questions.question: A sewer line is to be laid perpendicular to an existing main whose centerline is \(3x-4y+8=0\) (coordinates in meters), passing through the manhole at \((4,1)\). The equation of the new line is:
questions.explanation:
The existing main \(3x-4y+8=0\) has slope \(m_1=-A/B=-3/(-4)=3/4\). The perpendicular slope is \(m_2=-1/m_1=-4/3\). Point-slope form through \((4,1)\): \(y-1=-\tfrac{4}{3}(x-4)\), so \(3y-3=-4x+16\), or \(4x+3y-19=0\). Check: \(4(4)+3(1)-19=0\). ✓

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Straight Line.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is the line parallel to the main through \((4,1)\).
  • (C) has slope \(+4/3\) (sign error on the reciprocal).
  • (D) has slope \(-3/4\), the negative of \(m_1\) rather than the negative reciprocal.

A – Analytic geometry · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 1-1

questions.question: A parabolic reflector surface has the equation \((y-2)^2=8(x-1)\). The distance from the vertex to the focus is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Compare \((y-2)^2=8(x-1)\) with the Handbook form \((y-k)^2=2p(x-h)\): \(2p=8\), so \(p=4\). The focus is at \((h+p/2,k)=(1+2,2)=(3,2)\), a distance \(p/2=2\) from the vertex \((1,2)\).

Numerical entry: accepted answer 2 (range 1.95–2.05). The common wrong entry is 4 (reporting \(p\) instead of \(p/2\)).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Conic Sections, Case 1 (Parabola).

A – Analytic geometry · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 1-5

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^2(3x^2+2x)\,dx\) equals:
questions.explanation:
\[\int_0^2(3x^2+2x)\,dx=\left[x^3+x^2\right]_0^2=8+4=12\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Indefinite Integrals (entries 4, 5).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 6 results from integrating \(3x^2\) as \(x^2\) and \(2x\) as \(x\) \((4+2)\).
  • (B) 10 results from integrating \(2x\) as \(x\) \((8+2)\).
  • (D) 16 is the integrand evaluated at \(x=2\) with no integration.

B – Single-variable calculus · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 1-9

questions.question: The area of the region bounded by \(y=x^2\) and \(y=2x+3\) is ______ square units. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Intersections: \(x^2=2x+3\Rightarrow x^2-2x-3=(x-3)(x+1)=0\), so \(x=-1\) and \(x=3\). The line is above the parabola between them (at \(x=0\): \(3>0\)). \[A=\int_{-1}^{3}(2x+3-x^2)\,dx=\left[x^2+3x-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_{-1}^{3}=(9+9-9)-\left(1-3+\frac{1}{3}\right)=9-(-1.667)=10.67\]

Numerical entry: accepted answer 10.67 (range 10.6–10.7). Entering 11.33 means a sign slip on \(-x^3/3\) at \(x=-1\); entering 9 means the lower limit was dropped.

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Integral Calculus; Mathematics — Quadratic Equation.

B – Single-variable calculus · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 1-13

questions.question: The magnitude of \(\mathbf{A}=3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+6\mathbf{k}\) is:
questions.explanation:
\(|\mathbf{A}|=\sqrt{3^2+(-2)^2+6^2}=\sqrt{9+4+36}=\sqrt{49}=7\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Vectors (Length of Vector A).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 3.61 is \(\sqrt{9+4}\), omitting the \(\mathbf{k}\) component.
  • (C) 11 is the sum of the absolute values of the components.
  • (D) 49 is \(|\mathbf{A}|^2\).

C – Vector operations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 1-17

questions.question: A force \(\mathbf{F}=200\mathbf{i}+150\mathbf{j}-100\mathbf{k}\) N acts at the point \((2,1,3)\) m. The magnitude of the moment of the force about the origin is ______ N·m. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(\mathbf{r}=2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}\) m. \(\mathbf{M}_O=\mathbf{r}\times\mathbf{F}\):

  • \(\mathbf{i}\): \((1)(-100)-(3)(150)=-100-450=-550\)
  • \(\mathbf{j}\): \(-[(2)(-100)-(3)(200)]=-[-200-600]=+800\)
  • \(\mathbf{k}\): \((2)(150)-(1)(200)=300-200=100\)

\(\mathbf{M}_O=-550\mathbf{i}+800\mathbf{j}+100\mathbf{k}\) N·m; \(|\mathbf{M}_O|=\sqrt{550^2+800^2+100^2}=\sqrt{302{,}500+640{,}000+10{,}000}=\sqrt{952{,}500}=976\) N·m.

Numerical entry: accepted answer 976 N·m (range 970–980). Entering \(\mathbf{F}\times\mathbf{r}\) gives the same magnitude, so the order error is not caught by this question—but it would be if a component were asked for.

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Vectors (cross product).

C – Vector operations · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 1-21

questions.question: Five slump tests gave 4, 8, 6, 5, and 7 cm. The sample standard deviation is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\bar{X}=30/5=6\). Deviations: \(-2\), 2, 0, \(-1\), 1; squares sum to \(4+4+0+1+1=10\). \[s=\sqrt{\frac{10}{n-1}}=\sqrt{\frac{10}{4}}=\sqrt{2.5}=1.58\text{ cm}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values (sample standard deviation).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.41 is \(\sqrt{10/5}\), the population formula.
  • (C) 2.50 is the sample variance \(s^2\).
  • (D) 3.16 is \(\sqrt{10}\), forgetting to divide by \(n-1\).

D – Statistics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-25

questions.question: A pipe-wall thickness measurement has a known standard deviation of 2.0 mm. The number of measurements needed so that the 99% confidence interval on the mean has a half-width of no more than 0.5 mm is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Sample-size formula with \(Z_{\alpha/2}=2.5758\) for 99% (Values of \(Z_{\alpha/2}\) table), \(\sigma=2.0\) mm, and allowable error \(\bar{x}-\mu=0.5\) mm: \[n=\left[\frac{Z_{\alpha/2}\,\sigma}{\bar{x}-\mu}\right]^2=\left[\frac{2.5758\times2.0}{0.5}\right]^2=(10.30)^2=106.2\ \Rightarrow\ 107\text{ measurements}\]

Numerical entry: accepted answer 107 (the unrounded 106.2 must be rounded up; 106 does not meet the requirement). Using \(Z=1.96\) gives 62, the 95% answer.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Sample Size; Values of \(Z_{\alpha/2}\).

D – Statistics · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 1-29

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A quantity is normally distributed with mean 50 and standard deviation 5. Which statements are true?
choices: The points of inflection of the density curve are at 45 and 55.
The probability of a value greater than 60 is about 0.023.
About 68% of values lie between 40 and 60.
questions.explanation:
Convert each statement to the unit normal variable \(z=(x-50)/5\) and read the Unit Normal Distribution table where needed.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Normal Distribution (Gaussian Distribution); Unit Normal Distribution table.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the normal distribution is unimodal with mode at \(\mu=50\).
  • (B) True — the Handbook states the inflection points are at \(\mu\pm\sigma=45\) and 55.
  • (C) True — \(z=(60-50)/5=2.0\); \(R(2.0)=0.0228\approx0.023\).
  • (D) False — 40 to 60 is \(\mu\pm2\sigma\), which contains \(W(2.0)=95.45\%\) of values; 68% corresponds to \(\mu\pm\sigma\), i.e., 45 to 55.
  • (E) True — by symmetry the median equals the mean.

D – Statistics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-33

questions.question: A licensed geotechnical engineer recommends a deep foundation for a warehouse after borings reveal a soft clay layer. The developer, citing cost, directs the engineer to design shallow footings instead and states that “settlement is the owner’s problem, not yours.” The engineer’s analysis shows that differential settlement would exceed the tolerable limits for the structure and could compromise the roof framing. Under the NCEES Rules of Professional Conduct, the engineer’s most appropriate first action is to:
choices: Design the shallow footings as directed, since the developer has accepted the risk in writing.
Notify the developer in writing that the directive endangers public safety and that the engineer cannot proceed on that basis, and notify the appropriate authority if the directive stands.
Withdraw from the project without comment to avoid liability.
Report the developer to the state engineering licensing board.
questions.explanation:
Part A, item 1 of the Rules makes the health, safety, and welfare of the public the licensee’s foremost responsibility, and Part A, item 3 prescribes the response when professional judgment is overruled in a way that endangers the public: notify the employer or client and such other authority as may be appropriate. A written notice to the developer, followed by notice to the appropriate authority (for example, the building official) if the directive stands, is exactly that sequence. The engineer also may not seal shallow-footing plans that do not safeguard the public (Part A, item 2).

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — 2025–26 Model Rules, Section 240.15, Part A, items 1, 2, and 3.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) A client cannot waive the public’s safety; a structure with compromised roof framing endangers occupants, not just the owner’s wallet.
  • (C) Silent withdrawal fails the duty to notify.
  • (D) The board disciplines licensees; the developer is not a licensee, and reporting to the board is not the first step for an unsafe directive. The Rules direct notice to the client first, then to the appropriate authority.

A – Codes of ethics · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 2-1

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each situation (1–4) with the NCEES Rules of Professional Conduct provision (a–d) that most directly governs it.

  • (a) Obligations to Other Licensees — no misrepresentation of qualifications or degree of responsibility
  • (b) Obligations to the Public — report known violations to the board and cooperate
  • (c) Obligations to Employer and Clients — disclose known or potential conflicts of interest
  • (d) Obligations to the Public — notify employer or client and appropriate authority when judgment is overruled
pairs: An engineer’s employer directs a change that the engineer believes endangers the public; the engineer must inform the employer and, as appropriate, another authority.
An engineer’s spouse owns a share of a materials supplier that may bid on the engineer’s project; the engineer must inform the client.
A firm’s proposal describes a junior engineer as having been “lead designer” of a project on which she performed only drafting.
An engineer learns that a competitor’s firm is using the seal of an engineer who has retired and is no longer licensed.
questions.explanation:
1–(d): Part A, item 3 requires notifying the employer or client and appropriate authority when professional judgment is overruled and the public is endangered. 2–(c): Part B, item 6 requires disclosure of known or potential conflicts of interest, including circumstances that could appear to influence judgment—a spouse’s ownership interest in a potential bidder qualifies. 3–(a): Part C, item 1 prohibits misrepresenting or exaggerating an associate’s degree of responsibility in prior assignments; calling a drafter the “lead designer” does exactly that. 4–(b): Part A, item 8 requires a licensee who knows or has reason to believe that any person or firm has violated the laws governing practice to report it to the board; use of a retired, unlicensed engineer’s seal violates Model Law 150.30 A.4 and A.7.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — 2025–26 Model Rules, Section 240.15, Part A, items 3 and 8; Part B, item 6; Part C, item 1; Model Law, Section 150.30.

A – Codes of ethics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 2-5

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about professional liability for engineers are true?
choices: An engineer who contractually promises that the design will be “free of all defects” has assumed a duty greater than the ordinary standard of care.
Professional liability (errors and omissions) insurance generally covers claims arising from the engineer’s negligent errors and omissions but not from intentional misconduct.
A statute of repose begins to run when the plaintiff discovers the defect.
An engineer who exercised reasonable care is not liable in negligence merely because the completed structure later proved inadequate.
A limitation-of-liability clause in the engineer-owner agreement also limits the engineer’s liability to a third party injured by the design.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), and (D) correctly describe the standard of care and E&O coverage; (C) confuses repose with limitations, and (E) extends a contract clause to someone who never signed the contract.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice (liability doctrine is general; the Handbook’s Model Rules 240.15 Part B, item 1 and Model Law 150.10 A.2 address competence and negligence as licensing matters).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — A warranty of a defect-free design is a contractual promise beyond the ordinary standard of reasonable care; the engineer becomes liable for any defect regardless of negligence, and such promises are commonly excluded from E&O coverage.
  • (B) True — E&O policies cover negligent acts, errors, and omissions in professional services and exclude intentional or dishonest conduct.
  • (C) False — A statute of repose runs from substantial completion of the improvement; it is the statute of limitations that typically runs from discovery.
  • (D) True — Negligence requires a breach of the standard of care; an adverse outcome alone does not establish breach.
  • (E) False — A limitation-of-liability clause binds only the contracting parties; a third party who did not sign the agreement is not limited by it.

B – Professional liability · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 2-9

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Under the NCEES Model Law, which of the following individuals is practicing engineering, or offering to practice, in violation of the Act?
choices: An engineer intern who prepares stormwater calculations that are reviewed, modified, and sealed by the licensed engineer supervising the work.
An unlicensed graduate whose business card reads “Consulting Engineer” and who offers site-development design services to the public.
A licensee whose license has been placed on inactive status and who continues to seal drawings for clients in that jurisdiction.
A licensed architect who designs the architectural elements of a building within the scope of the architecture practice act.
A person who, having failed the PE exam, continues to use the letters “P.E.” after his name on proposals while awaiting a retake.
questions.explanation:
Check each person against the definitions of practice and inactive status, the prohibitions on unlicensed individuals, and the exemption clause. Three are in violation; the engineer intern and the architect fall within exemptions.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — Model Law, Section 110.20 A.3 and S; Section 150.10 A.9; Section 150.30 A; Section 170.20 A and C.

Option by option:

  • (A) False — Not a violation. The employees-and-subordinates exemption (Model Law 170.20 C) covers work that includes no final designs or decisions and is done under the responsible charge of, and verified by, a licensee.
  • (B) True — Violation. Model Law 150.30 A.1 through A.3 prohibit an unlicensed individual from offering to practice engineering and from using “engineer” or “engineering,” or any title conveying the impression of being a professional engineer, in a business activity.
  • (C) True — Violation. Model Law 110.20 S states that a licensee on inactive status may not practice or offer to practice in the jurisdiction, and 150.10 A.9 makes using a seal or practicing while the license is inactive a ground for discipline.
  • (D) False — Not a violation. Model Law 170.20 A exempts the practice of any other legally recognized profession within its own scope.
  • (E) True — Violation. Using “P.E.” without a license represents oneself as a professional engineer (110.20 A.3.b) and is prohibited by 150.30 A.3; it may also constitute fraud in relation to licensure.

C – Licensure · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 2-13

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each contract remedy (1–4) with its description (a–d).

  • (a) A court order requiring the breaching party to perform the promised act, available when money is an inadequate remedy
  • (b) A predetermined sum stated in the contract, such as a daily rate for late completion, enforceable when it is a reasonable forecast of actual loss
  • (c) Cancellation of the contract and restoration of the parties to their pre-contract positions
  • (d) A monetary award intended to place the injured party in the position it would have occupied had the contract been performed
questions.explanation:
1–(d): Compensatory damages are the ordinary money remedy, designed to give the injured party the benefit of the bargain. 2–(b): Liquidated damages are agreed in advance, most commonly as a daily rate for late completion; they are enforced when they are a reasonable pre-estimate of hard-to-measure loss and struck down when they are a penalty. 3–(a): Specific performance is equitable relief compelling performance, reserved for cases where damages are inadequate, such as the sale of unique property; courts do not order personal services. 4–(c): Rescission unwinds the contract and returns the parties to their starting positions, often paired with restitution of benefits conferred.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice (contract remedies are general legal doctrine).

D – Contracts and contract law · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 2-17

questions.question: A utility wants to accumulate $500,000 in 15 years to replace a well pump. If it makes equal end-of-year deposits into an account earning 8% per year, the required annual deposit is ______ dollars. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\[A = F\,(A/F, 8\%, 15) = 500{,}000 \times \frac{0.08}{(1.08)^{15}-1} = 500{,}000 \times \frac{0.08}{2.1722} = 500{,}000(0.03683) = \$18{,}415\] The 8.00% table gives (A/F, 8%, 15) = 0.0368, which yields $18,400. Accepted range: $18,300 to $18,500.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Factor Table (Sinking Fund); Interest Rate Tables, i = 8.00%.

A – Time value of money · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 3-3

questions.question: A parcel of land purchased for $30,000 is sold 9 years later for $60,000. Ignoring taxes and holding costs, the rate of return on the investment is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The rate of return makes \(P\,(F/P, i^*, 9) = F\): \((1 + i^*)^9 = 60{,}000/30{,}000 = 2\), so \(i^* = 2^{1/9} - 1 = 1.0801 - 1 = 0.0801 \approx 8\%\). Check with the table: (F/P, 8%, 9) = 1.9990, essentially 2.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Rate-of-Return; Factor Table (Single Payment Compound Amount); Interest Rate Tables, i = 8.00%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 9% uses \(n = 8\) instead of 9: \(2^{1/8} - 1 = 0.0905\), an off-by-one count of the compounding periods.
  • (C) 10% gives (F/P, 10%, 9) = 2.3579, which more than doubles the money.
  • (D) 11% (11.1%) is the simple-interest rate, 100%/9 years, which ignores compounding.

A – Time value of money · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 3-7

questions.question: Two years ago a firm paid $40,000 for a geotechnical investigation of a site it was considering purchasing. The firm is now deciding whether to purchase the site. In the purchase decision, the $40,000 should be treated as:
choices: a sunk cost that is not relevant to the decision
a fixed cost to be added to the purchase price
an opportunity cost of not purchasing
questions.explanation:
The investigation has already been paid for and cannot be recovered whether or not the site is purchased, so it is a sunk cost and has no bearing on the decision. Only future cash flows that differ between “purchase” and “do not purchase” are relevant.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — cost concepts (not tabulated in the Handbook; fundamental definitions).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) A fixed cost is one that does not vary with output; the past study is not a future cost of any kind.
  • (C) An opportunity cost is a forgone future benefit, not a past expenditure.
  • (D) An incremental cost is the additional future cost caused by choosing an alternative; the study cost is the same (already spent) under both alternatives.

B – Cost · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 3-11

questions.question: A precast plant has fixed costs of $80,000 per year, a variable cost of $12 per unit, and sells its product for $20 per unit. The breakeven production is:
questions.explanation:
\[Q^* = \frac{\text{FC}}{p - v} = \frac{80{,}000}{20 - 12} = 10{,}000 \text{ units/yr}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Breakeven Analysis.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 2,500 divides by \(p + v = 32\).
  • (B) 4,000 divides the fixed cost by the price alone, ignoring variable cost.
  • (C) 6,667 divides by the variable cost alone.

C – Analyses · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 3-15

questions.question: A soil-compaction roller costs $85,000, has a 6-year depreciable life, and an estimated salvage value of $10,000. Using straight-line depreciation, the book value at the end of year 4 is ______ dollars. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(D_j = (C - S_n)/n = (85{,}000 - 10{,}000)/6 = \$12{,}500\) per year. \(\text{BV}_4 = C - 4D_j = 85{,}000 - 4(12{,}500) = \$35{,}000\). Accepted answer: exactly 35,000.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Depreciation (Straight Line); Book Value.

C – Analyses · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 3-19

questions.question: The cost of repairing a culvert after a storm season depends on the season’s severity. A mild season (probability 0.5) will require $40,000 of repairs, a moderate season (probability 0.3) $70,000, and a severe season (probability 0.2) $120,000. The expected repair cost is ______ dollars. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(\text{EV} = 0.5(40{,}000) + 0.3(70{,}000) + 0.2(120{,}000) = 20{,}000 + 21{,}000 + 24{,}000 = \$65{,}000\). Probabilities sum to 1.0. Accepted answer: exactly 65,000. (The unweighted average of the three costs, $76,667, is a common wrong answer.)

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Economic Decision Trees (Expected Value).

D – Uncertainty · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 3-23

questions.question: Three coplanar forces act on an anchor bolt: 50 kN along the positive \(x\)-axis, 80 kN at 45° above the positive \(x\)-axis, and 60 kN straight down (negative \(y\)). The magnitude of the resultant is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\Sigma F_x = 50 + 80\cos 45^\circ + 0 = 50 + 56.57 = 106.57\) kN; \(\Sigma F_y = 0 + 80\sin 45^\circ - 60 = 56.57 - 60 = -3.43\) kN. \[F = \sqrt{106.57^2 + 3.43^2} = 106.6\,\text{kN}\] directed 1.8° below the positive \(x\)-axis.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Resultant (Two Dimensions).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the magnitude of the \(y\)-component alone;
  • (C) is \(\sqrt{50^2 + 80^2 + 60^2}\), a root-sum-square of magnitudes that ignores directions;
  • (D) is the arithmetic sum.

A – Resultants of force systems · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 4-3

questions.question: A cantilever beam projecting from a wall at O carries a downward force of 8 kN at 2.0 m from O and a counterclockwise couple of 10 kN·m. The system is equivalent to a single 8-kN downward force acting at a distance from O of:
questions.explanation:
Resultant force: 8 kN downward. Resultant moment about O (counterclockwise positive): \(-8(2.0) + 10 = -6\) kN·m, i.e., 6 kN·m clockwise. A downward 8-kN force produces a clockwise moment about O when it acts to the right of O, at \[d = \frac{6}{8} = 0.75\,\text{m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Systems of Forces.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is 10/8, the couple alone;
  • (C) ignores the couple;
  • (D) is (16 + 10)/8, adding the couple with the wrong sign.

B – Equivalent force systems · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 4-7

questions.question: The 12-ft cantilever in Figure 4.16(b) is fixed at B and carries a triangular load that increases from zero at the free end A to 600 lb/ft at the wall. The magnitude of the moment reaction at B is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The triangular load resultant is \(W = \tfrac{1}{2}(600)(12) = 3600\) lb, acting at the centroid of the triangle, one-third of the length from the wall (the peak end): \(12/3 = 4\) ft from B. Moments about B: \[M_B = 3600(4) = 14{,}400\,\text{ft·lb}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements; table of area properties (triangle centroid at \(h/3\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) places the resultant at midspan (6 ft);
  • (C) places it at \(2L/3 = 8\) ft from the wall, i.e., measured from the wrong end;
  • (D) uses the full length as the arm.

C – Equilibrium of rigid bodies · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-11

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about supports and equilibrium are true?
choices: A frictionless pin in a planar structure supplies two force components and no moment.
A roller supplies a single reaction force perpendicular to the surface on which it rolls.
A fixed support in a planar structure supplies three reaction components.
A ball-and-socket joint in three dimensions supplies three moment components.
A rigid body in three dimensions has six independent scalar equilibrium equations.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), (C), and (E) are true; (D) is false.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — a pin prevents translation in two directions but allows rotation.
  • (B) True.
  • (C) True — two forces and a moment.
  • (D) False — a ball-and-socket supplies three force components and no moments; it is free to rotate about any axis.
  • (E) True — three force equations and three moment equations.

C – Equilibrium of rigid bodies · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 4-15

questions.question: For the truss in Figure 4.17, the force in the top-chord member FG is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Cut through FG, FC, and BC and keep the left portion (A, B, F). Take moments about C (6, 0), where FC and BC intersect. Forces on the left portion: \(A_y = 35\) kN at \(x = 0\) (arm 6 m, clockwise about C), the 20-kN downward load at F (arm 3 m, counterclockwise about C), and \(F_{FG}\) acting in the \(+x\) direction at height 4 m if tensile (arm 4 m, clockwise about C). Counterclockwise positive: \[\Sigma M_C = -35(6) + 20(3) - 4F_{FG} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{FG} = \frac{-210 + 60}{4} = -37.5\,\text{kN}\] so FG carries 37.5 kN in compression.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Plane Truss: Method of Sections.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the force in AB (from moments about F);
  • (B) has the sign reversed—a top chord of a simply supported truss under gravity load is in compression;
  • (D) omits the 20-kN load at F.

D – Frames and trusses · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 4-19

questions.question: A pair of pliers has handles 120 mm long and jaws 30 mm long, measured from the common pivot pin. If a hand applies 50 N at the end of each handle, the gripping force at the tip of the jaws is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Each half of the pliers is a lever pivoting about the common pin. Moments about the pin for one half: \(50(120) = F_{\text{jaw}}(30)\), so \[F_{\text{jaw}} = 50\left(\frac{120}{30}\right) = 200\,\text{N}\] The mechanical advantage is 4.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) inverts the lever ratio;
  • (B) assumes no mechanical advantage;
  • (C) adds the two hand forces (2 × 50 N) and ignores the lever ratio; each jaw is loaded by its own handle through the 4:1 lever.

D – Frames and trusses · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 4-23

questions.question: A semicircular channel cross section is bounded by concentric semicircles of radii 10 in and 8 in, with the common diameter along the \(x\)-axis. The distance from the diameter to the centroid of the net area is ______ in. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Outer semicircle: \(A_1 = \pi(10)^2/2 = 157.08\) in², \(y_1 = 4(10)/(3\pi) = 4.244\) in. Inner semicircle: \(A_2 = \pi(8)^2/2 = 100.53\) in², \(y_2 = 4(8)/(3\pi) = 3.395\) in. \[y_c = \frac{157.08(4.244) - 100.53(3.395)}{157.08 - 100.53} = \frac{666.67 - 341.33}{56.55} = 5.75\,\text{in}\] Accepted range: 5.70–5.80 in. (In closed form \(y_c = \dfrac{4}{3\pi}\,\dfrac{a^3 - b^3}{a^2 - b^2}\); note the centroid of the thin ring lies well above both individual centroids, near \(2\bar{r}/\pi \approx 5.7\) in for the mean radius.)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — table of area properties (semicircle); Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes.

E – Centroid of area · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 4-27

questions.question: For the 6 in × 4 in × ½ in angle in Figure 4.19(b), the moment of inertia about the horizontal centroidal axis is ______ in\(^{4}\). [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Pieces: vertical leg 0.5 × 6 (\(a_1 = 3.0\) in², \(y_1 = 3.0\) in); horizontal leg 3.5 × 0.5 from \(x = 0.5\) to 4 (\(a_2 = 1.75\) in², \(y_2 = 0.25\) in). \(A = 4.75\) in². \[y_c = \frac{3.0(3.0) + 1.75(0.25)}{4.75} = \frac{9.4375}{4.75} = 1.987\,\text{in}\] \[\begin{aligned} I_{x_c} &= \left[\frac{0.5(6)^3}{12} + 3.0(3.0 - 1.987)^2\right] + \left[\frac{3.5(0.5)^3}{12} + 1.75(0.25 - 1.987)^2\right]\\ &= (9.000 + 3.079) + (0.036 + 5.280) = 17.4\,\text{in}^4 \end{aligned}\] Accepted range: 17.2–17.6 in\(^{4}\).

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Moment of Inertia Parallel Axis Theorem; table of area properties (rectangle).

F – Area moments of inertia · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 4-31

questions.question: In Figure 4.21 a 10° wedge is driven horizontally by a force \(P\) to raise a 2000-lb block that is guided by a smooth vertical wall. The coefficient of static friction is 0.25 on both the top and bottom faces of the wedge. The force \(P\) required to start raising the block is ______ lb. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Let \(\alpha = 10^\circ\), \(\mu = 0.25\), \(W = 2000\) lb. The wedge face descends toward its thin tip at angle \(\alpha\); when the wedge is driven right, the block rises and slides up the face relative to the wedge, so friction on the block acts down the face.

Block: normal force \(N_2\) from the wedge (perpendicular to the face), friction \(\mu N_2\) along the face, wall reaction \(N_w\) (horizontal, smooth), weight \(W\). Vertical equilibrium: \[N_2\cos\alpha - \mu N_2\sin\alpha - W = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad N_2 = \frac{2000}{\cos 10^\circ - 0.25\sin 10^\circ} = \frac{2000}{0.9848 - 0.0434} = 2124.5\,\text{lb}\] Wedge: \(P\) to the right; the equal-and-opposite contact forces \(N_2\) and \(\mu N_2\) from the block; floor normal \(N_3\) and floor friction \(\mu N_3\) to the left (opposing the wedge’s motion). Vertical equilibrium gives \(N_3 = N_2\cos\alpha - \mu N_2\sin\alpha = W = 2000\) lb. Horizontal equilibrium: \[P = N_2\sin\alpha + \mu N_2\cos\alpha + \mu N_3 = 2124.5(0.1736 + 0.2462) + 0.25(2000) = 891.9 + 500 = 1392\,\text{lb}\] Accepted range: 1380–1400 lb. A frictionless wedge would need only \(W\tan\alpha = 353\) lb; friction on the two faces quadruples the effort. Because \(\mu = 0.25 > \tan 10^\circ = 0.176\), the wedge is self-locking and stays in place when \(P\) is removed.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Friction; Equilibrium Requirements.

G – Static friction · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 4-35

questions.question: A particle moves along a straight line with acceleration \(a = 6t - 12\) m/s², where \(t\) is in seconds. At \(t = 0\) the particle is at \(s = 0\) with velocity \(v = 9\) m/s. The total distance traveled by the particle during the first 4 s is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Integrate: \(v = \int (6t - 12)\,dt + 9 = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 = 3(t - 1)(t - 3)\), and \(s = \int v\,dt + 0 = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t\). The velocity is zero at \(t = 1\) s and \(t = 3\) s, so the particle reverses twice. Positions: \(s(0) = 0\); \(s(1) = 1 - 6 + 9 = 4\) m; \(s(3) = 27 - 54 + 27 = 0\); \(s(4) = 64 - 96 + 36 = 4\) m. Distance traveled \(= |4 - 0| + |0 - 4| + |4 - 0| = 12\) m.

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Non-constant Acceleration; Particle Rectilinear Motion (variable \(a\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 4 m is the displacement \(s(4) - s(0)\), not the distance.
  • (B) 8 m counts only the first two legs (0 to 3 s).
  • (D) 36 m is \(v(0) \times 4\) s, assuming the initial velocity of 9 m/s is maintained; the velocity is not constant.

A – Kinematics · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 5-2

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A wheel of radius \(r\) rolls without slipping on a horizontal surface; its center moves at constant speed \(v\). Which of the following statements are true?
choices: The angular velocity of the wheel is \(v/r\).
The velocity of the point of the wheel in contact with the ground is zero.
The speed of the point at the top of the wheel is \(2v\).
The acceleration of the point of the wheel in contact with the ground is zero.
All points on the wheel have the same speed.
questions.explanation:
Treat the contact point as the instantaneous center of rotation; each statement is checked below.

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Instantaneous Center of Rotation; Plane Circular Motion; Translating Axes \(x\)-\(y\).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — with the contact point as the instant center, \(v = r\omega\) for the center, so \(\omega = v/r\).
  • (B) True — rolling without slipping means the wheel’s contact point has the same velocity as the fixed ground, which is zero; that is what makes it the instant center.
  • (C) True — the top point is \(2r\) from the instant center, so its speed is \(2r\omega = 2v\).
  • (D) False — the contact point’s velocity is zero only instantaneously; its acceleration is \(r\omega^2 = v^2/r\) directed toward the center, even at constant \(v\).
  • (E) False — the speed of a point is \(\omega\) times its distance from the contact point, which ranges from 0 at the bottom to \(2v\) at the top.

A – Kinematics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-6

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each body and axis (1–4) with its mass moment of inertia (a–d). \(M\) is the mass of the body.

  • (a) \(MR^2\)
  • (b) \(2MR^2/5\)
  • (c) \(ML^2/3\)
  • (d) \(MR^2/2\)
pairs: Slender rod of length \(L\), axis perpendicular to the rod through one end
Solid circular cylinder of radius \(R\), axis along the cylinder’s centerline
Solid sphere of radius \(R\), axis through the center
Thin ring of mean radius \(R\), axis through the center perpendicular to the plane of the ring
questions.explanation:
All four are direct table look-ups. (1) Slender rod about a perpendicular axis through an end: \(ML^2/3\), which is \(ML^2/12 + M(L/2)^2\). (2) Solid cylinder about its centerline: \(MR^2/2\), independent of length. (3) Solid sphere about a diameter: \(2MR^2/5\). (4) Thin ring about its central perpendicular axis: \(MR^2\), because every particle is at distance \(R\) from the axis. Remaining option check: \(MR^2/2\) is also the value for a thin ring about a diameter and for a thin disk about its central axis, so read the axis description carefully.

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — table of mass moments of inertia (slender rod; solid circular cylinder; solid sphere; thin ring).

B – Mass moments of inertia · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 5-10

questions.question: A 50-lb crate is already sliding on a horizontal floor (\(\mu_k = 0.30\)) under a 30-lb pull directed 20° above the horizontal. Using \(g = 32.2\) ft/s², the acceleration of the crate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Vertical equilibrium: \(N = W - P\sin 20^\circ = 50 - 30(0.3420) = 39.74\) lb. Friction: \(F = \mu_k N = 0.30(39.74) = 11.92\) lb. Horizontal: \(\Sigma F_x = P\cos 20^\circ - F = 30(0.9397) - 11.92 = 16.27\) lb. Mass: \(m = 50/32.2 = 1.553\) slug. \(a = 16.27/1.553 = 10.5\) ft/s².

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Particle Kinetics; Friction; Concept of Weight.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 8.5 uses \(N = W = 50\) lb, ignoring the upward component of the pull.
  • (C) 18.2 omits friction entirely.
  • (D) 25.8 adds the friction force to the pull instead of subtracting it; kinetic friction always opposes the sliding.

C – Force acceleration · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-14

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about work, energy, and power are true?
choices: If only conservative forces do work on a particle, the sum of its kinetic and potential energies is constant.
The work done by kinetic friction on a body sliding across a fixed surface is negative.
The change in elastic potential energy of a linear spring stretched from \(s_1\) to \(s_2\) is \(\tfrac12 k(s_2 - s_1)^2\).
A hoist that raises a 500-kg load at a constant 2.0 m/s with an overall efficiency of 80% must be supplied with about 12.3 kW.
Doubling a particle’s speed doubles its kinetic energy.
questions.explanation:
Check each statement against the Handbook’s Principle of Work and Energy, Elastic Potential Energy, Kinetic Energy, and Power and Efficiency headings; each is discussed below. For statement (D), the output power at constant speed is \(P_{out} = Wv = (500)(9.81)(2.0) = 9810\) W, and the input is \(P_{in} = P_{out}/\varepsilon = 9810/0.80 = 12\,260\) W ≈ 12.3 kW.

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Principle of Work and Energy; Elastic Potential Energy; Kinetic Energy; Power and Efficiency.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — this is the conservation-of-energy statement \(T_2 + V_2 = T_1 + V_1\) in the Handbook, which holds when \(U_{1\to2} = 0\).
  • (B) True — kinetic friction on a sliding body acts opposite to the motion, so its work \(-\mu_k Nd\) is negative; the Handbook notes that dissipative forces give negative \(U_{1\to2}\).
  • (C) False — the Handbook’s change in spring energy is \(\tfrac12 k(s_2^2 - s_1^2)\), which equals \(\tfrac12 k(s_2 - s_1)^2\) only when \(s_1 = 0\). For example, stretching from 0.1 m to 0.3 m with \(k = 100\) N/m stores \(\tfrac12(100)(0.09 - 0.01) = 4\) J, not 2 J.
  • (D) True — \(P_{in} = Wv/\varepsilon = (500)(9.81)(2.0)/0.80 = 12\,260\) W ≈ 12.3 kW; efficiency increases the required input.
  • (E) False — \(T = \tfrac12 mv^2\), so doubling \(v\) quadruples \(T\).

D – Work, energy, and power · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 5-18

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about shear and bending moment diagrams for a beam loaded only by transverse forces and couples are correct?
choices: The slope of the moment diagram at any section equals the shear force at that section.
A concentrated force produces a jump in the moment diagram.
A concentrated couple produces a jump in the moment diagram but not in the shear diagram.
The bending moment reaches a local maximum or minimum where the shear force is zero or changes sign.
Under a uniformly distributed load the shear diagram is parabolic.
questions.explanation:
Test each statement against the load–shear–moment relations \(w = -dV/dx\) and \(V = dM/dx\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Beams (load–shear–moment relations).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(V = dM/dx\).
  • (B) False — a concentrated force produces a jump in the shear diagram and a change of slope (a kink) in the moment diagram.
  • (C) True — a couple enters the moment equilibrium directly but not the vertical-force equilibrium.
  • (D) True — since \(dM/dx = V\), extrema of \(M\) occur where \(V = 0\) or changes sign.
  • (E) False — a uniform load makes the shear diagram linear (slope \(-w\)) and the moment diagram parabolic.

A – Shear and moment diagrams · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 6-4

questions.question: A 2-m steel bar (\(E = 200\) GPa) elongates 1.2 mm under an axial load. The axial stress is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\varepsilon = \delta/L = 1.2/2000 = 6.0\times10^{-4}\); \(\sigma = E\varepsilon = 200{,}000(6.0\times10^{-4}) = 120\) MPa.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Uniaxial Loading and Deformation (\(\varepsilon = \delta/L\), \(\sigma = E\varepsilon\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 60 MPa results from using \(L = 4\) m or halving.
  • (C) 240 MPa uses \(L = 1\) m.
  • (D) 1200 MPa reads \(\delta\) as 1.2 cm (12 mm).

B – Stresses and strains · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 6-8

questions.question: The doubly symmetric I-section in Figure 6.16 (flanges 200 mm × 20 mm, web 10 mm × 260 mm, overall depth 300 mm) carries a shear force of 150 kN. The maximum transverse shear stress in the section is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(I = 200(300)^3/12 - 190(260)^3/12 = 450.0\times10^6 - 278.3\times10^6 = 171.7\times10^6\) mm4. At the neutral axis, \(Q\) is the first moment of the half-section: flange \(200(20)(140) = 560{,}000\) mm3 plus half-web \(10(130)(65) = 84{,}500\) mm3, so \(Q = 644{,}500\) mm3. With \(b = 10\) mm (web width), \[\tau_{max} = \frac{VQ}{Ib} = \frac{150{,}000(644{,}500)}{171.7\times10^6(10)} = 56.3\,\text{MPa}\] The web-average approximation \(V/A_{web} = 150{,}000/(10\times260) = 57.7\) MPa is within 3%.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Stresses in Beams (\(\tau_{xy} = VQ/(Ib)\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 2.8 MPa uses the flange width \(b = 200\) mm instead of the web width.
  • (B) 14.2 MPa is the average shear on the gross area, \(V/A_{gross} = 150{,}000/10{,}600\), which ignores that the web carries almost all the shear.
  • (C) 48.9 MPa uses \(Q\) of the flange only, omitting the half-web contribution.

B – Stresses and strains · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 6-12

questions.question: An aluminum bar (\(E = 69\) GPa) with cross-sectional area 300 mm2 and length 1.5 m carries an axial tensile force of 18 kN. Its elongation is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\delta = PL/AE = 18{,}000(1500)/[300(69{,}000)] = 27.0\times10^6/20.7\times10^6 = 1.30\) mm.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Uniaxial Loading and Deformation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.87 mm uses \(L = 1\) m.
  • (C) 3.46 mm uses the shear modulus of aluminum (\(G = 26\) GPa) in place of \(E\).
  • (D) 13.0 mm makes a factor-of-10 slip converting \(E\), entering 69 GPa as 6,900 N/mm2 instead of 69,000 N/mm2: \(27.0\times10^6/[300(6{,}900)] = 13.0\) mm.

C – Deformations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 6-16

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A 2.4-m cantilever (\(E = 200\) GPa, \(I = 20\times10^6\) mm4) carries a uniformly distributed load of 3 kN/m over its full length and a 6-kN concentrated load at its free end. The deflection at the free end is ______ mm.
questions.explanation:
\(EI = 200\times10^9(20\times10^{-6}) = 4.0\times10^6\) N·m2 \(= 4000\) kN·m2. By superposition of the two cantilever cases: tip load \(PL^3/3EI = 6(2.4)^3/[3(4000)] = 82.94/12{,}000 = 6.91\) mm; uniform load \(wL^4/8EI = 3(2.4)^4/[8(4000)] = 99.53/32{,}000 = 3.11\) mm. Total = 10.0 mm.

FE Reference Handbook: Cantilevered Beam Slopes and Deflections; Mechanics of Materials — Principle of Superposition.

C – Deformations · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 6-20

questions.question: At a point in a plane-stress state, \(\sigma_x = 50\) MPa, \(\sigma_y = -10\) MPa, and \(\tau_{xy} = 40\) MPa. The principal stresses are most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(C = (50 - 10)/2 = 20\) MPa; \(R = \sqrt{[(50 + 10)/2]^2 + 40^2} = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50\) MPa. \(\sigma_{a,b} = 20 \pm 50 = 70\) MPa and \(-30\) MPa.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Principal Stresses; Mohr’s Circle—Stress, 2D.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the given \(\sigma_x\), \(\sigma_y\) — principal only if \(\tau_{xy} = 0\).
  • (B) uses \(R = 40\) (\(\tau_{xy}\) alone).
  • (D) uses \(R = 70\) (adding 30 and 40 instead of combining in quadrature).

D – Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 6-24

questions.question: A 60-mm-diameter solid shaft is subjected at a critical section to a bending moment of 1.2 kN·m and a torque of 1.6 kN·m. The maximum principal stress at the outer surface is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a solid circular shaft, \(\sigma = Mc/I = 32M/\pi d^3\) and \(\tau = Tr/J = 16T/\pi d^3\). With \(d = 60\) mm, \(\pi d^3 = 678{,}584\) mm3: \[\sigma_x = \frac{32(1.2\times10^6)}{678{,}584} = 56.6\,\text{MPa}, \qquad \tau_{xy} = \frac{16(1.6\times10^6)}{678{,}584} = 37.7\,\text{MPa}\] At the surface point of maximum bending stress, \(\sigma_y = 0\). \(C = 28.3\) MPa, \(R = \sqrt{28.3^2 + 37.7^2} = 47.2\) MPa, \(\sigma_1 = 28.3 + 47.2 = 75.5\) MPa (and \(\sigma_3 = -18.9\) MPa).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Stresses in Beams; Torsion; Principal Stresses.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 47.2 MPa is \(R\), the maximum shear stress.
  • (B) 56.6 MPa is the bending stress alone.
  • (D) 94.3 MPa is \(\sigma_x + \tau_{xy}\), adding stresses of different kinds directly.

D – Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 6-28

questions.question: A tension specimen of a ductile metal (\(E = 200\) GPa) is loaded to a total strain of 0.012, at which point the stress is 320 MPa, and is then completely unloaded. The permanent strain in the specimen is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Unloading is elastic along a line of slope \(E\): recovered strain \(= \sigma/E = 320/200{,}000 = 0.0016\). Permanent strain \(= 0.012 - 0.0016 = 0.0104\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Uniaxial Stress-Strain; Hooke’s Law (uniaxial).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.0016 is the recovered elastic strain, not the permanent strain.
  • (C) 0.012 assumes no elastic recovery.
  • (D) 0.0136 adds the elastic strain instead of subtracting it.

E – Elastic and plastic deformations · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-32

questions.question: A concrete batch contains 600 lb of cement and 33.0 gal of water (8.34 lb/gal). No other water is present. The water-cement ratio by mass is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Water mass = 33.0 gal × 8.34 lb/gal = 275.2 lb. w/c = 275.2/600 = 0.459 ≈ 0.46.

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Concrete (w/c is by weight).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is 33/600, forgetting to convert gallons to pounds.
  • (B) divides the water by the total mass of cement plus water instead of by the cement alone: 275.2/(600 + 275.2) = 0.31.
  • (D) uses the weight of an Imperial gallon of water (10.02 lb/gal) instead of the U.S. gallon (8.34 lb/gal): 33.0(10.02)/600 = 0.55.

A – Mix design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 7-3

questions.question: A bridge hanger cycles between a maximum stress of +120 MPa and a minimum stress of −40 MPa. The stress ratio \(R\) is:
questions.explanation:
\(R=\sigma_{min}/\sigma_{max}=(-40)/(120)=-0.333\).

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Properties of Materials — Mechanical (Fatigue, stress ratio).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) inverts the ratio.
  • (C) drops the sign; a negative \(R\) means the stress reverses sign during the cycle.
  • (D) inverts the ratio and drops the sign.

B – Test methods · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 7-7

questions.question: A steel member (\(E=200\) GPa, \(\alpha=11.7\times10^{-6}\)/°C) is fully restrained at both ends and heated 40°C. The stress induced is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Full restraint converts the thermal strain \(\alpha\Delta T=(11.7\times10^{-6})(40)=4.68\times10^{-4}\) into elastic strain: \(\sigma=E\alpha\Delta T=(200{,}000\,\text{MPa})(4.68\times10^{-4})=93.6\) MPa. Heating a restrained member produces compression.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Thermal Deformations; Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Thermal Properties.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) has the wrong sign—heating is compressive.
  • (C) assumes half restraint.
  • (D) doubles the strain.

C – Physical and mechanical properties · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 7-11

questions.question: A coarse aggregate sample has an oven-dry mass of 1,500 g, a saturated surface-dry mass of 1,524 g, and a submerged mass of 960 g. The absorption of the aggregate is ______ %. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Absorption \(=(B-A)/A\times100=(1{,}524-1{,}500)/1{,}500\times100=1.60\%\).

Accepted: 1.60 (1.59–1.61). Dividing by the SSD mass gives \(24/1{,}524=1.57\%\), which is outside the accepted range: absorption is always expressed on the oven-dry basis.

FE Reference Handbook: not given—definition supplied in the chapter.

B – Test methods · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 7-15

questions.question: A concrete mix per cubic meter contains 360 kg of cement (SG 3.15), 180 kg of water, and 1,100 kg of coarse aggregate (bulk SSD SG 2.70), with 4.0% air. The fine aggregate has a bulk SSD specific gravity of 2.62. Using the absolute-volume method, the SSD mass of fine aggregate per cubic meter is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Absolute volumes per m³ (water density 1,000 kg/m³):

  • Cement: \(360/(3.15\times1{,}000)=0.1143\) m³
  • Water: \(180/1{,}000=0.1800\) m³
  • Air: 0.040 m³
  • Coarse aggregate: \(1{,}100/(2.70\times1{,}000)=0.4074\) m³

Sum = 0.7417 m³; fine aggregate volume = 1 − 0.7417 = 0.2583 m³; mass = 0.2583 × 2.62 × 1,000 = 677 kg.

FE Reference Handbook: absolute-volume arithmetic must be known; Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Concrete for the principle.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 697 kg uses the coarse-aggregate specific gravity (2.70) for the sand.
  • (C) 782 kg omits the air volume.
  • (D) 976 kg omits the cement volume.

A – Mix design · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 7-19

questions.question: The mix of Question 7-22 contains 5.0% binder by total mass and the combined aggregate has a bulk specific gravity of 2.650. The voids filled with asphalt (VFA) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(P_s=100-5.0=95.0\%\). \[\text{VMA}=100-\frac{G_{mb}P_s}{G_{sb}}=100-\frac{2.350\times95.0}{2.650}=100-84.245=15.755\%\] From Question 7-22, \(V_a=4.277\%\) (carry the extra digit). \[\text{VFA}=100\,\frac{\text{VMA}-V_a}{\text{VMA}}=100\,\frac{15.755-4.277}{15.755}=72.9\%\]

FE Reference Handbook: not given—definitions supplied in the chapter.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 27.1% is \(100\,V_a/\text{VMA}\), the fraction of VMA that is air.
  • (B) 62.2% uses \(P_s=100\) in VMA (VMA = 11.3%).
  • (D) 84.2% is \(G_{mb}P_s/G_{sb}\), the aggregate volume percentage, not VFA.

A – Mix design · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 7-23

questions.question: Water rises in a clean glass tube of 1.0-mm inside diameter. Take surface tension 0.073 N/m, contact angle 0°, and specific weight 9.79 kN/m³. The capillary rise is ______ mm. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\[h=\frac{4\sigma\cos\beta}{\gamma d}=\frac{4(0.073)(1)}{9{,}790(0.0010)}=0.0298\ \text{m}=29.8\ \text{mm}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Definitions — Surface Tension and Capillarity.

B – Fluid properties · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-3

questions.question: Two horizontal pipes A and B carry water and have centerlines at the same elevation (Figure 8.9). A mercury manometer (SG = 13.6) connected between them shows a deflection of 150 mm, with the mercury lower on the A side. The pressure difference \(P_A-P_B\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Same fluid, same elevation: \(P_A-P_B=(\gamma_{Hg}-\gamma_w)h=9{,}810(13.6-1)(0.150)=18{,}541\ \text{Pa}\approx18.5\ \text{kPa}\).

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Characteristics of a Static Liquid — Manometers (\(h_1=h_2=h\) case).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses \(\gamma_w h\) only.
  • (C) uses \(\gamma_{Hg}h\) without subtracting the water column.
  • (D) uses \(\gamma_{Hg}h\) with an incorrect 0.20-m deflection.

C – Fluid statics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-7

questions.question: A concrete block of volume 2.0 ft³ and specific gravity 2.40 hangs from a cable, fully submerged in fresh water (\(\gamma=62.4\) lb/ft³). The tension in the cable is ______ lb. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(T=W-F_B=(SG-1)\gamma_wV=(2.40-1)(62.4)(2.0)=174.7\) lb.

questions.question: Oil with kinematic viscosity \(1.0\times10^{-4}\) m²/s flows at 1.5 m/s in a 50-mm pipe. The Darcy friction factor is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(Re=vD/\nu=1.5(0.050)/(1.0\times10^{-4})=750<2{,}100\), laminar. \(f=64/Re=64/750=0.085\).

questions.question: A pump delivers 0.050 m³/s of water (\(\gamma=9.81\) kN/m³) against a total head of 30 m. If the pump efficiency is 70 percent, the shaft (brake) power required is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\dot W=Q\gamma h/\eta=0.050(9{,}810)(30)/0.70=21{,}021\ \text{W}\approx21.0\) kW.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Fluid Flow Machinery — Pump Power Equation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses the density 1,000 kg/m³ in place of \(\gamma\) (omits \(g\)): \(0.050(1{,}000)(30)/0.70=2{,}143\) W.
  • (B) multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing.
  • (C) is the fluid (water) power with no efficiency applied.

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 8-19

questions.question: A 1:25 scale model of a spillway is tested using Froude similarity. If the prototype flow velocity at a point is 10 m/s, the corresponding model velocity is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Froude similarity, \(v^2/(lg)\) equal: \(v_m=v_p\sqrt{l_m/l_p}=10\sqrt{1/25}=2.0\) m/s.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Dimensional Homogeneity — Similitude (Froude number).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) keeps velocity equal, which is not similarity of any kind at reduced scale.
  • (C) inverts the scale ratio, multiplying by \(\sqrt{25}\) instead of dividing.
  • (D) is the Reynolds-similarity velocity for the same fluid (\(v_m=25v_p\)).

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 8-23

questions.question: A suppressed rectangular weir 2.0 m long operates under a head of 0.30 m. Using the Handbook coefficient, the discharge is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Suppressed rectangular weir, SI: \(Q=CLH^{3/2}=1.84(2.0)(0.30)^{1.5}=3.68(0.1643)=0.605\ \text{m}^3\text{/s}\approx0.60\) m³/s.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Weir Formulas (Rectangular, free discharge suppressed).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits the crest length \(L\) (\(1.84H^{3/2}=0.30\)).
  • (C) uses \(H^1\) (and is also what the USCS coefficient 3.33 would give in SI units).
  • (D) is the coefficient itself.

A – Flow measurement · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 8-27

questions.question: The azimuth of line PQ is 296°15′. The azimuth of line QP is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Back azimuth = forward azimuth ± 180°: \(296°15'-180°=116°15'\).

FE Reference Handbook: none needed.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(360°-296°15'\), the bearing angle of the forward line.

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 9-2

questions.question: In the traverse of Question 9-5, one course is 385.20 ft long. Using the compass rule, the correction to the latitude of that course is most nearly:
questions.explanation:

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 9-6

questions.question: The parcel in Figure 9.10 has corners P1 (E 100, N 100), P2 (E 260, N 140), P3 (E 300, N 320), P4 (E 120, N 280), all in meters. Its area is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Shoelace with X = E, Y = N in order P1–P2–P3–P4: \[\begin{aligned} \sum(X_iY_{i+1}-X_{i+1}Y_i)&=(100\cdot140-260\cdot100)+(260\cdot320-300\cdot140)\\ &\quad+(300\cdot280-120\cdot320)+(120\cdot100-100\cdot280)\\ &=(14{,}000-26{,}000)+(83{,}200-42{,}000)+(84{,}000-38{,}400)+(12{,}000-28{,}000)\\ &=-12{,}000+41{,}200+45{,}600-16{,}000=58{,}800 \end{aligned}\] Area \(=58{,}800/2=29{,}400\) m² \(=2.94\) ha.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Area formulas — Area by Coordinates; Units and Conversion Factors (hectare).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) omits the ½.
  • (C) is the area in acres (29,400 m² × 2.47104/10,000 = 7.26), not hectares.
  • (D) reports m²/1,000 — a hectare is 10,000 m².

B – Area computations · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 9-10

questions.question: A lot has an area of 125,000 ft². Its area in acres and hectares is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(125{,}000/43{,}560=2.870\) acres; \(2.870/2.47104=1.161\) ha.

FE Reference Handbook: Units and Conversion Factors (acre = 43,560 ft²; hectare = 2.47104 acres).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) swaps the two units.
  • (B) multiplies acres by 2.47104 instead of dividing.
  • (C) divides by 10,000 as if the area were in m².

B – Area computations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 9-14

questions.question: A level section in cut has a roadbed width of 12 m, side slopes of 1.5:1 (H:V), and a center cut of 3.2 m. The cross-section area is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A=d(w+sd)=3.2(12+1.5\times3.2)=3.2(16.8)=53.76\) m².

FE Reference Handbook: none needed (trapezoid geometry).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(w\times d\), ignoring the side slopes.
  • (B) inverts the slope ratio, using \(s=1/1.5=0.667\) horizontal per vertical: \(3.2(12+0.667\times3.2)=45.2\).
  • (C) uses \(s=1\).

C – Earthwork and volume computations · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 9-18

questions.question: Bank-measure earthwork between full stations is: 0+00 to 1+00, 600 yd³ cut; 1+00 to 2+00, 900 yd³ cut; 2+00 to 3+00, 300 yd³ cut and 500 yd³ fill; 3+00 to 4+00, 800 yd³ fill. Fill volumes are compacted measure and the shrinkage factor is 15% (fill increased by the factor). The mass diagram ordinate at Sta 4+00 is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Cumulative: 1+00: +600; 2+00: +1500; 3+00: 1500 + 300 − 1.15(500) = 1500 + 300 − 575 = +1225; 4+00: 1225 − 1.15(800) = 1225 − 920 = +305 yd³.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Earthwork formulas — Mass Haul Diagram.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) has the wrong sign.
  • (C) ignores shrinkage (1800 − 1300 = 500).
  • (D) applies the factor to the cut instead of the fill (1.15 × 1,800 − 1,300).

C – Earthwork and volume computations · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 9-22

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A level is set up between BM A (elevation 412.36 ft) and point P. The backsight on BM A is 5.87 ft and the foresight on P is 8.21 ft. Which statements are correct?
choices: The height of instrument is 418.23 ft.
The elevation of P is 410.02 ft.
Point P is higher than BM A.
The height of instrument is the elevation of the line of sight, not the height of the telescope above the ground.
If the backsight and foresight distances are equal, the effect of earth curvature on the elevation of P cancels.
questions.explanation:
HI \(=412.36+5.87=418.23\) ft; Elev P \(=418.23-8.21=410.02\) ft, so P is 2.34 ft below BM A. Statements (A), (B), (D), and (E) are correct.

FE Reference Handbook: none needed.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — HI = 412.36 + 5.87 = 418.23 ft.
  • (B) True — Elev P = 418.23 − 8.21 = 410.02 ft.
  • (C) False — P is 2.34 ft lower than BM A, because the foresight is larger than the backsight.
  • (D) True — HI is an elevation of the line of sight.
  • (E) True — equal sight lengths cancel curvature, refraction, and collimation error.

E – Leveling · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 9-26

questions.question: A watershed has a composite curve number of 78. A design storm delivers 3.5 in. of rainfall. Using the NRCS (SCS) rainfall-runoff method, determine the runoff depth in inches. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\[S = \frac{1000}{78} - 10 = 12.82 - 10 = 2.82\ \text{in.}, \qquad I_a = 0.2S = 0.564\ \text{in.} < 3.5\ \text{in.}\ \checkmark\] \[Q = \frac{(P - 0.2S)^2}{P + 0.8S} = \frac{(3.5 - 0.564)^2}{3.5 + 0.8(2.821)} = \frac{8.620}{5.756} = 1.497\ \text{in.}\]

Accepted range: 1.45–1.55 in. (report to two decimals; 1.5 in. is acceptable). A common wrong result is 2.94 in., which is \(P - I_a\) with the denominator omitted.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — NRCS/SCS Rainfall-Runoff.

A – Basic hydrology · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-2

questions.question: A rectangular concrete-lined channel is 2.0 m wide, has \(n = 0.013\) and is laid on a slope of 0.0025. At a normal depth of 0.80 m the discharge is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[A = by = 2.0(0.80) = 1.60\ \text{m}^2, \qquad P = b + 2y = 2.0 + 1.6 = 3.60\ \text{m}, \qquad R_H = \frac{1.60}{3.60} = 0.444\ \text{m}\] \[Q = \frac{K}{n}AR_H^{2/3}S^{1/2} = \frac{1.0}{0.013}(1.60)(0.4444)^{2/3}(0.0025)^{1/2} = 76.92(1.60)(0.5794)(0.050) = 3.58\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Manning’s Equation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 2.67 m3/s includes the free-surface width in the wetted perimeter (\(P = 5.6\) m).
  • (C) 4.10 m3/s raises \(R_H\) to the 1/2 power instead of 2/3.
  • (D) 5.30 m3/s uses \(R_H = y = 0.80\) m, valid only for a very wide channel.

B – Basic hydraulics · Easy · target ~3 min · Book question 10-6

questions.question: A rectangular channel 4.0 m wide has \(n = 0.014\) and a bed slope of 0.0016. Determine the normal depth, in meters, for a discharge of 15 m3/s. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Manning’s equation with \(A = 4y\) and \(P = 4 + 2y\): \[15 = \frac{1}{0.014}(4y)\left(\frac{4y}{4 + 2y}\right)^{2/3}(0.0016)^{1/2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad y\left(\frac{4y}{4 + 2y}\right)^{2/3} = 1.3125\] Trial \(y = 1.45\) m: \(A = 5.80\), \(P = 6.90\), \(R_H = 0.8406\), \(yR_H^{2/3} = 1.290\) (low). Trial \(y = 1.50\) m: \(A = 6.00\), \(P = 7.00\), \(R_H = 0.8571\), \(yR_H^{2/3} = 1.353\) (high). Interpolating, \(y_n = 1.467\) m, at which \(A = 5.868\) m2, \(P = 6.934\) m, \(R_H = 0.8462\) m and \(Q = 15.0\) m3/s ✓.

Accepted range: 1.44–1.50 m. Using \(R_H = y\) gives 1.18 m; using \(K = 1.486\) gives 1.11 m.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Manning’s Equation.

B – Basic hydraulics · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 10-10

questions.question: A pump handles 60°F water (vapor-pressure head 0.59 ft) at a site where the atmospheric pressure head is 33.9 ft. The sump water surface is 8.0 ft below the impeller centerline, and the suction piping loses 2.4 ft at the design flow. The net positive suction head available is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The sump surface is below the impeller, so the static suction head is negative: \(H_s = -8.0\) ft. \[NPSH_A = H_{pa} + H_s - \sum h_L - H_{vp} = 33.9 - 8.0 - 2.4 - 0.59 = 22.91\ \text{ft}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHA).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 23.5 ft drops the vapor-pressure head, which is the very quantity the margin is measured against.
  • (C) 38.9 ft takes the 8.0-ft suction lift as a positive static head and would wrongly certify a marginal installation.
  • (D) 44.9 ft adds every term instead of subtracting the losses and the lift.

C – Pumps · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 10-14

questions.question: A fire-hydrant flow test records a static pressure of 68 psi and a residual pressure of 42 psi while a total test flow of 1,100 gpm is discharged. Determine the rated capacity of the hydrant at 20 psi, in gpm. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\[H_R = P_S - 20 = 68 - 20 = 48\ \text{psi}, \qquad H_F = P_S - P_R = 68 - 42 = 26\ \text{psi}\] \[Q_R = Q_F\left(\frac{H_R}{H_F}\right)^{0.54} = 1100\left(\frac{48}{26}\right)^{0.54} = 1100(1.846)^{0.54} = 1100(1.3924) = 1532\ \text{gpm}\]

Accepted range: 1,500–1,560 gpm. Using the pressures themselves rather than the pressure drops (68/42) gives 1,427 gpm.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Formula for Calculating Rated Capacity at 20 psi from Fire Hydrant.

D – Water distribution systems · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-18

questions.question: A reservoir with a nearly constant surface area of 40 acres discharges over an uncontrolled spillway 60 ft long with \(C = 3.3\). At \(t = 0\) the pool is exactly at the crest and the inflow is zero; one hour later the inflow is 900 cfs. Using level-pool routing with a 1-hour time step and averaged inflows and outflows, determine the pool height above the crest at \(t = 1\) h, in feet. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Storage above the crest with a constant surface area: \(S = 40(43{,}560)h = 1.742\times10^6h\) ft3. Spillway rating: \(O = CLh^{3/2} = 3.3(60)h^{1.5} = 198\,h^{1.5}\) cfs. \(\Delta t\) = 3,600 s.

Continuity with averaged inflow and outflow, starting from \(S_1 = 0\), \(O_1 = 0\): \[\frac{0 + 900}{2}(3600) = 1.742\times10^6h_2 + \frac{0 + 198h_2^{1.5}}{2}(3600)\] \[1.620\times10^6 = 1.742\times10^6h_2 + 3.564\times10^5h_2^{1.5}\] Trial \(h_2 = 0.78\): \(1.359\times10^6 + 0.245\times10^6 = 1.605\times10^6\) (low). Trial \(h_2 = 0.79\): \(1.376\times10^6 + 0.250\times10^6 = 1.627\times10^6\) (high). Interpolating, \(h_2 = 0.787\) ft, at which \(O_2 = 198(0.787)^{1.5} = 138\) cfs.

Accepted range: 0.75–0.82 ft. Neglecting the outflow entirely (all inflow stored) gives 0.93 ft; using the start-of-step outflow only also gives 0.93 ft here, since \(O_1 = 0\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Weir Formulas; the continuity equation (\(dS/dt = I - O\)).

E – Flood control · Medium · target ~4 min · Book question 10-22

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about stormwater quantity and quality are correct?
choices: Urbanizing a watershed typically increases both the runoff volume and the peak discharge and shortens the time to peak.
A dry detention basin reduces the total volume of runoff leaving the site.
The “first flush” of a storm generally carries the highest pollutant concentrations.
Because settling in a pond is governed by the overflow rate \(Q/A_{surface}\), a shallow pond and a deep pond of the same surface area remove the same particle sizes.
Permeable pavement is classified as an infiltration BMP.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (C), (D) and (E) are correct; (B) is not (see the rationale for each statement below).

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Clarifier (overflow-rate concept); Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — impervious cover cuts infiltration and speeds conveyance.
  • (B) False — a dry detention basin delays and attenuates the hydrograph but releases essentially the same volume; only infiltration or retention BMPs reduce volume.
  • (C) True — pollutants accumulated between storms are washed off early.
  • (D) True — the critical settling velocity of an ideal basin is \(Q/A_{surface}\) and is independent of depth; depth affects detention time and scour, not the cut-off particle size.
  • (E) True — permeable pavement infiltrates runoff into a stone reservoir and the subgrade.

F – Stormwater · Easy · target ~3 min · Book question 10-26

questions.question: A 250-mm sanitary sewer (\(n = 0.013\)) must achieve a self-cleansing velocity of 0.60 m/s when flowing full. The minimum slope is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a full circular pipe \(R_H = D/4 = 0.250/4 = 0.0625\) m. \[v = \frac{1}{n}R_H^{2/3}S^{1/2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad S = \left(\frac{vn}{R_H^{2/3}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{0.60(0.013)}{(0.0625)^{2/3}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{0.00780}{0.15749}\right)^2 = (0.04953)^2 = 0.00245\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Manning’s Equation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.000386 uses \(R_H = D\).
  • (B) 0.000974 uses \(R_H = D/2\), a common slip; the hydraulic radius of a full circular pipe is \(D/4\).
  • (D) 0.0495 forgets to square, reporting \(S^{1/2}\) as the slope.

G – Collection systems · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 10-30

questions.question:
[Matching] Match each groundwater term (1–5) with the definition (A–E) that describes it. Each definition is used exactly once.

  • (A) Well discharge per unit of drawdown measured in the pumping well
  • (B) Hydraulic conductivity multiplied by the saturated thickness of the aquifer
  • (C) Volume of water released from storage per unit surface area of aquifer per unit decline in head
  • (D) Volume of water an unconfined aquifer releases by gravity drainage per unit bulk volume
  • (E) Fraction of the total volume consisting of interconnected voids available to conduct flow
questions.explanation:
1. Transmissivity — (B) \(T = Kb\), the discharge capacity of the full aquifer thickness per unit width per unit gradient (L2/T).
  2. Specific yield — (D) the drainable porosity of an unconfined aquifer, typically 0.1–0.3; it dominates unconfined storage.
  3. Specific capacity — (A) \(Q/D_w\) (for example gpm per foot of drawdown), a field index of well performance, not an aquifer property.
  4. Storativity — (C) the storage coefficient \(S\); for a confined aquifer it is 10−5–10−3 because water is released only by expansion of the water and compression of the skeleton, which is why confined cones of depression spread very far.
  5. Effective porosity — (E) the interconnected void fraction used to convert Darcy velocity to seepage velocity, \(v = q/n\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources (definitions of transmissivity and storativity; specific capacity \(Q/D_w\) under Dupuit’s Formula); Darcy’s Law. Specific yield is not defined in the Handbook.

H – Groundwater · Easy · target ~3 min · Book question 10-34

questions.question: A seeded BOD test uses 20 mL of an industrial wastewater plus seeded dilution water in a 300-mL bottle. The bottle DO falls from 8.9 to 2.7 mg/L in five days. A seed-control bottle holding 300 mL of the same seeded dilution water falls from 8.8 to 7.9 mg/L. Determine the BOD5 of the wastewater, in mg/L. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\[P = \frac{20}{300} = 0.0667, \qquad f = \frac{300 - 20}{300} = \frac{280}{300} = 0.9333\] \[BOD_5 = \frac{(D_1 - D_2) - (B_1 - B_2)f}{P} = \frac{(8.9 - 2.7) - (8.8 - 7.9)(0.9333)}{0.0667} = \frac{6.20 - 0.840}{0.0667} = \frac{5.36}{0.0667} = 80.4\ \text{mg/L}\] The test is valid: the depletion exceeds 2.0 mg/L and 2.7 mg/L of DO remains.

Accepted range: 78–83 mg/L. Omitting the seed correction gives 93.0 mg/L; omitting \(f\) over-corrects and gives 79.5 mg/L.

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — BOD Test Solution and Seeding Procedures.

J – Testing and standards · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-38

questions.question: A discrete particle of diameter 0.020 mm and specific gravity 2.65 settles in water at 20°C (\(\rho_f\) = 998.2 kg/m3, \(\mu = 1.002\times10^{-3}\) Pa·s). Using Stokes’ law, the terminal settling velocity expressed as an equivalent overflow rate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[v_t = \frac{g\rho_f(SG - 1)d^2}{18\mu} = \frac{9.81(998.2)(2.65 - 1)(2.0\times10^{-5})^2}{18(1.002\times10^{-3})} = \frac{6.463\times10^{-6}}{0.018036} = 3.583\times10^{-4}\ \text{m/s}\] \[v_t = 3.583\times10^{-4}(86{,}400) = 31.0\ \text{m/d}\] Check: \(Re = v_td\rho_f/\mu = 7.1\times10^{-3} \ll 1\), so Stokes’ law is valid. Using \(d\) = 0.020 m instead of 0.020 mm inflates the answer by 106.

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Settling Equations (Stokes’ Law); Clarifier (hydraulic loading rate = \(Q/A\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 50 m/d uses \(SG\) rather than \((SG - 1)\), i.e. it forgets the buoyant weight.
  • (C) 557 m/d drops the factor 18 from the denominator.
  • (D) 3,100 m/d misplaces the decimal in the diameter conversion, using \(d = 2.0\times10^{-4}\) m (0.20 mm); because \(v_t \propto d^2\), a tenfold diameter error is a hundredfold velocity error.

K – Water and wastewater treatment · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-42

questions.question: [Point-and-click] Figure 10.16 is the specific-energy curve for a wide rectangular channel carrying a unit discharge \(q\) = 2.5 m2/s. Five points on the curve carry the circled labels (A) through (E). The flow at point (A) passes through a short, smooth transition in which the specific energy is unchanged, and it leaves the transition supercritical. Name the labeled point that represents the depth downstream of the transition.
questions.explanation:
Specific energy for a rectangular channel is \[E = y + \frac{V^2}{2g} = y + \frac{q^2}{2gy^2}\] At point (A), \(y = 1.20\) m, so \(V = q/y = 2.5/1.20 = 2.083\) m/s and \[E_A = 1.20 + \frac{2.5^2}{2(9.81)(1.20)^2} = 1.20 + 0.221 = 1.421\ \text{m}\] Because the transition is loss-free, the downstream flow has the same specific energy. A given \(E\) above the minimum is shared by exactly two depths — the alternate depths — one subcritical (upper limb) and one supercritical (lower limb). Solving \(y + 0.3186/y^2 = 1.421\) for the small root gives \(y = 0.638\) m. That is the depth at point (D), the only labeled point on the lower limb lying on the same vertical line as (A).

Check that a supercritical alternate depth exists at all: \[y_c = \left(\frac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{2.5^2}{9.81}\right)^{1/3} = 0.860\ \text{m}, \qquad E_{min} = 1.5y_c = 1.291\ \text{m}\] Since \(E_A = 1.421\) m > \(E_{min}\), the flow can pass to the supercritical limb without a drop in energy.

Point (B) is at \(y = 0.95\) m on the upper limb, still subcritical, and its specific energy is 1.303 m — a different vertical line. Point (C) is the nose of the curve, the critical depth \(y_c = 0.860\) m at \(E_{min} = 1.291\) m; reaching it would require the flow to shed 0.13 m of specific energy, which a loss-free transition cannot do. Point (E) is supercritical (\(y = 0.45\) m) but sits at \(E = 2.02\) m, more energy than the flow ever had.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Specific Energy; Critical Depth; Froude Number.

B – Basic hydraulics · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-46

questions.question: The truss in Figure 11.16 carries a single 40-kN load at joint B. The force in member DE is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
By symmetry each reaction is 20 kN. Diagonal AD runs from (0, 0) to (2, 3), length \(\sqrt{13} = 3.606\) m, with direction cosines (0.5547, 0.8321).

Joint A, vertical: \(20 + 0.8321F_{AD} = 0 \Rightarrow F_{AD} = -24.04\) kN (compression).

Joint D (members AD, DB, DE). Vertical: \(-0.8321F_{AD} - 0.8321F_{DB} = 0 \Rightarrow F_{DB} = +24.04\) kN. Horizontal: \(-0.5547F_{AD} + 0.5547F_{DB} + F_{DE} = 0 \Rightarrow F_{DE} = -2(0.5547)(24.04) = -26.67\) kN, i.e., 26.7 kN compression.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Plane Truss: Method of Joints.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 13.3 kN tension is the bottom-chord force \(F_{AB}\).
  • (B) 24.0 kN compression is the end diagonal \(F_{AD}\).
  • (C) has the right magnitude but the wrong sense; the top chord of a simply supported truss under gravity load is always in compression.

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-4

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about shear and moment diagrams for a statically determinate beam are correct?
choices: The slope of the moment diagram at a section equals the shear at that section.
A concentrated couple applied to the beam produces a jump in the shear diagram equal to the couple.
Under a uniformly distributed load the shear diagram is linear and the moment diagram is parabolic.
The maximum bending moment occurs where the shear is zero or changes sign.
The change in shear between two sections equals the negative of the area under the load diagram between them.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (C), (D), and (E) follow directly from the two governing relationships \(dV/dx = -w\) and \(dM/dx = V\); statement (B) confuses the effect of a couple with that of a force.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Shearing Force and Bending Moment Sign Conventions.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(dM/dx = V\) is one of the two governing differential relationships.
  • (B) False — a concentrated couple produces a jump in the moment diagram equal to the couple and leaves the shear diagram unchanged. A concentrated force produces the jump in shear.
  • (C) True — with \(w\) constant, \(dV/dx = -w\) gives a straight line for \(V\), and \(dM/dx = V\) then gives a parabola for \(M\).
  • (D) True — \(M\) is stationary where \(dM/dx = V = 0\); at a concentrated load the shear changes sign discontinuously and the moment peaks there.
  • (E) True — integrating \(dV/dx = -w\) gives \(\Delta V = -\int w\,dx\).

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-8

questions.question: A simply supported steel beam spans 20 ft, has \(I = 800\,\text{in}^4\) and \(E = 29{,}000\) ksi, and carries a uniformly distributed load of 2.0 kip/ft together with a concentrated load of 10 kips at midspan. The midspan deflection is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Consistent units: \(L = 240\) in, \(w = 2.0/12 = 0.16667\) kip/in, \(P = 10\) kips. Superpose the two Handbook cases: \[\delta_w = \frac{5wL^4}{384EI} = \frac{5(0.16667)(240)^4}{384(29{,}000)(800)} = \frac{2.7648 \times 10^9}{8.9088 \times 10^9} = 0.310\,\text{in}\] \[\delta_P = \frac{PL^3}{48EI} = \frac{10(240)^3}{48(29{,}000)(800)} = \frac{1.3824 \times 10^8}{1.1136 \times 10^9} = 0.124\,\text{in}\] \[\delta = 0.310 + 0.124 = 0.435\,\text{in}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections; Principle of Superposition.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.12 in is the point-load contribution only.
  • (B) 0.31 in is the uniform-load contribution only.
  • (C) 0.39 in comes from smearing the 10-kip load into an equivalent uniform load \(P/L\) and using \(5wL^4/384EI\) for the total; a concentrated midspan load produces more deflection than the same weight spread along the span.

B – Deflection of determinate structures · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-12

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about elastic (Euler) column buckling are correct?
choices: The critical buckling load does not depend on the yield strength of the material.
When the unbraced length and end conditions are the same about both axes, buckling occurs about the axis with the smaller radius of gyration.
Doubling the unbraced length of a column reduces its Euler load to one-quarter of the original value.
Euler’s formula remains valid when the computed critical stress exceeds the proportional limit.
The theoretical effective-length factor for a column fixed at one end and free at the other is \(K = 0.5\).
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), and (C) follow from \(P_{cr} = \pi^2EI/(K\ell)^2\) and \(\sigma_{cr} = \pi^2E/(K\ell/r)^2\); statement (D) ignores the elastic assumption behind the formula, and statement (E) quotes the fixed-fixed factor.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Columns; Civil Engineering — Design of Steel Components — Columns.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(P_{cr} = \pi^2EI/(K\ell)^2\) contains \(E\) but not \(F_y\). Yield strength enters only in setting the upper bound on the usable stress.
