  • (B) True — \(\sigma_{cr} = \pi^2E/(K\ell/r)^2\) is smallest where \(K\ell/r\) is largest, i.e., where \(r\) is smallest.
  • (C) True — \(P_{cr} \propto 1/(K\ell)^2\), so doubling \(\ell\) divides the load by four.
  • (D) False — Euler’s derivation assumes linear elastic behavior. Above the proportional limit the true capacity falls below the Euler curve (inelastic buckling), which is why the AISC formula has two branches.
  • (E) False — \(K = 2.0\) for fixed-free; \(K = 0.5\) is the theoretical fixed-fixed value.

C – Column analysis · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-16

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following planar structures are unstable?
choices: A beam whose three reaction components are all vertical, loaded by a system that includes a horizontal force.
A frame whose three reaction components have lines of action that all pass through a single point.
A plane truss that satisfies \(m + r = 2j\) but contains one rectangular panel with no diagonal.
A beam supported by a pin at one end and a roller at the other, with no internal releases.
A beam with four reaction components and two internal hinges.
questions.explanation:
Structures (A), (B), and (C) pass or can pass the counting test but have a poor arrangement of members or reactions; structure (E) fails the count itself. Only (D) is stable.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — unstable: three parallel reactions cannot resist a force perpendicular to them, so the beam translates horizontally. The count \(r = 3\) is satisfied, which is exactly why counting alone is not sufficient.
  • (B) True — unstable: if all reaction lines pass through one point, their moment about that point is zero and the structure rotates about it.
  • (C) True — unstable: an untriangulated rectangular panel racks into a parallelogram. The global count can still equal \(2j\) if some other part of the truss has a redundant member — a local mechanism with a compensating redundancy elsewhere.
  • (D) False — stable and determinate: \(r = 3\), non-parallel, non-concurrent — the classic simple beam.
  • (E) True — unstable: \(r - 3 - c = 4 - 3 - 2 = -1\). There are more releases than redundancies, so the beam is a mechanism.

D – Determinacy and stability · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-20

questions.question: A beam fixed at both ends spans 10 m and carries a single concentrated load of 60 kN located 4 m from end A. The magnitude of the fixed-end moment at A is ______ kN·m. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
With \(a = 4\) m measured from A and \(b = 6\) m, \[FEM_{AB} = \frac{Pab^2}{L^2} = \frac{60(4)(6)^2}{(10)^2} = \frac{60(4)(36)}{100} = 86.4\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}\]

Numerical entry: accepted answer 86.4 kN·m (range 85.5–87.3). The common wrong entry is 57.6 kN·m, which is \(Pa^2b/L^2\) — the fixed-end moment at B. The moment is larger at the support nearer the load, so \(FEM_A > FEM_B\) here.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Member Fixed-End Moments.

E – Elementary indeterminate structures · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-24

questions.question: A roof structure carries nominal loads \(D = 30\) psf, \(L = 60\) psf, and \(S = 25\) psf, with no wind or seismic load considered. Using the ASD load combinations, the governing load is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Evaluate the ASD combinations with unfactored loads:

  • \(D + L = 30 + 60 = 90\) psf
  • \(D + S = 30 + 25 = 55\) psf
  • \(D + 0.75L + 0.75S = 30 + 45 + 18.75 = 93.75\) psf ← governs

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Load Combinations using Allowable Stress Design (ASD).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 55.0 psf is \(D + S\).
  • (B) 75.0 psf keeps the 0.75 factor on \(L\) but omits the companion snow term.
  • (C) 90.0 psf is \(D + L\), which loses to the three-load combination because the 0.75 reductions do not fully offset adding snow.

F – Loads and load combinations · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-28

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about tributary areas, load paths, and live-load reduction are correct?
choices: For a typical interior floor beam, the tributary width equals the spacing to the adjacent parallel beams.
In a regular rectangular column grid, a corner column’s tributary area is one-quarter of an interior column’s.
Live-load reduction may also be applied to the dead load when the tributary area is large.
The live-load element factor is \(K_{LL} = 4\) for a typical interior column and \(K_{LL} = 2\) for a typical interior beam.
For a member supporting a single floor, the reduced live load may not be taken less than \(0.50L_o\).
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), (D), and (E) restate the tributary-area geometry and the Handbook’s live-load reduction rules; statement (C) is false because the reduction applies to live load only.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Live Load Reduction; Structural Design — Loads (ASCE 7-16).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the tributary boundary lies halfway to each adjacent parallel member, so half a bay on each side sums to the full spacing.
  • (B) True — an interior column collects a full bay (halfway to the neighbor in each of four directions); a corner column collects only one quadrant of that.
  • (C) False — the reduction reflects the low probability that a large floor area is fully loaded with live load at one instant. Dead load is always present and is never reduced.
  • (D) True — these are the Handbook’s live-load element factors for the typical cases.
  • (E) True — the Handbook sets the floor at \(0.50L_o\) for members supporting one floor and \(0.40L_o\) for members supporting two or more.

F – Loads and load combinations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-32

questions.question: A compact, continuously braced W-shape of \(F_y = 50\) ksi steel must resist a factored moment \(M_u = 250\) kip-ft. The required plastic section modulus \(Z_x\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a compact, fully braced shape the limit state is yielding, \(M_n = M_p = F_yZ_x\), with \(\phi_b = 0.90\). Setting \(\phi_bF_yZ_x \ge M_u\) and converting kip-ft to kip-in: \[Z_x \ge \frac{M_u(12)}{\phi_bF_y} = \frac{250(12)}{0.90(50)} = \frac{3000}{45} = 66.7\,\text{in}^3\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Steel Components — Beams; AISC Table 3-2 (W Shapes — Selection by \(Z_x\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 55.6 in³ uses \(F_y = 60\) ksi.
  • (C) 80.0 in³ uses \(\phi = 0.75\) instead of 0.90.
  • (D) 83.3 in³ uses \(F_y = 36\) ksi and also omits \(\phi\) (\(3000/36\)); the table and the problem both specify 50-ksi steel.

G – Design of steel components · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-36

questions.question: For concrete with \(f'_c = 6000\) psi, the stress-block factor \(\beta_1\) is:
questions.explanation:
For \(4000 < f'_c < 8000\) psi, \[\beta_1 = 0.85 - 0.05\,\frac{f'_c - 4000}{1000} = 0.85 - 0.05\,\frac{2000}{1000} = 0.85 - 0.10 = 0.75\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) — Definitions (\(\beta_1\) table).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.85 applies only for \(f'_c \le 4000\) psi.
  • (B) 0.80 corresponds to \(f'_c = 5000\) psi.
  • (D) 0.65 is the floor value, reached at \(f'_c \ge 8000\) psi.

H – Design of reinforced concrete components · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 11-40

questions.question: A short tied column measures 18 in × 18 in and is reinforced with eight #9 bars (\(A_{st} = 8.00\,\text{in}^2\)). Take \(f'_c = 4000\) psi and \(f_y = 60{,}000\) psi. The design axial strength \(\phi P_n\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A_g = 18(18) = 324\,\text{in}^2\); \(\rho_g = 8.00/324 = 0.0247\), within the permitted range 0.01 to 0.08. \[\begin{aligned} \phi P_n &= \phi(0.80)\left[0.85f'_c(A_g - A_{st}) + A_{st}f_y\right] = 0.65(0.80)\left[0.85(4)(324 - 8.00) + 8.00(60)\right] \\ &= 0.52\left[1074.4 + 480.0\right] = 0.52(1554.4) = 808\,\text{kips} \end{aligned}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components — Short Columns; Resistance Factors.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 933 kips uses \(\phi = 0.75\), the spiral-column factor, with the tied-column 0.80; a tied column is compression-controlled with \(\phi = 0.65\).
  • (C) 1010 kips drops the 0.80 accidental-eccentricity factor.
  • (D) 1554 kips is the bracketed nominal quantity with neither 0.80 nor \(\phi\) applied.

H – Design of reinforced concrete components · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-44

questions.question: A clean sand contains 3% fines. Its grain-size curve gives \(D_{10} = 0.12\) mm, \(D_{30} = 0.32\) mm, and \(D_{60} = 0.90\) mm, and 85% of the coarse fraction passes the No. 4 sieve. The USCS group symbol is:
questions.explanation:
Fines are 3%, less than 5%, so this is a clean coarse-grained soil and the gradation criteria apply. More than half the coarse fraction passes the No. 4, so it is a sand. \[C_U = \frac{0.90}{0.12} = 7.5 \qquad C_C = \frac{(0.32)^2}{(0.12)(0.90)} = \frac{0.1024}{0.108} = 0.948\] For SW, ASTM D2487 requires \(C_U \ge 6\) and \(1 \le C_C \le 3\). The uniformity criterion is met but \(C_C = 0.95 < 1\), so the soil is SP.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Coefficient of Uniformity; Coefficient of Concavity (or Curvature); ASTM D2487-11 (USCS).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) accepts \(C_U \ge 6\) alone and ignores the \(C_C\) requirement.
  • (C) is the dual symbol required only when fines are between 5% and 12%.
  • (D) would require more than 12% fines classifying as ML or MH.

A – Index properties and soil classifications · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 12-2

questions.question: A sand deposit has \(e_{max} = 0.94\), \(e_{min} = 0.45\), and an in-situ void ratio of 0.60. The specific gravity of solids is 2.66. The relative density is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[D_r = \frac{e_{max} - e}{e_{max} - e_{min}}\times 100 = \frac{0.94 - 0.60}{0.94 - 0.45}\times 100 = \frac{0.34}{0.49}\times 100 = 69.4\%\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Relative Density.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) results from putting \((e - e_{min})\) in the numerator.
  • (B) divides \((e_{max} - e)\) by \(e_{max}\) instead of by the range.
  • (C) is what the unit-weight form gives when the closing factor \(\gamma_{d,max}/\gamma_{d,field}\) is omitted: \((16.31 - 13.45)/(18.00 - 13.45) = 62.9\%\).

A – Index properties and soil classifications · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-6

questions.question: A saturated soil has \(G_s = 2.68\) and \(e = 0.65\). Its submerged (effective) unit weight is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[\gamma_{sat} = \frac{(G_s+e)\gamma_w}{1+e} = \frac{(2.68+0.65)(9.81)}{1.65} = \frac{32.67}{1.65} = 19.80\,\text{kN/m}^3\] \[\gamma' = \gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w = 19.80 - 9.81 = 9.99\,\text{kN/m}^3\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Phase Relationships (saturated unit weight; effective (submerged) unit weight).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is the dry unit weight \(G_s\gamma_w/(1+e) = 26.29/1.65 = 15.93\) kN/m³, which removes the pore water instead of accounting for buoyancy.
  • (C) is the saturated unit weight, the intermediate result.
  • (D) is \(G_s\gamma_w\), the unit weight of the solid mineral.

B – Phase relations · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 12-10

questions.question: A laboratory standard Proctor test gives \(\gamma_{d,max} = 18.6\) kN/m³. A field density test on the compacted fill reads a moist unit weight of 20.5 kN/m³ at a water content of 15.0%. The relative compaction is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Convert the field reading to a dry unit weight first: \[\gamma_{d,field} = \frac{20.5}{1+0.15} = 17.83\,\text{kN/m}^3\] \[RC = \frac{17.83}{18.6}\times 100 = 95.8\%\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Relative Compaction; Phase Relationships (dry unit weight).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) divides the dry field value by the moist field value.
  • (B) estimates the dry unit weight by subtracting the water content instead of dividing by \((1+w)\): \(20.5(1-0.15) = 17.43\) kN/m³, and \(17.43/18.6 = 93.7\%\).
  • (D) compares the moist field unit weight directly to the laboratory maximum dry unit weight, a common error in field density work.

C – Laboratory and field tests · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 12-14

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A cofferdam excavation in a sand with \(\gamma_{sat} = 18.5\) kN/m³ has a computed upward exit gradient of 0.55. Determine the factor of safety against seepage liquefaction.
questions.explanation:
\[i_c = \frac{18.5 - 9.81}{9.81} = \frac{8.69}{9.81} = 0.886\] \[FS_s = \frac{i_c}{i_e} = \frac{0.886}{0.55} = 1.61\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Factor of Safety Against Seepage Liquefaction. Accepted range: 1.58 to 1.64. Inverting the ratio gives 0.62 and is not accepted; the factor of safety must be the capacity gradient over the demand gradient.

D – Effective stress · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-18

questions.question: A normally consolidated sand has \(\phi = 34°\). The at-rest earth pressure coefficient is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[K_0 = 1 - \sin\phi = 1 - \sin 34° = 1 - 0.559 = 0.441\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Horizontal Stress Profiles and Forces (at-rest forces on wall per unit length of wall).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the Rankine active coefficient \(\tan^2(45° - 17°) = 0.283\).
  • (C) is \(\sin\phi\) itself, not \(1 - \sin\phi\).
  • (D) is the passive coefficient.

E – Stability of retaining structures · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 12-22

questions.question: A consolidated-undrained triaxial test on a saturated normally consolidated clay fails at \(\sigma_3 = 150\) kPa and \(\sigma_1 = 390\) kPa, with a measured pore water pressure at failure of 60 kPa (Figure 12.17). Taking \(c' = 0\), the effective friction angle is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Shift both principal stresses left by the pore pressure to get effective stresses: \[\sigma'_3 = 150 - 60 = 90\,\text{kPa} \qquad \sigma'_1 = 390 - 60 = 330\,\text{kPa}\] The radius is unchanged; only the center moves: \[t = \frac{330 - 90}{2} = 120\,\text{kPa} \qquad s' = \frac{330 + 90}{2} = 210\,\text{kPa}\] \[\sin\phi' = \frac{t}{s'} = \frac{120}{210} = 0.5714 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \phi' = 34.8°\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Mohr-Coulomb failure envelope figure (with definitions of \(s\), \(t\), \(\theta\)); Effective Stress.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses \(\sigma_1\) in place of \(s'\).
  • (B) is the total-stress friction angle \(\arcsin(120/270) = 26.4°\), which is always smaller than \(\phi'\) for a normally consolidated clay.
  • (C) uses arctan in place of arcsin.

F – Shear strength · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-26

questions.question: A continuous footing 2.0 m wide is founded 1.5 m deep in a saturated clay with \(c = 60\) kPa and \(\phi = 0\). The soil unit weight is 18.0 kN/m³ and the water table is deep. Using \(N_c = 5.14\), \(N_q = 1.0\), \(N_\gamma = 0\) and a factor of safety of 3 applied to the gross ultimate capacity, the allowable bearing pressure is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[q_{ult} = cN_c + \gamma D_f N_q + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma BN_\gamma = 60(5.14) + 18.0(1.5)(1.0) + 0\] \[q_{ult} = 308.4 + 27.0 = 335.4\,\text{kPa} \qquad q_{all} = \frac{335.4}{3} = 111.8\,\text{kPa}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Ultimate Bearing Capacity. The factors were supplied in the problem.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the net allowable pressure \((335.4 - 27.0)/3 = 102.8\) kPa, correct only if the question had asked for net.
  • (C) uses the Terzaghi \(N_c = 5.7\) instead of the given 5.14.
  • (D) is the ultimate capacity with no factor of safety applied.

G – Bearing capacity · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-30

questions.question: A 0.30-m-diameter circular pile is driven 12 m into a saturated clay with \(c_u = 40\) kPa. Using \(f_s = \alpha c_u\) with \(\alpha = 0.85\) and \(q_p = N_c c_u\) with \(N_c = 9\), the ultimate pile capacity is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Shaft resistance uses the perimeter: \[A_s = \pi DL = \pi(0.30)(12) = 11.31\,\text{m}^2 \qquad f_s = 0.85(40) = 34\,\text{kPa}\] \[Q_s = 34(11.31) = 384.5\,\text{kN}\] End bearing uses the tip area: \[A_p = \frac{\pi(0.30)^2}{4} = 0.07069\,\text{m}^2 \qquad q_p = 9(40) = 360\,\text{kPa}\] \[Q_p = 360(0.07069) = 25.4\,\text{kN} \qquad Q_{ult} = 384.5 + 25.4 = 410\,\text{kN}\]

FE Reference Handbook: not in Handbook 10.6 — the pile-capacity relationships were supplied in the problem statement.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses the cross-sectional area in place of the perimeter when computing \(A_s\).
  • (B) omits end bearing.
  • (D) uses \(\alpha = 1.0\) instead of the given 0.85.

H – Foundation types · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-34

questions.question: A clay has a liquid limit of 52. Using the Handbook correlations for compression index and recompression index, the recompression index is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[C_C = 0.009(LL - 10) = 0.009(52 - 10) = 0.009(42) = 0.378\] \[C_R = \frac{C_C}{6} = \frac{0.378}{6} = 0.063\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Compression Index (correlation to liquid limit); Recompression Index (correlation to compression index).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) divides by 10 instead of 6.
  • (C) omits the \(-10\) inside the correlation.
  • (D) is \(C_C\), not \(C_R\); the recompression index is roughly one sixth as large, which is why unloading and reloading produce so much less settlement than first loading.

I – Consolidation and differential settlement · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 12-38

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about slope stability are correct?
choices: For a dry cohesionless infinite slope the factor of safety does not depend on the depth to the slip surface
An embankment built rapidly on soft saturated clay is most critical immediately after construction
A cut slope in stiff clay is most critical in the long term, after negative pore pressures have dissipated
In the ordinary (Fellenius) method of slices the factor of safety is obtained without iteration
Raising the water table in a slope increases the driving shear force but leaves the available shear strength unchanged
questions.explanation:
Statements (A) through (D) are correct; (E) misplaces the main effect of a rising water table, which acts on the resisting side through the effective normal stress.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Slope Failure Along Planar Surface; Effective Stress.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — For \(c' = 0\) the infinite-slope factor of safety reduces to \(\tan\phi/\tan\beta\), in which \(H\) cancels — a dry sand slope is equally safe at all depths, and stands exactly at \(\beta = \phi\).
  • (B) True — The foundation clay has not yet consolidated, so its undrained strength is at its lowest; as consolidation proceeds the strength increases and the factor of safety rises.
  • (C) True — Excavation unloads the clay and generates negative pore pressures that temporarily raise effective stress; as they dissipate the clay swells and weakens, so the long-term drained case governs.
  • (D) True — The ordinary method assumes \(N = W\cos\alpha\), so the factor of safety follows from a single pass; Bishop’s simplified method has \(FS\) on both sides and requires iteration.
  • (E) False — Raising the water table increases the pore pressure on the slip surface, which reduces the effective normal stress and therefore reduces the available frictional strength. That reduction, not a change in driving force, is the main effect.

J – Slope stability · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 12-42

questions.question: [Point-and-click] A fine-grained soil has a liquid limit of 62 and a plastic limit of 24. Figure 12.19 is a USCS-style plasticity chart on which five zones carry the circled labels (A) through (E). Name the labeled zone in which this soil plots.
questions.explanation:
First the plasticity index: \[PI = LL - PL = 62 - 24 = 38\] Now locate \((LL, PI) = (62, 38)\) on the chart. Two boundaries decide the zone: \[\text{A-line at } LL = 62: \quad PI = 0.73(LL - 20) = 0.73(42) = 30.7\] \[\text{U-line at } LL = 62: \quad PI = 0.9(LL - 8) = 0.9(54) = 48.6\] The point has \(PI = 38 > 30.7\), so it lies above the A-line, and \(38 < 48.6\), so it is below the U-line and the result is a physically admissible combination of limits. With \(LL = 62 \ge 50\) the soil is of high plasticity. Above the A-line and to the right of \(LL = 50\) is the CH zone, marked (D).

Zone (A) is the hatched CL-ML band, which requires \(4 \le PI \le 7\); this soil’s PI is 38. Zone (B) is CL — above the A-line but with \(LL < 50\). Zone (C) is ML or OL — \(LL < 50\) and below the A-line. Zone (E) is MH or OH: it has the right liquid limit but lies below the A-line, and it is the answer you get if you compare PI against the A-line ordinate at the wrong liquid limit, or forget that the A-line rises with LL.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Plasticity Index; ASTM D2487-11 Standard Practice for Classification of Soils for Engineering Purposes (Unified Soil Classification System) and its plasticity chart.

A – Index properties and soil classifications · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-46

questions.question: A curve has \(R=400\) m and \(I=60^\circ\). The external distance is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(E=R[1/\cos(I/2)-1]=400[1/\cos30^\circ-1]=400(1.1547-1)=61.9\) m.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the middle ordinate \(R(1-\cos30^\circ)=53.6\) m.
  • (C) is the tangent \(R\tan30^\circ\).
  • (D) is the long chord \(2R\sin30^\circ\).

A – Geometric design · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-4

questions.question: Which of the following changes increase the required stopping sight distance? [Select all that apply]
choices: A change from a level road to a downgrade
A change from a downgrade to an upgrade
questions.explanation:
Both terms of \(SSD=1.47Vt+V^2/[30(a/32.2\pm G)]\) must be examined: speed and reaction time lengthen it, a downgrade lengthens the braking term, and a higher deceleration or an upgrade shortens it.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Stopping Sight Distance.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — both terms grow with \(V\) (the braking term with \(V^2\)).
  • (B) True — a downgrade makes \(G\) negative, reducing the denominator \(30(a/32.2+G)\) and lengthening the braking distance.
  • (C) True — the reaction distance \(1.47Vt\) grows with \(t\).
  • (D) False — a higher \(a\) increases the denominator and shortens braking.
  • (E) False — an upgrade (positive \(G\)) shortens braking distance.

A – Geometric design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-8

questions.question: A sag vertical curve joins a −3.5% grade to a +2.5% grade on a road with a design speed of 50 mph and a stopping sight distance of 450 ft. Considering both the headlight and the comfort criteria, the minimum curve length is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A=|2.5-(-3.5)|=6.0\). Headlight, assume \(S\le L\): \(L=AS^2/(400+3.5S)=6(450)^2/(400+1575)=1{,}215{,}000/1975=615\) ft \(\ge450\), consistent. Comfort: \(L=AV^2/46.5=6(50)^2/46.5=323\) ft. The larger (headlight) value governs: 615 ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Vertical Curves: Sight Distance Related to Curve Length (Sag Vertical Curve).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) takes the algebraic difference of the grades with the sign of \(g_1\) dropped, \(A=|2.5-3.5|=1.0\): headlight \(1.0(450)^2/1975=103\) ft governs over comfort \(1.0(50)^2/46.5=54\) ft. For a sag, \(A=|g_2-g_1|=|2.5-(-3.5)|=6.0\).
  • (B) is the comfort length, which does not satisfy the headlight criterion.
  • (C) uses the \(S>L\) headlight formula \(2S-(400+3.5S)/A=900-329=571\) ft, although the \(S\le L\) result (615 ft) is consistent with its own assumption.

A – Geometric design · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 13-12

questions.question: A flexible pavement has 5.0 in of asphalt concrete (\(a_1=0.42\)), 6.0 in of crushed-stone base (\(a_2=0.14\), \(m_2=1.0\)), and 8.0 in of gravel subbase (\(a_3=0.08\), \(m_3=0.80\)). The structural number is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(SN=0.42(5.0)+0.14(6.0)(1.0)+0.08(8.0)(0.80)=2.10+0.84+0.51=3.45\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Highway Pavement Design (AASHTO Structural Number Equation).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits the subbase.
  • (B) applies \(m=0.80\) to the base as well: \(2.10+0.84(0.80)+0.51=3.28\).
  • (D) ignores the drainage coefficient (\(m_3=1.0\)).

B – Pavement design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-16

questions.question: Which statements about pavement systems are correct? [Select all that apply]
choices: A rigid pavement distributes wheel loads over a large area through the bending stiffness of the concrete slab.
In a flexible pavement, layer stiffness generally decreases with depth, and each layer spreads the load to reduce stress on the layer below.
The AASHTO structural number is the design index used for rigid (concrete) pavements.
CBR and resilient modulus are both measures of subgrade support.
A drainage coefficient less than 1.0 reduces the structural contribution of a base layer, requiring greater thickness for the same structural number.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), (D), and (E) describe flexible and rigid pavement behavior, subgrade characterization, and drainage correctly; the structural number in (C) belongs to flexible, not rigid, design.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Highway Pavement Design.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — slab action is the defining feature of rigid pavement.
  • (B) True — a flexible pavement is a layered system with stiffness decreasing downward.
  • (C) False — the structural number is the flexible-pavement design index; rigid pavements are designed for slab thickness.
  • (D) True — CBR is an index of penetration resistance and \(M_R\) a modulus from repeated loading; both characterize subgrade support and can be correlated.
  • (E) True — \(a_iD_im_i\) is reduced when \(m_i<1\), so \(D_i\) must increase to hold \(SN\).

B – Pavement design · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-20

questions.question: A lane carries a flow of 1,440 veh/h at a space-mean speed of 60 km/h. Which statements are correct? [Select all that apply]
choices: The average spacing is about 41.7 m.
If the flow doubled at the same speed, the average spacing would be halved.
questions.explanation:
Use \(V=DS\) with headway \(h=3600/V\) and spacing \(s=1000/D\) (metric): \(h=2.5\) s, \(D=24\) veh/km, \(s=41.7\) m.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity (\(D=v_p/S\)); Traffic Flow Relationships.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(h=3600/1440=2.5\) s.
  • (B) True — \(D=V/S=1440/60=24\) veh/km.
  • (C) True — \(s=1000/24=41.7\) m (also \(s=S\times h=16.67\ \text{m/s}\times2.5\ \text{s}\)).
  • (D) False — 86 comes from \(S\times V/1000\), which is not a density.
  • (E) True — at constant speed, density is proportional to flow, and spacing is the inverse of density.

C – Traffic flow · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 13-24

questions.question: Vehicles arrive at a single-booth toll plaza as a Poisson process at 240 veh/h and are served with exponentially distributed service times averaging 12 s. The average time a vehicle spends waiting in the queue (before service begins) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\mu=3600/12=300\) veh/h; \(\lambda=240\) veh/h; \(\rho=0.80\). \(W_q=\lambda/[\mu(\mu-\lambda)]=240/[300(60)]=0.01333\) h = 48 s.

FE Reference Handbook: Industrial and Systems Engineering — Queueing Models (Single Server Models, Poisson Input—Exponential Service Time).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the service time \(1/\mu\).
  • (B) uses the constant-service (M/D/1) result \(W_q=\rho/[2\mu(1-\rho)]\), which does not apply to exponential service.
  • (D) is the total time in the system \(W=1/(\mu-\lambda)=60\) s.

C – Traffic flow · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 13-28

questions.question: A crosswalk is 72 ft long and serves 8 pedestrians per interval. Using the default pedestrian walking speed, the minimum pedestrian green time, in seconds, is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(G_p=3.2+L/S_p+0.27N_{ped}=3.2+72/3.5+0.27(8)=3.2+20.57+2.16=25.9\) s.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Traffic Signal Timing (\(G_p\), default \(S_p=3.5\) ft/s).

D – Traffic control devices · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-32

questions.question:
Match each step of the four-step travel demand model (1–4) with the tool most closely associated with it (a–d). [Drag-and-drop / matching]

  • (a) Gravity model
  • (b) Logit model
  • (c) User-equilibrium route loading
  • (d) Trip rates per dwelling unit
questions.explanation:
Trip generation uses trip rates (or regression) per dwelling unit or employee; distribution uses the gravity model; mode choice uses the logit model; assignment loads trips onto network routes, most rigorously by user equilibrium.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Gravity Model; Logit Models.

E – Transportation planning · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-36

questions.question: Three countermeasures with crash reduction factors of 0.25, 0.15, and 0.10 are applied at one site. The overall crash reduction factor is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(CR=CR_1+(1-CR_1)CR_2+(1-CR_1)(1-CR_2)CR_3=0.25+0.75(0.15)+0.75(0.85)(0.10)=0.25+0.1125+0.0638=0.426\approx0.43\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Traffic Safety Equations (Crash Reduction).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the first factor alone.
  • (C) is the simple sum, which overstates the effect because later measures act only on remaining crashes.
  • (D) is 1 − 0.25, the fraction remaining after the first measure.

E – Transportation planning · Hard · target ~1 min · Book question 13-40

questions.question:
A contractor bids the following unit-price schedule on the owner’s estimated quantities:

Item Estimated quantity Unit price
Roadway excavation 8,000 m³ $12.50/m³
Aggregate base course 3,200 m² $28.00/m²
450-mm storm pipe 1,900 m $95.00/m

The instructions to bidders state that mobilization, estimated by the contractor at $100,000, is to be included in the unit prices and will not be paid as a separate item. The total bid is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Total the extended amounts:

\(8{,}000(12.50)=\$100{,}000\); \(3{,}200(28.00)=\$89{,}600\); \(1{,}900(95.00)=\$180{,}500\).

\(\text{Total}=100{,}000+89{,}600+180{,}500=\$370{,}100\). Mobilization is already inside the unit prices, so it is neither added to nor deducted from the extended total.

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $189,600 omits the pipe item.
  • (B) $270,100 deducts the $100,000 mobilization from the extended total. The instructions say mobilization is already carried inside the unit prices, so the extended amounts are the bid; nothing is added or removed.
  • (C) $289,460 extends the base course at $2.80/m² instead of $28.00/m² (a decimal slip): 100,000 + 3,200(2.80) + 180,500 = 100,000 + 8,960 + 180,500 = $289,460.

A – Project administration · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-2

questions.question: A construction manager at risk holds a cost-plus contract with a fee of 6% of allowable cost and a guaranteed maximum price of $1,500,000 covering cost plus fee. Savings below the GMP are shared 70% owner / 30% CM. Final allowable cost is $1,320,000. What does the owner pay?
questions.explanation:
\(\text{Fee}=0.06(1{,}320{,}000)=\$79{,}200\).

\(\text{Cost plus fee}=1{,}320{,}000+79{,}200=\$1{,}399{,}200\), which is below the GMP, so the cap does not bind.

\(\text{Savings}=1{,}500{,}000-1{,}399{,}200=\$100{,}800\). The CM’s 30% share is \(0.30(100{,}800)=\$30{,}240\).

\(\text{Owner pays}=1{,}399{,}200+30{,}240=\$1{,}429{,}440\).

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $1,399,200 forgets that the owner must pay the CM its share of the savings.
  • (C) $1,469,760 gives the CM the owner’s 70% share.
  • (D) $1,500,000 pays the guaranteed maximum price, which is a cap, not the amount earned.

A – Project administration · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 14-6

questions.question: A 3-m-deep precast manhole is being entered to install a drop connection. Which condition, by itself, would make the manhole a permit-required confined space?
choices: It has limited means of entry and exit.
It is not designed for continuous occupancy.
A ladder is required to reach the bottom.
Atmospheric testing detects hydrogen sulfide above the permissible exposure limit.
questions.explanation:
A space becomes permit-required when, in addition to being a confined space, it contains or may contain a hazardous atmosphere, contains material that could engulf an entrant, has converging walls or a tapering floor that could trap an entrant, or contains any other recognized serious hazard. Hydrogen sulfide above the permissible exposure limit is a hazardous atmosphere — and, being heavier than air, it collects at the bottom of a manhole, which is where the sensor must be lowered.

FE Reference Handbook: Safety — Confined Space Safety.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Limited entry and exit is one of the two defining features of a confined space itself; it makes the manhole confined but not yet permit-required.
  • (B) Not being designed for continuous occupancy is the other defining feature of a confined space; by itself it does not trigger a permit.
  • (C) Needing a ladder is a matter of access, not a permit trigger.

B – Construction operations and methods · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-10

questions.question: [Numerical entry] Only 5 trucks are available for the operation of Questions 14-12 and 14-13, so the trucks govern production. The material swells 25%. Determine the fleet production in bank cubic meters per hour, working a 50-minute hour.
questions.explanation:
Truck payload \(=5\) passes \(\times2.55=12.75\) LCM. With fewer trucks than the balance number, the trucks govern: \[P=\frac{n\,q_{truck}\times60E}{C_{truck}}=\frac{5(12.75)(50)}{21.0}=151.8\ \text{LCM/hr}\] Convert to bank measure with the load factor \(LF=1/(1+s_w)=1/1.25=0.80\): \[P=151.8(0.80)=121.4\ \text{BCM/hr}\] Accepted range: 119–124 BCM/hr (report 121). Two traps: using the loader’s 212.5 LCM/hr (the loader now idles part of every cycle, so it does not govern), and multiplying by 1.25 instead of dividing, which gives 190 BCM/hr — bank volume is always smaller than the loose volume that carried it.

FE Reference Handbook: none.

B – Construction operations and methods · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 14-14

questions.question: For the network of Figure 14.12, the total float of activity C is:
questions.explanation:
Backward pass from \(LF_G=17\): G: LS 13, LF 17. E: LF = \(LS_G\) = 13, LS 10. F: LF 13, LS 11. C: LF = \(LS_E\) = 10, LS 6. D: LF = \(LS_F\) = 11, LS 5. B: LF = \(LS_D\) = 5, LS 0. A: LF = min(\(LS_C\), \(LS_D\)) = min(6, 5) = 5, LS 3. \[TF_C=LS_C-ES_C=6-2=4\ \text{days}\quad(\text{check: }LF_C-EF_C=10-6=4)\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — Nomenclature (Float = LS − ES or LF − EF).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0 treats C as critical; the critical path is B–D–F–G.
  • (B) 3 days is the total float of A.
  • (D) 11 days subtracts \(EF_C\) from the project duration (\(17-6\)), which ignores the fact that E and G must still follow C and therefore consume that time.

C – Project controls · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-18

questions.question: A 20-day project has a single critical path A–B–C–D with crash cost slopes of $600, $450, $900, and $300 per day, respectively. Noncritical activity E has a cost slope of $200 per day and 4 days of total float. Indirect cost is $500 per day. To reduce the project duration by one day at the least total cost, the contractor should crash:
choices: activity E, because it has the lowest cost slope
activity B, because it is nearest the middle of the path
nothing, because every cost slope exceeds the indirect cost
activity D, for a net saving of $200
questions.explanation:
Only a critical activity can shorten the project, so E is irrelevant no matter how cheap it is. Among A, B, C, D the lowest cost slope is D at $300/day. Crashing D one day costs $300 in direct cost and saves $500 in indirect cost: \[\text{net saving}=500-300=\$200/\text{day}\]

FE Reference Handbook: none — the time-cost trade-off is the standard method stated in Section 14.7.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Crashing E spends $200 and shortens no path that controls the finish date; E already has 4 days of float.
  • (B) B costs $450/day; it would still net a $50 saving, but D is cheaper, and “least total cost” means taking the lowest slope first.
  • (C) is false: D’s $300/day slope is below the $500/day indirect cost, so the step is economical.

C – Project controls · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 14-22

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A project has a budget at completion of $5,000,000. At the status date the earned value is $2,000,000 and the actual cost is $2,300,000. Determine the to-complete performance index (TCPI) required to finish the remaining work within the original budget. Report to two decimal places.
questions.explanation:
\[TCPI=\frac{BAC-EV}{BAC-AC}=\frac{5{,}000{,}000-2{,}000{,}000}{5{,}000{,}000-2{,}300{,}000}=\frac{3{,}000{,}000}{2{,}700{,}000}=1.111\] The remaining $3.0 million of budgeted work must be performed for the $2.7 million of budget that is left, an efficiency of 1.11 — well above the \(CPI=2{,}000{,}000/2{,}300{,}000=0.87\) achieved so far, which is a strong signal that the budget will not be recovered.

Accepted range: 1.10–1.12 (report 1.11). Inverting the fraction gives 0.90, and using \(AC\) in the numerator gives 0.90 as well — both are wrong; the numerator is always the work remaining and the denominator the money remaining.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — Earned-Value Analysis (BAC and the variance/index definitions; TCPI is derived from them as stated in Section 14.8).

C – Project controls · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 14-26

questions.question: A masonry crew of two masons at $38.00/hr and one laborer at $26.00/hr places 45 m² of block wall in an 8-hour day. Material and equipment cost $32.00/m². The contractor marks the work up 15% for overhead and profit. The unit price is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Crew rate \(=2(38.00)+1(26.00)=\$102.00\)/hr.

Daily crew cost \(=102.00(8)=\$816.00\) for 45 m², so labor \(=816.00/45=\$18.13/\text{m}^2\).

Direct cost \(=18.13+32.00=\$50.13/\text{m}^2\).

Unit price \(=50.13(1.15)=\$57.65/\text{m}^2\).

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $50.13 is the direct cost with the markup left off.
  • (B) $52.34 omits the laborer from the crew ($76/hr).
  • (D) $58.98 divides by 0.85 instead of multiplying by 1.15 — that treats 15% as a margin on the selling price rather than a markup on cost. On the FE, “marked up 15%” means multiply by 1.15.

D – Construction estimating · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 14-30

questions.question: [Numerical entry] Figure 14.14 is an excerpt from a grading plan with existing contours at a 1-m interval. Point P lies on the line of steepest slope between the EG 104 and EG 105 contours, 12.0 m from the 104 contour along the 30.0-m contour spacing; the ground rises uniformly between the two contours. The proposed spot elevation at P is 102.50. Determine the depth of cut at P in meters.
questions.explanation:
Interpolate linearly between the contours. The ground rises 1.00 m over the 30.0 m between the EG 104 and EG 105 contours, so the slope is \(1.00/30.0=0.0333\) m/m and the existing elevation at P, 12.0 m from the 104 contour, is \[EG_P=104.00+\frac{12.0}{30.0}(1.00)=104.00+0.40=104.40\] Depth of cut \(=EG-FG=104.40-102.50=1.90\) m.

Accepted range: 1.85–1.95 m (report 1.90 m). Interpolating from the wrong contour gives \(105.00-(12/30)(1.00)=104.60\) and a cut of 2.10 m; forgetting to interpolate at all gives 1.50 m. Because the proposed grade is below existing ground, the work is cut, not fill.

FE Reference Handbook: none — contour interpolation is a drawing convention; the resulting depths feed the Civil Engineering — Earthwork Formulas.

E – Interpretation of engineering drawings · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-34

questions.question: Two property lines have slopes \(m_1=0.5\) and \(m_2=3\). The acute angle between them is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[\alpha=\arctan\left[\frac{m_2-m_1}{1+m_2m_1}\right]=\arctan\left[\frac{3-0.5}{1+(3)(0.5)}\right]=\arctan\left[\frac{2.5}{2.5}\right]=\arctan(1)=45.0^\circ\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Straight Line.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 71.6° is \(\arctan(3)\), the inclination of line 2 alone.
  • (C) 78.7° uses \(1-m_2m_1\) in the denominator: \(\arctan[2.5/(1-1.5)]=\arctan(-5)\), reported as 78.7°.
  • (D) 90° would require \(1+m_1m_2=0\), i.e., \(m_2=-2\).

A – Analytic geometry · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-2

questions.question: An elliptical arch has the equation \(9x^2+25y^2-18x-100y-116=0\). The eccentricity of the ellipse is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Complete the square: \(9(x^2-2x)+25(y^2-4y)=116\Rightarrow9(x-1)^2-9+25(y-2)^2-100=116\Rightarrow9(x-1)^2+25(y-2)^2=225\). Divide by 225: \[\frac{(x-1)^2}{25}+\frac{(y-2)^2}{9}=1\quad\Rightarrow\quad a=5,\ b=3\] \[e=\sqrt{1-b^2/a^2}=\sqrt{1-9/25}=\sqrt{0.64}=0.80\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Conic Sections, Case 2 (Ellipse).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.60 is \(b/a\).
  • (C) 1.25 is \(1/e=a/c\). An eccentricity of 1 or more cannot describe an ellipse, which eliminates (C) and (D) immediately.
  • (D) 1.67 is \(a/b\).

A – Analytic geometry · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 1-6

questions.question: The function \(f(x)=-2x^3+9x^2-12x+5\) has a local maximum at \(x\) equal to:
questions.explanation:
\(f'(x)=-6x^2+18x-12=-6(x^2-3x+2)=-6(x-1)(x-2)\), zero at \(x=1\) and \(x=2\). \(f''(x)=-12x+18\): \(f''(1)=+6>0\) (minimum); \(f''(2)=-6<0\) (maximum). The local maximum is at \(x=2\), where \(f(2)=-16+36-24+5=1\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Differential Calculus (Test for a Maximum).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) \(x=1\) is the local minimum.
  • (B) \(x=1.5\) is the inflection point (\(f''=0\)).
  • (D) \(x=3\) is not a critical point.

B – Single-variable calculus · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-10

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1 xe^{2x}\,dx\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Handbook entry 23: \(\int xe^{ax}\,dx=(e^{ax}/a^2)(ax-1)\) with \(a=2\): \[\int_0^1 xe^{2x}\,dx=\left[\frac{e^{2x}}{4}(2x-1)\right]_0^1=\frac{e^2}{4}(1)-\frac{1}{4}(-1)=1.847+0.250=2.097\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Indefinite Integrals (entry 23).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.250 writes the bracket as \((x-1)\) instead of \((ax-1)\), so the upper limit contributes zero and only the lower-limit term survives.
  • (B) 1.597 is a sign error on the lower-limit term \((1.847-0.25)\).
  • (C) 1.847 omits the lower limit entirely.

B – Single-variable calculus · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 1-14

questions.question: For \(\mathbf{A}=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+3\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{B}=4\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k}\), the dot product \(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}\) is:
questions.explanation:
\(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=(2)(4)+(-1)(2)+(3)(-1)=8-2-3=3\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Vectors (dot product).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) \(-3\) is an overall sign error.
  • (C) 9 results from \(8-2+3\) (sign error on the last term).
  • (D) 13 ignores all signs \((8+2+3)\).

C – Vector operations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 1-18

questions.question: The scalar projection of \(\mathbf{B}=4\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}\) onto the direction of \(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Scalar projection of \(\mathbf{B}\) on \(\mathbf{A}\) is \(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{A}|\). \(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=4+8+4=16\); \(|\mathbf{A}|=\sqrt{1+4+4}=3\). Projection \(=16/3=5.33\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Vectors (dot product “represents the projection of B onto A times |A|”).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.889 is \(\cos\theta=\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}/(|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|)=16/18\), a direction cosine between the vectors, not a projection.
  • (B) 1.78 divides by \(|\mathbf{A}|^2=9\) (that is the scale factor for the vector projection, not the scalar projection).
  • (C) 2.67 divides by \(|\mathbf{B}|=6\), giving the projection of \(\mathbf{A}\) on \(\mathbf{B}\) instead.

C – Vector operations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-22

questions.question: Cylinder strengths for a concrete mix are normally distributed with mean 30.0 MPa and standard deviation 2.5 MPa. The probability that a cylinder tests below 25.0 MPa is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(z=(25.0-30.0)/2.5=-2.0\). \(P(X<25)=F(-2.0)=1-F(2.0)=R(2.0)=0.0228\) from the Unit Normal Distribution table.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Normal Distribution; Unit Normal Distribution table.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 0.0455 is \(2R(2.0)\), the two-tailed area.
  • (C) 0.5 ignores the standard deviation.
  • (D) 0.9772 is \(F(2.0)\), the probability of testing above 25 MPa.

D – Statistics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-26

questions.question: Five observations of \(x\) and \(y\) are: (1, 2.1), (2, 3.9), (3, 6.2), (4, 7.8), (5, 10.1). The slope of the least-squares line \(\hat{y}=\hat{a}+\hat{b}x\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(n=5\); \(\sum x=15\), \(\sum y=30.1\), \(\sum xy=2.1+7.8+18.6+31.2+50.5=110.2\), \(\sum x^2=55\). \[S_{xy}=110.2-\frac{(15)(30.1)}{5}=110.2-90.3=19.9;\qquad S_{xx}=55-\frac{15^2}{5}=55-45=10\] \[\hat{b}=\frac{S_{xy}}{S_{xx}}=\frac{19.9}{10}=1.99;\qquad\hat{a}=\bar{y}-\hat{b}\bar{x}=6.02-1.99(3)=0.05\]

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Linear Regression and Goodness of Fit (Least Squares).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.05 is the intercept \(\hat{a}\).
  • (B) 0.43 computes \(S_{xx}\) as \(\sum x^2-\bar{x}^2=55-9=46\) (forgetting the factor \(n\)), so \(\hat{b}=19.9/46\).
  • (C) 0.50 is \(S_{xx}/S_{xy}\), the inverted ratio.

D – Statistics · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 1-30

questions.question: A column carries an independent dead load with mean 40 kN and standard deviation 4.5 kN and a live load with mean 25 kN and standard deviation 6.0 kN, both normally distributed. The probability that the total load exceeds 80 kN is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Total \(T=D+L\): \(\mu_T=40+25=65\) kN. For independent variables, variances add: \(\sigma_T^2=4.5^2+6.0^2=20.25+36=56.25\), so \(\sigma_T=7.5\) kN. Then \(z=(80-65)/7.5=2.0\) and \(P(T>80)=R(2.0)=0.0228\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Combinations of Random Variables; Unit Normal Distribution table.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.0013 corresponds to \(z=3\), which would need \(\sigma_T=5\) kN.
  • (C) 0.0764 results from adding standard deviations (\(\sigma_T=10.5\), \(z=1.43\)).
  • (D) 0.9772 is \(F(2.0)\), the probability the total is less than 80 kN.

D – Statistics · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 1-34

questions.question: A resident engineer representing a county on a highway project receives, from the paving contractor, an unsolicited gift of a weekend at a resort “in appreciation of a smooth partnership.” The paving is 60% complete and quantities are still being measured for payment. Under the NCEES Rules of Professional Conduct, the engineer should:
choices: Accept the gift, since it was not requested and the contractor’s work has been satisfactory.
Accept the gift and disclose it to the county in the next monthly report.
Accept the gift only if its value is less than the county’s threshold for reportable gifts.
Decline the gift, because licensees may not accept gratuities from contractors in connection with work for a client.
questions.explanation:
Part B, item 5 states that licensees shall not solicit or accept gratuities, directly or indirectly, from contractors, their agents, or other parties in connection with work for employers or clients. The rule has no exception for unsolicited gifts, satisfactory performance, disclosure, or value thresholds—and here the engineer is still measuring quantities that determine the contractor’s payment, so the appearance of influence is acute.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — 2025–26 Model Rules, Section 240.15, Part B, item 5.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) The Rules prohibit accepting, not merely soliciting.
  • (B) Disclosure is the remedy for conflicts of interest (Part B, item 6), not for gratuities, which are flatly prohibited.
  • (C) The Rules contain no monetary threshold; an employer’s gift policy cannot authorize what the Rules forbid.

A – Codes of ethics · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 2-2

questions.question: An owner sues an engineer for negligence, alleging that a drainage design was inadequate. Which of the following is NOT an element the owner must prove to prevail?
choices: The engineer owed the owner a duty of care.
The engineer intended to produce a deficient design.
The engineer’s breach caused the owner’s loss.
questions.explanation:
Negligence requires proof of duty, breach of the standard of care, causation, and damages. Intent is not an element; negligence is precisely the theory that applies when harm results from carelessness rather than deliberate conduct. Intentional wrongdoing would be a different tort (fraud, for example) and is generally excluded from professional liability insurance.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice (negligence elements are general legal doctrine; the Handbook does not tabulate them).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Duty is one of the four required elements.
  • (C) Causation is one of the four required elements.
  • (D) Damages is one of the four required elements; the fourth, not listed among the options, is breach.

B – Professional liability · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 2-6

questions.question: Under the NCEES Model Law, which of the following correctly orders the steps by which an engineering graduate typically becomes a licensed professional engineer?
choices: Pass the PE exam; gain progressive experience; pass the FE exam; obtain licensure.
Gain progressive experience; graduate from an accredited program; pass the FE exam; obtain licensure.
Graduate from an accredited program; pass the PE exam; be certified as an engineer intern; obtain licensure.
Graduate from an accredited program; pass the FE exam; gain progressive experience; pass the PE exam; obtain licensure.
questions.explanation:
The Model Law pathway is education (an EAC/ABET or ETAC/ABET degree or equivalent), then the FE exam (which with the education qualifies the candidate for engineer intern certification), then progressive engineering experience, then the PE exam and any jurisdiction-specific exam, then licensure by the board upon also showing good character and five references.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — Model Law, Section 130.10 General Requirements for Licensure, parts A and B.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Reverses the FE and PE exams.
  • (B) Experience must be after the qualifying degree is conferred to count, and the PE exam is omitted.
  • (C) Engineer intern certification requires the FE exam, not the PE exam, and comes before the experience period, not after the PE exam.

C – Licensure · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 2-10

questions.question: A jurisdiction requires 30 professional development hours (PDH) per two-year renewal period. Its rules state that 1 continuing education unit (CEU) equals 10 PDH, that 1 college semester credit hour equals 45 PDH, and that a maximum of 15 PDH may be carried forward from the previous renewal period. During the current period an engineer completed 8 hours of qualifying technical seminars and a 0.9-CEU online course, and had 4 PDH of eligible carryover from the previous period. The engineer took no college courses. The number of additional PDH the engineer must earn before renewal is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Convert all activities to PDH using the conversion factors stated in the question:

  • Seminars: 8 hours = 8 PDH
  • Online course: 0.9 CEU × 10 PDH/CEU = 9 PDH
  • Carryover: 4 PDH (below the 15-PDH cap, so all of it counts)
  • College courses: 0

Total credited = 8 + 9 + 4 = 21 PDH. Shortfall = 30 − 21 = 9 PDH.

Accepted answer: 9 (exact integer). A common wrong answer is 13, obtained by omitting the carryover, or 17.1, obtained by treating 0.9 CEU as 0.9 PDH.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — Model Law, Section 150.10 A.4 (failure to comply with board rules is a ground for discipline; the CPC hour requirement and conversion factors are jurisdiction rules supplied in the question).

C – Licensure · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 2-14

questions.question: An engineer administering a construction contract is authorized by the owner-engineer agreement to interpret the contract documents and to review and certify the contractor’s monthly payment applications. Without consulting the owner, the engineer verbally directs the contractor to install an additional 200 m of storm sewer not shown on the drawings, and the contractor submits a $95,000 change-order request. Which statement best describes the situation?
choices: The owner is bound to pay the $95,000, because the engineer is the owner’s agent for all purposes on the project.

The engineer acted outside the actual authority granted by the agreement; the owner is not automatically bound, and the engineer may be personally liable to the contractor or the owner for the unauthorized direction.
The contractor cannot recover from anyone, because a verbal directive can never modify a written construction contract.
The engineer’s professional liability insurance will pay the $95,000 as a covered error.
questions.explanation:
An agent binds the principal only within the scope of the authority the principal has granted (actual authority) or has led third parties reasonably to believe exists (apparent authority). The agreement gave the engineer authority to interpret documents and certify payments—not to order additional work or commit the owner’s money. Ordering $95,000 of extra sewer exceeds that authority. The owner may ratify the change, but is not automatically bound; and an agent who exceeds authority may be personally liable to the third party who relied on the direction (the contractor) or to the principal for the resulting loss. It also breaches the NSPE Fundamental Canon to act for each client as a faithful agent or trustee, since the engineer committed the client without consent.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice (agency principles are general legal doctrine; see 2025–26 Model Rules, Section 240.15, Part B, for the licensee’s duties to clients).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) An agent’s authority is limited to what was granted; “agent for all purposes” is not what the agreement says.
  • (C) Oral directives can modify contracts unless the contract or the statute of frauds requires a writing, and even then the contractor may have quantum meruit or ratification arguments; the categorical “never” is wrong.
  • (D) E&O insurance covers negligent professional errors, not the cost of work the engineer had no authority to order.

D – Contracts and contract law · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 2-18

questions.question: Maintenance costs on a piece of equipment are $10,000 at the end of the first year and increase by $1,000 each year for 8 years. At \(i = 8\%\), the equivalent uniform annual cost of the maintenance is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The series is a base \(A_1 = \$10{,}000\) plus a gradient \(G = \$1{,}000\) with \(n = 8\). \[(A/G, 8\%, 8) = \frac{1}{0.08} - \frac{8}{(1.08)^8 - 1} = 12.5 - \frac{8}{0.8509} = 12.5 - 9.4015 = 3.0985 \text{ (table: 3.0985)}\] \(A = 10{,}000 + 1{,}000(3.0985) = \$13{,}099 \approx \$13{,}100\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Factor Table (Uniform Gradient Uniform Series); Interest Rate Tables, i = 8.00%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $11,000 adds one year’s gradient only.
  • (C) $13,500 is the arithmetic average of the eight costs, which ignores the time value of money (the equivalent annual amount is always less than the simple average for an increasing series).
  • (D) $17,000 is the year-8 cost.

A – Time value of money · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 3-4

questions.question: A foundation will pay a scholarship of $5,000 at the end of each year for 4 years, with the first payment at the end of year 6. At \(i = 6\%\) per year, the present worth (at year 0) of the four payments is ______ dollars. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
The four payments occur at years 6, 7, 8, and 9. The (P/A) factor places their worth one period before the first payment, at year 5; then (P/F, 6%, 5) brings that amount to year 0: \[P_5 = 5{,}000\,(P/A, 6\%, 4) = 5{,}000(3.4651) = \$17{,}326\] \[P_0 = 17{,}326\,(P/F, 6\%, 5) = 17{,}326(0.7473) = \$12{,}948\] Accepted range: $12,900 to $13,000. (The table factors 3.4651 and 0.7473 give $12,948; the unrounded closed-form factors give $12,947.)

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Factor Table (Uniform Series Present Worth; Single Payment Present Worth); Interest Rate Tables, i = 6.00%.

A – Time value of money · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 3-8

questions.question: A pipe-fabrication shop has fixed costs of $120,000 per year and a variable cost of $35 per unit. At an output of 4,000 units per year, the average cost per unit is:
questions.explanation:
Average cost \(= \text{TC}/Q = \text{FC}/Q + v = 120{,}000/4{,}000 + 35 = 30 + 35 = \$65\) per unit.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — cost concepts (fundamental definitions; not tabulated in the Handbook).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $30 is the fixed cost per unit alone.
  • (B) $35 is the variable (incremental) cost per unit, not the average.
  • (D) $155 adds the fixed cost per unit in the wrong units (120 + 35, treating $120,000 as $120 per unit).

B – Cost · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 3-12

questions.question: A rooftop photovoltaic array costs $180,000 installed. It is expected to generate 220,000 kWh per year, displacing electricity purchased at $0.11 per kWh, and to require $1,700 per year in maintenance. The simple payback period is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Annual energy savings \(= 220{,}000 \text{ kWh} \times \$0.11/\text{kWh} = \$24{,}200\). Net annual benefit \(= 24{,}200 - 1{,}700 = \$22{,}500\). Simple payback \(= 180{,}000/22{,}500 = 8.0\) years.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Breakeven Analysis (payback period).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 7.4 years omits the maintenance cost (\(180{,}000/24{,}200\)).
  • (C) 11 years is the last year in which the discounted savings still fall short of the cost at 6% (Question 3-17); it is neither the simple nor the discounted payback.
  • (D) 12 years is the discounted payback at 6% (Question 3-17), not the simple payback.

C – Analyses · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 3-16

questions.question: A $140,000 piece of construction equipment is 7-year MACRS property. The MACRS depreciation charge in year 2 is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
From the MACRS Factors table, 7-year recovery period, year 2: 24.49%. \(D_2 = 0.2449 \times 140{,}000 = \$34{,}286 \approx \$34{,}300\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Depreciation (Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System); MACRS Factors table.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $20,000 is straight-line over 7 years with no salvage (and, coincidentally, nearly the year-1 MACRS charge of \(14.29\% \times \$140{,}000 = \$20{,}006\)).
  • (B) $24,500 is the year-3 factor (17.49%) applied to the cost.
  • (D) $44,800 uses the 5-year column’s year-2 factor (32.00%).

C – Analyses · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 3-20

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A utility must decide whether to replace an aging valve now, at a certain cost of $60,000, or wait one year. If it waits, there is a 0.6 probability the valve survives the year and is replaced next year at a deferred cost equivalent to $20,000 today, and a 0.4 probability it fails during the year, in which case emergency replacement and damage cost $150,000. Which of the following statements are correct?
choices: The expected cost of waiting is $72,000.
On an expected-value basis, replacing now is the lower-cost choice.
If the probability of failure were 0.3 instead of 0.4, waiting would have the lower expected cost.
The expected-value criterion accounts for the utility’s aversion to the $150,000 outcome.
The failure probability at which the two choices have equal expected cost is 0.4.
questions.explanation:
Expected cost of waiting \(= 0.6(20{,}000) + 0.4(150{,}000) = 12{,}000 + 60{,}000 = \$72{,}000\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Economic Decision Trees (Expected Value); Breakeven Analysis.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(0.6(20{,}000) + 0.4(150{,}000) = \$72{,}000\).
  • (B) True — $60,000 certain is less than the $72,000 expected cost of waiting.
  • (C) True — with \(p = 0.3\): \(0.7(20{,}000) + 0.3(150{,}000) = 14{,}000 + 45{,}000 = \$59{,}000 < \$60{,}000\), so waiting would have the lower expected cost.
  • (D) False — expected value weights outcomes only by probability and is indifferent to the spread of outcomes; risk aversion is not captured.
  • (E) False — the breakeven probability solves \(20{,}000(1 - p) + 150{,}000p = 60{,}000\), giving \(130{,}000p = 40{,}000\) and \(p = 0.308\), not 0.4.

D – Uncertainty · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 3-24

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about force systems are true?
choices: The resultant of a concurrent coplanar force system is a single force whose line of action passes through the point of concurrency.
Two forces of equal magnitude and opposite direction acting along different parallel lines have zero resultant force but a nonzero resultant moment.
The magnitude of the resultant of a force system can never be less than the magnitude of the largest force in the system.
A two-force member in equilibrium carries two forces that are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and collinear.
The direction cosines of any force satisfy \(\cos^2\theta_x + \cos^2\theta_y + \cos^2\theta_z = 1\).
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), (D), and (E) are true; (C) is false.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Resultant (Two Dimensions); Moments (Couples); Concurrent Forces; Resolution of a Force.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — concurrent forces add to a single force through the common point, with no residual couple.
  • (B) True — this is the definition of a couple: zero force resultant, moment \(Fd\).
  • (C) False — two equal and opposite collinear forces have a resultant of zero, smaller than either force; in general the resultant can be anything from the difference to the sum of the magnitudes.
  • (D) True — this is the Handbook statement under Concurrent Forces.
  • (E) True — the direction cosines are the components of a unit vector, so their squares sum to one.

A – Resultants of force systems · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-4

questions.question: Four columns rest on a rectangular footing. Taking the corner column as the origin, the column loads are 200 kN at (0, 0), 300 kN at (4, 0), 250 kN at (0, 3), and 350 kN at (4, 3), with coordinates in meters. The \(x\)-coordinate of the point where the resultant of the four loads acts is ______ m. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
The resultant of parallel forces is \(R = 200 + 300 + 250 + 350 = 1100\) kN. Its location is where its moment about each axis equals the total moment (the same formula as a centroid, weighting by force): \[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum F_n x_n}{R} = \frac{200(0) + 300(4) + 250(0) + 350(4)}{1100} = \frac{2600}{1100} = 2.364\,\text{m}\] \[\bar{y} = \frac{250(3) + 350(3)}{1100} = \frac{1800}{1100} = 1.636\,\text{m}\] Accepted range: 2.35–2.38 m (the footing’s geometric center is at (2.0, 1.5), so the resultant is shifted toward the heavier columns, as expected).

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Systems of Forces; Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes.

B – Equivalent force systems · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 4-8

questions.question: The overhanging beam in Figure 4.16(c) is pinned at A and supported by a roller at B, 8 m from A, with a 3-m overhang to C. It carries 12 kN/m over AB, a 30-kN load at C, and a 40-kN·m counterclockwise couple at midspan of AB. The reaction at B is ______ kN. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Uniform-load resultant: \(12(8) = 96\) kN at 4 m from A. Moments about A (counterclockwise positive), with the couple entering directly: \[B_y(8) - 96(4) - 30(11) + 40 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad B_y = \frac{384 + 330 - 40}{8} = 84.25\,\text{kN}\] Check: \(A_y = 96 + 30 - 84.25 = 41.75\) kN; moments about B: \(-41.75(8) + 96(4) - 30(3) + 40 = -334 + 384 - 90 + 40 = 0\). ✓

Accepted range: 84.0–84.5 kN. (Reversing the sign of the couple gives 94.25 kN; omitting it gives 89.25 kN.)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements; Moments (Couples).

C – Equilibrium of rigid bodies · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 4-12

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each support (1–4) with the reactions it supplies in a planar structure (a–d).

  • (a) Two force components and one moment
  • (b) Two force components
  • (c) One force normal to the supporting surface
  • (d) One tensile force along the member axis
questions.explanation:
A pin resists translation in both in-plane directions (two force components, no moment). A roller resists only translation normal to its surface. A fixed support resists both translations and rotation (two forces plus a moment). A cable is a two-force member that can only pull, so it supplies one tensile force along its axis.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements; Concurrent Forces (two-force members).

C – Equilibrium of rigid bodies · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 4-16

questions.question: For the truss in Figure 4.17, the force in diagonal member FC is ______ kN (enter a positive value for tension, negative for compression). [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Using the same section as Question 4-19, sum vertical forces on the left portion. The chords FG and BC are horizontal and contribute nothing; FC runs from F (3, 4) to C (6, 0), unit vector (0.6, −0.8), and a tensile force pulls the left portion toward C: \[\Sigma F_V = 35 - 20 - 0.8F_{FC} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{FC} = 18.75\,\text{kN (tension)}\] Accepted: 18.7 to 18.8 (positive). A full joint solution confirms \(F_{HC} = 18.75\) kN (T) by symmetry, \(F_{CG} = 30\) kN (C), and the bottom chord uniformly 26.25 kN (T).

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Plane Truss: Method of Sections.

D – Frames and trusses · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 4-20

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about plane trusses are true?
choices: In an ideal truss, loads are applied only at the joints and every member is a two-force member.
If three members meet at an unloaded joint and two of them are collinear, the third member carries no force.
A zero-force member can be removed from a truss without affecting its stability under any loading.
The method of sections can determine the force in an interior member without first solving the joints between it and a support.
A plane truss satisfying \(m + r = 2j\) is necessarily stable.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), and (D) are true; (C) and (E) are false.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Statically Determinate Truss; Plane Truss: Method of Sections.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — these are the idealizing assumptions of truss analysis.
  • (B) True — this is the Handbook’s second zero-force rule.
  • (C) False — a zero-force member carries no force under the given loading; it may be essential for stability or under other load cases (and it commonly braces compression members).
  • (D) True — that is the purpose of the method of sections.
  • (E) False — \(m + r = 2j\) is necessary for determinacy but not sufficient for stability; members must also be arranged properly (for example, a rectangular panel without a diagonal collapses even if the count works out).

D – Frames and trusses · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-24

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each shape (1–4) with the distance from its base to its centroid (a–d). All shapes have their base on the \(x\)-axis; \(h\) is the height, \(a\) the radius of the semicircle, and for the trapezoid \(a\) is the top width and \(b\) the bottom width.

  • (a) \(h/3\)
  • (b) \(h/2\)
  • (c) \(4a/(3\pi)\)
  • (d) \(h(2a + b)/[3(a + b)]\)
pairs: Semicircle of radius \(a\) (flat side on the base)
questions.explanation:
Rectangle: \(h/2\) by symmetry. Triangle: \(h/3\) from the base (any triangle). Semicircle: \(4a/(3\pi) \approx 0.424a\) from the diameter. Trapezoid: \(h(2a+b)/[3(a+b)]\) from the base of width \(b\); check that it reduces to \(h/3\) when \(a = 0\) (triangle) and to \(h/2\) when \(a = b\) (rectangle).

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — table of area properties.

E – Centroid of area · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 4-28

questions.question: A 40 mm × 80 mm rectangle has one corner at the origin, with the 40-mm side along the \(x\)-axis and the 80-mm side along the \(y\)-axis. Its product of inertia \(I_{xy}\) with respect to the \(x\)- and \(y\)-axes is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a rectangle with a corner at the origin and sides along the axes, the table gives \(I_{xy} = Abh/4 = b^2h^2/4\): \[I_{xy} = \frac{(40)^2(80)^2}{4} = 2.56 \times 10^6\,\text{mm}^4\] Equivalently, by the parallel-axis theorem from the centroid: \(I_{x_c y_c} = 0\) (symmetry) and \(d_x d_y A = (20)(40)(3200) = 2.56 \times 10^6\) mm\(^{4}\).

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Product of Inertia; table of area properties (rectangle).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the centroidal product of inertia, zero by symmetry;
  • (B) is half the correct value;
  • (D) is \(b^2h^2/2\).

F – Area moments of inertia · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 4-32

questions.question: A rope is wrapped around a fixed horizontal bollard, \(\mu_s = 0.30\). A worker can pull with at most 100 N and must hold a 2000-N load on the other end. The minimum wrap of rope around the bollard, expressed in turns, is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
With the load side about to slip, \(F_1 = 2000\) N and \(F_2 = 100\) N. From \(F_1 = F_2 e^{\mu\theta}\): \[\theta = \frac{1}{\mu}\ln\frac{F_1}{F_2} = \frac{\ln 20}{0.30} = \frac{2.996}{0.30} = 9.99\,\text{rad}\] \[\text{turns} = \frac{9.99}{2\pi} = 1.59 \approx 1.6\ \text{turns}\] (In practice the worker would take two full turns.)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Belt Friction.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) understates the wrap and would require the worker to hold about 780 N;
  • (B) uses the common logarithm instead of the natural logarithm: \(\log_{10}20/0.30 = 4.34\) rad \(= 0.69\) turn;
  • (C) understates the wrap and would require the worker to hold about 300 N.

G – Static friction · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-36

questions.question: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a vertical cliff 30 m high. Neglecting air resistance and using \(g = 9.81\) m/s², the horizontal distance from the base of the cliff to the point where the stone strikes the level ground below is ______ m. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Horizontal launch means \(\theta = 0\): \(v_{0x} = 15\) m/s, \(v_{0y} = 0\). With \(y_0 = 30\) m and \(y = 0\) at the ground, \(0 = -\tfrac12(9.81)t^2 + 0 + 30\), so \(t = \sqrt{2(30)/9.81} = 2.473\) s. Then \(x = v_0\cos(0)\,t = 15(2.473) = 37.1\) m.

Numerical entry: accepted range 36.8–37.4 m. A common wrong entry is 26.2 m (using \(t = \sqrt{30/9.81}\), i.e., dropping the factor of 2 in \(\tfrac12 gt^2\)).

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Projectile Motion.

A – Kinematics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-3

questions.question: A wheel of diameter 0.6 m rolls without slipping to the right with its center moving at 4 m/s. The speed of the point on the rim located at the forward end of the horizontal diameter (level with the center) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(r = 0.3\) m, so \(\omega = v_O/r = 4/0.3 = 13.33\) rad/s. The forward point on the horizontal diameter is at distance \(\sqrt{r^2 + r^2} = \sqrt{2}\,r = 0.4243\) m from the contact point (instant center), so its speed is \(\omega\sqrt{2}\,r = 13.33(0.4243) = 5.66\) m/s. Alternatively, \(\mathbf{v}_A = \mathbf{v}_O + \boldsymbol{\omega}\times\mathbf{r}_{A/O} = 4\mathbf{i} + (-13.33\mathbf{k})\times(0.3\mathbf{i}) = 4\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}\) m/s, magnitude \(4\sqrt{2} = 5.66\) m/s.

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Instantaneous Center of Rotation; Translating Axes \(x\)-\(y\).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 4.0 is the speed of the center; the rim point has an additional relative velocity \(r\omega = 4\) m/s perpendicular to the radius.
  • (C) 8.0 is the speed of the top point.
  • (D) 11.3 uses the 0.6-m diameter in place of the radius when finding the distance from the instant center (\(\sqrt{2}(0.6) = 0.849\) m) while keeping \(\omega = 13.33\) rad/s, doubling the answer.

A – Kinematics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-7

questions.question: An 800-kg elevator car accelerates upward at 1.5 m/s². Using \(g = 9.81\) m/s², the tension in the hoisting cable is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Free-body diagram of the car: tension \(T\) up, weight \(mg\) down, acceleration \(a\) up. \(\Sigma F_y = ma\): \(T - mg = ma\), so \(T = m(g + a) = 800(9.81 + 1.5) = 9048\) N ≈ 9.0 kN.

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Particle Kinetics; Concept of Weight.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.2 kN is \(ma\) alone, omitting the weight.
  • (B) 6.6 kN is \(m(g - a)\), the tension for a downward acceleration.
  • (C) 7.8 kN is the weight, correct only at constant velocity.

C – Force acceleration · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 5-11

questions.question: A 1500-kg car traveling at 72 km/h on a level road is brought to rest by a constant braking (friction) force of 6.0 kN. The distance traveled during braking is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(v_1 = 72/3.6 = 20\) m/s. Work-energy from moving to rest on a level road (\(V_1 = V_2\)): \(T_2 = T_1 + U_{1\to2}\), with \(T_2 = 0\) and \(U_{1\to2} = -Fd\): \[0 = \tfrac12(1500)(20)^2 - 6000\,d \quad\Rightarrow\quad d = \frac{300\,000}{6000} = 50\ \text{m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Principle of Work and Energy; Kinetic Energy; Work (constant force).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 25 m is \(mv^2/(4F)\), an extra factor of \(\tfrac12\).
  • (C) 100 m omits the \(\tfrac12\) in the kinetic energy.
  • (D) 491 m uses the weight \(mg = 14\,715\) N in place of the mass in the kinetic energy: \(\tfrac12(14\,715)(20)^2/6000\).

D – Work, energy, and power · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-15

questions.question: A simply supported beam spans 8 m and carries a uniformly distributed load of 5 kN/m over its entire length. The maximum bending moment is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a simply supported beam under a full-length uniform load, \(M_{max} = wL^2/8 = 5(8)^2/8 = 40\) kN·m at midspan.

FE Reference Handbook: Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections (maximum moment column).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 80 kN·m is \(wL^2/4\).
  • (C) 160 kN·m is \(wL^2/2\), the wall moment of a cantilever.
  • (D) 320 kN·m is \(wL^2\), omitting the factor 1/8 altogether.

A – Shear and moment diagrams · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 6-1

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A 12-ft simply supported beam carries a distributed load that increases linearly from zero at the left support to 3 kip/ft at the right support. Using the Handbook beam table, the maximum bending moment in the beam is ______ kip·ft.
questions.explanation:
The Handbook beam table lists, for a simply supported beam with a triangular load of peak intensity \(w_0\), \(M_{max} = w_0L^2/(9\sqrt{3})\) at \(x = L/\sqrt{3}\) from the light end. \(M_{max} = 3(12)^2/(9\sqrt{3}) = 432/15.59 = 27.7\) kip·ft, at \(12/\sqrt{3} = 6.93\) ft from the left support. Without the table: \(R_A = W/3 = 6\) kip, \(V(x) = 6 - x^2/8 = 0\) at \(x = 6.93\) ft, \(M = 6(6.93) - (6.93)^3/24 = 41.57 - 13.86 = 27.7\) kip·ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections (triangular load, \(M_{max} = w_0L^2/(9\sqrt{3})\)).

A – Shear and moment diagrams · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 6-5

questions.question: A 50-mm-diameter, 1-m-long rod elongates 0.8 mm under an axial tensile load. Poisson’s ratio for the material is 0.30. The change in diameter of the rod is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Axial strain \(\varepsilon = 0.8/1000 = 8\times10^{-4}\). Lateral strain \(= -\nu\varepsilon = -0.30(8\times10^{-4}) = -2.4\times10^{-4}\). \(\Delta d = -2.4\times10^{-4}(50) = -0.012\) mm (decrease).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Shear Stress-Strain (\(\nu = -\) lateral strain / longitudinal strain).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 0.024 mm applies the lateral strain to \(2d\).
  • (C) 0.040 mm increase is the axial strain applied to the diameter with the wrong sign.
  • (D) 0.240 mm applies the lateral strain to the 1000-mm length instead of the 50-mm diameter.

B – Stresses and strains · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 6-9

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A 25-m length of steel rail (\(\alpha = 11.7\times10^{-6}/^\circ\text{C}\)) is free to expand. When its temperature rises 45°C, its change in length is ______ mm.
questions.explanation:
\(\delta_t = \alpha L\Delta T = 11.7\times10^{-6}(25{,}000\,\text{mm})(45) = 13.16\) mm. Since the rail is free to expand, no stress develops.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Thermal Deformations.

B – Stresses and strains · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-13

questions.question: A solid circular shaft 40 mm in diameter and 1.2 m long (\(G = 80\) GPa) carries a torque of 400 N·m. The angle of twist between its ends is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
