\(J = \pi(40)^4/32 = 251{,}327\) mm4. \(\phi = TL/GJ = 400{,}000\,\text{N·mm}(1200)/[80{,}000(251{,}327)] = 0.0239\) rad \(= 1.37^\circ\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Torsion (\(\phi = TL/GJ\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.024° is the answer in radians mislabeled as degrees.
  • (C) 2.74° is double (e.g., using \(J = \pi d^4/64\)).
  • (D) 21.9° puts the radius (20 mm) into the diameter formula \(J = \pi d^4/32\), making \(J\) 16 times too small.

C – Deformations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 6-17

questions.question: A prismatic bar is rigidly fixed at both ends A and B, 900 mm apart. An axial force of 60 kN is applied at a point 300 mm from end A, directed toward B. The reaction at end A is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Equilibrium: \(R_A + R_B = 60\) kN. Compatibility: segment AC (300 mm) is in tension under \(R_A\) while segment CB (600 mm) is in compression under \(R_B\), and the total length change is zero: \(R_A(300)/AE = R_B(600)/AE\), so \(R_A = 2R_B\). Then \(3R_B = 60\), \(R_B = 20\) kN, \(R_A = 40\) kN. In general \(R_A = Pb/L = 60(600)/900 = 40\) kN — the support nearer the load carries more.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Uniaxial Loading and Deformation (\(\delta = PL/AE\) with compatibility).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 20 kN is \(R_B\), the reaction at the far end.
  • (B) 30 kN assumes the load splits equally, which ignores compatibility.
  • (D) 60 kN assumes A carries everything, which would be true only if B were free.

C – Deformations · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 6-21

questions.question: At a point on the free surface of a member, \(\sigma_x = 100\) MPa, \(\sigma_y = 20\) MPa (both tension), and \(\tau_{xy} = 0\). The absolute maximum shear stress at the point is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
With no shear, the given stresses are principal: \(\sigma_1 = 100\), \(\sigma_2 = 20\), \(\sigma_3 = 0\) (free surface). The in-plane maximum shear is \((100 - 20)/2 = 40\) MPa, but the absolute maximum is \((\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2 = (100 - 0)/2 = 50\) MPa, on planes at 45° between the \(x\) direction and the surface normal.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Mohr’s Circle—Stress, 2D (\(\tau_{max} = (\sigma_1 - \sigma_3)/2\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 40 MPa is the in-plane maximum only.
  • (C) 60 MPa is \((\sigma_1 + \sigma_2)/2\), the center of the circle.
  • (D) 100 MPa is \(\sigma_1\).

D – Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-25

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A bar of rectangular cross-section 50 mm wide and 100 mm deep carries an axial tensile force of 40 kN together with a bending moment of 3 kN·m about the axis parallel to the 50-mm side. The maximum tensile normal stress in the section is ______ MPa.
questions.explanation:
\(A = 50(100) = 5000\) mm2; \(S = bh^2/6 = 50(100)^2/6 = 83{,}333\) mm3. \(\sigma_{axial} = 40{,}000/5000 = 8\) MPa; \(\sigma_{bending} = 3\times10^6/83{,}333 = 36\) MPa. Maximum tension \(= 8 + 36 = 44\) MPa on the tension face; the opposite face has \(8 - 36 = -28\) MPa.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Uniaxial Loading and Deformation; Stresses in Beams.

D – Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 6-29

questions.question: [Point-and-click] Figure 6.17 is Mohr’s circle for a point in plane stress with \(\sigma_x = 90\) MPa, \(\sigma_y = 30\) MPa (both tension) and \(\tau_{xy} = 40\) MPa. Five points on the diagram carry the circled labels (A) through (E). Name the labeled point whose coordinates give the maximum in-plane shear stress together with the normal stress acting on that plane.
questions.explanation:
The circle is centered on the average normal stress and its radius is the maximum in-plane shear stress: \[\sigma_{avg} = \frac{\sigma_x + \sigma_y}{2} = \frac{90 + 30}{2} = 60\,\text{MPa}\] \[R = \sqrt{\left(\frac{\sigma_x - \sigma_y}{2}\right)^2 + \tau_{xy}^2} = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50\,\text{MPa}\] The largest shear ordinate on the circle is \(R = 50\) MPa, and it occurs at the top (and bottom) of the circle, directly above the center — that is, at \((\sigma, \tau) = (60, 50)\) MPa. Point (D) sits there. The plane of maximum in-plane shear therefore carries \(\tau_{max} = 50\) MPa together with a normal stress of 60 MPa; it is \(45^\circ\) from the principal planes on the element, which is \(90^\circ\) on the circle.

The other labels: (A) is the \(x\)-face point (90, 40 ccw), plotted below the axis under the Handbook convention — the state you were given, not the maximum. (B) is the center (60, 0): the right normal stress but zero shear. (C) is the right-hand intercept, \(\sigma_1 = 60 + 50 = 110\) MPa with \(\tau = 0\). (E) is the left-hand intercept, \(\sigma_2 = 60 - 50 = 10\) MPa with \(\tau = 0\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Mohr’s Circle—Stress, 2D; Stress and Strain — Principal Stresses.

D – Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 6-33

questions.question: A tension specimen with a 2.00-in gauge length measures 2.56 in between gauge marks after fracture. The percent elongation is ______ %. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Elongation \(=(L_f-L_0)/L_0\times100=(2.56-2.00)/2.00\times100=28\%\).

Accepted: 28 (27.9–28.1). Dividing by the final length (21.9%) is the common error.

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Properties of Materials — Mechanical (Ductility).

B – Test methods · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 7-4

questions.question: A plain carbon steel has a Brinell hardness number of 200. Using the Handbook’s approximate relationship, its tensile strength is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
TS (psi) ≈ 500 × BHN = 500 × 200 = 100,000 psi = 100 ksi (equivalently 3.5 × 200 = 700 MPa).

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Relationship Between Hardness and Tensile Strength.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses 100 × BHN.
  • (B) uses 250 × BHN.
  • (D) uses 1,000 × BHN.

B – Test methods · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 7-8

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about corrosion of metals are correct?
choices: Oxidation, and therefore metal loss, occurs at the anode.
Cold-worked regions of carbon steel are cathodic to regions that have not been cold worked.
Corrosion requires an electrolyte in contact with both the anode and the cathode.
When two dissimilar metals are in contact, the more electropositive metal becomes the cathode.
Grain boundary regions are anodic to the bulk grain.
questions.explanation:
Corrosion needs an anode, a cathode, and an electrolyte; metal is lost by oxidation at the anode, and the Handbook’s list of anodic regions includes cold-worked regions, grain boundaries, and the more electropositive of two dissimilar metals.

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Corrosion.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the anode reaction is oxidation, \(\text{M}\rightarrow\text{M}^{n+}+ne^-\), and the anode loses metal.
  • (B) False — the Handbook states cold-worked regions are anodic to non-cold-worked regions.
  • (C) True — an anode and a cathode in electrical contact in the presence of an electrolyte are all required.
  • (D) False — the more electropositive (more active) metal becomes the anode.
  • (E) True — grain boundary regions are anodic to the bulk grain.

C – Physical and mechanical properties · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 7-12

questions.question: For the aggregate of Question 7-15, the bulk specific gravity on the SSD basis is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(G_{sb,\text{SSD}}=B/(B-C)=1{,}524/(1{,}524-960)=1{,}524/564=2.70\).

FE Reference Handbook: not given—definition supplied in the chapter.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 2.66 is the bulk OD specific gravity, \(A/(B-C)=1{,}500/564\).
  • (C) 2.78 is the apparent specific gravity, \(A/(A-C)=1{,}500/540\).
  • (D) 2.82 is \(B/(A-C) = 1{,}524/540\): the SSD mass (numerator of the SSD formula) divided by the apparent, pore-free volume \(A - C\) (denominator of the apparent formula), mixing the two definitions.

B – Test methods · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 7-16

questions.question: The theoretical unit weight (density) of the concrete in Question 7-19 is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Unit weight = (360 + 180 + 1,100 + 677)/1 m³ = 2,317 ≈ 2,320 kg/m³, a typical value for air-entrained normal-weight concrete.

FE Reference Handbook: not given—sum of masses per unit volume.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits the water: 2,317 − 180 = 2,137 kg/m³.
  • (C) omits the air, dividing the 2,317 kg of material by 0.96 m³ instead of 1 m³: 2,317/0.96 = 2,414 kg/m³.
  • (D) carries forward the Question 7-19 error of omitting the cement volume (976 kg of sand instead of 677 kg): 360 + 180 + 1,100 + 976 = 2,616 kg/m³.

A – Mix design · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 7-20

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each laboratory test (1–5) with the property or characteristic it measures (A–E). Each letter is used once.

  • (A) Theoretical maximum specific gravity \(G_{mm}\)
  • (B) Consistency/workability of fresh concrete
  • (C) Resistance of a compacted asphalt mix to deformation under load at 60°C
  • (D) Aggregate gradation
  • (E) Energy absorbed in fracture and ductile-to-brittle transition
pairs: Rice (vacuum) test on loose asphalt mixture
questions.explanation:
1–B: The slump cone measures the consistency (workability) of fresh concrete. 2–E: The Charpy V-notch test measures the energy absorbed in fracture and, over a range of temperatures, the ductile-to-brittle transition. 3–A: The Rice test de-airs loose mix under vacuum to obtain the theoretical maximum specific gravity \(G_{mm}\). 4–D: Sieve analysis gives the particle-size distribution (gradation). 5–C: Marshall stability is the maximum load resisted by a compacted asphalt specimen loaded diametrally at 60°C, an index of resistance to deformation.

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Impact Test (Charpy); others from this chapter.

B – Test methods · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 7-24

questions.question: Which of the following statements about fluid properties are correct? [Select all that apply]
choices: Kinematic viscosity equals dynamic viscosity divided by density.
The viscosity of a liquid increases as its temperature increases.
A fluid in which shear stress is directly proportional to the velocity gradient is Newtonian.
The specific gravity of a liquid is its density divided by the density of water at standard conditions.
The vapor pressure of water decreases as its temperature increases.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (C), and (D) are the Handbook definitions; (B) and (E) reverse the temperature trends shown in the Properties of Water table.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Definitions; Properties of Water (SI Metric Units).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the Handbook defines \(\nu=\mu/\rho\).
  • (B) False — liquid viscosity decreases with temperature (see the water table: 0.001781 Pa·s at 0 °C, 0.000282 Pa·s at 100 °C); gas viscosity increases.
  • (C) True — \(\tau_t=\mu(dv/dy)\) defines a Newtonian fluid.
  • (D) True — \(SG=\rho/\rho_w\) with \(\rho_w=1{,}000\) kg/m³.
  • (E) False — vapor pressure rises with temperature (2.34 kPa at 20 °C, 101.33 kPa at 100 °C).

B – Fluid properties · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-4

questions.question: A vertical rectangular gate 5 ft wide and 8 ft tall has its top edge at the water surface (\(\gamma=62.4\) lb/ft³). The resultant hydrostatic force on the gate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(h_C=4\) ft, \(A=40\) ft². \(F_R=\gamma h_CA=62.4(4)(40)=9{,}984\ \text{lb}\approx9{,}980\) lb. (It acts at \(\tfrac{2}{3}(8)=5.33\) ft below the surface.)

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Forces on Submerged Surfaces and the Center of Pressure.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is half the correct force (using \(h_C=2\) ft).
  • (C) uses the center-of-pressure depth (5.33 ft) instead of the centroid depth in \(\gamma h_CA\).
  • (D) uses the bottom pressure times the full area.

C – Fluid statics · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 8-8

questions.question: A rectangular barge 20 m long and 8 m wide floats in fresh water (\(\gamma=9.81\) kN/m³). When a 50-kN load is placed on board, the barge sinks an additional:
questions.explanation:
Additional displaced weight equals the load: \(\gamma A\,\Delta d=50{,}000\) N, so \(\Delta d=50{,}000/[9{,}810(20\times8)]=0.0319\ \text{m}\approx32\) mm.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Archimedes Principle and Buoyancy.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is a decimal error.
  • (C) uses half the plan area.
  • (D) is a decimal error.

C – Fluid statics · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 8-12

questions.question: Water at 20 °C (kinematic viscosity \(1.003\times10^{-6}\) m²/s) flows at 2.0 m/s through 200 m of 100-mm cast-iron pipe with relative roughness \(\varepsilon/D=0.0025\). Using the Moody diagram, the friction head loss is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(Re=vD/\nu=2.0(0.100)/(1.003\times10^{-6})=1.99\times10^5\). On the Moody diagram at \(Re\approx2\times10^5\) and \(\varepsilon/D=0.0025\), \(f\approx0.026\) (Colebrook: 0.0256). \[h_f=f\,\frac{L}{D}\,\frac{v^2}{2g}=0.026\left(\frac{200}{0.100}\right)\frac{(2.0)^2}{2(9.81)}=0.026(2{,}000)(0.2039)=10.6\ \text{m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Consequences of Fluid Flow — Head Loss Due to Flow; Moody, Darcy, or Stanton Friction Factor Diagram; Properties of Water (SI Metric Units).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) forgets to square the velocity: \(0.026(2{,}000)(2.0)/[2(9.81)]=5.3\) m.
  • (B) reads the smooth-pipe curve (\(f\approx0.0156\) at this \(Re\)) instead of the \(\varepsilon/D=0.0025\) curve.
  • (C) uses a generic turbulent value \(f=0.020\) instead of reading the chart at \(\varepsilon/D=0.0025\).

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 8-16

questions.question: Two pipes of equal length and equal friction factor run in parallel between the same two junctions. Pipe A has twice the diameter of pipe B. The fraction of the total flow carried by pipe A is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Equal head loss: \(f\dfrac{L}{D_A}\dfrac{v_A^2}{2g}=f\dfrac{L}{D_B}\dfrac{v_B^2}{2g}\), so \(v_A/v_B=\sqrt{D_A/D_B}=\sqrt{2}\). Then \(Q_A/Q_B=(D_A/D_B)^2(v_A/v_B)=4\sqrt{2}=5.66\), and \(Q_A/(Q_A+Q_B)=5.66/6.66=0.85\).

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Characteristics of Selected Flow Configurations — Multipath Pipeline Problems; Head Loss Due to Flow.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) splits the flow in proportion to velocity alone (\(\sqrt{2}/(1+\sqrt{2})=0.59\)), forgetting the area ratio.
  • (B) assumes flow splits in proportion to diameter.
  • (C) assumes flow splits in proportion to area (4 : 1).

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 8-20

questions.question: Water flows steadily through a long horizontal pipe of constant diameter with friction. Which statements are correct? [Select all that apply]
choices: The energy line slopes downward in the direction of flow.
The hydraulic grade line is parallel to the energy line.
The pressure decreases in the direction of flow.
The velocity decreases in the direction of flow.
The vertical distance between the energy line and the hydraulic grade line increases downstream.
questions.explanation:
With constant diameter the velocity head is constant, so friction shows up only as a steady fall in both lines and in the pressure.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Hydraulic Gradient (Grade Line); Energy Line (Bernoulli Equation); Energy Equation.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — friction removes total head, so the EGL falls at slope \(h_f/L\).
  • (B) True — constant diameter means constant velocity head, so the HGL lies a fixed \(v^2/2g\) below the EGL.
  • (C) True — with \(z\) and \(v\) constant, the energy equation gives \(P_1-P_2=\gamma h_f>0\).
  • (D) False — continuity fixes the velocity in a constant-diameter pipe.
  • (E) False — the separation is \(v^2/2g\), which is constant.

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-24

questions.question: A vertical cylindrical tank 2.0 m in diameter drains through a 25-mm sharp-edged orifice (\(C=0.61\)) in its base. The time for the water level to fall from 3.0 m to 1.0 m above the orifice is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A_t=\pi(2.0)^2/4=3.142\) m²; \(A_0=\pi(0.025)^2/4=4.909\times10^{-4}\) m². \[t=\frac{2A_t\left(h_1^{1/2}-h_2^{1/2}\right)}{CA_0\sqrt{2g}}=\frac{2(3.142)\left(\sqrt{3.0}-\sqrt{1.0}\right)}{0.61(4.909\times10^{-4})\sqrt{2(9.81)}}=\frac{6.283(0.732)}{1.326\times10^{-3}}=3{,}468\ \text{s}=57.8\ \text{min}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Fluid Flow Measurement — Time required to drain a tank.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) divides by \(2g\) instead of \(\sqrt{2g}\) in the denominator.
  • (B) is half the answer, from dropping the factor of 2 in the numerator.
  • (C) divides the drained volume (6.28 m³) by the initial discharge (2.30 L/s) as if the rate stayed constant.

A – Flow measurement · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 8-28

questions.question: The seven interior angles of a closed traverse are measured and sum to 900°01′45″. The correction to be applied to each angle is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Theoretical sum \(=(7-2)180°=900°\). Misclosure \(=+1'45''=+105''\). Correction per angle \(=-105''/7=-15''\).

FE Reference Handbook: none needed.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the total misclosure, not the per-angle correction.
  • (B) divides by 5 (from \(n-2\)) instead of by the 7 angles.
  • (D) has the wrong sign — the measured sum is too large, so each angle must be reduced.

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 9-3

questions.question: A steel tape standardized at 20°C (\(\alpha=11.6\times10^{-6}\) per °C) is used at 5°C to measure a horizontal distance recorded as 187.450 m. The corrected distance is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(C_T=\alpha(T-T_s)L=11.6\times10^{-6}(5-20)(187.450)=-0.0326\) m. The cold tape is short, so it reads long; corrected distance \(=187.450-0.033=187.417\) m.

FE Reference Handbook: none needed.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) applies no correction.
  • (C) has the wrong sign.
  • (D) doubles the correction with the wrong sign.

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 9-7

questions.question: Offsets from a base line to a fence are measured at 15 ft intervals: 4.2, 6.8, 9.1, 10.4, 8.7, 5.3 ft. By the trapezoidal rule the area between the base line and the fence is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A=w[(h_1+h_6)/2+h_2+h_3+h_4+h_5]=15[(4.2+5.3)/2+6.8+9.1+10.4+8.7]=15[4.75+35.0]=15(39.75)=596.3\) ft².

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Area formulas — Trapezoidal Rule.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits the end offsets entirely (15 × 35.0 = 525).
  • (C) adds all six offsets at full weight (15 × 44.5 = 668).
  • (D) is twice the correct area — multiplying the bracket by 2 instead of halving the end offsets.

B – Area computations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 9-11

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about area computation are correct?
choices: Simpson’s 1/3 rule requires an odd number of offsets.
The DMD of the last course of a closed traverse should equal the negative of its departure.
The area-by-coordinates formula gives a negative result if the points are taken counterclockwise, and the absolute value is used.
The trapezoidal rule is exact for a boundary that is a parabola between offsets.
The DMD method requires that latitudes and departures be balanced first.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), and (E) are correct. Statement (C) is false: the sign of the coordinate sum depends on both the direction of travel and which coordinate is taken as X. With X = E and Y = N, counterclockwise order gives a positive sum (Question 9-10) and clockwise order a negative one (Worked Example 9.5); swapping X and Y reverses the sign. Only the absolute value is meaningful. Statement (D) is false because the trapezoidal rule is exact only for straight-line boundaries.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Area formulas.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — Simpson’s 1/3 rule needs an even number of intervals, i.e., an odd number of offsets, as the Handbook notes.
  • (B) True — the DMD check.
  • (C) False — the sign depends on the direction of travel and on which coordinate is taken as X. With X = E and Y = N, counterclockwise order gives a positive sum and clockwise a negative one; only the absolute value is meaningful.
  • (D) False — the trapezoidal rule is exact only for straight-line boundaries; Simpson’s rule is exact for parabolic ones.
  • (E) True — an unbalanced traverse does not close, so its “area” is undefined; balancing is a prerequisite for DMD (and for coordinates).

B – Area computations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 9-15

questions.question:
[Numerical entry] A borrow pit is laid out on a 15 m square grid with nine corner points (three rows of three). The depths of cut, in meters, are:

Column 1 Column 2 Column 3
Row 1 0.8 1.4 1.1
Row 2 1.5 2.2 1.9
Row 3 1.0 1.6 1.2

Enter the volume of excavation in m³ to the nearest 10 m³.
questions.explanation:
Four squares of \(A=15^2=225\) m². Multiplicity 1 (grid corners): 0.8 + 1.1 + 1.0 + 1.2 = 4.1. Multiplicity 2 (edge midpoints): 1.4 + 1.5 + 1.9 + 1.6 = 6.4. Multiplicity 4 (center): 2.2. \[V=(225/4)[4.1+2(6.4)+4(2.2)]=56.25[4.1+12.8+8.8]=56.25(25.7)=1{,}445.6\,\text{m}^3\ \to\ 1{,}450\,\text{m}^3\ \text{to the nearest 10}\]

Accepted 1,440–1,450. The unrounded value is 1,445.6 m³ (1,446 if entered to the nearest m³).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Earthwork formulas (average end area applied to each grid square).

C – Earthwork and volume computations · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 9-19

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each term (1–5) with its description (a–e).

  • (a) Product of the grid scale factor and the elevation factor, used to convert ground distance to grid distance
  • (b) Horizontal datum on which U.S. latitude, longitude, and state plane coordinates are defined
  • (c) Equipotential surface of the earth’s gravity field that approximates mean sea level; the reference for orthometric heights
  • (d) Plane northing and easting coordinates on a conformal projection defined zone by zone for each state
  • (e) Vertical datum for orthometric elevations of U.S. benchmarks
questions.explanation:
NAD83 is the horizontal datum (b); NAVD88 is the vertical datum for benchmark elevations (e); state plane coordinates are zone-by-zone plane N/E coordinates on a conformal projection (d); the combined factor converts ground to grid distance (a); the geoid is the mean-sea-level equipotential surface referenced by orthometric heights (c).

FE Reference Handbook: none printed; conceptual.

D – Coordinate systems · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 9-23

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A level run starts at BM 10 (elevation 250.000 m). Backsights in order are 2.315, 1.087, 2.654, 0.921 m and foresights in order are 1.006, 2.492, 1.135, 3.208 m, ending on BM 11. Enter the elevation of BM 11 in meters to three decimal places.
questions.explanation:
\(\sum\text{BS}=2.315+1.087+2.654+0.921=6.977\) m; \(\sum\text{FS}=1.006+2.492+1.135+3.208=7.841\) m. Elev BM 11 \(=250.000+6.977-7.841=249.136\) m.

The data carry three decimals, so no rounding ambiguity arises; the ±0.001 tolerance allows only for a keying slip in the last digit.

FE Reference Handbook: none needed.

E – Leveling · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 9-27

questions.question: A reservoir has a nearly constant water-surface area of 2.5 km2. Over a 30-day month the average surface inflow is 3.0 m3/s and the average outflow (releases) is 2.2 m3/s. Precipitation on the lake surface totals 20 mm and evaporation totals 90 mm. Groundwater exchange and bank storage are negligible. The change in reservoir water-surface elevation over the month is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Apply the hydrologic mass balance in volume units over \(\Delta t = 30(86{,}400) = 2.592\times10^6\) s.

Net surface flow: \((3.0 - 2.2)(2.592\times10^6) = 2.074\times10^6\) m3. Precipitation on the lake: \(0.020(2.5\times10^6) = 5.0\times10^4\) m3. Evaporation: \(0.090(2.5\times10^6) = 2.25\times10^5\) m3. \[\Delta S = 2.074\times10^6 + 0.050\times10^6 - 0.225\times10^6 = 1.899\times10^6\ \text{m}^3\] \[\Delta h = \frac{1.899\times10^6}{2.5\times10^6} = 0.759\ \text{m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Hydrologic Mass Balance (Budget).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 0.79 m applies a pan coefficient of 0.7 to the 90 mm, but the problem already gives lake evaporation, not pan evaporation.
  • (C) 0.83 m neglects precipitation and evaporation entirely.
  • (D) 0.90 m reverses both signs, adding evaporation and subtracting precipitation.

A – Basic hydrology · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-3

questions.question: A rectangular channel 12 ft wide carries 300 cfs. Determine the critical depth, in feet. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\[q = \frac{Q}{B} = \frac{300}{12} = 25\ \text{cfs/ft}, \qquad y_c = \left(\frac{q^2}{g}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{625}{32.2}\right)^{1/3} = (19.41)^{1/3} = 2.687\ \text{ft}\]

Accepted range: 2.65–2.72 ft. Using the total discharge instead of the unit discharge gives 14.1 ft, which is physically impossible for this channel.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Critical Depth.

B – Basic hydraulics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 10-7

questions.question: Water flows in a rectangular channel at a depth of 0.60 m with a mean velocity of 3.5 m/s. The Froude number and flow regime are:
questions.explanation:
For a rectangular section the hydraulic depth equals the flow depth. \[Fr = \frac{v}{\sqrt{gy_h}} = \frac{3.5}{\sqrt{9.81(0.60)}} = \frac{3.5}{2.426} = 1.44 > 1 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{supercritical}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Froude Number.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.69 is the reciprocal, \(\sqrt{gy}/v\), and inverts the regime as well.
  • (B) has the right number but the wrong classification: \(Fr > 1\) is supercritical (rapid), not subcritical.
  • (D) 2.04 uses \(y/2\) in place of the hydraulic depth.

B – Basic hydraulics · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-11

questions.question: At 1,200 rpm a pump operating at one point on its characteristic curve delivers 450 gpm at 60 ft of head and absorbs 9.0 hp. Applying the affinity laws, the corresponding point at 1,500 rpm is:
questions.explanation:
With the impeller diameter fixed, the speed ratio is \(r = 1500/1200 = 1.25\): \[Q_2 = rQ_1 = 1.25(450) = 563\ \text{gpm}, \qquad H_2 = r^2H_1 = 1.5625(60) = 93.8\ \text{ft}, \qquad \dot W_2 = r^3\dot W_1 = 1.953(9.0) = 17.6\ \text{hp}\] Note that these are points on the pump curve; the actual operating flow shifts differently because the system curve has a static-head intercept.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Fluid Flow Machinery — Scaling Laws; Affinity Laws.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) leaves the flow unscaled.
  • (B) scales head and power linearly with speed.
  • (C) scales power with \(N^2\) rather than \(N^3\).

C – Pumps · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 10-15

questions.question: Two pipes of the same material (\(C = 120\)) and the same 500-m length run in parallel between the same two junctions: pipe A is 300 mm in diameter and pipe B is 250 mm. The total flow is 0.200 m3/s. The flow carried by pipe A is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Parallel branches share the same head loss, so with equal \(C\) and equal \(L\) the Hazen–Williams form \(Q = k_1CAR_H^{0.63}S^{0.54}\) gives \(Q \propto D^2 \cdot D^{0.63} = D^{2.63}\). \[\frac{Q_A}{Q_{total}} = \frac{0.30^{2.63}}{0.30^{2.63} + 0.25^{2.63}} = \frac{0.04215}{0.04215 + 0.02610} = 0.618\] \[Q_A = 0.618(0.200) = 0.124\ \text{m}^3/\text{s} \qquad (Q_B = 0.076\ \text{m}^3/\text{s})\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hazen-Williams Equation; Fluid Mechanics — Multipath Pipeline Problems.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.100 m3/s splits the flow equally, ignoring the diameters.
  • (B) 0.109 m3/s splits in proportion to diameter.
  • (C) 0.118 m3/s splits in proportion to cross-sectional area (\(D^2\)), which neglects the \(R_H^{0.63}\) term.

D – Water distribution systems · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-19

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about reservoirs and level-pool routing are correct?
choices: The peak outflow occurs at the instant the receding inflow hydrograph crosses the rising outflow hydrograph.
The peak outflow is smaller than the peak inflow and occurs later.
Level-pool routing requires both a storage–elevation relationship and an outflow–elevation (spillway rating) relationship.
Freeboard is the vertical distance from the spillway crest up to the maximum pool level reached during the design flood.
Using the outflow at the start of each time step instead of the average of the start and end outflows makes the computed pool rise too small.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B) and (C) are correct; (D) and (E) are not (see the rationale for each statement below).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Weir Formulas (spillway rating); continuity.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — continuity gives \(dS/dt = I - O\), so storage (and therefore pool elevation and spillway outflow) peaks exactly when \(I = O\). Because the outflow is still rising while the inflow is falling, that crossing lies on the inflow recession.
  • (B) True — this is attenuation and lag; the reservoir borrows volume from the peak and returns it later.
  • (C) True — the two auxiliary curves close the single continuity equation; the storage-indication (modified Puls) method simply repackages them as \(2S/\Delta t + O\) versus \(O\).
  • (D) False — freeboard is measured from the maximum pool level up to the top of the dam, not from the crest up to the pool.
  • (E) False — using \(O_1\) alone understates the outflow during the step, so the computed storage increase, and the pool rise, come out too large.

E – Flood control · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-23

questions.question: A sanitary sewer serves 8,000 people at 380 L/cap·d. The peaking factor from the sewage flow ratio curve is 2.8 and the infiltration/inflow allowance is 5.5 L/s. The peak design flow is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[Q_{avg} = \frac{8000(380)}{86{,}400} = 35.2\ \text{L/s}\] \[Q_{design} = PF\times Q_{avg} + Q_{I/I} = 2.8(35.19) + 5.5 = 98.5 + 5.5 = 104.0\ \text{L/s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Sewage Flow Ratio Curves.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 40.7 L/s omits the peaking factor.
  • (B) 98.5 L/s omits the infiltration/inflow allowance.
  • (D) 114 L/s applies the peaking factor to the infiltration as well; infiltration is a groundwater phenomenon and is added after peaking the sanitary flow.

G – Collection systems · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-27

questions.question: A sand aquifer has a hydraulic conductivity of \(2.5\times10^{-4}\) m/s and an effective porosity of 0.30. The hydraulic gradient is 0.008. The specific discharge (Darcy velocity) and the average seepage velocity are, respectively, most nearly:
choices: \(2.0\times10^{-6}\) m/s and \(6.0\times10^{-7}\) m/s
\(2.0\times10^{-6}\) m/s and \(2.0\times10^{-6}\) m/s
\(6.7\times10^{-6}\) m/s and \(2.0\times10^{-6}\) m/s
\(2.0\times10^{-6}\) m/s and \(6.7\times10^{-6}\) m/s
questions.explanation:
\[q = Ki = (2.5\times10^{-4})(0.008) = 2.0\times10^{-6}\ \text{m/s}\] \[v = \frac{q}{n} = \frac{2.0\times10^{-6}}{0.30} = 6.7\times10^{-6}\ \text{m/s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Darcy’s Law.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) multiplies by the porosity instead of dividing, making the pore velocity smaller than the Darcy velocity — impossible, since the flow is squeezed through only a fraction of the area.
  • (B) omits the porosity correction entirely; a contaminant would then be predicted to arrive 3.3 times later than it actually does.
  • (C) interchanges the two velocities.

H – Groundwater · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-31

questions.question: A groundwater contains Ca2+ = 60 mg/L and Mg2+ = 18 mg/L. Using equivalent weights of 20.0 for Ca2+, 12.2 for Mg2+ and 50.0 for CaCO3, the total hardness is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Convert each cation to CaCO3 equivalents by multiplying by 50.0 divided by the ion’s equivalent weight: \[\text{Ca}^{2+}: 60\left(\frac{50.0}{20.0}\right) = 150\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3, \qquad \text{Mg}^{2+}: 18\left(\frac{50.0}{12.2}\right) = 73.8\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3\] \[TH = 150 + 73.8 = 224\ \text{mg/L as CaCO}_3\ \text{("very hard")}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Common Radicals in Water (molecular and equivalent weights); Chemistry.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 78 mg/L adds the raw ion concentrations, which mixes unlike equivalents.
  • (B) 150 mg/L counts only the calcium.
  • (C) 187 mg/L converts magnesium with its molecular weight (24.3) rather than its equivalent weight (12.2), halving the magnesium contribution.

I – Water quality · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-35

questions.question: Three noise sources produce sound pressure levels of 78 dB, 78 dB and 72 dB at a receptor when operated individually. Operated together, the level at the receptor is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Decibels combine on an energy basis: \[\begin{aligned} SPL_{total} &= 10\log_{10}\left(10^{7.8} + 10^{7.8} + 10^{7.2}\right) = 10\log_{10}\left(1.262\times10^8 + 0.1585\times10^8\right)\\ &= 10\log_{10}\left(1.420\times10^8\right) = 81.5\ \text{dB} \end{aligned}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Safety — Noise Pollution.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 78.0 dB reports only the loudest source and ignores the others.
  • (C) 82.8 dB treats all three sources as 78 dB (adding \(10\log_{10}3\) = 4.8 dB).
  • (D) 228 dB adds the levels arithmetically, which is meaningless — the total can never exceed the loudest source by more than \(10\log_{10}N\) = 4.8 dB here.

J – Testing and standards · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 10-39

questions.question: An activated-sludge aeration basin has a volume of 3,000 m3 and an MLSS concentration of 2,800 mg/L. It receives 9,000 m3/d of primary effluent containing 150 mg/L of BOD5. The food-to-microorganism ratio is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[F{:}M = \frac{Q_0S_0}{VX_A} = \frac{9000\ \text{m}^3/\text{d}\times150\ \text{mg/L}}{3000\ \text{m}^3\times2800\ \text{mg/L}} = \frac{1.35\times10^6}{8.40\times10^6} = 0.161\ \text{d}^{-1}\] The concentration units cancel, so both may be left in mg/L. The value is just below the conventional range (0.2–0.4) and above the extended-aeration range (0.05–0.15).

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Wastewater Treatment and Technologies — Activated Sludge; Design and Operational Parameters for Activated-Sludge Treatment.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.6 × 10−4 converts only \(S_0\) to kg/m3 and leaves \(X_A\) in mg/L.
  • (C) 0.45 is the volumetric organic loading \(Q_0S_0/V\) in kg BOD/m3·d, a different parameter.
  • (D) 6.2 is the reciprocal of F:M.

K – Water and wastewater treatment · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 10-43

questions.question: A cantilever beam 5 m long is fixed at A and free at B. It carries a uniformly distributed load of 8 kN/m over its entire length and a concentrated load of 12 kN at the free end B. The magnitude of the maximum bending moment is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
In a cantilever both loads bend the beam the same way, and the moment grows from zero at the free end to its maximum at the fixed support A. Taking moments of everything to the right of a cut just beside A (the uniform load acts at its centroid, \(L/2\) from A; the point load acts at the full length \(L\)): \[M_{max} = \frac{wL^2}{2} + PL = \frac{8(5)^2}{2} + 12(5) = 100 + 60 = 160\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}\] The moment is hogging (tension on the top fiber). The support also carries a vertical reaction \(wL + P = 40 + 12 = 52\) kN.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Cantilevered Beam Slopes and Deflections; Shearing Force and Bending Moment Sign Conventions.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 40 kN·m uses the simple-span formulas \(wL^2/8 + PL/4 = 25 + 15\); a cantilever is not a simply supported beam.
  • (B) 85 kN·m keeps the correct tip-load term \(PL = 60\) but uses the simple-span coefficient \(wL^2/8 = 25\) for the uniform load instead of \(wL^2/2 = 100\).
  • (C) 100 kN·m is the uniform-load contribution \(wL^2/2\) alone; the 12-kN tip load adds \(PL = 60\) kN·m at the support.

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 11-1

questions.question: The Pratt truss in Figure 11.17 spans 12 m in four 3-m panels, is 4 m deep, and carries 30 kN at each of the bottom joints B, C, and D. The force in top-chord member FG is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Reactions: \(R_A = R_E = (3 \times 30)/2 = 45\) kN. Cut a section through FG, FC, and BC and take the left portion. Members FC and BC intersect at C (6, 0), so moments about C leave only \(F_{FG}\), whose line of action is 4 m above C: \[45(6) - 30(3) + F_{FG}(4) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{FG} = -\frac{270 - 90}{4} = -45.0\,\text{kN}\] Negative means compression.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Plane Truss: Method of Sections.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 33.8 kN tension is the bottom-chord force \(F_{AB} = F_{BC} = 33.75\) kN.
  • (C) reverses the sense.
  • (D) 56.3 kN compression is the end diagonal \(F_{AF} = -56.25\) kN, found at joint A.

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-5

questions.question: A simply supported beam of span 8 m carries a concentrated load of 40 kN at midspan. \(EI = 12{,}000\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}^2\). The midspan deflection is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[v_{max} = \frac{PL^3}{48EI} = \frac{40(8)^3}{48(12{,}000)} = \frac{20{,}480}{576{,}000} = 0.03556\,\text{m} = 35.6\,\text{mm}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections (central concentrated load).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 8.9 mm uses \(PL^3/192EI\), the fixed-fixed case.
  • (B) 17.8 mm uses \(PL^3/96EI\).
  • (C) 22.2 mm uses \(5PL^3/384EI\), the uniform-load coefficient applied to a concentrated load; a load concentrated at midspan deflects the beam more than the same total load spread along the span.

B – Deflection of determinate structures · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-9

questions.question: A pinned-pinned column is 6 m long, has \(I = 25 \times 10^6\,\text{mm}^4\) about its weak axis, and \(E = 200\) GPa. The Euler critical buckling load is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Pinned-pinned means \(K = 1.0\), so \(K\ell = 6000\) mm. With \(E = 200{,}000\,\text{N/mm}^2\): \[P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2EI}{(K\ell)^2} = \frac{\pi^2(200{,}000)(25 \times 10^6)}{(6000)^2} = \frac{4.9348 \times 10^{13}}{3.6 \times 10^7} = 1.371 \times 10^6\,\text{N} = 1371\,\text{kN}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Columns.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 343 kN uses \(K = 2.0\) (fixed-free).
  • (C) 2800 kN uses \(K = 0.7\) (fixed-pinned), which multiplies the pinned value by \(1/0.7^2 = 2.04\).
  • (D) 5480 kN uses \(K = 0.5\) (fixed-fixed), four times the pinned value.

C – Column analysis · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-13

questions.question: A steel column is fixed at its base, and its top is free to both translate and rotate. AISC Table C-A-7.1 recommends a design value of \(K\) for this case of:
questions.explanation:
The theoretical value for a column fixed at one end and free (both to translate and to rotate) at the other is \(K = 2.0\); because real “fixed” bases rotate slightly, AISC Table C-A-7.1 recommends the higher design value \(K = 2.10\) for that case.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Steel Components — AISC Table C-A-7.1 (Approximate Values of Effective Length Factor, K).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.65 is the recommended value for fixed-fixed (theoretical 0.5).
  • (B) 1.20 is the recommended value for a column fixed at both ends but free to sidesway (theoretical 1.0).
  • (C) 2.00 is the theoretical fixed-free value, not the recommended design value the question asks for.

C – Column analysis · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 11-17

questions.question:
[Matching] Match each structure (1–4) with its classification (W–Z). Each classification is used exactly once.

  • (W) Statically determinate
  • (X) Statically indeterminate to the first degree
  • (Y) Statically indeterminate to the second degree
  • (Z) Statically indeterminate to the third degree
pairs: A beam with a pin at one end and a roller at the other, no internal releases
A propped cantilever (fixed at one end, roller at the other), no internal releases
A beam fixed at both ends, no internal releases
A beam continuous over four supports (one pin and three rollers), no internal releases
questions.explanation:
For a beam without internal releases the degree of indeterminacy is \(r - 3\):

  1. Pin (2) + roller (1): \(r = 3\), degree 0 → W, statically determinate.
  2. Fixed (3) + roller (1): \(r = 4\), degree 1 → X.
  3. Fixed (3) + fixed (3): \(r = 6\), degree 3 → Z.
  4. Pin (2) + three rollers (3): \(r = 5\), degree 2 → Y.

A common mis-assignment is giving a fixed support two components instead of three, which turns structure 3 into a first-degree problem and structure 2 into a determinate one.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures.

D – Determinacy and stability · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-21

questions.question: Three prismatic members meet at rigid joint B and all of their far ends are fixed: member BA has moment of inertia \(I\) and length 6 m, member BC has \(2I\) and length 8 m, and member BD has \(I\) and length 4 m. All members have the same \(E\). The moment distribution factor \(DF_{BC}\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Because every far end is fixed, each member’s stiffness is \(4EI/L\), and with \(E\) common the relative stiffnesses are proportional to \(I/L\): \[k_{BA} \propto \frac{1}{6} = 0.1667 \qquad k_{BC} \propto \frac{2}{8} = 0.2500 \qquad k_{BD} \propto \frac{1}{4} = 0.2500\] \[DF_{BC} = \frac{0.2500}{0.1667 + 0.2500 + 0.2500} = \frac{0.2500}{0.6667} = 0.375\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Beam Stiffness and Moment Carryover.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.250 is the relative stiffness \(I/L\) of BC without dividing by the total.
  • (B) 0.333 assumes three members of equal stiffness.
  • (D) 0.600 comes from comparing BC with BA only, ignoring member BD.

E – Elementary indeterminate structures · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-25

questions.question: An interior column supports two identical floors. The tributary area of each floor is 400 ft², the live-load element factor is \(K_{LL} = 4\), and the unreduced live load is \(L_o = 100\) psf. Using the Handbook live-load reduction equation with the \(0.40L_o\) floor for members supporting two or more floors, the reduced live load is ______ psf. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
A column supporting two floors collects both tributary areas: \(A_T = 2(400) = 800\,\text{ft}^2\). With \(K_{LL} = 4\), \[K_{LL}A_T = 4(800) = 3200\,\text{ft}^2 \quad (\ge 400\,\text{ft}^2\text{, so the reduction is permitted})\] \[L = L_o\left(0.25 + \frac{15}{\sqrt{K_{LL}A_T}}\right) = 100\left(0.25 + \frac{15}{56.57}\right) = 100(0.25 + 0.2652) = 51.5\,\text{psf}\] The floor for a member supporting two or more floors is \(0.40L_o = 40\) psf, which does not govern.

Numerical entry: accepted answer 51.5 psf (range 50.5–52.5). Common wrong entries are 62.5 psf (using only one floor’s 400 ft²) and 40.0 psf (assuming the floor always governs).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Live Load Reduction.

F – Loads and load combinations · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-29

questions.question: [Ranking] A uniform pressure is applied to a floor of a steel-framed building supported on spread footings. Arrange the following elements in the order in which the gravity load reaches the ground, starting with the element that receives the load first.
questions.explanation:
The gravity load path in a typical steel-framed floor runs: floor slab (2) collects the pressure and spans to the floor beams (5); the beams span to the girders (1) on the column lines; the girders deliver concentrated reactions to the columns (4); the columns carry the accumulated load down to the spread footings (3), which spread it into the soil.

A common ranking error is swapping beam and girder. The girder is the member that receives beam reactions; it is downstream of the beam, closer to the column.

FE Reference Handbook: Load-path and tributary-area concepts (not tabulated in the Handbook); \(A_T\) appears under Civil Engineering — Live Load Reduction.

F – Loads, load combinations, and load paths · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 11-33

questions.question: A W16×40 beam of \(F_y = 50\) ksi steel has an unbraced length \(L_b = 12\) ft with \(C_b = 1.14\). AISC Table 3-2 gives \(\phi_bM_{px} = 274\) kip-ft, \(\phi_bBF = 10.1\) kips, \(L_p = 5.55\) ft, and \(L_r = 15.9\) ft. The design flexural strength \(\phi_bM_n\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(L_p = 5.55\,\text{ft} < L_b = 12\,\text{ft} < L_r = 15.9\) ft, so the beam is in the inelastic lateral-torsional-buckling zone and the Table 3-2 straight-line form applies: \[\begin{aligned} \phi_bM_n &= C_b\left[\phi_bM_{px} - \phi_bBF(L_b - L_p)\right] = 1.14\left[274 - 10.1(12 - 5.55)\right] \\ &= 1.14[274 - 65.1] = 1.14(208.9) = 238\,\text{kip-ft} \le \phi_bM_{px} = 274\,\text{kip-ft}\ ✓ \end{aligned}\] Without \(C_b\) the result would be 209 kip-ft—conservative, but not what the question asks.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Steel Components — Beams; AISC Table 3-2.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 267 kip-ft measures the reduction from the wrong end of the zone, using \(L_r - L_b = 3.9\) ft instead of \(L_b - L_p = 6.45\) ft: \(1.14[274 - 10.1(3.9)] = 267\) kip-ft.
  • (C) 274 kip-ft is \(\phi_bM_{px}\), valid only if \(L_b \le L_p\).
  • (D) 312 kip-ft applies \(C_b\) to \(\phi_bM_{px}\) itself; the \(C_b\)-amplified value may never exceed \(\phi_bM_{px}\), so 312 kip-ft is impossible.

G – Design of steel components · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-37

questions.question: A singly reinforced rectangular beam has \(b = 14\) in, \(d = d_t = 22\) in, \(A_s = 3.16\,\text{in}^2\), \(f'_c = 4000\) psi, and \(f_y = 60{,}000\) psi. The design moment strength \(\phi M_n\) is ______ kip-ft. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Depth of the Whitney stress block (work in kips and inches, \(f_y = 60\) ksi, \(f'_c = 4\) ksi): \[a = \frac{A_sf_y}{0.85f'_cb} = \frac{3.16(60)}{0.85(4)(14)} = \frac{189.6}{47.6} = 3.98\,\text{in}\] Check the strain: \(\beta_1 = 0.85\), so \(c = a/\beta_1 = 4.69\) in and \[\varepsilon_t = \frac{0.003(d_t - c)}{c} = \frac{0.003(22 - 4.69)}{4.69} = 0.0111 \ge 0.005 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \phi = 0.90\] \[M_n = A_sf_y\left(d - \frac{a}{2}\right) = 189.6(22 - 1.99) = 3794\,\text{kip-in} = 316.1\,\text{kip-ft}\] \[\phi M_n = 0.90(316.1) = 284.5\,\text{kip-ft}\]

Numerical entry: accepted answer 284 kip-ft (range 281–288). Common wrong entries are 316 kip-ft (\(M_n\), with \(\phi\) omitted) and 3794 (kip-in, not converted).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components — Beams—Flexure; Unified Design Provisions; Resistance Factors.

H – Design of reinforced concrete components · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-41

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about the development length \(l_d\) of a straight deformed bar in tension are correct?
choices: \(l_d\) increases in proportion to the bar diameter.
\(l_d\) decreases as the specified concrete compressive strength increases.
A “top bar,” with more than 12 in of fresh concrete cast below it, requires a longer \(l_d\) than the same bar near the bottom of the member.
Epoxy coating of the bar reduces the required development length.
A standard hook can reduce the embedment length required at a discontinuous end of a member.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), (C), and (E) describe how bond and anchorage behave; statement (D) reverses the effect of epoxy coating.

The FE Handbook does not print the full \(l_d\) expression; a question requiring the arithmetic must supply the formula.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (development and splice concepts).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the required length scales with \(d_b\): a bar’s yield force grows with \(d_b^2\) while its bond perimeter grows with \(d_b\), so the length needed grows linearly with diameter.
  • (B) True — bond strength rises with \(\sqrt{f'_c}\), which appears in the denominator of \(l_d\).
  • (C) True — bleed water and settlement under a bar with a deep layer of fresh concrete beneath it weaken the bond, so a top-bar factor (commonly 1.3) lengthens \(l_d\).
  • (D) False — epoxy coating reduces bond and therefore increases the required development length.
  • (E) True — a standard hook develops part of the bar force by bearing on the concrete inside the bend, so the required embedment at a discontinuous end is shorter than for a straight bar.

H – Design of reinforced concrete components · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-45

questions.question: A fine-grained inorganic soil has a liquid limit of 60 and a plasticity index of 35. Using the plasticity chart of Figure 12.2, its USCS group symbol is:
questions.explanation:
Evaluate the “A” line at LL = 60: \(PI_A = 0.73(60 - 20) = 29.2\). The soil’s PI of 35 exceeds 29.2, so it plots above the “A” line and is a clay. Its liquid limit of 60 is 50 or more, so it is a high-plasticity (fat) clay: CH.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — ASTM D2487-11 (USCS) plasticity chart.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) requires LL < 50.
  • (B) would require the point to plot below the “A” line.
  • (C) requires an organic soil, identified by the oven-dried liquid limit ratio, not by position on the chart alone.

A – Index properties and soil classifications · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 12-3

questions.question: A soil sample has a moist unit weight of 19.6 kN/m³ at a water content of 14%. Its dry unit weight is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[\gamma_d = \frac{\gamma}{1+w} = \frac{19.6}{1.14} = 17.19\,\text{kN/m}^3\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Phase Relationships (dry unit weight, water content).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) subtracts \(w\gamma_w\) from the moist unit weight, treating the water content as a volume fraction of water: \(19.6 - 0.14(9.81) = 18.2\) kN/m³. The water content is a ratio of masses, \(W_w/W_s\), so divide by \((1+w)\).
  • (C) is the moist unit weight unchanged, ignoring the water content.
  • (D) multiplies by \((1+w)\) instead of dividing.

B – Phase relations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 12-7

questions.question: A soil with \(G_s = 2.65\) is compacted at a water content of 18%. The zero-air-voids dry unit weight at that water content is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Setting \(S = 100\%\) gives \(e = wG_s\), so \[\gamma_{zav} = \frac{G_s\gamma_w}{1+wG_s} = \frac{2.65(62.4)}{1+0.18(2.65)} = \frac{165.36}{1.477} = 112.0\ \text{pcf}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Phase Relationships (dry unit weight, degree of saturation, specific gravity of soil solids).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) uses \((1+w)\) in the denominator instead of \((1+wG_s)\).
  • (C) divides the water content by \(G_s\) instead of multiplying: \(165.36/(1 + 0.18/2.65) = 154.8\) pcf.
  • (D) omits the denominator entirely and is simply \(G_s\gamma_w\).

B – Phase relations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-11

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following tests can yield effective-stress shear strength parameters \(c'\) and \(\phi'\)?
choices: Consolidated-undrained (CU) triaxial test with pore pressure measurement
Slow direct shear test on a clean sand
questions.explanation:
A test yields \(c'\) and \(\phi'\) only if the effective stresses at failure are known — either because the test is drained (\(u = 0\)) or because the pore pressure is measured.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Mohr-Coulomb failure envelope figure (with definitions of \(s\), \(t\), \(\theta\)); Effective Stress; Shear Stress at Failure.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — In a CD test drainage is permitted throughout and shearing is slow enough that \(u = 0\), so total and effective stresses coincide and the envelope is the effective-stress envelope.
  • (B) True — In a CU test the pore pressure at failure is measured, so each total-stress circle can be shifted left by \(u_f\) to give the effective-stress circle and hence \(c'\) and \(\phi'\).
  • (C) False — A UU test on a saturated clay drains at no stage and no pore pressure is measured; it gives only the total-stress result \(\phi_u = 0\), \(c = c_u\).
  • (D) False — The unconfined compression test is a UU test at zero cell pressure; it gives \(c_u = q_u/2\) and nothing about effective stress.
  • (E) True — A direct shear test on a clean sand sheared slowly is fully drained, so the measured envelope is an effective-stress envelope.

C – Laboratory and field tests · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-15

questions.question: Water flows through a sand with \(K = 2.0\times 10^{-4}\) m/s under a hydraulic gradient of 0.30. The effective porosity is 0.35. The average seepage velocity is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Darcy (discharge) velocity: \[q = Ki = (2.0\times 10^{-4})(0.30) = 6.0\times 10^{-5}\,\text{m/s}\] Seepage velocity, which accounts for flow through the void area only: \[v = \frac{q}{n} = \frac{6.0\times 10^{-5}}{0.35} = 1.71\times 10^{-4}\,\text{m/s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Darcy’s Law (specific discharge and average seepage velocity).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) multiplies by \(n\) instead of dividing.
  • (B) is the Darcy velocity, which is smaller than the true pore-water speed.
  • (C) divides by the solids fraction \((1-n) = 0.65\) instead of by the porosity: \(6.0\times 10^{-5}/0.65 = 9.23\times 10^{-5}\) m/s.

D – Effective stress · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-19

questions.question: The 5.0-m smooth vertical wall of Figure 12.16 retains a dry sand backfill (\(\gamma = 19.0\) kN/m³, \(\phi = 32°\), \(c = 0\), level surface) carrying a uniform surcharge of 15 kPa. The total active thrust per meter of wall is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[K_A = \tan^2\left(45° - \frac{32°}{2}\right) = \tan^2 29° = 0.3073\] The surcharge contributes a rectangular pressure block of constant magnitude \(K_A q\) over the full height, and the soil weight contributes the usual triangle: \[P_{rect} = K_A qH = 0.3073(15.0)(5.0) = 23.04\,\text{kN/m}\] \[P_{tri} = \tfrac{1}{2}K_A\gamma H^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.3073)(19.0)(5.0)^2 = 72.97\,\text{kN/m}\] \[P = 23.04 + 72.97 = 96.0\,\text{kN/m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Horizontal Stress Profiles and Forces; Vertical Stress Profiles with Surcharge.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits the surcharge entirely.
  • (B) treats the whole diagram as one triangle with the base value \(K_A(q + \gamma H)\), which under-counts the surcharge block by half.
  • (D) uses \(K_0 = 1 - \sin 32° = 0.470\) instead of \(K_A\); the at-rest coefficient applies only to walls that cannot move.

E – Stability of retaining structures · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-23

questions.question: A triaxial specimen of sand with \(\phi = 32°\) fails. The failure plane is inclined to the horizontal at:
questions.explanation:
\[\theta = 45° + \frac{\phi}{2} = 45° + 16° = 61°\] measured from the plane on which the major principal stress acts, which in a triaxial test is horizontal.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Mohr-Coulomb failure envelope figure (the \(2\theta\) construction on the circle, with definitions of \(s\), \(t\), \(\theta\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(45° - \phi/2\), the complementary conjugate plane.
  • (B) is the friction angle itself, which is the slope of the envelope, not the orientation of the failure plane.
  • (C) is the plane of maximum shear stress, which does not fail because it carries a higher normal stress (the circle center \(s\)) than the failure plane, so its available strength exceeds the shear stress on it.

F – Shear strength · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 12-27

questions.question: A 2.0-m-wide strip footing is founded 1.5 m deep in sand with \(\phi = 30°\) and \(c = 0\). Above the water table \(\gamma = 19.0\) kN/m³; below it \(\gamma_{sat} = 21.0\) kN/m³. Use \(N_q = 18.4\) and \(N_\gamma = 15.7\). If the water table rises from far below the footing to the ground surface, the ultimate bearing capacity becomes most nearly:
questions.explanation:
With the water table at the ground surface, both the surcharge zone and the failure wedge are submerged, so \(\gamma'\) replaces \(\gamma\) everywhere: \[\gamma' = 21.0 - 9.81 = 11.19\,\text{kN/m}^3\] \[q_{ult} = 0 + \gamma' D_f N_q + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma' BN_\gamma = 11.19(1.5)(18.4) + \tfrac{1}{2}(11.19)(2.0)(15.7)\] \[q_{ult} = 308.8 + 175.7 = 484.5\,\text{kPa}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Ultimate Bearing Capacity; Phase Relationships (effective/submerged unit weight).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) submerges only the surcharge term.
  • (C) submerges only the self-weight term.
  • (D) is the deep-water-table value, \(19.0(1.5)(18.4) + \tfrac{1}{2}(19.0)(2.0)(15.7) = 822.7\) kPa; the rise costs 41% of the capacity.

G – Bearing capacity · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 12-31

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following are valid reasons to select a mat foundation?
choices: The combined area of the required spread footings would exceed about half the building plan area
The soil is erratic and differential settlement between columns must be limited
The structure has a basement below the water table and requires a watertight slab
The structure is light and founded on a deep, uniform dense gravel
The load must be transferred past 20 m of soft clay to bedrock
questions.explanation:
A mat pays off when footings would nearly merge anyway, when its stiffness is needed to control differential settlement, or when a watertight slab is required; it is the wrong choice for light loads on good soil and for loads that must reach deep bearing strata.

FE Reference Handbook: not tabulated in Handbook 10.6; conceptual foundation selection.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — Once individual footings would cover roughly half the footprint, the incremental cost of joining them into one slab is small and the mat is usually cheaper.
  • (B) True — A mat’s flexural stiffness redistributes load away from soft zones, which is precisely what limits differential settlement.
  • (C) True — A mat below the water table doubles as a watertight structural slab resisting uplift.
  • (D) False — A light structure on dense uniform gravel is the ideal case for small, inexpensive spread footings; a mat would be wasteful.
  • (E) False — Transferring load past 20 m of soft clay to bedrock is a deep-foundation problem; a mat bears at shallow depth and would settle excessively.

H – Foundation types · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-35

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about consolidation are correct?
choices: Doubling the thickness of a doubly drained clay layer quadruples the time to reach a given degree of consolidation

An overconsolidated clay settles less than a normally consolidated clay of the same thickness under the same stress increase, provided the final effective stress stays below the preconsolidation pressure
The coefficient of consolidation \(c_v\) has units of length squared per unit time
Secondary compression occurs only while excess pore water pressure is dissipating and ceases when it reaches zero
Installing prefabricated vertical drains reduces the ultimate primary consolidation settlement
questions.explanation:
Statements (A) through (C) follow directly from \(T_v = c_v t/H_{dr}^2\) and the recompression branch of the \(e\)–log \(\sigma'\) curve; (D) and (E) confuse rate with magnitude or primary with secondary compression.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Variation of Time Factor with Degree of Consolidation; Soil Consolidation Curve Over Consolidated Clay; Recompression Index.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(t = T_v H_{dr}^2/c_v\), and doubling \(H\) doubles \(H_{dr}\), so \(t\) increases by a factor of four at any fixed \(T_v\).
  • (B) True — Below \(\sigma'_c\) the soil follows the recompression branch with slope \(C_R \approx C_C/6\), so settlement is roughly one sixth of the virgin-compression value.
  • (C) True — From \(T_v = c_v t/H_{dr}^2\), \(c_v\) has units of length² per unit time (m²/yr, cm²/s).
  • (D) False — Secondary compression occurs at essentially constant effective stress after primary consolidation is complete, and continues indefinitely at a decreasing rate.
  • (E) False — Wick drains shorten the drainage path and so reduce the time; the ultimate magnitude of primary settlement is set by the stress change and the compressibility, and is unchanged.

I – Consolidation and differential settlement · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-39

questions.question: A highway subgrade is a clay with a plasticity index of 28 and a severe shrink–swell problem. The most appropriate chemical stabilizer is:
questions.explanation:
Lime is the standard treatment for plastic clays. Calcium ions displace sodium on the clay particle surfaces, causing flocculation that raises the plastic limit and lowers the plasticity index, sharply reducing shrink–swell potential; a slower pozzolanic reaction with the clay’s silica and alumina then cements the particles and builds long-term strength.

FE Reference Handbook: not covered in Handbook 10.6; conceptual soil stabilization.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) Portland cement works best on granular and low-plasticity soils, where it can be mixed uniformly; high-PI clay forms clods that cement cannot penetrate.
  • (C) Bituminous emulsions waterproof and bind granular soils and are ineffective on wet plastic clay.
  • (D) Salt is used chiefly as a dust palliative and construction aid, not as a structural stabilizer for shrink–swell clay.

K – Soil stabilization · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 12-43

questions.question: A horizontal curve has a degree of curve of \(5^\circ00'\) (arc definition). Its radius is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(R=5729.58/D=5729.58/5=1145.9\approx1{,}146\) ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves (\(R=5729.58/D\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is half the radius.
  • (C) is the radius for \(D=4^\circ\).
  • (D) is twice the radius (the diameter).

A – Geometric design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-1

questions.question: A freeway ramp is designed for 70 mph with a maximum superelevation of 8% and a maximum side-friction factor of 0.10. The minimum radius is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(R_{min}=V^2/[15(0.01e+f)]=70^2/[15(0.08+0.10)]=4900/2.70=1{,}815\) ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves (Side friction factor).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is half the correct value.
  • (C) uses friction only (\(f=0.10\), no superelevation).
  • (D) uses superelevation only.

A – Geometric design · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-5

questions.question: An 800-ft equal-tangent sag curve joins a −4.0% grade to a +2.0% grade. The PVC is at station 20+00, elevation 500.00 ft. The elevation of the curve at station 24+00 is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(a=(g_2-g_1)/(2L)=(0.02+0.04)/(2\times800)=3.75\times10^{-5}\ \text{ft}^{-1}\). At Sta 24+00, \(x=400\) ft: \[Y=500.00+(-0.04)(400)+3.75\times10^{-5}(400)^2=500.00-16.00+6.00=490.00\ \text{ft}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Vertical Curves.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) subtracts the offset instead of adding it (on a sag the curve is above the back tangent).
  • (B) is the tangent elevation without the parabolic offset.
  • (D) uses \(a=(g_2-g_1)/L\), doubling the offset.

A – Geometric design · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 13-9

questions.question: A horizontal curve has a radius of 1,200 ft to the centerline of the inside lane. To provide a sight distance of 500 ft along the curve, the required clearance from that centerline to a sound wall on the inside of the curve is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(HSO=R[1-\cos(28.65S/R)]=1200[1-\cos(28.65\times500/1200)]=1200[1-\cos11.94^\circ]=1200(0.02163)=26\) ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves (Sight Distance to see around obstruction).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is twice the correct value.
  • (C) uses the full central angle \(57.3S/R\) instead of half.
  • (D) evaluates \(\cos(11.94)\) with the calculator in radian mode.

A – Geometric design · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-13

questions.question: Using the AASHTO load equivalency factors in the Handbook, a 22,000-lb single axle causes how many times the pavement damage of a standard 18,000-lb single axle?
questions.explanation:
From the Handbook table, the single-axle LEF at 22,000 lb is 2.18; the 18,000-lb axle is the reference with LEF 1.000. The ratio is 2.18.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Highway Pavement Design (Load Equivalency Factors).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) reads the tandem-axle column at 22,000 lb instead of the single-axle column.
  • (B) is the ratio of the loads, 22/18 = 1.22.
  • (C) is that ratio squared, 1.49; the fourth-power rule of thumb, \((22/18)^4=2.23\), is the one that approximates the table value 2.18.

B – Pavement design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-17

questions.question: A design lane carries 500 ESALs per day in the first year. Traffic grows 4% per year. The cumulative ESALs over a 15-year design period are most nearly:
questions.explanation:
First-year ESALs \(=500\times365=182{,}500\). Growth factor \(=[(1.04)^{15}-1]/0.04=(1.8009-1)/0.04=20.02\).

Cumulative \(=182{,}500\times20.02=3.65\times10^6\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics (uniform-series compound-amount factor, \((F/A,i,n)\)); Civil Engineering — Transportation — Highway Pavement Design.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the first-year total only.
  • (B) uses the present-worth factor \((P/A,4\%,15)=11.12\) instead of the compound-amount factor \((F/A)\).
  • (C) ignores growth (\(15\times182{,}500\)).

B – Pavement design · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 13-21

questions.question: A basic freeway segment has a demand flow rate of 1,500 pc/h/ln and an average speed of 62 mph. The density, in pc/mi/ln, is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(D=v_p/S=1500/62=24.2\) pc/mi/ln. (This is in the >18–26 range, LOS C.)

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity.

C – Traffic flow · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-25

questions.question: Traffic approaches a signal at 1,800 veh/h with a density of 40 veh/mi. When the signal turns red, vehicles stop at a jam density of 160 veh/mi. Using \(w=(q_2-q_1)/(k_2-k_1)\), the speed and direction of the shockwave at the rear of the stopped queue are:
questions.explanation:
\(w=(0-1800)/(160-40)=-15\) mph. The negative sign means the boundary of the stopped queue moves upstream (against traffic) at 15 mph.

FE Reference Handbook: not in the Handbook (formula supplied in the question); \(V=DS\) is in Traffic Flow Relationships.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) divides by \(k_j\) alone.
  • (C) has the wrong direction — the back of a growing queue always moves upstream.
  • (D) is the approach speed \(q_1/k_1\), not the wave speed.

C – Traffic flow · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-29

questions.question: A signalized intersection has a total lost time of 12 s per cycle and a sum of critical flow ratios of 0.62. Using Webster’s equation \(C_0=(1.5L+5)/(1-Y)\), the optimum cycle length is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(C_0=(1.5\times12+5)/(1-0.62)=23/0.38=60.5\approx60\) s.

FE Reference Handbook: not in the Handbook (Webster’s equation supplied in the question).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) divides by \(Y\) instead of \(1-Y\).
  • (B) omits the 1.5 multiplier on \(L\).
  • (D) doubles the lost time.

D – Traffic control devices · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-33

questions.question: In a two-mode logit model, the utility of auto is −1.2 and the utility of transit is −1.8. The probability that a traveler chooses auto is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(P(A)=e^{U_A}/(e^{U_A}+e^{U_T})=e^{-1.2}/(e^{-1.2}+e^{-1.8})=0.3012/(0.3012+0.1653)=0.646\approx0.65\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Logit Models.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the transit probability.
  • (B) is the ratio of the utilities 1.2/3.0, which is not how the logit works.
  • (C) is 1.8/3.0.

E – Transportation planning · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-37

questions.question: A transit agency’s ridership has a fare elasticity of −0.3. If fares are raised 20%, ridership is expected to:
questions.explanation:
\(\%\Delta Q=\eta\times\%\Delta P=(-0.3)(+20\%)=-6\%\): ridership falls about 6%.

FE Reference Handbook: not in the Handbook (elasticity definition).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) treats the elasticity as −1.
  • (C) has the wrong sign.
  • (D) divides instead of multiplying.

E – Transportation planning · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-41

questions.question: At a public bid opening, the apparent low bidder’s proposal is complete and properly signed and is accompanied by the required 5% bid bond, but the bidder did not acknowledge Addendum No. 2, which added a section of retaining wall to the work. Which statement is correct?
choices: The bid is nonresponsive and must be rejected.
The bidder is not responsible and must be disqualified from future work.
The bid is valid; the owner simply issues a change order for the retaining wall after award.
The bid is valid because the bid bond cures any defect in the bid form.
questions.explanation:
Acknowledgment of every addendum is a material requirement of the invitation to bid. Without it the owner cannot know that the bidder priced the retaining wall, so the bid fails to conform and is nonresponsive. Responsiveness is judged from the bid documents alone, at the moment of opening.

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) “Responsible” describes the bidder’s capacity, experience, and integrity — nothing here suggests the firm cannot perform.
  • (C) A change order cannot be used to add work the bidder never priced; that would defeat competitive bidding.
  • (D) A bid bond guarantees that a bidder will sign the contract; it does not repair a defective bid.

A – Project administration · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-3

questions.question:
[Matching] Match each document (1–5) with the description (a–e) that fits it. Each is used once.

  • (a) Contractor’s written question to the designer about an ambiguity or conflict in the documents
  • (b) Fabrication information submitted by the contractor for the designer’s review before fabrication
  • (c) Issued to all bidders before bid opening to modify or clarify the bidding documents
  • (d) Project-specific modifications to the standard general conditions
  • (e) Bilateral written modification of contract scope, price, and/or time after award
questions.explanation:
An addendum (1) is issued before bid opening and becomes part of the bidding documents (c). A change order (2) is signed after award by both parties and modifies scope, price, and/or time (e). An RFI (3) is a question, not a change (a). A shop drawing (4) is a contractor submittal reviewed for general conformance with the design intent (b). Supplementary conditions (5) tailor the standard general conditions to the project (d).

The discriminator is timing and direction: addendum = before bids, owner to bidders; change order = after award, bilateral; RFI = contractor to designer, a question; shop drawing = contractor to designer, information; supplementary conditions = part of the contract from the start.

FE Reference Handbook: none.

A – Project administration · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-7

questions.question: A cut yields 1,500 BCY of silty clay that swells 20% and shrinks 12%. The loose volume hauled and the compacted volume it will produce in the embankment are most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[V_{loose}=V_{bank}(1+s_w)=1{,}500(1.20)=1{,}800\ \text{LCY}\] \[V_{compacted}=V_{bank}(1-s_h)=1{,}500(0.88)=1{,}320\ \text{CCY}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Earthwork Formulas (fill is adjusted for shrinkage).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) applies the shrinkage as an increase, \(1{,}500(1.12)=1{,}680\).
  • (C) divides rather than multiplies for swell (\(1{,}500/1.20=1{,}250\)) and then treats shrinkage backwards (\(1{,}500/0.88=1{,}705\)).
  • (D) swaps the two answers; the loose volume must be the largest of the three states and the compacted volume the smallest.

B – Construction operations and methods · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-11

questions.question: Which statement about silt fence is correct?
choices: It is installed along the contour downslope of a disturbed area, where it ponds sheet flow so that sediment settles.
It filters runoff, removing suspended sediment as water passes through the fabric.
It is installed across swales and ditches to trap sediment carried in concentrated flow.
It replaces the need for a sediment basin on drainage areas of any size.
questions.explanation:
Silt fence is a sediment-control BMP installed on the contour, downslope of disturbed ground. It works by ponding sheet flow behind the fabric so that suspended soil settles out; the fabric passes water slowly and is not a filter medium in the usual sense.

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) Overstates the fabric’s role; removal is by settling in the ponded water, not by straining.
  • (C) Is a common field failure — concentrated flow overtops or undermines a silt fence within one storm; check dams, rock lining, or a sediment trap belong in a channel.
  • (D) Silt fence has strict drainage-area and slope-length limits (on the order of 1/4 acre per 100 ft of fence); larger areas need a sediment trap or basin.

B – Construction operations and methods · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-15

questions.question: For the network of Figure 14.12, the total float and free float of activity A are:
questions.explanation:
From the passes above, A has ES 0, EF 2, LS 3, LF 5, so \[TF_A=LS_A-ES_A=3-0=3\ \text{days}\] \[FF_A=\min(ES_{successors})-EF_A=\min(ES_C,ES_D)-EF_A=\min(2,5)-2=0\] A has three days of total float but no free float: any delay to A immediately pushes the early start of C. A’s 3 days of total float are limited by its link to the critical activity D (\(LS_D-EF_A=5-2=3\)). The A–C–E chain itself has 4 days of float, held as free float by E at the end of the chain (\(FF_E=ES_G-EF_E=13-9=4\)).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — Nomenclature (Float); free float is the standard definition stated in Section 14.6.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the answer if you mistake A for critical.
  • (C) sets FF equal to TF, which is only true for the last activity in a float chain.
  • (D) TF = 4 is the float of C and E, not A (A is also tied to the critical activity D); FF = 3 then wrongly equates A’s free float with its total float.

C – Project controls · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 14-19

questions.question: At the status date a project reports a planned value of $540,000, an earned value of $450,000, and an actual cost of $500,000. The cost performance index is:
questions.explanation:
\[CPI=\frac{BCWP}{ACWP}=\frac{EV}{AC}=\frac{450{,}000}{500{,}000}=0.90\] Below 1.0, so the project is spending more than it is earning.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — Earned-Value Analysis, Indices.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.83 is \(EV/PV=450/540\), the schedule performance index.
  • (C) 1.11 inverts the ratio, \(AC/EV\).
  • (D) 1.20 is \(PV/EV\). Earned value is always the numerator of both indices.

C – Project controls · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-23

questions.question: Resource leveling is best described as:
choices: shifting noncritical activities within their available float to smooth the resource histogram without extending the project
adding crews so that every activity is performed at its crash duration
extending the project duration until the daily resource demand never exceeds the available supply
reassigning float from critical activities to noncritical ones
questions.explanation:
Resource leveling shifts noncritical activities within their available float to smooth peaks and valleys in the resource histogram, holding the project duration fixed. Float is the currency: activities with the most float are moved first.

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) Describes an all-crash schedule, a time-cost decision, not leveling.
  • (C) Describes resource-constrained scheduling (resource allocation), which accepts a longer duration when the limit cannot be met within float.
  • (D) Is meaningless — critical activities have no float to give.

C – Project controls · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-27

questions.question: A similar water treatment plant was built for $8.2 million when the applicable construction cost index stood at 520. The index is now 715. Neglecting differences in size and location, the escalated cost is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[C_2=C_1\frac{I_2}{I_1}=8.2\left(\frac{715}{520}\right)=8.2(1.375)=\$11.3\ \text{million}\]
