FE Reference Handbook: Chemical Engineering — Cost Estimation — Cost Indexes (Current $ = Cost in year M × Current Index / Index in year M); cross-referenced from Engineering Economics.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $5.96 million inverts the ratio.
  • (B) $8.20 million ignores escalation entirely.
  • (C) $9.80 million treats the index difference (\(715-520=195\)) as a 19.5% increase; only the ratio of two index values has meaning, never their difference or their absolute size.

D – Construction estimating · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-31

questions.question: From the foundation plan, section, and footing schedule in Figure 14.11, determine the mass of reinforcing steel in one F2 footing. Bars run the full footing width less 75 mm of cover at each end, and 16-mm bars have a mass of 1.58 kg/m.
questions.explanation:
From the footing schedule, an F2 footing is 1500 × 1500 mm with 5-16 mm bars each way, so \(5+5=10\) bars. Section A/S-2 shows 75 mm of cover all sides, so each bar is \[1500-2(75)=1350\ \text{mm}=1.35\ \text{m}\] Mass \(=10(1.35)(1.58)=21.3\) kg.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components — ASTM Standard Reinforcement Bars (bar mass per unit length; the metric bar mass is given on the drawing).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 10.7 kg counts only one direction (5 bars).
  • (C) 23.7 kg uses the full 1.50-m footing width and ignores cover.
  • (D) 42.7 kg counts 5 bars in each of four faces, or doubles the mat.

E – Interpretation of engineering drawings · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-35

questions.question: A circular roadway curve is described by \(x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0\) (units of meters). The radius of the curve is:
questions.explanation:
Match \(x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0\) to the normal form \(x^2+y^2+2ax+2by+c=0\): \(a=-3\), \(b=2\), \(c=-12\). Center \((-a,-b)=(3,-2)\); radius \(r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2-c}=\sqrt{9+4+12}=\sqrt{25}=5.0\) m.

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Conic Section Equation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.0 results from a sign error, \(\sqrt{9+4-12}\).
  • (B) 3.46 is \(\sqrt{12}\), treating the constant as \(r^2\) without completing the square.
  • (D) 25 is \(r^2\), not \(r\).

A – Analytic geometry · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 1-3

questions.question: [Select all that apply] For the curve \(9x^2-16y^2=144\), which of the following statements are true?
choices: The vertices are at \((\pm4,0)\).
The foci are at \((\pm3,0)\).
The curve passes through the origin.
questions.explanation:
Divide by 144: \(x^2/16-y^2/9=1\), so \(a=4\), \(b=3\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Conic Sections, Case 3 (Hyperbola).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the difference of squared terms equal to 1 is the hyperbola standard form (equivalently, \(B^2-4AC=0-4(9)(-16)>0\)).
  • (B) True — vertices at \((\pm a,0)=(\pm4,0)\).
  • (C) True — \(e=\sqrt{1+b^2/a^2}=\sqrt{1+9/16}=\sqrt{25/16}=1.25\).
  • (D) False — foci are at \((\pm ae,0)=(\pm5,0)\), not \((\pm3,0)\); the value 3 is \(b\).
  • (E) False — at the origin, \(0-0=0\neq144\); the curve never comes closer to the origin than the vertices at \(x=\pm4\).

A – Analytic geometry · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 1-7

questions.question: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{e^{2x}-1}{\sin3x}\) equals:
questions.explanation:
At \(x=0\) both numerator and denominator are zero. L’Hôpital: differentiate separately, \[\frac{2e^{2x}}{3\cos3x}\to\frac{2}{3}\quad\text{as }x\to0\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — L’Hospital’s Rule; Mathematics — Derivatives (entries 14, 16).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 1 assumes both go to zero at the same rate.
  • (C) 3/2 is the reciprocal (derivatives assigned to the wrong parts).
  • (D) 2 drops the chain-rule factor 3 on the denominator, \(d(\sin3x)/dx\) taken as \(\cos3x\), giving \(2e^{0}/\cos0=2\).

B – Single-variable calculus · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 1-11

questions.question: Depths in a stream were measured at 2.0-m intervals across the 12-m width shown in Figure 1.8. Using Simpson’s rule, the cross-sectional area of flow is ______ m². [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Seven ordinates at \(\Delta x=2.0\) m give \(n=6\) intervals (even, so Simpson’s rule applies). Coefficient pattern 1, 4, 2, 4, 2, 4, 1: \[\begin{aligned} A&\approx\frac{\Delta x}{3}\left[d_0+4(d_1+d_3+d_5)+2(d_2+d_4)+d_6\right]=\frac{2.0}{3}\left[0+4(1.2+2.6+1.5)+2(2.0+2.4)+0\right]\\ &=\frac{2.0}{3}\left[21.2+8.8\right]=\frac{2.0}{3}(30.0)=20.0\text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}\] For comparison, the trapezoidal rule gives \(2.0\,[0/2+1.2+2.0+2.6+2.4+1.5+0/2]=19.4\) m², slightly lower because the section is concave.

Numerical entry: accepted answer 20.0 m² (range 19.9–20.1). An entry of 19.4 indicates the trapezoidal rule was used instead of Simpson’s.

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Numerical Integration (Simpson’s Rule/Parabolic Rule).

B – Single-variable calculus · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 1-15

questions.question: The angle between \(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{B}=2\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\) is:
questions.explanation:
\(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=(1)(2)+(2)(-2)+(2)(1)=2-4+2=0\). Since neither vector is zero, \(\cos\theta=0\) and \(\theta=90^\circ\); the vectors are perpendicular. (Both have magnitude 3, which is irrelevant once the dot product is zero.)

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Vectors (dot product; Identities).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0° would require \(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|=9\).
  • (B) 45° corresponds to \(\cos\theta=0.707\), i.e., a dot product of 6.4, which does not occur here.
  • (C) 60° corresponds to \(\cos\theta=0.5\), i.e., a dot product of 4.5, which does not occur here.

C – Vector operations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-19

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each vector expression (1–4) with its geometric meaning (a–d), for nonzero vectors \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\).

  • (a) area of the parallelogram with sides \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\)
  • (b) \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are parallel
  • (c) scalar projection of \(\mathbf{B}\) on \(\mathbf{A}\)
  • (d) \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\) are perpendicular
questions.explanation:
1. \(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}=|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\cos\theta=0\) with nonzero vectors means \(\cos\theta=0\): perpendicular — (d).
  2. \(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\sin\theta\,\mathbf{n}=\mathbf{0}\) means \(\sin\theta=0\): parallel — (b).
  3. \(|\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}|=|\mathbf{A}||\mathbf{B}|\sin\theta\) is base × height of the parallelogram — (a).
  4. \(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}/|\mathbf{A}|=|\mathbf{B}|\cos\theta\) is the scalar projection of \(\mathbf{B}\) on \(\mathbf{A}\) — (c).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Vectors (dot product, cross product, Identities).

C – Vector operations · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 1-23

questions.question: Cut lengths of reinforcing bars are normally distributed with mean 6.000 m and standard deviation 4 mm. The specification allows ±6 mm. The percentage of bars that will be rejected is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Tolerance ±6 mm at \(\sigma=4\) mm is \(z=\pm1.5\). The accepted fraction is \(W(1.5)=0.8664\); the rejected fraction is \(1-0.8664=0.1336=13.4\%\) (equivalently \(2R(1.5)=2\times0.0668\)).

FE Reference Handbook: Unit Normal Distribution table (\(W(x)\) and \(R(x)\) columns).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 3.4% is roughly half of one tail.
  • (B) 6.7% is a single tail, \(R(1.5)\), ignoring the short bars.
  • (D) 86.6% is the accepted fraction.

D – Statistics · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 1-27

questions.question: For the data of Question 1-30, the coefficient of determination \(R^2\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\sum y^2=4.41+15.21+38.44+60.84+102.01=220.91\); \(S_{yy}=220.91-30.1^2/5=220.91-181.20=39.71\). \[R^2=\frac{S_{xy}^2}{S_{xx}S_{yy}}=\frac{19.9^2}{(10)(39.71)}=\frac{396.0}{397.1}=0.997\]

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Sample Correlation Coefficient (R) and Coefficient of Determination (R²).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.050 is \(S_{xy}/(S_{xx}S_{yy})\), forgetting to square \(S_{xy}\).
  • (B) 0.501 is \(S_{xy}/S_{yy}\).
  • (D) 1.99 is the least-squares slope \(\hat{b}=S_{xy}/S_{xx}=19.9/10\) from Question 1-30, not a measure of fit; \(R^2\) always lies between 0 and 1. (The correlation coefficient here is \(R=\sqrt{0.997}=0.999\); do not confuse \(R\) with \(R^2\) either.)

D – Statistics · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 1-31

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] For the sample data set \(\{3, 5, 5, 8, 14\}\), match each statistic (1–4) with its value (a–d).

  • (a) 4.30
  • (b) 5
  • (c) 7
  • (d) 11
questions.explanation:
Sorted data: 3, 5, 5, 8, 14; \(n=5\).

  1. Mean \(=(3+5+5+8+14)/5=35/5=7\) — (c).
  2. Median = 3rd value of 5 = 5 — (b).
  3. Range \(=14-3=11\) — (d).
  4. Squared deviations from 7: \(16+4+4+1+49=74\); \(s=\sqrt{74/4}=\sqrt{18.5}=4.30\) — (a).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values.

D – Statistics · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 1-35

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following actions are permitted under the NCEES Rules of Professional Conduct?
choices: A licensee publicly criticizes a proposed dam design, disclosing that a downstream homeowners’ association paid for the licensee’s review and identifying that association as the party on whose behalf the licensee is speaking.
A licensee accepts a fee from both the owner and the equipment vendor for the same pump-station project after full written disclosure to, and agreement by, both parties.
A licensee discloses a client’s confidential soil-contamination data to a regulator when a statute requires the report.
A licensee seals a bridge-rehabilitation drawing set prepared entirely by another firm after a one-day review, because the licensee is confident in that firm’s reputation.
A licensee coordinates a multidisciplinary building project and seals the overall cover sheet, with each technical discipline’s sheets sealed by the licensee responsible for that discipline.
questions.explanation:
Test each action against the specific rule that governs it. Four of the five comply with a stated condition of the Rules; only the sealing of another firm’s completed work, (D), is prohibited.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — 2025–26 Model Rules, Section 240.15, Part A, item 6; Part B, items 2, 3, 4, and 7; Model Law, Section 110.20 E (Responsible Charge).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — Permitted. Part A, item 6 prohibits statements inspired or paid for by interested parties unless the licensee explicitly identifies those parties and reveals any interest; the licensee did both.
  • (B) True — Permitted. Part B, item 7 allows compensation from more than one party for the same project when the circumstances are fully disclosed and agreed to in writing by all interested parties.
  • (C) True — Permitted. Part B, item 4 prohibits revealing confidential information except as authorized or required by law or rules; a statutory reporting requirement is such an exception.
  • (D) False — Not permitted. Part B, item 2 prohibits sealing any document not prepared under the licensee’s responsible charge; a one-day review of another firm’s completed set does not satisfy the four elements of responsible charge, and Model Law 150.10 A.10 makes this a ground for discipline.
  • (E) True — Permitted. Part B, item 3 expressly allows a licensee to coordinate an entire project when each technical segment is sealed by the licensee responsible for it.

A – Codes of ethics · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 2-3

questions.question: In a professional negligence action against a civil engineer, the standard of care against which the engineer’s conduct is measured is best described as:
choices: The degree of care and skill ordinarily exercised by reasonably prudent engineers in the same discipline under similar circumstances.
The highest level of skill attainable by the leading engineers in the discipline.
A design that is completely free of errors and omissions.
Compliance with the minimum requirements of the applicable building code, regardless of site conditions.
questions.explanation:
The professional standard of care is the care and skill ordinarily exercised by reasonably prudent members of the same profession, in the same discipline, under similar circumstances. It is established by comparison with peers, generally through expert testimony.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice (standard of care is general legal doctrine; see also Model Rules 240.15 Part B, item 1 on practicing within competence).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) The standard is ordinary reasonable care, not the best attainable.
  • (C) Perfection is not required; an error that a reasonably prudent engineer might also have made is not negligence, though an engineer who promises an error-free design has contractually raised the bar.
  • (D) Code compliance is evidence of reasonable care but does not define it; a reasonably prudent engineer responds to site conditions the code does not address.

B – Professional liability · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 2-7

questions.question: A candidate received a bachelor’s degree in civil engineering technology from an ETAC/ABET-accredited program, conferred in June 2019, passed the FE exam, and began full-time progressive engineering experience under a licensed engineer on July 1, 2019. The candidate holds no graduate degree. Under the NCEES Model Law, the earliest date on which the candidate satisfies the experience requirement for PE licensure is:
questions.explanation:
The Model Law requires six years of progressive engineering experience after a qualifying degree from an ETAC/ABET-accredited engineering technology bachelor’s program (path c), versus four years for an EAC/ABET engineering degree. Experience is counted from when the qualifying work began, after the degree was conferred: \[\text{July 1, 2019} + 6\text{ years} = \text{July 1, 2025}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — Model Law, Section 130.10 B.2.a(1)(c) and B.2.a(3) Experience Requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Three years applies to an EAC/ABET graduate who also holds an acceptable master’s degree; this candidate has neither.
  • (B) Four years is the EAC/ABET engineering-degree requirement.
  • (C) Five years applies to an ETAC/ABET graduate who also holds an acceptable master’s degree; this candidate has none.

C – Licensure · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 2-11

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a required element of an enforceable contract for engineering services?
choices: An offer and an acceptance of its terms
questions.explanation:
The elements of an enforceable contract are offer, acceptance, consideration, capacity of the parties, and legality of purpose. Notarization is not required for validity; even a writing is required only for the categories covered by the statute of frauds, and a professional-services agreement can in principle be oral, though prudence dictates a written agreement.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice (contract elements are general legal doctrine).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Offer and acceptance together constitute mutual assent, a required element.
  • (B) Consideration is required.
  • (D) Legality is required; an agreement to violate the licensing law, for example, is void.

D – Contracts and contract law · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 2-15

questions.question: A municipality deposits $15,000 in a fund earning 4% per year, compounded annually. The amount in the fund after 10 years is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(F = P\,(F/P, 4\%, 10) = 15{,}000\,(1.04)^{10} = 15{,}000(1.4802) = \$22{,}203 \approx \$22{,}200\). The 4.00% table gives (F/P, 4%, 10) = 1.4802.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Factor Table (Single Payment Compound Amount); Interest Rate Tables, i = 4.00%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $10,100 is \(P\,(P/F, 4\%, 10)\), discounting instead of compounding.
  • (B) $18,200 uses only \((1+i)^5\): \(15{,}000(1.2167) = \$18{,}250\).
  • (C) $21,000 is simple interest, \(15{,}000(1 + 0.04 \times 10)\).

A – Time value of money · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 3-1

questions.question: A construction loan is quoted at 8% nominal annual interest, compounded quarterly. The effective annual interest rate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(i_e = (1 + r/m)^m - 1 = (1 + 0.08/4)^4 - 1 = (1.02)^4 - 1 = 1.0824 - 1 = 8.24\%\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Non-Annual Compounding.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 8.00% is the nominal rate.
  • (B) 8.16% is the effective rate for semiannual compounding, \((1.04)^2 - 1\).
  • (D) 8.30% is the effective rate for monthly compounding, \((1 + 0.08/12)^{12} - 1\).

A – Time value of money · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 3-5

questions.question: A monument requires an initial investment of $1,200,000 and perpetual maintenance of $25,000 per year. At \(i = 5\%\), the capitalized cost of the monument is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Capitalized cost of the perpetual maintenance is \(P = A/i = 25{,}000/0.05 = \$500{,}000\). Total capitalized cost \(= 1{,}200{,}000 + 500{,}000 = \$1{,}700{,}000\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Capitalized Costs.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $1,200,000 omits the maintenance entirely.
  • (B) $1,450,000 adds only 10 years of maintenance undiscounted.
  • (D) $2,200,000 adds 40 years of maintenance undiscounted.

A – Time value of money · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 3-9

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A general contractor is analyzing the costs of a building project. Which of the following statements are correct?
choices: The wages of a crane operator assigned full time to the project are direct labor.
The salary of the home-office accountant is direct labor for the project.
The annual lease on the contractor’s main office is a fixed cost.
The interest the contractor’s cash could have earned had it not been tied up in equipment for the project is an opportunity cost.
The cost of a feasibility study completed last year is an opportunity cost of the project.
questions.explanation:
Labor traceable to a specific project is direct labor; overhead support staff are indirect labor. A lease incurred regardless of the volume of work is fixed. Forgone interest is the opportunity cost of capital, and a completed, paid-for study is sunk.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — cost concepts (fundamental definitions).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — labor traceable to a specific project is direct labor.
  • (B) False — the accountant supports all projects and is indirect labor charged through overhead.
  • (C) True — the lease is incurred regardless of the volume of work, so it is fixed.
  • (D) True — forgone interest is the classic opportunity cost of capital.
  • (E) False — a completed and paid-for study is a sunk cost, not an opportunity cost.

B – Cost · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 3-13

questions.question: For the photovoltaic array of Question 3-16, the discounted payback period at \(i = 6\%\) per year is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Discounted payback is the smallest \(n\) for which \(22{,}500\,(P/A, 6\%, n) \geq 180{,}000\), i.e., \((P/A, 6\%, n) \geq 8.000\). Scanning the P/A column of the 6.00% table: \(n = 11\) gives 7.8869 (\(22{,}500 \times 7.8869 = \$177{,}455 < \$180{,}000\)); \(n = 12\) gives 8.3838 (\(\$188{,}636 > \$180{,}000\)). The discounted payback period is 12 years.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Breakeven Analysis (payback period); Interest Rate Tables, i = 6.00%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 8 years is the simple payback, which ignores interest.
  • (B) 11 years falls short: the present worth of 11 years of savings is $177,455.
  • (D) 15 years is longer than necessary.

C – Analyses · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 3-17

questions.question: In one year a small engineering firm has revenue of $90,000, operating expenses of $30,000, and depreciation of $25,000 on its equipment. The income-tax rate is 30%. The firm’s after-tax cash flow for the year is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Taxable income \(= R - E - D = 90{,}000 - 30{,}000 - 25{,}000 = \$35{,}000\). Tax \(= 0.30 \times 35{,}000 = \$10{,}500\). Depreciation is not a cash flow, so after-tax cash flow \(= (R - E) - \text{Tax} = 60{,}000 - 10{,}500 = \$49{,}500\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Taxation; Depreciation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $24,500 is taxable income less tax—it wrongly subtracts depreciation from the cash flow.
  • (B) $40,500 leaves the operating expenses out of the tax calculation, taxing \(R - D = \$65{,}000\) (tax $19,500) and subtracting that from $60,000.
  • (C) $42,000 taxes the full $60,000 without the depreciation deduction.

C – Analyses · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 3-21

questions.question: Two forces act on a bracket: 150 lb along the positive \(x\)-axis and 200 lb at 120° counterclockwise from the positive \(x\)-axis. The magnitude of the resultant is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\Sigma F_x = 150 + 200\cos 120^\circ = 150 - 100 = 50\) lb; \(\Sigma F_y = 200\sin 120^\circ = 173.2\) lb. \[F = \sqrt{50^2 + 173.2^2} = 180.3\,\text{lb}\] at \(\theta = \arctan(173.2/50) = 73.9^\circ\) from the positive \(x\)-axis.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Resultant (Two Dimensions).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the magnitude of the difference of the two magnitudes;
  • (C) results from treating the forces as perpendicular (\(\sqrt{150^2 + 200^2}\));
  • (D) is the arithmetic sum of the magnitudes, correct only for collinear forces.

A – Resultants of force systems · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 4-1

questions.question: A 500-N force directed 30° above the positive \(x\)-axis is applied at the point (0.8, 0.3) m. The moment of the force about the origin is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(F_x = 500\cos 30^\circ = 433.0\) N, \(F_y = 500\sin 30^\circ = 250.0\) N. Using \(M_z = xF_y - yF_x\) with \((x, y) = (0.8, 0.3)\) m: \[M_O = 0.8(250.0) - 0.3(433.0) = 200.0 - 129.9 = 70.1\,\text{N·m}\] Positive means counterclockwise.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Moments (Couples).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) keeps only the \(xF_y\) term;
  • (C) keeps only the \(-yF_x\) term;
  • (D) adds the two terms instead of subtracting, ignoring the sign of the second.

B – Equivalent force systems · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 4-5

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about equivalent force systems are true?
choices: A force together with a couple whose moment is perpendicular to the force can always be replaced by a single force.
A wrench consists of a force and a couple whose moment vector is parallel to the force.
A force can be moved to a parallel line of action without changing the external effect on a rigid body, provided no couple is added.
The moment of a couple is the same about every point in space.
Any general three-dimensional force system can be reduced to a single force.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), and (D) are true; (C) and (E) are false.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Moments (Couples); Systems of Forces.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — sliding the force a distance \(M/F\) perpendicular to both the force and the moment absorbs the couple entirely; this is why coplanar and parallel systems reduce to a single force.
  • (B) True — that is the definition of a wrench.
  • (C) False — moving a force off its line of action changes the moment; a couple \(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\) must be added to keep the systems equivalent.
  • (D) True — a couple is a free vector.
  • (E) False — a general 3-D system reduces to a wrench (force plus parallel couple), which is a single force only when the parallel couple component happens to be zero.

B – Equivalent force systems · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-9

questions.question: An 800-lb sign hangs from a ring supported by two cables. Cable 1 rises to the left at 30° above horizontal and cable 2 rises to the right at 60° above horizontal. The tension in cable 1 is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Equilibrium of the ring (concurrent forces): \(\Sigma F_x = -T_1\cos 30^\circ + T_2\cos 60^\circ = 0\), so \(T_2 = T_1\cos 30^\circ/\cos 60^\circ = 1.732T_1\). \(\Sigma F_y = T_1\sin 30^\circ + T_2\sin 60^\circ - 800 = 0\): \[0.5T_1 + 1.732(0.866)T_1 = 800 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2.0T_1 = 800 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_1 = 400\,\text{lb}\] and \(T_2 = 693\) lb. (Because the cables are 90° apart, each tension is simply \(W\) times the sine of its own angle: \(T_1 = 800\sin 30^\circ\).)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements; Concurrent Forces.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) uses \(T_1 = W\tan 30^\circ = 800/\sqrt{3}\) (tangent instead of sine of the cable’s own angle);
  • (C) is the tension in cable 2;
  • (D) assumes cable 1 carries the whole weight.

C – Equilibrium of rigid bodies · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-13

questions.question: For the Pratt truss in Figure 4.17, loaded at the top-chord joints F, G, and H, the number of zero-force members is:
questions.explanation:
At joint B, members AB and BC are collinear, BF is the third member, and no load or reaction acts at B, so BF is a zero-force member. Joint D is identical (DH is zero-force). Joint G has the collinear chords FG and GH plus CG, but the 30-kN load acts at G, so CG is not zero-force (it carries 30 kN in compression). Joint C has five members and no rule applies. Two zero-force members: BF and DH.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Statically Determinate Truss.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) misses both BF and DH;
  • (B) misses one of BF and DH;
  • (D) incorrectly counts CG, which carries the load applied at G.

D – Frames and trusses · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 4-17

questions.question: The frame in Figure 4.18 consists of vertical member AB (3 m) and horizontal member BC (4 m), pinned together at B and pinned to the supports at A and C. A 6-kN horizontal force acts at D, the midpoint of AB, and an 8-kN vertical force acts at E, the midpoint of BC. The magnitude of the horizontal reaction at C is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Member BC carries the 8-kN load at its midpoint and is pinned at both ends, so it is a three-force member. Its FBD: \(B_x\), \(B_y\) at B (0, 3); \(C_x\), \(C_y\) at C (4, 3); 8 kN down at (2, 3). Moments about B: \(C_y(4) - 8(2) = 0\), so \(C_y = 4\) kN.

Whole frame, moments about A (counterclockwise positive), with \(C_x\) assumed to act in the \(+x\) direction at (4, 3) and \(C_y = 4\) kN up: \[\Sigma M_A = 4C_y - 3C_x - 8(2) - 6(1.5) = 16 - 3C_x - 16 - 9 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad C_x = -3\,\text{kN}\] The horizontal reaction at C is 3 kN (directed to the left). Then \(A_x = -6 - C_x = -3\) kN and \(A_y = 8 - 4 = 4\) kN.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) would be correct if C were a roller, but C is a pin;
  • (C) is the vertical reaction at C;
  • (D) assumes C resists the entire 6-kN horizontal load, ignoring the pin at A.

D – Frames and trusses · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 4-21

questions.question: A right triangle has legs of 9 in along the \(x\)-axis and 6 in along the \(y\)-axis, with the right angle at the origin. The \(y\)-coordinate of its centroid is:
questions.explanation:
For a right triangle with the right angle at the origin, the Handbook table gives the centroid at one-third of each leg from the right angle: \(y_c = h/3 = 6/3 = 2\) in (and \(x_c = b/3 = 3\) in).

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — table of area properties (right triangle).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is \(x_c\);
  • (C) is \(2h/3\), measured from the wrong vertex;
  • (D) is \(b/2\).

E – Centroid of area · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 4-25

questions.question: A rectangular concrete section is 300 mm wide and 500 mm deep. Its moment of inertia about a horizontal axis along its base is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a rectangle about its base the table gives \(I_x = bh^3/3\): \[I_x = \frac{300(500)^3}{3} = 1.25 \times 10^{10} = 12.5 \times 10^9\,\text{mm}^4\]

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — table of area properties (rectangle).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(I_{y_c} = 500(300)^3/12\);
  • (B) is the centroidal value \(bh^3/12\);
  • (C) uses the base formula with the width and depth interchanged, \(500(300)^3/3\) (the cube must go on the dimension perpendicular to the axis).

F – Area moments of inertia · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 4-29

questions.question: A 20-kg crate rests on a ramp inclined at 25° to the horizontal; \(\mu_s = 0.50\) between crate and ramp. The minimum force parallel to the ramp required to start the crate moving up the ramp is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(W = 20(9.81) = 196.2\) N. First check that the crate is at rest without a push: \(\tan 25^\circ = 0.466 < 0.50\), so it does not slide by itself. For impending motion up the ramp, friction acts down the ramp at its limiting value \(\mu_s N\) with \(N = W\cos 25^\circ\): \[P = W\sin 25^\circ + \mu_s W\cos 25^\circ = 196.2(0.4226 + 0.50 \times 0.9063) = 196.2(0.8758) = 172\,\text{N}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Friction.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses the 20-kg mass as if it were the weight in newtons (omits \(g\)): \(20(0.8758) = 17.5\);
  • (B) is \(W\sin\theta\) alone (a frictionless ramp);
  • (C) is \(\mu_s W\cos\theta\) alone.

G – Static friction · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 4-33

questions.question: [Point-and-click] The truss in Figure 4.22 is a statically determinate plane truss loaded only at joints J2, J3 and J4. Five of its members carry the circled labels (A) through (E). Name the labeled region that marks the member carrying zero force.
questions.explanation:
Look for the standard zero-force patterns before computing anything. Joint J7 carries no external load and joins exactly three members: the two top-chord members J6–J7 and J7–J8, which are collinear, and the vertical J3–J7. Summing forces perpendicular to the collinear pair leaves only the vertical, so \[F_{J3J7} = 0\] Region (C) marks that vertical.

A method-of-joints sweep confirms that no other labeled member is unloaded. By symmetry the reactions are \(R_{J1} = R_{J5} = (20 + 10 + 20)/2 = 25\) kN. The diagonals rise 4 m over 3 m, so their length is 5 m and their direction cosines are (0.6, 0.8).

At J1: \(25 + 0.8F_{J1J6} = 0 \Rightarrow F_{J1J6} = -31.25\) kN (compression), and \(F_{J1J2} = 18.75\) kN (tension). At J2 the vertical takes the panel load, \(F_{J2J6} = 20\) kN. At J6, vertical equilibrium gives \(25 - 20 - 0.8F_{J6J3} = 0\), so \(F_{J6J3} = +6.25\) kN (tension); horizontal equilibrium then gives \(F_{J6J7} = -22.5\) kN (compression). At J3, with \(F_{J3J7} = 0\), horizontal equilibrium gives \(F_{J3J4} = 18.75\) kN (tension).

Why the other labels are wrong: (A) is the end diagonal J1–J6, which carries the whole 25-kN reaction into the truss at −31.25 kN. (B) is the top chord J6–J7 at −22.5 kN. (D) is the diagonal J6–J3 at +6.25 kN — small, but not zero, because the 20-kN load at J2 is smaller than the vertical component the end diagonal delivers to J6. (E) is the bottom chord J3–J4 at +18.75 kN.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Plane Truss: Method of Joints; Statically Determinate Truss.

D – Frames and trusses · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-37

questions.question: A projectile is fired on level ground with an initial speed of 120 ft/s at 30° above the horizontal. Using \(g = 32.2\) ft/s² and neglecting air resistance, the horizontal range is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
On level ground the time of flight follows from \(y = 0\): \(0 = -\tfrac12 gt^2 + v_0\sin\theta\,t\), so \(t = 2v_0\sin\theta/g = 2(120)(0.5)/32.2 = 3.727\) s. Range \(= v_0\cos\theta\,t = 120(0.8660)(3.727) = 387\) ft. (Equivalently \(v_0^2\sin 2\theta/g = 14400(0.8660)/32.2 = 387\) ft.)

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Projectile Motion.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 194 ft omits the factor of 2 in the time of flight (it is \(v_0^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g\)).
  • (B) 224 ft is \(v_0^2\sin\theta/g\).
  • (D) 447 ft is \(v_0^2/g\), dropping the trigonometric factor entirely.

A – Kinematics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-4

questions.question: A solid-cylinder flywheel has a mass of 500 kg and a diameter of 1.2 m. Its mass moment of inertia about its axis of rotation is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a solid cylinder about its longitudinal axis, \(I = MR^2/2\) with \(R = 0.6\) m: \(I = \tfrac12(500)(0.6)^2 = 90\) kg·m².

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — table of mass moments of inertia (solid circular cylinder, \(I_{y_c} = MR^2/2\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 180 is \(MR^2\), the thin-ring formula.
  • (C) 270 is \(3MR^2/2\), the value about a parallel axis tangent to the rim; the parallel-axis shift does not apply because the flywheel rotates about its own centerline.
  • (D) 360 is \(MD^2/2\), using the diameter in place of the radius.

B – Mass moments of inertia · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 5-8

questions.question: A highway curve of radius 300 m is to be banked so that a vehicle traveling at 100 km/h requires no friction force to stay on the curve. Using \(g = 9.81\) m/s², the required banking angle is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(v = 100/3.6 = 27.78\) m/s. With no friction, \(\tan\theta = v^2/(gR) = 27.78^2/[(9.81)(300)] = 771.6/2943 = 0.2622\), so \(\theta = \arctan(0.2622) = 14.7^\circ\).

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Normal and Tangential Kinetics for Planar Problems (\(\Sigma F_n = mv^2/\rho\)); Particle Kinetics.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 15.2° is \(\arcsin(0.2622)\) instead of arctan.
  • (C) 27.7° is \(\arctan(0.5244)\), the angle whose tangent is twice the correct value (an extra factor of 2 in \(v^2/gR\)).
  • (D) 73.6° results from using 100 km/h directly in \(v^2/gR\) without converting to m/s.

C – Force acceleration · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-12

questions.question: A 2-kg collar is released from rest and falls 0.5 m before striking the free end of a vertical spring of stiffness 800 N/m, which is undeformed before contact. Using \(g = 9.81\) m/s², the maximum compression of the spring is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Take the datum at maximum compression \(x\). Between release (1) and maximum compression (2), \(T_1 = T_2 = 0\); the collar drops \(0.5 + x\); the spring goes from undeformed to compression \(x\). Conservation of energy, \(T_2 + V_2 = T_1 + V_1\): \[0 + \tfrac12(800)x^2 = 0 + 2(9.81)(0.5 + x)\] \[400x^2 - 19.62x - 9.81 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = \frac{19.62 + \sqrt{19.62^2 + 4(400)(9.81)}}{800} = \frac{19.62 + 126.8}{800} = 0.183\ \text{m} = 183\ \text{mm}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Principle of Work and Energy; Potential Energy; Elastic Potential Energy.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 25 mm is the static deflection \(mg/k\), which is the equilibrium compression, not the maximum dynamic one.
  • (B) 49 mm is \(2mg/k\), the maximum compression if the collar were released from rest at the spring’s free end (zero drop height).
  • (C) 157 mm omits the work of gravity during the compression itself (solving \(\tfrac12 kx^2 = mgh\)).

D – Work, energy, and power · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 5-16

questions.question: A 10-ft simply supported beam carries a single 12-kip concentrated load 3 ft from the left support. The maximum bending moment is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Reactions: \(R_A = Pb/L = 12(7)/10 = 8.4\) kip, \(R_B = 3.6\) kip. The shear is constant at +8.4 kip to the load and \(-3.6\) kip beyond, so the moment peaks under the load: \(M_{max} = R_Aa = 8.4(3) = 25.2\) kip·ft. Equivalently, \(Pab/L = 12(3)(7)/10 = 25.2\) kip·ft from the beam table.

FE Reference Handbook: Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections (\(M_{max} = Pab/L\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 30.0 kip·ft is \(PL/4\), the midspan-load formula.
  • (C) 36.0 kip·ft is \(P\times a\) with no reaction computed.
  • (D) 84.0 kip·ft is \(P\times b\), the load times the longer segment, again with no reaction computed.

A – Shear and moment diagrams · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 6-2

questions.question: The shear force at the left support of a 6-m simply supported beam carrying a uniformly distributed load is +24 kN. The maximum bending moment in the beam is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a uniform load the shear is linear from +24 kN at the left support to zero at midspan (3 m). The change in moment equals the area under the shear diagram: \(M_{max} = \tfrac{1}{2}(3)(24) = 36\) kN·m. Alternatively, \(wL/2 = 24\) gives \(w = 8\) kN/m and \(wL^2/8 = 8(36)/8 = 36\) kN·m.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Beams (\(M_2 - M_1 = \int V\,dx\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 72 kN·m is the full triangle area over 6 m instead of 3 m (the shear reverses sign at midspan).
  • (C) 144 kN·m is \(VL\).
  • (D) 288 kN·m is \(wL^2\) with \(w = 8\) kN/m, omitting the factor 1/8.

A – Shear and moment diagrams · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 6-6

questions.question: A hollow circular shaft has an outside diameter of 100 mm and an inside diameter of 60 mm. It transmits a torque of 8 kN·m. The maximum shear stress in the shaft is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(J = \pi(100^4 - 60^4)/32 = \pi(1.0\times10^8 - 1.296\times10^7)/32 = 8.545\times10^6\) mm4. \(\tau_{max} = Tr/J = 8\times10^6(50)/8.545\times10^6 = 46.8\) MPa.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Torsion (\(\tau = Tr/J\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 28.1 MPa uses the inner radius (30 mm) instead of the outer radius.
  • (B) 40.7 MPa uses the \(J\) of a solid 100-mm shaft.
  • (D) 93.6 MPa uses the diameter in place of the radius.

B – Stresses and strains · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 6-10

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A steel plate (\(E = 200\) GPa, \(\nu = 0.30\)) is in plane stress with \(\sigma_x = 120\) MPa and \(\sigma_y = 40\) MPa (both tension) and no shear stress. The normal strain in the \(x\) direction is ______ \(\times10^{-6}\).
questions.explanation:
Plane-stress Hooke’s law: \(\varepsilon_x = (\sigma_x - \nu\sigma_y)/E = [120 - 0.30(40)]/200{,}000 = 108/200{,}000 = 5.40\times10^{-4} = 540\times10^{-6}\). (Note \(\varepsilon_y = [40 - 0.3(120)]/200{,}000 = 20\times10^{-6}\) and \(\varepsilon_z = -0.3(160)/200{,}000 = -240\times10^{-6}\); the plate thins even though \(\sigma_z = 0\).)

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Hooke’s Law (plane stress case).

B – Stresses and strains · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-14

questions.question: A 3-m cantilever beam with \(EI = 12{,}000\) kN·m2 carries a uniformly distributed load of 8 kN/m over its full length. The deflection at the free end is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Cantilever with uniform load: \(v_{max} = wL^4/8EI = 8(3)^4/[8(12{,}000)] = 648/96{,}000 = 0.00675\) m \(= 6.75\) mm.

FE Reference Handbook: Cantilevered Beam Slopes and Deflections.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.70 mm uses the simply supported beam formula \(5wL^4/384EI = 5(8)(3)^4/[384(12{,}000)] = 0.70\) mm instead of the cantilever case.
  • (B) 1.80 mm uses the cantilever formula for a triangular load (zero at the free end), \(w_0L^4/30EI = 648/360{,}000 = 1.80\) mm, instead of the uniform-load case.
  • (C) 5.63 mm replaces the uniform load by its 24-kN resultant acting as a point load at midlength, \(Pa^2(3L - a)/6EI\) with \(a = 1.5\) m. A resultant is valid for reactions, not for deflections.

C – Deformations · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-18

questions.question: An aluminum bar (\(E = 69\) GPa, \(\alpha = 23.6\times10^{-6}/^\circ\text{C}\)) is held rigidly between two immovable supports at zero stress. Its temperature then rises 40°C. The stress in the bar is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Fully restrained: \(\alpha L\Delta T = PL/AE\) gives \(\sigma = E\alpha\Delta T = 69{,}000(23.6\times10^{-6})(40) = 65.1\) MPa compression.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Thermal Deformations; Uniaxial Loading and Deformation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is wrong because the supports prevent expansion, so stress develops.
  • (B) 24.5 MPa uses the shear modulus of aluminum (\(G = 26\) GPa) in place of \(E\).
  • (C) 32.6 MPa halves the result (e.g., using \(\Delta T = 20^\circ\)C).

C – Deformations · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-22

questions.question: A thin-walled cylindrical pressure vessel has an inside diameter of 48 in. and a wall thickness of 0.5 in. It contains gas at 200 psi. Using the mean radius as in the Handbook, the hoop stress in the wall is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(r_i = 24\) in, \(r_o = 24.5\) in, \(r = 24.25\) in. \(\sigma_t = pr/t = 200(24.25)/0.5 = 9700\) psi \(= 9.7\) ksi. (\(t/r = 0.02\), so thin-wall theory applies.)

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Cylindrical Pressure Vessel (thin-walled, \(\sigma_t = pr/t\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 2.4 ksi is \(pr/2t\) with an additional halving.
  • (B) 4.85 ksi is the axial stress \(pr/2t\).
  • (D) 19.4 ksi uses the diameter in place of the radius.

D – Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-26

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A plane-stress element has \(\sigma_x = 40\) MPa, \(\sigma_y = 40\) MPa (both tension), and \(\tau_{xy} = 0\). Which statements are correct?
choices: Every direction in the plane is a principal direction.
The maximum in-plane shear stress is zero.
The absolute maximum shear stress at the point is zero.
Mohr’s circle for the in-plane stresses degenerates to a single point.
The normal stress on a plane inclined at 45° to the \(x\) axis is 20 MPa.
questions.explanation:
\(C = 40\) MPa, \(R = \sqrt{0 + 0} = 0\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Mohr’s Circle—Stress, 2D.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — with \(R = 0\) the normal stress is 40 MPa and the shear is zero on every in-plane orientation.
  • (B) True — \(\tau_{in} = R = 0\).
  • (C) False — \(\sigma_3 = 0\) (free surface), so \(\tau_{max} = (40 - 0)/2 = 20\) MPa on planes inclined 45° to the surface.
  • (D) True — the circle has zero radius.
  • (E) False — the normal stress on any in-plane orientation, including 45°, is \(C = 40\) MPa.

D – Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 6-30

questions.question: An aluminum-alloy rod 10.0 mm in diameter and 250 mm long carries an axial tensile load of 8.00 kN and elongates 0.364 mm within the elastic range. The modulus of elasticity of the alloy is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A_0=\pi(10.0)^2/4=78.54\,\text{mm}^2\). \(\sigma=8{,}000\,\text{N}/78.54\,\text{mm}^2=101.9\,\text{MPa}\). \(\varepsilon=0.364/250=1.456\times10^{-3}\). \[E=\sigma/\varepsilon=101.9/0.001456=69{,}960\,\text{MPa}\approx 70\,\text{GPa}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Properties of Materials — Mechanical.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) results from doubling the area (using \(\pi d^2/2\)), which halves the stress.
  • (C) is twice the correct value, from halving the area (using \(\pi d^2/8\)) or the strain.
  • (D) is the modulus of steel, not aluminum.

C – Physical and mechanical properties · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 7-1

questions.question: Which test is used to determine the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature of a structural steel?
choices: Brinell hardness test at several loads
Tension test at several strain rates
Charpy V-notch impact test at several temperatures
questions.explanation:
The Handbook states that the Charpy impact test finds the energy required to fracture and identifies the ductile-to-brittle transition; tests are repeated over a range of temperatures.

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Impact Test.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Hardness measures penetration resistance.
  • (B) Fatigue tests give the S-N curve.
  • (C) Strain rate affects the transition but a tension test does not define it.

B – Test methods · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 7-5

questions.question: A steel operates in the steady-state creep regime with stress sensitivity \(n=4\). If the applied stress is increased by 50% at constant temperature, the steady-state creep rate increases by a factor of most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Steady-state creep: \(\dot\varepsilon=A\sigma^n e^{-Q/(RT)}\). At constant \(T\), \(\dot\varepsilon_2/\dot\varepsilon_1=(\sigma_2/\sigma_1)^n=(1.5)^4=5.06\approx5.1\).

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Properties of Materials — Mechanical (Creep).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \((1.5)^{1/4}=1.107\), applying the exponent as \(1/n\) (as in the Basquin form) instead of \(n\).
  • (B) assumes the rate is linear in stress.
  • (C) is \(n\) itself.

C – Physical and mechanical properties · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 7-9

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about wood as a structural material are correct?
choices: Strength and stiffness are greater parallel to the grain than perpendicular to it.
Below the fiber saturation point (about 30% moisture content), drying causes shrinkage and increases strength.
Wood is isotropic, so a single modulus of elasticity applies in all directions.
Increasing the moisture content from 10% to 18% increases the bending strength.
Moisture content is expressed as the mass of water divided by the oven-dry mass of the wood.
questions.explanation:
Wood is strongest and stiffest parallel to grain, its properties change with moisture only below the fiber saturation point, and moisture content is referred to oven-dry mass.

FE Reference Handbook: not covered (definitions from this chapter).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the aligned fiber structure makes wood far stronger and stiffer parallel to grain.
  • (B) True — above the fiber saturation point only free water is lost with no property change; below it, bound water leaves, causing shrinkage and strength gain.
  • (C) False — wood is strongly anisotropic (orthotropic), with different moduli longitudinally, radially, and tangentially.
  • (D) False — raising moisture content below the fiber saturation point decreases strength.
  • (E) True — moisture content is referred to oven-dry mass, as for soils.

C – Physical and mechanical properties · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 7-13

questions.question: Which of the following changes to a concrete mix will most reliably increase its 28-day compressive strength?
choices: Reducing the water-cement ratio while maintaining workability with a superplasticizer
Adding water at the truck to raise the slump from 3 in to 5 in
Increasing the entrained air content from 4% to 7%
Storing the test cylinders in laboratory air instead of the moist room
questions.explanation:
Water-cement ratio is the primary factor controlling strength; lowering it raises strength, and a superplasticizer restores the workability lost.

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Concrete.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) Adding water without cement raises w/c and lowers strength.
  • (C) Each additional percent of entrained air lowers strength (the Handbook figure shows the air-entrained curve below the non-air-entrained curve).
  • (D) The Handbook curing figure shows that air-stored concrete reaches far lower strength than moist-cured concrete.

A – Mix design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 7-17

questions.question: Using the Handbook (ACI 318) expression, the modulus of elasticity of a concrete with unit weight 150 lb/ft³ and \(f'_c=4{,}000\) psi is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[E_c=33\,w_c^{1.5}\sqrt{f'_c}=33(150)^{1.5}\sqrt{4{,}000}=33(1{,}837.1)(63.25)=3.83\times10^{6}\ \text{psi}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components (ACI 318-14) — Definitions (\(E_c\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) \(3.13\times10^5\) uses \(w_c^{1.0}\) instead of \(w_c^{1.5}\) (\(33\times150\times63.25\)).
  • (B) \(4.70\times10^5\) multiplies \(w_c\) by 1.5 instead of raising it to the 1.5 power (\(33\times225\times63.25\)).
  • (C) \(3.60\times10^6\) is \(57{,}000\sqrt{f'_c}\), the normal-weight shortcut that assumes \(w_c=145\) pcf rather than the 150 pcf given.

C – Physical and mechanical properties · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 7-21

questions.question: An oil has a density of 850 kg/m³. Its specific weight is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\gamma=\rho g=850\ \text{kg/m}^3\times9.81\ \text{m/s}^2=8{,}339\ \text{N/m}^3\approx8.34\ \text{kN/m}^3\).

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Definitions — Density, Specific Volume, Specific Weight, and Specific Gravity.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the specific gravity (0.85) mislabeled with units.
  • (C) is the specific weight of water.
  • (D) uses the USCS value \(g = 32.2\) ft/s² with the SI density: \(850(32.2) = 27{,}370\) N/m³ \(= 27.4\) kN/m³. In SI, \(g = 9.81\) m/s².

B – Fluid properties · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 8-1

questions.question: A liquid has a specific gravity of 1.26. Its mass density in USCS consistent units is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\rho=SG\,\rho_w=1.26(1.94\ \text{slug/ft}^3)=2.44\ \text{slug/ft}^3\) (water: \(62.4/32.2=1.94\)).

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Definitions; Properties of Water (English Units) (mass density column).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) treats SG as if it were already in slugs.
  • (C) is the specific weight of water in lbf/ft³.
  • (D) is the specific weight of the liquid (\(1.26\times62.4\)), not its mass density.

B – Fluid properties · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 8-5

questions.question: The vertical gate in Figure 8.10 is 4 ft wide and 6 ft tall, hinged along its top edge, which is 2 ft below the water surface (\(\gamma=62.4\) lb/ft³). It is held closed by a horizontal force \(P\) applied at the bottom edge. Neglecting the gate’s weight, the force \(P\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Centroid depth \(h_C=2+3=5\) ft; \(A=24\) ft². \(F_R=62.4(5)(24)=7{,}488\) lb.

Center of pressure: \(I_{xC}=4(6)^3/12=72\) ft\(^4\); \(h_{CP}=5+72/[5(24)]=5.6\) ft below the surface, i.e., 3.6 ft below the hinge.

Moments about the hinge: \(P(6)=7{,}488(3.6)\), so \(P=4{,}493\ \text{lb}\approx4{,}490\) lb.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Forces on Submerged Surfaces and the Center of Pressure; Statics — Moment of Inertia (Area).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses a 2-ft lever arm (the hinge’s depth below the surface) in place of the 3.6-ft distance from the hinge to the center of pressure.
  • (B) applies the force at the centroid (3 ft below the hinge).
  • (D) is the full hydrostatic force, ignoring the moment balance.

C – Fluid statics · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 8-9

questions.question: Water flows at 2.0 m/s in a 200-mm pipe that reduces to a 100-mm pipe. The velocity in the 100-mm pipe is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(v_2=v_1(D_1/D_2)^2=2.0(200/100)^2=8.0\) m/s.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Principles of One-Dimensional Fluid Flow — The Continuity Equation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) inverts the ratio.
  • (B) ignores the change.
  • (C) scales with diameter instead of diameter squared.

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 8-13

questions.question: Oil with dynamic viscosity 0.20 Pa·s and density 900 kg/m³ flows at \(5.0\times10^{-5}\) m³/s through a 20-mm-diameter tube 10 m long. The flow is laminar. The pressure drop due to friction is ______ kPa. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Check the regime: \(v=Q/A=5.0\times10^{-5}/[\pi(0.02)^2/4]=0.159\) m/s; \(Re=\rho vD/\mu=900(0.159)(0.020)/0.20=14\), laminar. \[\Delta P_f=\frac{128\mu LQ}{\pi D^4}=\frac{128(0.20)(10)(5.0\times10^{-5})}{\pi(0.020)^4}=25{,}460\ \text{Pa}=25.5\ \text{kPa}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Consequences of Fluid Flow — Pressure Drop for Laminar Flow (Hagen-Poiseuille).

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-17

questions.question: A 50-mm-diameter water jet (\(\rho=1{,}000\) kg/m³) at 20 m/s strikes a fixed flat plate at right angles. The force on the plate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A=\pi(0.05)^2/4=0.001963\) m²; \(Q=Av=0.03927\) m³/s. Fixed blade with \(\alpha=90°\): \(F_x=Q\rho v_1=0.03927(1{,}000)(20)=785\) N.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Deflectors and Blades — Fixed Blade; The Impulse-Momentum Principle.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is a decimal error.
  • (B) is half the answer, from \(\rho v^2A/2\) (a dynamic pressure, not a momentum flux).
  • (D) is double, appropriate for a jet reversed through 180°.

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-21

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each measuring device (1–4) with the relation that governs it (a–d).

  • (a) \(Q=CH^{5/2}\)
  • (b) \(v=\sqrt{2(P_0-P_s)/\rho}\)
  • (c) \(Q=CA_0\sqrt{2gh}\) with \(C\approx0.61\)
  • (d) \(Q=\dfrac{C_vA_2}{\sqrt{1-(A_2/A_1)^2}}\sqrt{2g\,\Delta h}\)
pairs: Sharp-edged orifice discharging from a tank
questions.explanation:
The pitot tube converts velocity head to stagnation pressure, (b). The venturi combines Bernoulli and continuity with the approach-velocity factor \(1/\sqrt{1-(A_2/A_1)^2}\), (d). A sharp-edged orifice discharging from a tank uses \(Q=CA_0\sqrt{2gh}\) with \(C\approx0.61\), (c). The V-notch weir discharge varies as \(H^{5/2}\), (a).

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Fluid Flow Measurement — Pitot Tubes; Venturi Meters; Orifices; Orifice Discharging Freely into Atmosphere; Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Weir Formulas.

A – Flow measurement · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-25

questions.question: [Point-and-click] Figure 8.11 shows a pump lifting 20 °C water from a sump to an elevated delivery tank. All of the elevations, losses and heads needed are printed on the figure. Five points in the system carry the circled labels (A) through (E). Name the labeled point at which cavitation is most likely to begin.
questions.explanation:
Cavitation begins wherever the absolute pressure falls to the vapor pressure of the liquid, so work out the absolute pressure head at each labeled point with the energy equation, starting from the sump surface (absolute head 10.33 m, velocity negligible): \[\frac{p}{\gamma}=H_{pa}-\Delta z-\sum h_L-\frac{V^2}{2g}\]

    1. sump surface: \(p/\gamma=10.33\) m (atmospheric).
    1. \(10.33-3.0-1.2-0.30=5.83\) m.
    1. pump suction flange: \(10.33-6.5-2.8-0.30=0.73\) m.
    1. pump discharge flange: the pump adds 45.0 m, so \(0.73+45.0=45.73\) m.
    1. high point of the delivery line: \(45.73-(14.0-6.5)-1.6=36.63\) m.

The vapor-pressure head at 20 °C is 0.24 m of water. Point (C) is the only place in the system that comes anywhere near it: the absolute pressure head there is only \(0.73-0.24=0.49\) m above the vapor-pressure head, and the Handbook’s net positive suction head available is \(NPSH_A=H_{pa}+H_s-\sum h_L-H_{vp}=10.33-6.5-2.8-0.24=0.79\) m (the pressure margin plus the 0.30-m velocity head). Point (C) therefore has the smallest cavitation margin in the system. Whether cavitation actually occurs depends on the pump’s required NPSH at the operating point, which is not given, so (C) is the location most susceptible to cavitation. Everything downstream of the impeller is pressurized by the pump and is in no danger.

Why the others are wrong: (A) is at atmospheric pressure by definition — the highest absolute pressure in the suction line, not the lowest. (B) is on the suction side but only 3.0 m above the sump and has taken only 1.2 m of loss, so it still stands at 5.83 m. (D) is 45.73 m absolute, immediately after the pump has done its work. (E) is the highest elevation in the system, which makes it a tempting wrong answer, but the pump has already put 45 m of head into the water, leaving 36.63 m there.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Energy Equation; Fluid Flow Machinery — Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHA).

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 8-29

questions.question: A traverse course is 325.60 ft long on a bearing of S 48°30′ E. Its latitude and departure are most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Azimuth \(=180°-48°30'=131°30'\). \(\text{Lat}=325.60\cos131.5°=-215.75\) ft; \(\text{Dep}=325.60\sin131.5°=+243.86\) ft. Check with the bearing letters: S → latitude negative; E → departure positive.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Latitudes and Departures.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) has the wrong latitude sign (S is negative).
  • (B) swaps cosine and sine.
  • (C) swaps them and has both signs wrong.

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 9-4

questions.question: With a level whose stadia interval factor is 100 and stadia constant is zero, the upper and lower stadia hairs read 2.870 m and 1.625 m on a vertical rod with a horizontal line of sight. The horizontal distance to the rod is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(s=2.870-1.625=1.245\) m; \(D=ks+C=100(1.245)+0=124.5\) m.

FE Reference Handbook: none needed.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) doubles the interval.
  • (C) multiplies the upper-hair reading alone by 100 (100 × 2.870) instead of the rod interval between the hairs.
  • (D) uses the sum of the readings instead of their difference.

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 9-8

questions.question: Offsets at 8 m spacing from a base line to a curved shoreline are 2.4, 5.1, 6.9, 7.5, 6.2, 4.4, 1.8 m. By Simpson’s 1/3 rule the area is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(n=7\) (odd), \(w=8\) m. Even-numbered offsets \((h_2,h_4,h_6)\): 5.1 + 7.5 + 4.4 = 17.0. Odd interior \((h_3,h_5)\): 6.9 + 6.2 = 13.1. \[A=(8/3)[2.4+4(17.0)+2(13.1)+1.8]=(8/3)[2.4+68.0+26.2+1.8]=(8/3)(98.4)=262.4\,\text{m}^2\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Area formulas — Simpson’s 1/3 Rule.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) swaps the 2 and 4 weights (\(\tfrac{8}{3}(90.6)=241.6\)).
  • (B) is the trapezoidal-rule result (257.6 m²).
  • (D) omits the division by 3.

B – Area computations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 9-12

questions.question: Cross-section end areas at two stations 100 ft apart are 320 ft² and 410 ft², both in fill. The volume of embankment between the stations by the average end area method is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(V=L(A_1+A_2)/2=100(320+410)/2=36{,}500\) ft³ \(=36{,}500/27=1{,}352\) yd³.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Earthwork formulas — Average End Area Formula.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) omits the division by 2 in the average end area formula (100 × 730 = 73,000 ft³ = 2,704 yd³).
  • (C) divides by 10.
  • (D) is the volume in ft³.

C – Earthwork and volume computations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 9-16

questions.question: A project section requires 7,100 yd³ of compacted embankment and provides 6,400 yd³ of bank-measure cut. The soil shrinks 10% from bank to compacted. Using the Handbook convention of increasing fill by the shrinkage factor, the bank volume of borrow required is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Adjusted fill (bank measure) \(=7{,}100(1+0.10)=7{,}810\) yd³. Borrow \(=7{,}810-6{,}400=1{,}410\) yd³.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Earthwork formulas (shrinkage statement).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) ignores shrinkage (7,100 − 6,400).
  • (B) applies the shrinkage factor to the cut as well as to the fill (7,810 − 7,040).
  • (D) divides the fill by (1 − 0.10) instead of multiplying by (1 + 0.10) — a different convention that the question excludes.

C – Earthwork and volume computations · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 9-20

questions.question: A ground distance of 2,540.60 m is measured at a site where the combined (grid) factor is 0.99978. The corresponding state plane grid distance is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Grid = ground × CF \(=2{,}540.60\times0.99978=2{,}540.04\) m.

FE Reference Handbook: none printed.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) doubles the reduction.
  • (C) applies no factor.
  • (D) divides by the factor (grid-to-ground direction).

D – Coordinate systems · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 9-24

questions.question: A sag vertical curve has \(g_1=-4.0\%\), \(g_2=+2.0\%\), \(L=400\) ft, and PVC at Sta 20+00, elevation 180.00 ft. The curve elevation at Sta 21+50 is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(a=(g_2-g_1)/(2L)=(0.02+0.04)/(800)=7.5\times10^{-5}\) per ft; \(x=150\) ft. \[Y=180.00+(-0.04)(150)+7.5\times10^{-5}(150)^2=180.00-6.00+1.69=175.69\,\text{ft}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Vertical Curves.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) subtracts the offset — on a sag curve the curve lies above the back tangent.
  • (B) is the tangent elevation with no offset.
  • (D) uses \(L\) instead of \(2L\) in the parabola constant.

E – Leveling · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 9-28

questions.question: The 2-hour unit hydrograph for a watershed has ordinates, in cfs per inch, of 0, 80, 200, 120, 40 and 0 at \(t\) = 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 h. A storm produces 1.5 in. of rainfall excess during its first 2 hours and 0.5 in. during its second 2 hours. Baseflow is constant at 30 cfs. The peak total streamflow is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Scale the unit hydrograph by each block’s excess depth and lag the second block by one UH duration (2 h), then add ordinates and baseflow.

\(t\) (h) 1.5 × UH 0.5 × UH lagged 2 h DRH (cfs)
0 0 — 0
2 120 0 120
4 300 40 340
6 180 100 280
8 60 60 120
10 0 20 20
12 — 0 0

Peak DRH = 340 cfs at \(t = 4\) h; peak streamflow = 340 + 30 = 370 cfs.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources (unit hydrograph definition and convolution).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 300 cfs uses only the first rainfall block (and omits baseflow).
  • (B) 340 cfs is the direct-runoff peak with baseflow forgotten.
  • (D) 400 cfs applies the total 2.0 in. of excess to the UH peak at one instant, which ignores the 2-hour lag between blocks, and omits the 30-cfs baseflow.

A – Basic hydrology · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 10-4

questions.question: Water flows in a wide rectangular channel at a depth of 0.40 m with a mean velocity of 8.0 m/s and then passes through a hydraulic jump. The depth immediately downstream of the jump is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[Fr_1 = \frac{v_1}{\sqrt{gy_1}} = \frac{8.0}{\sqrt{9.81(0.40)}} = \frac{8.0}{1.981} = 4.04\ \text{(supercritical ✓)}\] \[y_2 = \frac{y_1}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8Fr_1^2} - 1\right) = \frac{0.40}{2}\left(\sqrt{1 + 8(4.039)^2} - 1\right) = 0.20(12.47 - 1) = 2.09\ \text{m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Hydraulic Jump; Froude Number.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.69 m is the height of the jump, \(y_2 - y_1\), not the sequent depth.
  • (C) 3.62 m is the alternate depth from the specific-energy curve (\(E_1 = 3.66\) m held constant); a jump destroys energy, so the sequent depth is always smaller than the alternate depth.
  • (D) 4.19 m omits the factor \(y_1/2\), using \(y_1\) instead.

B – Basic hydraulics · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-8

questions.question: A rectangular channel is to be built as the best hydraulic section for a discharge of 6.0 m3/s with \(n = 0.015\) and a bed slope of 0.001. The required flow depth is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The best hydraulic rectangular section is half a square: \(b = 2y\), so \(A = 2y^2\), \(P = 4y\) and \(R_H = y/2\). \[Q = \frac{1}{n}(2y^2)\left(\frac{y}{2}\right)^{2/3}S^{1/2} = \frac{2(0.6300)(0.03162)}{0.015}y^{8/3} = 2.656\,y^{8/3}\] \[y^{8/3} = \frac{6.0}{2.656} = 2.259 \quad\Rightarrow\quad y = (2.259)^{3/8} = 1.357\ \text{m} \qquad (b = 2.71\ \text{m})\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Manning’s Equation (the best-hydraulic-section geometry follows from minimizing \(P\) at constant \(A\) and is not printed in the Handbook).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 1.61 m uses \(R_H = y/4\), borrowing the full-circular-pipe rule \(R_H = D/4\); for the half-square section \(R_H = y/2\).
  • (C) 1.95 m assumes a square section (\(b = y\), \(R_H = y/3\)), which is not the most efficient shape.
  • (D) 2.71 m is the bottom width, not the depth.

B – Basic hydraulics · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 10-12

questions.question: A pump has the characteristic \(H = 90 - 0.0004Q^2\) and serves a system whose head requirement is \(H_{sys} = 30 + 0.0006Q^2\), with \(H\) in feet and \(Q\) in gpm. The operating flow rate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The operating point is the intersection of the pump and system curves: \[90 - 0.0004Q^2 = 30 + 0.0006Q^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 0.001Q^2 = 60 \quad\Rightarrow\quad Q = 245\ \text{gpm}\] with \(H = 30 + 0.0006(60{,}000) = 66\) ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Fluid Flow Machinery — Centrifugal Pump Characteristics.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 300 gpm drops the 30-ft static head from the system curve.
  • (C) 387 gpm is the flow at which the pump curve falls to the 30-ft static head (\(90 - 0.0004Q^2 = 30\)), i.e., the system friction term is ignored.
  • (D) 548 gpm subtracts the \(Q^2\) coefficients instead of adding them when moving them to one side (\(0.0002Q^2 = 60\)).

C – Pumps · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 10-16

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about pipe networks and friction formulas are correct?
choices: For pipes in parallel, the head loss between the common junctions is the same in every branch and the branch discharges add.
For pipes in series, the discharge is the same in every pipe and the head losses add.
Doubling the diameter of a pipe while holding the discharge constant reduces the Hazen–Williams head loss by roughly a factor of 29.
The Hazen–Williams coefficient \(C\) of an unlined cast-iron main increases as the pipe ages.
The Darcy–Weisbach equation applies to any fluid in any flow regime, whereas Hazen–Williams is an empirical fit for water in turbulent flow.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), (C) and (E) are correct; (D) is not (see the rationale for each statement below).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hazen-Williams Equation; Values of Hazen-Williams Coefficient C; Fluid Mechanics — Head Loss Due to Flow; Multipath Pipeline Problems.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — this is the defining condition for parallel paths.
  • (B) True — continuity fixes \(Q\); losses accumulate along the path.
  • (C) True — \(h_f \propto D^{-4.87}\), and \(2^{4.87} = 29.2\).
  • (D) False — tuberculation and corrosion roughen the interior, so \(C\) decreases with age (new cast iron ≈ 130, twenty-year-old cast iron ≈ 100).
  • (E) True — Darcy–Weisbach is dimensionally general and uses \(f\) from the Moody diagram; Hazen–Williams is calibrated for water in turbulent pipe flow.

D – Water distribution systems · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-20

questions.question: A post-development runoff hydrograph is approximately triangular with a peak of 12.0 cfs and a time base of 60 min. The allowable release rate is the pre-development peak of 5.0 cfs. Using the triangular-hydrograph approximation, the required detention storage is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
With the outflow assumed to rise linearly from zero until it reaches the allowable peak on the inflow recession limb, and then to follow the recession, the outflow hydrograph is a triangle of base \(t_b\) and height \(Q_{allow}\). The required storage is the area between the inflow triangle and the outflow triangle: \[V \approx \tfrac{1}{2}t_b(Q_{post} - Q_{allow}) = \tfrac{1}{2}(60\times60\ \text{s})(12.0 - 5.0) = \tfrac{1}{2}(3600)(7.0) = 12{,}600\ \text{ft}^3\] The result is 0.29 acre-ft.

FE Reference Handbook: no printed formula — this triangular approximation follows from \(dS/dt = I - O\); the Handbook’s continuity relation is the basis.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 21,600 ft3 is the total inflow volume, as if nothing were released during the storm.
  • (C) 25,200 ft3 omits the factor of 1/2 for the triangular area.
  • (D) 30,600 ft3 adds the allowable release to the post-development peak instead of subtracting it.

F – Stormwater · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 10-24

questions.question: [Ranking] A circular sewer of fixed diameter, slope and Manning \(n\) (constant with depth) flows at the four depth ratios listed below. Rank them in order of increasing discharge ratio \(Q/Q_f\), smallest first.
questions.explanation:
With \(\theta = 2\cos^{-1}(1 - 2d/D)\), \(A/A_f = (\theta - \sin\theta)/2\pi\) and \(R/R_f = (\theta - \sin\theta)/\theta\), so \(Q/Q_f = (A/A_f)(R/R_f)^{2/3}\):

\(d/D\) \(A/A_f\) \(v/v_f\) \(Q/Q_f\)
0.25 0.196 0.701 0.137
0.50 0.500 1.000 0.500
0.94 0.976 1.103 1.076
1.00 1.000 1.000 1.000

The counter-intuitive result is that the just-full pipe is not the pipe of greatest capacity. Near \(d/D = 0.94\) the flow area is already 98% of full while the wetted perimeter is appreciably less, so the hydraulic radius — and hence the velocity — peaks above the full-pipe value; discharge peaks at about \(1.08Q_f\). (Velocity itself peaks slightly lower, near \(d/D\) = 0.81.) At \(d/D = 0.50\) exactly, \(R_H = R_{H,f}\), so \(v = v_f\) and \(Q = 0.5Q_f\) — a pair of values worth memorizing. Read the same ranking straight off the \(Q/Q_f\) curve.

A frequent wrong ordering puts item 4 last, on the assumption that a full pipe must carry the most; another halves the velocity at \(d/D = 0.5\) along with the area, which would give \(Q/Q_f = 0.25\) rather than 0.50.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydraulic-Element (Partial Flow) Graph for Circular Sewers; Manning’s Equation.

G – Collection systems · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-28

questions.question: A confined aquifer has a transmissivity of 250 m2/d. A fully penetrating well pumps 2,000 m3/d at steady state. An observation well 50 m from the pumping well shows a drawdown of 1.20 m. The drawdown at a radius of 5 m is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The Thiem equation for a confined aquifer gives the head difference between two radii: \[h_2 - h_1 = \frac{Q\ln(r_2/r_1)}{2\pi T} = \frac{2000\ln(50/5)}{2\pi(250)} = \frac{2000(2.3026)}{1570.8} = 2.932\ \text{m}\] Because the head is lower nearer the well, the drawdown is larger there by the same amount: \[s_{5\,\text{m}} = s_{50\,\text{m}} + 2.932 = 1.20 + 2.93 = 4.13\ \text{m}\] Subtracting rather than adding gives −1.73 m, which is not physical.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Thiem Equation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.27 m uses \(\log_{10}\) in place of ln and then reports the head difference alone.
  • (B) 2.47 m makes the same base-10 error but does add the 1.20 m.
  • (C) 2.93 m reports the head difference rather than the drawdown at 5 m; it omits the 1.20 m already present at 50 m.

H – Groundwater · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-32

questions.question: A wastewater has a 5-day BOD of 180 mg/L and a base-\(e\) rate constant \(k = 0.20\) d−1 at 20°C. The ultimate carbonaceous BOD is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[BOD_t = L_o\left(1 - e^{-kt}\right) \quad\Rightarrow\quad L_o = \frac{BOD_5}{1 - e^{-5k}} = \frac{180}{1 - e^{-0.20(5)}} = \frac{180}{1 - 0.3679} = \frac{180}{0.6321} = 284.8\ \text{mg/L}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Microbial Kinetics — BOD Exertion.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 114 mg/L multiplies by \((1 - e^{-kt})\) instead of dividing, which runs the exertion curve backwards.
  • (B) 200 mg/L treats \(k = 0.20\) as a base-10 constant (\(k_e = 2.303K = 0.46\) d−1); the Handbook equation is base \(e\).
  • (D) 993 mg/L uses \(t = 1\) d instead of the 5 d of the standard test.

I – Water quality · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 10-36

questions.question: Nitrogen dioxide (molecular weight 46 g/mol) is present in ambient air at 0.050 ppm by volume at 25°C and 1 atm. Using \(R = 0.0821\) L·atm/(mol·K), the mass concentration is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[\frac{\text{mg}}{\text{m}^3} = \text{ppm}\times\frac{P\times MW}{RT} = 0.050\times\frac{(1\ \text{atm})(46\ \text{g/mol})}{0.0821(298)} = \frac{2.30}{24.47} = 0.0940\ \text{mg/m}^3 = 94\ \mu\text{g/m}^3\] (Equivalently, at 25°C and 1 atm the molar volume is 24.5 L/mol, so 1 ppm ≈ 40.9 MW µg/m3.)

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Air Pollution (concentration conversions and nomenclature).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.094 µg/m3 leaves the answer in mg/m3 but labels it µg/m3.
  • (B) 2.3 µg/m3 multiplies ppm by MW without dividing by \(RT\).
  • (D) 2,300 µg/m3 multiplies by 1,000 without dividing by the molar volume.

J – Testing and standards · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-40

questions.question: An aeration basin of 2,000 m3 operates at an MLSS of 3,000 mg/L. Waste activated sludge is drawn from the return line at 60 m3/d with a solids concentration of 10,000 mg/L; solids leaving in the final effluent are negligible. The solids residence time (sludge age) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Solids residence time is the biomass inventory divided by the biomass leaving per day. With effluent solids neglected and wasting from the return line at \(X_r\): \[\theta_c = \frac{VX_A}{Q_wX_w + Q_eX_e} \approx \frac{VX_A}{Q_wX_r} = \frac{2000(3000)}{60(10{,}000)} = \frac{6.0\times10^6}{6.0\times10^5} = 10\ \text{d}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Wastewater Treatment and Technologies — Activated Sludge.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.10 d inverts the ratio.
  • (C) 33 d uses the aeration-basin MLSS (3,000 mg/L) as the wasted-sludge concentration, appropriate only when sludge is wasted directly from the aeration basin.
  • (D) 111 d interchanges \(X_A\) and \(X_r\).

K – Water and wastewater treatment · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 10-44

questions.question: For the overhanging beam in Figure 11.15, the vertical reaction at support B is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Loads: the 12 kN/m over the 8-m span gives a resultant of \(12(8) = 96\) kN at \(x = 4\) m from A; the point load is 30 kN at \(x = 10\) m. Sum moments about A (counterclockwise positive): \[R_B(8) - 96(4) - 30(10) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad R_B = \frac{384 + 300}{8} = \frac{684}{8} = 85.5\,\text{kN}\] (Check: \(R_A = 96 + 30 - 85.5 = 40.5\) kN.)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 40.5 kN is \(R_A\), not \(R_B\).
  • (B) 63.0 kN is half the total load, correct only if the loading were symmetric about the supports.
  • (D) 126.0 kN is the total applied load \(96 + 30\).

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-2

questions.question: For the same truss (Figure 11.17), the force in the center vertical member CG is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Work at joint C, where five members meet: BC and CD (horizontal), the vertical CG, and the two diagonals FC and CH. Each diagonal runs 3 m horizontally and 4 m vertically, so its vertical direction cosine is 0.8.

By symmetry \(F_{FC} = F_{CH}\). Section through FG, FC, BC (Question 11-5), left portion, vertical equilibrium: \[45 - 30 - 0.8F_{FC} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{FC} = 18.75\,\text{kN (tension)}\] Joint C, vertical equilibrium (the two diagonals pull upward toward F and H, the 30-kN load acts down): \[0.8(18.75) + 0.8(18.75) + F_{CG} - 30 = 15 + 15 + F_{CG} - 30 = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{CG} = 0\] The two diagonals meeting at the center panel point carry the entire 30-kN load there, so the center vertical is a zero-force member for this symmetric loading. (It is still needed for stability and for unsymmetric load cases.)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Plane Truss: Method of Joints; Method of Sections.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 15.0 kN compression is the vertical component of one diagonal only.
  • (C) 30.0 kN tension is the force in the other verticals BF and DH, where only one diagonal frames in.
  • (D) 45.0 kN is the reaction.

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-6

questions.question: A steel cantilever 12 ft long has \(I = 300\,\text{in}^4\) and \(E = 29{,}000\) ksi, and carries a uniformly distributed load of 1.5 kip/ft over its full length. The deflection at the free end is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Work in inches and kips: \(L = 12(12) = 144\) in and \(w = 1.5/12 = 0.125\) kip/in. \[\delta = \frac{wL^4}{8EI} = \frac{0.125(144)^4}{8(29{,}000)(300)} = \frac{5.375 \times 10^7}{6.96 \times 10^7} = 0.772\,\text{in}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Cantilevered Beam Slopes and Deflections (uniform load).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.39 in halves the result, as if the formula were \(wL^4/16EI\).
  • (C) 2.06 in results from lumping the total load \(W = wL = 18\) kips at the tip and using \(PL^3/3EI\); the tip-load formula gives a much larger deflection than the same total load spread out.
  • (D) 9.27 in leaves \(w\) in kip/ft while \(L\) is in inches — a factor of 12.

B – Deflection of determinate structures · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-10

questions.question: A W12×58 column (\(A_g = 17.0\,\text{in}^2\), \(F_y = 50\) ksi) has an effective slenderness ratio \(KL/r = 60\). AISC Table 4-14 gives \(\phi_cF_{cr} = 34.6\) ksi at \(KL/r = 60\) for \(F_y = 50\) ksi. The LRFD design compressive strength is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The table value is already a stress that includes \(\phi_c = 0.90\), so it is multiplied by the gross area only: \[\phi_cP_n = (\phi_cF_{cr})A_g = 34.6(17.0) = 588\,\text{kips}\] As a check by formula: \(F_e = \pi^2(29{,}000)/60^2 = 79.5\) ksi; since \(60 < 4.71\sqrt{29{,}000/50} = 113\), \(F_{cr} = 0.658^{50/79.5}(50) = 38.4\) ksi and \(\phi_cF_{cr} = 34.6\) ksi.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Steel Components — Columns; AISC Table 4-14.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 653 kips is \(F_{cr}A_g\) with the resistance factor omitted.
  • (C) 765 kips is \(0.90F_yA_g\), the squash load reduced by \(\phi\), which ignores buckling.
  • (D) 850 kips is \(F_yA_g\), the unfactored yield load.

C – Column analysis · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-14
