questions.question: A plane truss has 18 members, 10 joints, and 3 independent reaction components, and all panels are triangulated. The structure is:
choices: statically indeterminate to the first degree
statically indeterminate to the third degree
questions.explanation:
For a plane truss compare \(m + r\) with \(2j\): \[m + r = 18 + 3 = 21 \qquad 2j = 2(10) = 20 \qquad 21 > 20\] The structure is statically indeterminate to degree \(m + r - 2j = 1\). Because the panels are all triangulated and the reactions are neither parallel nor concurrent, it is stable.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) would require \(m + r < 2j\).
  • (B) would require \(m + r = 2j\) exactly.
  • (D) would require \(m + r - 2j = 3\), i.e., two more members (or reaction components) than this truss has.

D – Determinacy and stability · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-18

questions.question: A propped cantilever (fixed at A, roller at B) spans 8 m and carries a single concentrated load of 32 kN at midspan. The reaction at the prop B is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Force method: remove the prop to get a cantilever fixed at A. From the Handbook’s cantilever table, a load \(P\) at distance \(a = L/2\) from the fixed end deflects the tip by \[\Delta_{BB} = \frac{Pa^2(3L - a)}{6EI} = \frac{P(L/2)^2(3L - L/2)}{6EI} = \frac{5PL^3}{48EI}\] The redundant \(B_y\) acting alone at the tip lifts it by \(B_yL^3/3EI\). Compatibility (\(\Delta_{BB} = \delta_{BB}\)): \[\frac{B_yL^3}{3EI} = \frac{5PL^3}{48EI} \quad\Rightarrow\quad B_y = \frac{5P}{16} = \frac{5(32)}{16} = 10.0\,\text{kN}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Elementary Statically Indeterminate Structures by Force Method of Analysis; Mechanics of Materials — Cantilevered Beam Slopes and Deflections.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 12.0 kN is \(3P/8\), the prop reaction for a uniformly loaded propped cantilever applied to a point load.
  • (C) 16.0 kN is \(P/2\), the simply supported answer, which ignores the fixity at A.
  • (D) 22.0 kN is \(A_y = 11P/16\), the reaction at the fixed end.

E – Elementary indeterminate structures · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-22

questions.question: A beam of constant \(EI\) is continuous over three supports forming two equal spans of 6 m each, and carries a uniformly distributed load of 20 kN/m over its full 12-m length. The reaction at the center support is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Take the middle support as the redundant. The primary structure is a simple beam of total length \(L = 12\) m carrying \(w = 20\) kN/m; its midspan deflection is \(5wL^4/384EI\). A single force \(B_y\) at midspan lifts it \(B_yL^3/48EI\). Compatibility: \[\frac{B_yL^3}{48EI} = \frac{5wL^4}{384EI} \quad\Rightarrow\quad B_y = \frac{5wL}{8} = \frac{5(20)(12)}{8} = 150\,\text{kN}\] Equivalently, \(1.25w\ell = 1.25(20)(6) = 150\) kN with \(\ell\) the individual span length. The end reactions are \((240 - 150)/2 = 45\) kN each.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Elementary Statically Indeterminate Structures by Force Method of Analysis; Mechanics of Materials — Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 75 kN evaluates \(5wL/8\) with the single-span length \(\ell = 6\) m; in the Handbook case \(L\) is the total length between the end supports (12 m).
  • (B) 90 kN applies the propped-cantilever factor \(3wL/8\) with \(L = 12\) m (the total length); per span, \(3w\ell/8 = 45\) kN is the correct end reaction, not the center reaction.
  • (C) 120 kN is half the total load, the answer if the beam were two independent simple spans (each end reaction \(w\ell/2 = 60\) kN, summing to 120 kN at the middle).

E – Elementary indeterminate structures · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-26

questions.question: A simply supported beam spans 12 m. A single concentrated live load of 90 kN may be placed anywhere on the span. Using the influence line for bending moment at section C, 5 m from support A, the maximum moment at C is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The influence line for the moment at a section of a simple span is a triangle whose peak, directly under the section, is \(ab/L\). With \(a = 5\) m and \(b = 7\) m: \[\text{peak ordinate} = \frac{ab}{L} = \frac{5(7)}{12} = 2.917\,\text{m}\] A single load is placed at the peak, so \(M_C = 90(2.917) = 262.5\) kN·m.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Influence Lines for Beams and Trusses.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 188 kN·m uses \(a = b = 5\) m.
  • (C) 270 kN·m is \(PL/4\), the largest moment anywhere on the span (at midspan), not the moment at C.
  • (D) 315 kN·m uses \(ab/L\) with \(L = 10\) m instead of 12 m.

F – Loads and load combinations · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-30

questions.question: An A36 plate (\(F_y = 36\) ksi, \(F_u = 58\) ksi) is 6 in wide and 3/8 in thick and is connected at its end by two 7/8-in-diameter bolts in a single line across the width (\(U = 1.0\)). Using \(d_h = d_b + 1/16\) in plus an additional 1/16 in for damage, the LRFD design tensile strength of the plate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Gross area: \(A_g = 6(0.375) = 2.25\,\text{in}^2\).

Hole allowance per bolt: \(d_h + 1/16 = (7/8 + 1/16) + 1/16 = 1.0\) in. Two holes on the same line: \[A_n = [6 - 2(1.0)](0.375) = 4.0(0.375) = 1.50\,\text{in}^2, \qquad A_e = UA_n = 1.50\,\text{in}^2\] Yielding: \(\phi P_n = 0.90F_yA_g = 0.90(36)(2.25) = 72.9\) kips. Rupture: \(\phi P_n = 0.75F_uA_e = 0.75(58)(1.50) = 65.25\) kips ← governs.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Steel Components — Tension Members.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 72.9 kips is the yielding limit state, which does not govern here because two holes remove a third of the width.
  • (C) 81.0 kips is \(F_yA_g\) with no resistance factor.
  • (D) 97.9 kips is \(0.75F_uA_g\), using the gross area in the rupture check; rupture always uses the effective net area.

G – Design of steel components · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-34

questions.question: A W18×50 beam has \(d = 18.0\) in and \(t_w = 0.355\) in, with \(F_y = 50\) ksi, \(C_{v1} = 1.0\), and \(\phi_v = 1.00\). The design shear strength is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The web area for a rolled I-shape is the overall depth times the web thickness: \[A_w = dt_w = 18.0(0.355) = 6.39\,\text{in}^2\] \[\phi_vV_n = \phi_v(0.6F_yA_wC_{v1}) = 1.00(0.6)(50)(6.39)(1.0) = 192\,\text{kips}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Steel Components — Beams (shear).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 128 kips uses a 0.4 coefficient instead of 0.6.
  • (C) 213 kips divides by \(\phi = 0.90\), but the shear resistance factor for most rolled shapes is 1.00.
  • (D) 320 kips uses \(F_y\) rather than \(0.6F_y\); the 0.6 converts tension yield to shear yield.

G – Design of steel components · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-38

questions.question: A rectangular beam section of \(f'_c = 5000\) psi concrete has a Whitney stress-block depth \(a = 6.0\) in and an extreme-tension-steel depth \(d_t = 18\) in. Using the Handbook’s unified design provisions, the strength reduction factor \(\phi\) for flexure is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For \(f'_c = 5000\) psi, \(\beta_1 = 0.85 - 0.05(1000/1000) = 0.80\), so the neutral-axis depth is \[c = \frac{a}{\beta_1} = \frac{6.0}{0.80} = 7.50\,\text{in}\] \[\varepsilon_t = \frac{0.003(d_t - c)}{c} = \frac{0.003(18 - 7.50)}{7.50} = \frac{0.0315}{7.50} = 0.0042\] Since \(0.002 < 0.0042 < 0.005\), the section is in the transition zone: \[\phi = 0.48 + 83\varepsilon_t = 0.48 + 83(0.0042) = 0.48 + 0.349 = 0.829 \approx 0.83\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components — Unified Design Provisions; Resistance Factors.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.65 is the compression-controlled value for tied members, which would require \(\varepsilon_t \le 0.002\).
  • (B) 0.75 is the shear and torsion factor, not a flexural \(\phi\).
  • (D) 0.90 assumes the section is tension-controlled; with \(\varepsilon_t = 0.0042 < 0.005\) it is not, and using 0.90 would overstate the strength by about 9%.

H – Design of reinforced concrete components · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-42

questions.question: [Point-and-click] Figure 11.21 shows a simply supported beam with an overhang. A single 60-kN wheel load may be parked at any one of the five stations carrying the circled labels (A) through (E). Name the labeled station at which the load produces the largest-magnitude bending moment at section X.
questions.explanation:
Build the influence line for the bending moment at section X. Measure \(x\) from S1; the span is \(L = 12\) m and \(a = 4\) m to section X.

For a unit load inside the span, the ordinate is \(x(L - a)/L\) while the load is left of X and \(a(L - x)/L\) while it is right of X, so the influence line is a triangle peaking directly under the section at \[\eta_{max} = \frac{a(L - a)}{L} = \frac{4(8)}{12} = 2.667\,\text{m}\] For a unit load on the overhang a distance \(d\) beyond S2, the S1 reaction is \(-d/L\) (downward) and the ordinate is \(-ad/L\), which at \(d = 4\) m gives \(-4(4)/12 = -1.333\) m.

Multiplying by the 60-kN load:

Station Ordinate (m) \(M_X\) (kN·m)
(A) \(x = 0\) 0 0
(B) \(x = 4\) +2.667 +160
(C) \(x = 8\) +1.333 +80
(D) \(x = 12\) 0 0
(E) \(d = 4\) −1.333 −80

The load produces the largest-magnitude moment at section X when it stands directly over the section, at station (B): \(M_X = 160\) kN·m.

Stations (A) and (D) sit directly over the supports, where the influence ordinate is zero and no moment is produced at X. (C) is inside the span but on the far side of the section, giving 80 kN·m — half the peak. (E) is on the overhang and produces a moment of the opposite sign, −80 kN·m; it governs the negative moment envelope at X but is only half the magnitude of (B).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Influence Lines for Beams and Trusses.

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-46

questions.question: A soil has 68% passing the No. 10 sieve, 48% passing the No. 40 sieve, and 22% passing the No. 200 sieve. On the minus-No. 40 fraction, LL = 38 and PI = 12. Its AASHTO classification is:
questions.explanation:
Only 22% passes the No. 200 sieve, which is 35% or less, so the soil is a granular material. Test the granular columns left to right: A-1-a requires ≤ 50% passing the No. 10, and 68% fails it; A-1-b requires \(PI \le 6\), and \(PI = 12\) fails it; A-3 requires ≥ 51% passing the No. 40, and 48% fails it. That leaves A-2, whose only sieve requirement (≤ 35% passing the No. 200) is met. Within A-2, \(LL = 38 \le 40\) and \(PI = 12 \ge 11\) gives A-2-6.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — AASHTO Soil Classification.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) fails the plasticity index limit of 6.
  • (C) requires \(PI \le 10\).
  • (D) requires more than 35% passing the No. 200 sieve.

A – Index properties and soil classifications · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-4

questions.question: A soil with \(G_s = 2.70\) has a dry unit weight of 16.2 kN/m³. Its void ratio is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[\gamma_d = \frac{G_s\gamma_w}{1+e} \quad\Rightarrow\quad e = \frac{G_s\gamma_w}{\gamma_d} - 1 = \frac{2.70(9.81)}{16.2} - 1 = 1.635 - 1 = 0.635\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Phase Relationships (dry unit weight, void ratio, specific gravity of soil solids).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(1 - 0.635\).
  • (B) is the porosity \(n = e/(1+e) = 0.388\).
  • (D) omits the subtraction of 1.

B – Phase relations · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 12-8

questions.question: A falling-head permeability test uses a specimen 12.0 cm long with a cross-sectional area of 32.0 cm² and a standpipe of area 0.60 cm². The head falls from 90 cm to 30 cm in 240 s. The coefficient of permeability is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[K = 2.303\,\frac{aL}{At_e}\log_{10}\frac{h_1}{h_2} = 2.303\,\frac{(0.60)(12.0)}{(32.0)(240)}\log_{10}\frac{90}{30}\] \[K = 2.303\left(9.375\times 10^{-4}\right)(0.4771) = 1.03\times 10^{-3}\,\text{cm/s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Hydraulic Conductivity/Permeability (from falling head test).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) divides by 2.303 instead of multiplying: \((9.375\times 10^{-4})(0.4771)/2.303 = 1.94\times 10^{-4}\) cm/s.
  • (B) omits the 2.303 factor.
  • (D) uses \(\ln(h_1/h_2) = 1.099\) while retaining the 2.303, overstating \(K\) by that factor.

C – Laboratory and field tests · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-12

questions.question: A standard penetration test records a field blow count of 22 using a hammer with a measured energy ratio of 75%. Using \(N_{60} = N(ER/60)\), the corrected blow count is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[N_{60} = N\,\frac{ER}{60} = 22\left(\frac{75}{60}\right) = 27.5 \approx 28\] A hammer that delivers more than 60% of the theoretical energy drives the sampler farther per blow, so the measured count understates the equivalent 60%-energy count; the correction must increase N.

FE Reference Handbook: not in Handbook 10.6 — the correction was supplied in the problem statement.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) inverts the ratio to 60/75, giving 17.6.
  • (B) applies no correction.
  • (D) applies the 75/60 ratio twice, giving 34.4.

C – Laboratory and field tests · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 12-16

questions.question: For the profile in Figure 12.15 — 2.5 m of moist sand (\(\gamma = 17.0\) kN/m³) over a fully saturated capillary zone from 2.5 m to the water table at 4.0 m (\(\gamma_{sat} = 19.5\) kN/m³) — the effective vertical stress at a depth of 2.5 m is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
At 2.5 m the total vertical stress is the weight of the moist sand above: \[\sigma = 17.0(2.5) = 42.5\,\text{kPa}\] The point lies 1.5 m above the water table inside a fully saturated capillary zone, so the pore pressure is negative: \[u = -\gamma_w(1.5) = -9.81(1.5) = -14.7\,\text{kPa}\] \[\sigma' = \sigma - u = 42.5 - (-14.7) = 57.2\,\text{kPa}\] Capillary suction increases effective stress, which is why moist sand stands in a vertical cut.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Effective Stress; Vertical Stress Profiles.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) treats the moist sand above the capillary zone as if it were submerged, using \(\gamma - \gamma_w\): \((17.0 - 9.81)(2.5) = 18.0\) kPa.
  • (B) subtracts the suction instead of adding it.
  • (C) ignores capillarity and takes \(u = 0\).

D – Effective stress · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 12-20

questions.question: [Numerical entry] For the wall of Question 12-23, determine the height above the base of the wall at which the resultant active thrust acts, in meters.
questions.explanation:
The rectangular block acts at mid-height and the triangular block at one third of the height: \[\bar{y} = \frac{P_{rect}(H/2) + P_{tri}(H/3)}{P_{rect} + P_{tri}} = \frac{23.04(2.50) + 72.97(1.667)}{96.02}\] \[\bar{y} = \frac{57.61 + 121.62}{96.02} = \frac{179.23}{96.02} = 1.87\,\text{m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Horizontal Stress Profiles and Forces. Accepted range: 1.80 to 1.95 m. Answering 1.67 m (the triangle alone) or 2.50 m (the rectangle alone) is not accepted; the resultant must lie between those two values, closer to the larger force.

E – Stability of retaining structures · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 12-24

questions.question: An unconsolidated-undrained triaxial test on a saturated clay at a cell pressure of 100 kPa fails at a major principal stress of 260 kPa. The undrained shear strength is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a saturated clay in a UU test the total-stress envelope is horizontal (\(\phi_u = 0\)), so the undrained shear strength equals the radius of the Mohr circle: \[c_u = \frac{\sigma_1 - \sigma_3}{2} = \frac{260 - 100}{2} = 80\,\text{kPa}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Mohr-Coulomb failure envelope figure (with definitions of \(s\), \(t\), \(\theta\)); Shear Stress at Failure.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) halves the cell pressure.
  • (C) is the deviator stress \(\sigma_1 - \sigma_3\), which is twice \(c_u\).
  • (D) is the mean normal stress \(s = (\sigma_1 + \sigma_3)/2\), the circle center rather than its radius.

F – Shear strength · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-28

questions.question: [Numerical entry] An 8.0-ft-square footing is founded 5.0 ft below grade in a saturated clay with \(c = 1{,}500\) psf and \(\phi = 0\). The soil unit weight is 120 pcf and the water table is deep. Using \(q_{ult} = 1.3cN_c + \gamma D_f N_q + 0.4\gamma BN_\gamma\) with \(N_c = 5.7\), \(N_q = 1.0\), \(N_\gamma = 0\), determine the allowable column load in kips for a factor of safety of 3 on the gross ultimate capacity.
questions.explanation:
\[q_{ult} = 1.3(1{,}500)(5.7) + (120)(5.0)(1.0) + 0.4(120)(8.0)(0) = 11{,}115 + 600 = 11{,}715\ \text{psf}\] \[q_{all} = \frac{11{,}715}{3} = 3{,}905\ \text{psf}\] \[Q_{all} = q_{all}A = 3{,}905(8.0)(8.0) = 249{,}900\ \text{lb} = 250\ \text{kip}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Ultimate Bearing Capacity. The shape modification and factors were supplied in the problem. Accepted range: 248 to 252 kip. Applying the 1.3 factor to the surcharge term as well gives 254 kip and is not accepted; omitting the 1.3 entirely gives 195 kip.

G – Bearing capacity · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-32

questions.question: A 3.0-m-thick normally consolidated clay layer has \(e_0 = 1.10\) and \(C_C = 0.45\). The effective stress at mid-depth is 100 kPa before loading and increases by 80 kPa. The primary consolidation settlement is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The clay is normally consolidated, so \(\sigma'_0 \ge \sigma'_c\) and the single virgin-compression branch applies. With \(\sigma'_f = 100 + 80 = 180\) kPa: \[\Delta H = \frac{H_0}{1+e_0}C_C\log_{10}\frac{\sigma'_f}{\sigma'_0} = \frac{3.0}{2.10}(0.45)\log_{10}\frac{180}{100}\] \[\Delta H = 1.4286(0.45)(0.2553) = 0.1641\,\text{m} = 164\,\text{mm}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Soil Consolidation Curve Over Consolidated Clay (second case); Compression Index; Ultimate Consolidation Settlement in Soil Layer.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses \(C_R = C_C/6\), appropriate only if the loading stayed within the recompression range.
  • (C) omits the \((1+e_0)\) divisor.
  • (D) uses the natural logarithm instead of \(\log_{10}\).

I – Consolidation and differential settlement · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-36

questions.question: A long cohesionless slope inclined at 20° has \(\phi' = 34°\) and \(\gamma_{sat} = 20.0\) kN/m³. After prolonged rain the water table rises to the ground surface with seepage parallel to the slope. Using \(FS = (\gamma'/\gamma_{sat})(\tan\phi'/\tan\beta)\), the factor of safety is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[\gamma' = 20.0 - 9.81 = 10.19\,\text{kN/m}^3\] \[FS = \frac{\gamma'}{\gamma_{sat}}\cdot\frac{\tan\phi'}{\tan\beta} = \frac{10.19}{20.0}\cdot\frac{\tan 34°}{\tan 20°} = 0.5095\left(\frac{0.6745}{0.3640}\right) = 0.5095(1.853) = 0.944\] The factor of safety is below 1.0, so the slope fails — the familiar rainfall-triggered shallow landslide.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Effective Stress. The infinite-slope expression is not in Handbook 10.6 and was supplied in the problem statement.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the ratio \(\gamma'/\gamma_{sat}\) alone.
  • (C) is the dry-slope value \(\tan\phi'/\tan\beta = 1.85\); seepage roughly halves it.
  • (D) inverts the unit-weight ratio: \((20.0/10.19)(1.853) = 3.64\).

J – Slope stability · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-40

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A woven geotextile is placed between a soft silty-clay subgrade and a crushed-stone base course. Which functions does the geotextile perform in this application?
choices: Separation of the aggregate from the subgrade fines
Filtration — allowing water to pass while retaining soil particles
Acting as an essentially impermeable hydraulic barrier
In-plane drainage sufficient to serve as the roadway’s edge drain
Reduction of the plasticity index of the subgrade clay
questions.explanation:
A geotextile between subgrade and base performs separation and filtration; barrier, in-plane drainage, and chemical modification belong to other products.

FE Reference Handbook: not covered in Handbook 10.6; conceptual geosynthetic functions.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — Separation is the primary function: the fabric keeps the crushed stone from punching into the soft subgrade and keeps subgrade fines from pumping up into the aggregate voids under traffic.
  • (B) True — The fabric is permeable and its opening size is chosen so that water can pass while soil particles are retained — the definition of the filtration function.
  • (C) False — A barrier function requires an essentially impermeable geomembrane, typically HDPE; a woven geotextile is deliberately permeable.
  • (D) False — A thin geotextile has negligible in-plane transmissivity. Conveying water within the plane of the product is the drainage function, performed by a geonet or geocomposite.
  • (E) False — A geosynthetic is a physical inclusion; it does not chemically alter the clay’s Atterberg limits. Lowering PI requires a chemical additive such as lime.

K – Soil stabilization · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-44

questions.question: A circular curve of radius 250 m has an intersection angle of \(40^\circ\). The tangent distance is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(T=R\tan(I/2)=250\tan20^\circ=250\times0.36397=91.0\) m.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is the arc length \(L=RI\pi/180=250(40)\pi/180\), not a tangent distance.
  • (C) is \(2T=2(91.0)=182.0\) m, the total length along both tangents from the PC through the PI to the PT, instead of one tangent distance.
  • (D) is \(R\tan I\), using the full angle.

A – Geometric design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-2

questions.question: A curve of radius 350 m is to carry traffic at 90 km/h. If the side-friction factor is limited to 0.13, the superelevation rate required is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Use the SI form \(e+f=v^2/(gR)\): \(v=90/3.6=25.0\) m/s. \(v^2/(gR)=625/(9.81\times350)=0.1820\). \(e=0.1820-0.13=0.052=5.2\%\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves (the Handbook’s \(0.01e+f=V^2/(15R)\) is the same relation in mph and ft; converting \(V=55.9\) mph and \(R=1148\) ft gives 0.1815, the same result).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is the friction factor alone expressed as a percent.
  • (C) is the full demand \(v^2/(gR)\) without subtracting friction.
  • (D) adds the friction factor to the demand (\(0.182+0.13\)) instead of subtracting it.

A – Geometric design · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 13-6

questions.question: For the curve in Question 13-9, the elevation of the low point, in feet, is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(x_m=g_1L/(g_1-g_2)=(-0.04)(800)/(-0.04-0.02)=533.3\) ft from the PVC (Sta 25+33.3).

\(Y_{low}=500.00-0.04(533.3)+3.75\times10^{-5}(533.3)^2=500.00-21.33+10.67=489.33\) ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Vertical Curves (\(x_m\) and curve elevation). The low point is not at the PVI (Sta 24+00, elevation 490.00) because the grades are unequal in magnitude.

A – Geometric design · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 13-10

questions.question: A minor road intersects a major road with a design speed of 55 mph at a stop-controlled intersection. If the time gap for a passenger car turning left from the minor road onto the major road is 7.5 s, the required intersection sight distance along the major road is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(ISD=1.47V_{major}t_g=1.47(55)(7.5)=606\) ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Stopping Sight Distance (\(ISD\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits the 1.47 mph-to-ft/s conversion.
  • (B) is the level-road stopping sight distance for 55 mph (\(t=2.5\) s, \(a=11.2\) ft/s²), not the ISD.
  • (C) uses \(t_g=6.5\) s, the AASHTO gap for a right turn or crossing maneuver, not the 7.5 s left-turn gap given.

A – Geometric design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-14

questions.question: A five-axle tractor–semitrailer has a 10,000-lb single steering axle and two 34,000-lb tandem axle groups. Using the Handbook load equivalency factors (single 10,000 lb: 0.0877; tandem 34,000 lb: 1.095), the truck factor in ESALs per truck is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Truck factor \(=0.0877+1.095+1.095=2.278\approx2.28\) ESALs per truck.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Highway Pavement Design (Load Equivalency Factors). Reading the tandem group from the single-axle column (11.18 each) would give 22.4, ten times too large.

B – Pavement design · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-18

questions.question: An approach carries 1,800 veh in the peak hour, and the busiest 15-minute period within that hour carries 520 veh. The peak hour factor is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(PHF=V/(4V_{15})=1800/(4\times520)=1800/2080=0.865\approx0.87\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Peak Hour Factor.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(V_{15}/V\).
  • (C) is the inverse, \(4V_{15}/V\).
  • (D) is \(V/V_{15}\).

C – Traffic flow · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-22

questions.question: A freeway on level terrain carries 10% trucks. The heavy-vehicle adjustment factor \(f_{HV}\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Level terrain, \(E_T=2.0\): \(f_{HV}=1/[1+0.10(2.0-1)]=1/1.10=0.909\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity (\(f_{HV}\) and the PCE table).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses \(E_T=3.0\) (rolling terrain).
  • (C) is the reciprocal, \(1+P_T(E_T-1)\).
  • (D) uses \(E_T\) instead of \(E_T-1\) and does not take the reciprocal (\(1+0.10\times2.0\)).

C – Traffic flow · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-26

questions.question: Under MUTCD conventions, a diamond-shaped sign with a black legend on a yellow background is a:
questions.explanation:
Yellow background, black legend, diamond shape identifies a warning sign.

FE Reference Handbook: not in the Handbook (MUTCD convention).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Regulatory signs are white rectangles (with the red STOP octagon and YIELD triangle).
  • (B) Guide signs are green, blue, or brown rectangles.
  • (C) Temporary traffic control signs are orange.

D – Traffic control devices · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-30

questions.question: Which statements about signal timing and signal warrants are correct? [Select all that apply]
choices: Total lost time per cycle increases as the number of phases increases.
Increasing the cycle length always reduces average delay at an intersection.
The capacity of a lane group equals its saturation flow rate multiplied by its effective green ratio \(g/C\).
MUTCD signal warrants describe conditions under which a signal may be justified; meeting a warrant does not by itself require installation.
For a fixed total lost time, a longer cycle increases the fraction of the cycle that is effective green.
questions.explanation:
Lost time accrues per phase, capacity is \(s\,g/C\), warrants permit rather than require a signal, and \((C-L)/C\) grows with \(C\); only the claim that longer cycles always reduce delay is false.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Traffic Signal Timing (intervals); other items are concepts.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — each phase contributes start-up and clearance lost time.
  • (B) False — beyond the optimum, longer cycles increase delay because vehicles wait through longer reds; Webster’s \(C_0\) is a minimum-delay optimum.
  • (C) True — \(c=s\,g/C\).
  • (D) True — warrants indicate that a signal may be justified after an engineering study; they do not mandate one.
  • (E) True — effective green fraction is \((C-L)/C\), which rises with \(C\) for fixed \(L\).

D – Traffic control devices · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-34

questions.question: An intersection with a total entering ADT of 12,400 veh/day experienced 9 crashes in one year. The crash rate, in crashes per million entering vehicles, is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(V=12{,}400\times365=4.526\times10^6\). \(R_{MEV}=9\times10^6/4.526\times10^6=1.99\) crashes per million entering vehicles.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Traffic Safety Equations (Crash Rates at Intersections).

E – Transportation planning · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-38

questions.question: [Point-and-click] Figure 13.14 shows a simple horizontal curve with \(R=250.00\) m and \(\Delta=70^\circ\). The station of the PC is 2+460.000. Five points carry the circled labels (A) through (E). Name the labeled point whose station is 2+612.716.
questions.explanation:
Stationing runs along the alignment, which means along the arc between the PC and the PT — never along the tangents. The curve length is \[L=\frac{R\Delta\pi}{180}=\frac{250(70)\pi}{180}=305.433\ \text{m}\] Half of that is 152.716 m, so the point 2+612.716 lies \[2460.000+152.716=2612.716\ \text{m}\] along the arc from the PC — the midpoint of the curve, point (D). It is the point at which the middle ordinate \(M=R(1-\cos(\Delta/2))=250(1-0.8192)=45.21\) m is measured from the long chord, and the external distance \(E=R(\sec(\Delta/2)-1)=55.19\) m is measured back to the PI.

Point (A) is the PC, station 2+460.000 by definition. Point (B) is the PI: it is not on the alignment at all, and the tempting arithmetic \(PC+T=2460.000+250\tan35^\circ=2460.000+175.052\) = 2+635.052 is a common error — the tangent distance is a chainage along the tangent, not along the road. Point (C) is the PT, at \(PC+L\) = 2+765.433. Point (E) is the midpoint of the long chord, which lies 45.21 m inside the pavement and is not a point on the alignment, so it has no station.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves.

A – Geometric design · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 13-42

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following are characteristics of construction manager at risk (CMAR) delivery?
choices: The construction manager is engaged during design to provide estimating, constructability review, and scheduling.
The construction manager holds the trade contracts.
The owner holds a separate contract with the design professional.
The construction manager commits to a guaranteed maximum price.
The construction manager acts solely as the owner’s fee-based agent and bears no cost risk.
questions.explanation:
Under CMAR the construction manager joins during design for preconstruction services (A), later holds the trade contracts as the builder (B), and commits to a guaranteed maximum price, bearing the cost risk above it (D). The owner keeps a separate design contract, so the designer remains the owner’s agent (C).

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the CM is hired during design to provide preconstruction services.
  • (B) True — as the builder, the CM at risk holds the trade contracts.
  • (C) True — the owner keeps a separate design contract, so the designer remains the owner’s agent.
  • (D) True — the CM commits to a GMP and bears the cost risk above it.
  • (E) False — this describes CM as agent (“pure CM”), where the CM is a fee-based consultant, the owner holds the trade contracts, and the CM guarantees nothing. The “at risk” in CMAR is precisely the difference.

A – Project administration · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-4

questions.question: A trench 4.5 m deep with a 1.2-m-wide bottom is to be open-cut in saturated sand, which classifies as Type C soil. Using the maximum allowable slope of 1 1/2 : 1 (H:V), the required top width of the excavation is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Saturated sand is Type C, maximum allowable slope \(1\tfrac{1}{2}:1\), so \(m=1.5\) (horizontal per unit of vertical depth) on each side. \[W_{top}=b+2mH=1.2+2(1.5)(4.5)=1.2+13.5=14.7\ \text{m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: none (OSHA slope values; the trapezoid geometry matches the end area used in Civil Engineering — Earthwork Formulas).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 7.2 m inverts the ratio, using 1 horizontal per 1.5 vertical.
  • (B) 10.2 m applies the Type B slope of 1:1.
  • (C) 13.5 m is the total horizontal slope offset alone, omitting the 1.2-m trench bottom.

B – Construction operations and methods · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-8

questions.question: A track loader has a 3.0-m³ bucket, a bucket fill factor of 0.85, and a cycle time of 0.60 min. Working a 50-minute hour, its production is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Volume per cycle \(q=3.0(0.85)=2.55\ \text{m}^3\) (loose). \[P=\frac{q\times60\times E}{C}=\frac{2.55(50)}{0.60}=212.5\ \text{LCM/hr}\] (The 50-minute hour is \(60E=50\).)

FE Reference Handbook: none — equipment cycle analysis is not in the Handbook.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 177 LCM/hr applies the job efficiency twice, once as the 50-minute hour and again as the factor 50/60 = 0.833: \(2.55(50)(0.833)/0.60=177\) LCM/hr.
  • (C) 255 LCM/hr uses a full 60-minute hour, i.e., \(E=1.0\): \(2.55(60)/0.60=255\) LCM/hr.
  • (D) 294 LCM/hr divides the heaped capacity by the fill factor instead of multiplying: \((3.0/0.85)(50)/0.60=294\) LCM/hr.

B – Construction operations and methods · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-12

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A mobile crane will set a rooftop air handler. Which of the following statements about planning the lift are correct?
choices: The gross capacity read from the load chart must be reduced by the weight of the hook block, slings, shackles, and spreader bar.
Chart capacity decreases as the operating radius increases.
The lift must be checked at the largest radius through which the load will swing, not only at the set point.
A jib stowed on the boom need not be deducted because it is not carrying load.
Ground conditions under the outriggers must be adequate and the crane must be level within the manufacturer’s tolerance.
questions.explanation:
Net capacity is the gross chart capacity at the governing radius less every deduction, and the governing radius is the largest one the load passes through. Statements (A), (B), (C), and (E) are correct; (D) is false because a stowed jib is a deduction from chart capacity.

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — net capacity equals gross chart capacity minus all deductions: hook block, slings, shackles, spreader bars.
  • (B) True — capacity falls as radius grows because the overturning moment is load times radius.
  • (C) True — the governing case is the largest radius the load passes through, not necessarily the set point.
  • (D) False — a jib stowed on the boom is a deduction from chart capacity even when it is not rigged for use, because it adds moment about the tipping axis.
  • (E) True — OSHA requires adequate supporting ground (mats or cribbing) and a level machine.

B – Construction operations and methods · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-16

questions.question: In Figure 14.13, activity Q (4 days) has two predecessors: activity M, whose early start is day 10, linked start-to-start with a 3-day lag; and activity N, whose early finish is day 11, linked finish-to-start with no lag. The early start and early finish of Q are:
questions.explanation:
Apply each relationship and take the latest result:

  • SS + 3 from M: \(ES_Q\ge ES_M+3=10+3=13\)
  • FS from N: \(ES_Q\ge EF_N=11\)

\(ES_Q=\max(13,11)=13\) and \(EF_Q=13+4=17\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — CPM Precedence Relationships (start-to-start: the start of B depends on the start of A).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) uses \(ES_M\) without adding the lag.
  • (B) applies only the finish-to-start link and ignores the SS constraint, which governs here.
  • (D) treats the SS + 3 as a finish-to-start with lag, \(EF_M+3=(10+6)+3=19\) — a common lag error.

C – Project controls · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-20

questions.question: A project with a budget at completion of $3,000,000 reports an earned value of $1,200,000 and an actual cost of $1,350,000. Using the Handbook forecasting relations, the estimate at completion is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[CPI=\frac{EV}{AC}=\frac{1{,}200{,}000}{1{,}350{,}000}=0.8889\] \[ETC=\frac{BAC-BCWP}{CPI}=\frac{3{,}000{,}000-1{,}200{,}000}{0.8889}=\$2{,}025{,}000\] \[EAC=ACWP+ETC=1{,}350{,}000+2{,}025{,}000=\$3{,}375{,}000\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — Earned-Value Analysis, Forecasting (\(ETC=(BAC-BCWP)/CPI\), \(EAC=ACWP+ETC\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $2,025,000 reports the ETC, not the EAC.
  • (B) $3,000,000 is the BAC and ignores the overrun to date.
  • (C) $3,150,000 uses \(AC+(BAC-EV)\), i.e., assumes the remaining work is done exactly on budget (\(CPI=1\)) — a legitimate forecast, but not the Handbook form.

C – Project controls · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-24

questions.question: A slab on grade is 40 m by 25 m by 150 mm thick. The estimator adds 6% for waste and over-excavation and orders whole cubic meters. The concrete to be ordered is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Net placed volume \(=40(25)(0.150)=150\ \text{m}^3\).

Ordered \(=150(1.06)=159.0\rightarrow159\ \text{m}^3\).

FE Reference Handbook: none (quantity takeoff conventions).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 141 m³ subtracts 6% instead of adding it.
  • (B) 150 m³ is the placed volume, which is what the owner pays for, but not what must be ordered.
  • (D) 1,590 m³ uses a slab thickness of 1.5 m instead of 0.150 m — always confirm whether a thickness is given in millimeters or meters.

D – Construction estimating · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-28

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following belong in job (project) overhead, as distinct from direct cost or home-office overhead?
choices: The project superintendent’s salary for the duration of the job
Ready-mix concrete delivered for the footings
The temporary site office, its utilities, and site sanitation
Performance and payment bond premiums for this project
questions.explanation:
Job (project) overhead — the “general conditions” cost — is the cost of running this site that cannot be charged to a single work item: supervision (A), the temporary office, utilities, and sanitation (C), and project-specific bond premiums, permits, and builder’s risk insurance (E).

The distinction matters on the exam because markups are applied in sequence: direct cost, then job overhead, then home-office overhead and profit.

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — site supervision for this job is job overhead.
  • (B) False — ready-mix concrete for the footings is a direct cost, traceable to a specific item of work.
  • (C) True — the temporary office, its utilities, and sanitation are general-conditions costs of this site.
  • (D) False — the corporate accounting department is home-office (general) overhead, spread across all the company’s projects as a percentage of volume.
  • (E) True — bond premiums for this project are job overhead.

D – Construction estimating · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-32

questions.question:
[Matching] Using Figure 14.11, match each annotation (1–5) with its meaning (a–e). Each is used once.

  • (a) Concrete cover from the face of the concrete to the reinforcement
  • (b) A section cut whose view is drawn on sheet S-2
  • (c) A footing mark keyed to the footing schedule
  • (d) A column grid line identifier
  • (e) A column type repeated throughout unless noted otherwise
pairs: “F2” next to a dashed square on the plan
The circled letter “B” on a dash-dot line
questions.explanation:
A mark such as “F2” (1) identifies a repeated element by type and sends the reader to the corresponding schedule for size, thickness, and reinforcement (c) — the plan itself carries no dimensions for the footing. A circled letter or number on a dash-dot line (2) is a column grid line (d); grids are usually lettered one way and numbered the other so that any column can be named “B-1.” The flag with a letter over a sheet number (3) is a section marker: section A is cut here and drawn on sheet S-2 (b), with the arrow giving the direction of view. “typ.” after a callout (4) means the note applies to every similar condition unless noted otherwise (e). “clr.” (5) is clear cover, the distance from the concrete face to the nearest bar surface (a).

Reading a set is a matter of following these cross-references: plan gives location and mark, schedule gives size and reinforcement, section gives cover and arrangement.

FE Reference Handbook: none — drawing conventions are not in the Handbook.

E – Interpretation of engineering drawings · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-36

questions.question: The curve \(4x^2-4xy+y^2+3x-8=0\) is a:
questions.explanation:
\(A=4\), \(B=-4\), \(C=1\): \(B^2-4AC=16-16=0\), so the conic is a parabola (rotated, because \(B\neq0\)).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Conic Section Equation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) A circle requires \(A=C\) and \(B=0\).
  • (B) An ellipse requires \(B^2-4AC<0\).
  • (C) A hyperbola requires \(B^2-4AC>0\).

A – Analytic geometry · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 1-4

questions.question: For \(f(x)=x^2\sin x\), the value of \(f'(\pi)\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Product rule: \(f'(x)=2x\sin x+x^2\cos x\). At \(x=\pi\): \(\sin\pi=0\), \(\cos\pi=-1\), so \(f'(\pi)=0+\pi^2(-1)=-9.87\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Derivatives (entries 5, 8, 16).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) \(-6.28\) is \(-2\pi\), from multiplying the two derivatives, \((2x)(\cos x)\) at \(x=\pi\), instead of using the product rule.
  • (C) 0 comes from ignoring the product rule and using \(2x\sin x\) alone.
  • (D) 9.87 is a sign error on \(\cos\pi\).

B – Single-variable calculus · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 1-8

questions.question: The radius of curvature of \(y=x^3/3\) at \(x=1\) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(y'=x^2=1\) and \(y''=2x=2\) at \(x=1\). \[R=\frac{\left[1+(y')^2\right]^{3/2}}{|y''|}=\frac{(1+1)^{3/2}}{2}=\frac{2.828}{2}=1.414\]

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — The Radius of Curvature.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.500 is the shallow-curve approximation \(R\approx1/|y''|\), which is not valid here because the slope \(y'=1\) is not small.
  • (B) 0.707 is the curvature \(K=1/R\).
  • (C) 1.000 omits the 3/2 power: \((1+1)/2\).

B – Single-variable calculus · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-12

questions.question: [Select all that apply] For \(f(x)=x^3-3x\), which statements are true?
choices: \(f\) has a local maximum at \(x=-1\).
\(f\) has a local minimum at \(x=1\).
\(f\) has a point of inflection at \(x=0\).
\(f\) has an absolute maximum at \(x=-1\).
\(f\) is increasing for all \(x>1\).
questions.explanation:
\(f'(x)=3x^2-3=3(x-1)(x+1)\); \(f''(x)=6x\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Differential Calculus (Tests for Maximum, Minimum, and Point of Inflection).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(f'(-1)=0\) and \(f''(-1)=-6<0\): local maximum, \(f(-1)=2\).
  • (B) True — \(f'(1)=0\) and \(f''(1)=6>0\): local minimum, \(f(1)=-2\).
  • (C) True — \(f''(0)=0\) and \(f''\) changes sign from negative to positive through \(x=0\).
  • (D) False — a cubic is unbounded above (\(f\to\infty\) as \(x\to\infty\)), so it has no absolute maximum; \(x=-1\) is only a local maximum.
  • (E) True — for \(x>1\), both factors of \(f'\) are positive, so \(f'>0\) and \(f\) is increasing.

B – Single-variable calculus · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 1-16

questions.question: For \(\mathbf{A}=2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}+\mathbf{k}\) and \(\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}+2\mathbf{k}\), the cross product \(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\) is:
questions.explanation:
\[\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf{i}&\mathbf{j}&\mathbf{k}\\2&3&1\\1&-1&2\end{vmatrix}=\mathbf{i}[(3)(2)-(1)(-1)]-\mathbf{j}[(2)(2)-(1)(1)]+\mathbf{k}[(2)(-1)-(3)(1)]=7\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}-5\mathbf{k}\] Check: \((7,-3,-5)\cdot(2,3,1)=14-9-5=0\) ✓ and \((7,-3,-5)\cdot(1,-1,2)=7+3-10=0\) ✓.

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Vectors (cross product); Mathematics — Determinants.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) forgets the minus sign on the \(\mathbf{j}\) cofactor.
  • (C) is \(\mathbf{B}\times\mathbf{A}\), the negative of the correct result.
  • (D) has the \(\mathbf{i}\) and \(\mathbf{k}\) magnitudes exchanged, with the sign of the \(\mathbf{i}\) component also wrong.

C – Vector operations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-20

questions.question: Eight traffic counts (vehicles per 15 min) were recorded: 12, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 15, 23. The median of the data is:
questions.explanation:
Sorted: 12, 15, 15, 15, 18, 20, 22, 23. With \(n=8\) (even), the median is the average of the 4th and 5th values: \((15+18)/2=16.5\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Dispersion, Mean, Median, and Mode Values.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 17.5 is the mean \((140/8)\).
  • (C) 18.0 is the 5th sorted value alone, not the average of the two middle values.
  • (D) 19.0 averages the 4th and 5th values of the list as recorded, \((18+20)/2\), without sorting it first.

D – Statistics · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 1-24

questions.question: Ten tensile tests on steel coupons give a sample mean yield strength of 42.0 ksi with a sample standard deviation of 3.0 ksi. The 95% confidence interval for the mean yield strength is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\sigma\) is unknown, so use \(t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\) with \(\alpha/2=0.025\) and \(v=9\): from the Student’s t-Distribution table, \(t_{0.025,9}=2.262\). \[E=2.262\times\frac{3.0}{\sqrt{10}}=2.262\times0.9487=2.146\text{ ksi};\qquad 42.0\pm2.15\ \Rightarrow\ 39.85\text{ to }44.15\text{ ksi}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Confidence Interval for the Mean µ of a Normal Distribution, case (B); Student’s t-Distribution table.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(\bar{X}\pm s\), with no multiplier and no \(\sqrt{n}\).
  • (C) uses \(Z_{0.025}=1.960\) instead of \(t\) \((E=1.86)\).
  • (D) divides by \(n\) instead of \(\sqrt{n}\) \((E=0.68)\).

D – Statistics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-28

questions.question: Each of five independent soil samples has a 10% probability of failing a gradation test. The probability that at least one sample fails is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Binomial with \(n=5\), \(p=0.10\), \(q=0.90\). \(P(\text{at least one fails})=1-P(0)=1-C(5,0)\,p^0q^5=1-0.9^5=1-0.5905=0.4095\approx0.41\). The Handbook’s Cumulative Binomial Probabilities table confirms \(P(X\le0)=5.90\times10^{-1}\) for \(n=5\), \(p=0.10\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Binomial Distribution; Cumulative Binomial Probabilities table.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.10 is the single-sample probability.
  • (C) 0.50 adds probabilities as if they were mutually exclusive \((5\times0.1)\).
  • (D) 0.59 is \(P(0)\), the probability that no sample fails.

D – Statistics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 1-32

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Regarding a confidence interval for a population mean, which statements are true?
choices: Increasing the sample size, other things equal, narrows the interval.
A 99% interval is wider than a 95% interval computed from the same data.
The \(t\) distribution is used when the population standard deviation is unknown.
As the sample size becomes very large, \(t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\) approaches \(Z_{\alpha/2}\).
A 95% confidence interval contains 95% of the individual sample values.
questions.explanation:
The half-width of the interval is \(Z_{\alpha/2}\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) (or \(t_{\alpha/2}s/\sqrt{n}\)); each statement follows from this form.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Probability and Statistics — Confidence Interval for the Mean µ of a Normal Distribution; Student’s t-Distribution table.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the half-width is proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\).
  • (B) True — \(Z_{0.005}=2.5758>Z_{0.025}=1.9600\) (and likewise for \(t\)), so more confidence requires a wider interval.
  • (C) True — case (B) of the Handbook’s confidence-interval formulas uses \(t_{\alpha/2}\) with \(s\).
  • (D) True — the \(\infty\) row of the \(t\) table equals the normal fractiles (e.g., 1.960 at \(\alpha=0.025\)).
  • (E) False — a confidence interval bounds the population mean, not individual observations; the interval for individual values would be roughly \(\bar{X}\pm2s\), far wider than \(\bar{X}\pm2s/\sqrt{n}\).

D – Statistics · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 1-36

questions.question: While reviewing a set of publicly available construction documents for a neighboring site, a licensed structural engineer notices that the sealed drawings for a pedestrian bridge appear to omit lateral bracing that, in the engineer’s judgment, is necessary for stability under design wind loads. The drawings were sealed by another licensee whom the engineer does not know. Under the NCEES Rules of Professional Conduct, the engineer’s most appropriate action is to:
choices: Make a reasonable effort to inform the sealing licensee of the apparent material omission, since it may affect public safety.
Do nothing, because the engineer has no contractual relationship with the project and criticizing another licensee’s work is prohibited.
Post a detailed critique of the design on a professional discussion forum to warn the public.
File a complaint with the licensing board before contacting the other licensee, since the omission suggests incompetence.
questions.explanation:
Part C, item 4 requires a licensee who believes another licensee’s work contains a material discrepancy, error, or omission that may affect public health, safety, or welfare to make a reasonable effort to inform that licensee, unless legally prohibited. Missing lateral bracing on a pedestrian bridge is exactly such a matter. The rule is aimed at the sealing engineer first because that engineer can verify whether the bracing is shown elsewhere, was intentionally omitted with justification, or is a genuine error—and can correct it fastest.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — 2025–26 Model Rules, Section 240.15, Part C, items 3 and 4; Part A, item 5.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) The Rules prohibit malicious, false, or indiscriminate criticism (Part C, item 3), not a good-faith notification of a possible safety error, and the absence of a contract does not remove the duty.
  • (C) A public critique of a design the engineer has only partially reviewed risks violating Part A, item 5 (public opinions only on adequate knowledge) and Part C, item 3, and does nothing to fix the bridge.
  • (D) Reporting to the board (Part A, item 8) applies to known or reasonably believed violations; an apparent omission whose explanation is unknown does not yet rise to that level, and the Rules direct the licensee to the other engineer first. If the sealing engineer refuses to address a confirmed danger, a report to the board and notice to the authority having jurisdiction would then be appropriate.

A – Codes of ethics · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 2-4

questions.question: A jurisdiction’s statute of limitations for claims against design professionals is 3 years from the date the defect is discovered, and its statute of repose is 10 years from substantial completion of the improvement. A bridge designed by an engineer reached substantial completion on June 30, 2014. A latent design defect was discovered on March 1, 2023, and the owner filed suit on January 15, 2025. The suit is:
choices: Timely, because it was filed within 3 years of discovery.
Barred by the statute of limitations.
Barred by the statute of repose.
Timely, because the statute of repose is tolled once the defect is discovered.
questions.explanation:
Compute both deadlines. Statute of limitations: 3 years from discovery on March 1, 2023, gives March 1, 2026. Statute of repose: 10 years from substantial completion on June 30, 2014, gives June 30, 2024. The suit filed January 15, 2025 is within the limitations period but about 6.5 months after the repose period ended. A claim must satisfy both statutes, so it is barred by the statute of repose.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice (statutes of limitations and repose are general legal doctrine; the periods are supplied in the question).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Checks only the limitations statute.
  • (B) The limitations period runs to March 1, 2026, so the suit was within it.
  • (D) The distinguishing feature of a statute of repose is that it runs from substantial completion regardless of discovery; it is not tolled by the discovery rule.

B – Professional liability · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 2-8

questions.question: A licensed engineer who owns a small firm is asked by a developer to seal a set of site-grading plans that were prepared by an out-of-state consultant not licensed in the jurisdiction. The engineer had no involvement while the plans were being prepared but performs a careful two-day review, finds the plans acceptable, and seals them. Under the NCEES Model Law and Rules of Professional Conduct, this action is:
choices: Permissible, because the engineer performed a thorough review and accepted responsibility.
Permissible, because the plans were prepared by a competent engineer licensed elsewhere.
A violation, because the plans were not prepared under the engineer’s responsible charge.
A violation only if the plans are later found to contain an error.
questions.explanation:
Responsible charge (Model Law 110.20 E) requires that the licensee have and exercise authority to review and to change, reject, or approve the work throughout its development, be personally aware of the project’s scope and parameters, be able to answer for the decisions in detail, and accept full responsibility. A review performed only after the plans were complete cannot satisfy the first element. Sealing the plans violates Rules Part B, item 2 and is a ground for discipline under Model Law 150.10 A.10. This is the practice known as plan stamping.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice — Model Law, Section 110.20 E (Responsible Charge); Section 150.10 A.10; 2025–26 Model Rules, Section 240.15, Part B, item 2.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Thoroughness after the fact does not create authority during development.
  • (B) The preparer’s competence elsewhere is irrelevant; the preparer is not licensed in this jurisdiction and the sealing engineer was not in responsible charge.
  • (D) The violation is the act of sealing work not under responsible charge; it does not depend on whether an error is later found.

C – Licensure · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 2-12

questions.question: A contractor submits a bid of $4.2 million to construct a pump station. The owner responds, “Your bid is accepted at $4.0 million with the completion date moved up by 30 days.” The contractor replies that it will not perform at $4.0 million. The owner then attempts to hold the contractor to its original $4.2 million bid. Which statement is correct?
choices: No contract exists, because the owner’s response was a counteroffer that rejected the bid, and the contractor declined the counteroffer.
A contract exists at $4.2 million, because the contractor’s bid was an offer and the owner accepted it.
A contract exists at $4.0 million, because the contractor did not object to the price within a reasonable time.
A contract exists at $4.2 million with the original completion date, because the owner’s changed terms are severable.
questions.explanation:
The bid was an offer. The owner’s response changed two material terms—price and completion date—so it was not an acceptance but a counteroffer, and a counteroffer operates as a rejection of the original offer. The contractor then declined the counteroffer. With the original offer rejected and the counteroffer refused, there is no mutual assent and no contract; the owner cannot revive the $4.2 million bid unilaterally.

FE Reference Handbook: Ethics and Professional Practice (offer, acceptance, and counteroffer are general contract-law doctrine).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) The owner never accepted the bid; it modified it.
  • (C) Silence is not acceptance, and the contractor in fact objected.
  • (D) Material terms cannot be severed to manufacture an acceptance the offeree did not give.

D – Contracts and contract law · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 2-16

questions.question: A city borrows $250,000 at 6% per year to purchase a fire truck and will repay the loan in 20 equal end-of-year payments. The annual payment is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[A = P\,(A/P, 6\%, 20) = 250{,}000 \times \frac{0.06(1.06)^{20}}{(1.06)^{20}-1} = 250{,}000(0.0872) = \$21{,}800\] The 6.00% table gives (A/P, 6%, 20) = 0.0872.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Factor Table (Capital Recovery); Interest Rate Tables, i = 6.00%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $6,800 uses the sinking-fund factor (A/F, 6%, 20) = 0.0272.
  • (B) $12,500 is the principal divided by 20 with no interest.
  • (C) $15,000 is interest only (\(0.06 \times 250{,}000\)) with no principal repayment.

A – Time value of money · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 3-2

questions.question: An engineer deposits $2,000 at the end of each year for 10 years into an account earning 6% per year. No further deposits are made. The balance in the account 5 years after the last deposit is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Bring the deposits to the time of the last deposit (year 10) with (F/A), then compound the lump sum 5 more years with (F/P): \[F_{10} = 2{,}000\,(F/A, 6\%, 10) = 2{,}000(13.1808) = \$26{,}362\] \[F_{15} = 26{,}362\,(F/P, 6\%, 5) = 26{,}362(1.3382) = \$35{,}278 \approx \$35{,}300\] Both factors match the 6.00% table (13.1808 and 1.3382).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Factor Table (Uniform Series Compound Amount; Single Payment Compound Amount); Interest Rate Tables, i = 6.00%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $26,400 stops at year 10 and omits the 5 years of further growth.
  • (C) $37,400 compounds the year-10 balance for 6 years instead of 5, \(26{,}362\,(F/P, 6\%, 6) = 26{,}362(1.4185)\)—an off-by-one count of the periods from year 10 to year 15.
  • (D) $46,600 is \(2{,}000\,(F/A, 6\%, 15)\), which wrongly assumes deposits continued through year 15.

A – Time value of money · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 3-6

questions.question: A $1,000 face-value bond pays 6% annual coupons ($60 at the end of each year) and matures in 10 years. An investor who requires an 8% annual return should pay most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Bond value is the present worth of the coupons and the face value at the investor’s required rate of 8%: \[\text{Value} = 60\,(P/A, 8\%, 10) + 1{,}000\,(P/F, 8\%, 10) = 60(6.7101) + 1{,}000(0.4632) = 402.6 + 463.2 = \$865.8 \approx \$866\] Both factors match the 8.00% table. The bond sells at a discount because the required return exceeds the coupon rate.

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Bonds; Interest Rate Tables, i = 8.00%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) $1,000 would be correct only if the required rate equaled the 6% coupon rate.
  • (C) $1,147 results from swapping the rates—discounting an $80 coupon at 6%.
  • (D) $1,403 discounts the coupons (\(60 \times 6.7101 = \$402.6\)) but adds the $1,000 face value undiscounted, as if it were received today rather than at year 10.

A – Time value of money · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 3-10

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each cost term (1–4) with its description (a–d).

  • (a) The additional cost of producing one more unit of output
  • (b) A cost that does not change with the level of output
  • (c) A cost already incurred that cannot be recovered by any current decision
  • (d) The benefit forgone by not choosing the next-best alternative
questions.explanation:
A sunk cost (1) is already incurred and unrecoverable (c). An opportunity cost (2) is the benefit forgone from the next-best alternative (d). An incremental cost (3) is the added cost of one more unit (a). A fixed cost (4) does not vary with output (b).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — cost concepts (fundamental definitions).

B – Cost · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 3-14

questions.question: A proposed pedestrian bridge has a first cost of $4,500,000, a 25-year life with no salvage value, annual operation and maintenance costs of $90,000, and annual benefits to users valued at $620,000. At \(i = 8\%\), the conventional benefit-cost ratio (O&M counted as a cost) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Annual cost \(= 4{,}500{,}000\,(A/P, 8\%, 25) + 90{,}000 = 4{,}500{,}000(0.0937) + 90{,}000 = 421{,}650 + 90{,}000 = \$511{,}650\). The 8.00% table gives (A/P, 8%, 25) = 0.0937. \[B/C = 620{,}000/511{,}650 = 1.21\]

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Benefit-Cost Analysis; Factor Table (Capital Recovery); Interest Rate Tables, i = 8.00%.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 1.26 is the modified ratio, \((620{,}000 - 90{,}000)/421{,}650\), with O&M moved to the numerator—a valid ratio but not the conventional one requested.
  • (C) 1.47 omits the O&M cost from the denominator.
  • (D) 2.30 spreads the first cost over the life with no interest, \(4{,}500{,}000/25 = \$180{,}000\) per year, so \(C = \$270{,}000\) and \(620{,}000/270{,}000 = 2.30\); the capital recovery factor is required.

C – Analyses · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 3-18

questions.question: A contract will pay $80,000 in actual (then-current) dollars at the end of year 6. The real (inflation-free) interest rate is 5% per year and general inflation is expected to be 3% per year. The present worth of the payment is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The payment is in actual dollars, so use the inflation-adjusted rate: \(d = i + f + if = 0.05 + 0.03 + 0.0015 = 0.0815\). \[P = 80{,}000\,(1.0815)^{-6} = 80{,}000/1.6001 = \$49{,}995 \approx \$50{,}000\] Equivalently, deflate to constant dollars, \(80{,}000/(1.03)^6 = \$66{,}999\), then discount at the real rate, \(66{,}999/(1.05)^6 = \$49{,}995\).

FE Reference Handbook: Engineering Economics — Inflation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) $41,900 counts inflation twice: it discounts at the inflation-adjusted rate \(d\) and then deflates again by \((1.03)^6\).
  • (C) $59,700 discounts at the real rate only, ignoring inflation.
  • (D) $67,000 deflates for inflation but never discounts for the time value of money.

C – Analyses · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 3-22

questions.question: A 700-N force acts along the line from point P (1, 2, 3) m toward point Q (5, −1, −9) m. The \(z\)-component of the force is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
The direction vector from P to Q is \((5-1,\ -1-2,\ -9-3) = (4, -3, -12)\) m, with length \(R = \sqrt{16 + 9 + 144} = 13\) m. By \(F_z = (z/R)F\): \[F_z = \frac{-12}{13}(700) = -646\,\text{N}\] (The full vector is \(215\mathbf{i} - 162\mathbf{j} - 646\mathbf{k}\) N, and \(\theta_z = \arccos(-12/13) = 157.4^\circ\).)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Resolution of a Force.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is the magnitude of the \(x\)-component with a wrong sign;
  • (C) is the \(y\)-component;
  • (D) results from taking the direction vector from Q to P instead of from P to Q.

A – Resultants of force systems · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-2

questions.question: A force \(\mathbf{F} = 50\mathbf{i} - 20\mathbf{j} + 40\mathbf{k}\) lb acts at the point (3, 1, −2) ft. The moment of the force about the \(z\)-axis is:
questions.explanation:
The moment about the \(z\)-axis is the \(z\)-component of \(\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}\) with \(\mathbf{r} = (3, 1, -2)\): \[M_z = xF_y - yF_x = 3(-20) - 1(50) = -110\,\text{ft·lb}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Moments (Couples).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(M_x = yF_z - zF_y = 1(40) - (-2)(-20) = 0\);
  • (C) is \(M_y = zF_x - xF_z = (-2)(50) - 3(40) = -220\) ft·lb;
  • (D) has the wrong sign (the \(z\)-component is \(xF_y - yF_x\), not \(yF_x - xF_y\)).

B – Equivalent force systems · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 4-6

questions.question: The 10-m simply supported beam in Figure 4.16(a) carries a uniform load of 5 kN/m over its full length and a 20-kN concentrated load 3 m from the pin at A. The vertical reaction at A is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Uniform-load resultant: \(5(10) = 50\) kN at midspan (5 m from A). Moments about A: \[B_y(10) - 50(5) - 20(3) = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad B_y = 31\,\text{kN}\] \[A_y = 50 + 20 - 31 = 39\,\text{kN}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the share of the point load alone, \(20(7)/10 = 14\) kN, with the uniform load forgotten;
  • (B) is half of the uniform load only;
  • (C) is the reaction at B.

C – Equilibrium of rigid bodies · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 4-10

questions.question: A highway sign weighing 400 N is mounted on a vertical post fixed at its base. The center of the sign is 4.0 m above the base and offset 1.5 m horizontally from the post axis. A wind force of 600 N acts horizontally on the center of the sign, perpendicular to the plane containing the post axis and the sign center. The torsional moment (moment about the post axis) at the base is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Put the post axis along \(z\), the arm to the sign along \(x\) (sign center at (1.5, 0, 4.0) m), and the wind along \(y\): \(\mathbf{F}_w = 600\mathbf{j}\) N; weight \(\mathbf{W} = -400\mathbf{k}\) N. The base reaction must balance the moment of both forces about the base: \[\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}_w = (1.5, 0, 4.0) \times (0, 600, 0) = (0 \cdot 0 - 4.0 \cdot 600,\ 4.0 \cdot 0 - 1.5 \cdot 0,\ 1.5 \cdot 600 - 0) = (-2400, 0, 900)\,\text{N·m}\] \[\mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{W} = (1.5, 0, 4.0) \times (0, 0, -400) = (0, 600, 0)\,\text{N·m}\] The torsional moment about the post axis is the \(z\)-component: \(M_z = 900\) N·m (wind force × horizontal offset). The bending moments are 2400 N·m about \(x\) (wind × height) and 600 N·m about \(y\) (weight × offset).

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Moments (Couples); Equilibrium Requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the bending moment from the sign weight;
  • (C) is the bending moment from the wind about the horizontal axis;
  • (D) is the resultant bending moment \(\sqrt{2400^2 + 600^2}\), not the torsion.

C – Equilibrium of rigid bodies · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 4-14

questions.question: For the truss in Figure 4.17, the force in member AF is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Reactions: the loading is symmetric, so \(A_y = E_y = (20 + 30 + 20)/2 = 35\) kN. At joint A, member AF runs from A (0, 0) to F (3, 4): unit vector (0.6, 0.8). Assuming tension, \[\Sigma F_V = 35 + 0.8F_{AF} = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad F_{AF} = -43.75\,\text{kN}\] that is, 43.8 kN compression. Then \(\Sigma F_H\): \(F_{AB} = -0.6(-43.75) = 26.25\) kN tension.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Plane Truss: Method of Joints.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the force in AB;
  • (B) is the reaction itself;
  • (D) divides the reaction by 0.6 instead of 0.8 (using the horizontal component of the diagonal in the vertical equation).

D – Frames and trusses · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-18

questions.question: For the frame in Figure 4.18, the magnitude of the resultant force transmitted through the pin at B is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
From the FBD of member BC (Question 4-21): \(\Sigma F_x = B_x + C_x = 0\) gives \(B_x = 3\) kN; \(\Sigma F_y = B_y + 4 - 8 = 0\) gives \(B_y = 4\) kN. The resultant pin force is \[B = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5\,\text{kN}\] (Check on member AB: it carries \(A_x = -3\) kN, \(A_y = 4\) kN at A, the 6-kN load at D, and the reversed pin forces −3 kN and −4 kN at B. \(\Sigma F_x = -3 + 6 - 3 = 0\); \(\Sigma F_y = 4 - 4 = 0\); moments about A: the 6-kN force at height 1.5 m gives −9 kN·m and the −3-kN horizontal force at height 3 m gives +9 kN·m, for a sum of zero. ✓)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(B_x\) alone;
  • (B) is \(B_y\) alone;
  • (D) adds the components arithmetically instead of vectorially.

D – Frames and trusses · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-22

questions.question: The plate in Figure 4.19(a) is a 200 mm × 300 mm rectangle with a 120 mm × 200 mm rectangular notch removed from its upper right and a 40-mm-diameter hole centered at (40, 250) mm. The \(y\)-coordinate of the centroid of the net area is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Treat the notch and hole as negative areas (reference axes at the lower-left corner):

Piece \(a_n\) (mm²) \(y_n\) (mm) \(y_n a_n\) (mm³)
Rectangle 200 × 300 60,000 150 9,000,000
Notch 120 × 200 (from \(x\) = 80 to 200, \(y\) = 100 to 300) −24,000 200 −4,800,000
Hole \(-\pi(20)^2\) −1,256.6 250 −314,159
Sum 34,743.4 3,885,841

\[y_c = \frac{3{,}885{,}841}{34{,}743.4} = 111.8\,\text{mm}\] (For reference, \(x_c = [60{,}000(100) - 24{,}000(140) - 1{,}256.6(40)]/34{,}743.4 = 74.5\) mm.)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Centroids of Masses, Areas, Lengths, and Volumes.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the \(x\)-coordinate of the centroid;
  • (C) is \(y_c\) with the hole ignored (116.7 mm);
  • (D) is the centroid of the full rectangle.

E – Centroid of area · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 4-26

questions.question: A hollow circular pipe has an outside diameter of 10 in and an inside diameter of 9 in. Its radius of gyration about a centroidal axis is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a hollow circle with outer radius \(a\) and inner radius \(b\), the table gives \(r_{x_c}^2 = (a^2 + b^2)/4\). With \(a = 5\) in and \(b = 4.5\) in: \[r = \sqrt{\frac{5^2 + 4.5^2}{4}} = \frac{\sqrt{45.25}}{2} = 3.36\,\text{in}\] (Equivalently \(r = \sqrt{I/A}\) with \(I = \pi(a^4 - b^4)/4 = 168.8\) in\(^{4}\) and \(A = \pi(a^2 - b^2) = 14.92\) in².)

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — table of area properties (hollow circle); Radius of Gyration.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) subtracts the squares instead of adding them, \(\sqrt{(5^2 - 4.5^2)/4}\);
  • (B) is \(a/2\), the value for a solid circle;
  • (D) is the mean radius, a common but incorrect guess.

F – Area moments of inertia · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 4-30

questions.question: The uniform 5-m ladder in Figure 4.20 weighs 200 N and leans against a smooth wall. The coefficient of static friction between the ladder and the floor is 0.30. The minimum angle \(\theta\) between the ladder and the floor at which the ladder will not slip is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
FBD of the ladder: weight \(W\) at the midpoint, normal force \(N_A\) from the smooth wall (horizontal), and at the floor a normal force \(N_B = W\) and friction \(F_B\). Moments about B: \(N_A(L\sin\theta) = W(L/2)\cos\theta\), so \(N_A = W/(2\tan\theta)\). Horizontal equilibrium: \(F_B = N_A\). Slip impends when \(F_B = \mu_s N_B = \mu_s W\): \[\frac{W}{2\tan\theta} = \mu_s W \quad\Rightarrow\quad \tan\theta_{\min} = \frac{1}{2\mu_s} = \frac{1}{0.60} = 1.667 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \theta_{\min} = 59.0^\circ\] The length and weight cancel out.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Friction; Equilibrium Requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(\arctan(\mu_s)\), the angle of friction, which has nothing to do with the ladder geometry;
  • (B) is \(\arctan(2\mu_s)\), the complement of the correct angle;
  • (C) has no basis in the numbers.

G – Static friction · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 4-34

questions.question: A vehicle accelerates uniformly from 20 km/h to 80 km/h over a distance of 200 m. The acceleration is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Convert: \(v_0 = 20/3.6 = 5.556\) m/s; \(v = 80/3.6 = 22.22\) m/s. Time is neither given nor asked, so use \(v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a_0(s - s_0)\): \[a_0 = \frac{v^2 - v_0^2}{2(s - s_0)} = \frac{22.22^2 - 5.556^2}{2(200)} = \frac{493.8 - 30.9}{400} = 1.16\ \text{m/s}^2\]

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Particle Rectilinear Motion (constant acceleration).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 1.23 is \(v^2/2s\), ignoring the initial velocity.
  • (C) 2.31 omits the factor of 2 in \(2a_0(s - s_0)\).
  • (D) 15.0 uses the speeds in km/h without converting: \((80^2 - 20^2)/[2(200)]\).

A – Kinematics · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 5-1

questions.question: A car traveling at 90 km/h on a horizontal circular curve of radius 250 m applies its brakes, reducing its speed at a rate of 2.0 m/s². At the instant braking begins, the magnitude of the car’s total acceleration is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(v = 90/3.6 = 25\) m/s. Normal component: \(a_n = v^2/\rho = 25^2/250 = 2.5\) m/s². Tangential component: \(a_t = 2.0\) m/s² (opposite to the velocity, but only the magnitude matters here). Total: \(a = \sqrt{2.0^2 + 2.5^2} = 3.20\) m/s².

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Normal and Tangential Components.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.5 subtracts the tangential component from the normal component algebraically (treating the braking as if it cancels part of \(a_n\)); the components are perpendicular and must be combined as vectors.
  • (B) 2.0 is the tangential component alone.
  • (C) 2.5 is the normal component alone.

A – Kinematics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-5

questions.question: A slender uniform rod has a mass of 15 kg and a length of 3.0 m. Its mass moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the rod and located 0.5 m from one end is ______ kg·m². [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
The rod’s centroid is at midlength, 1.5 m from either end; the axis is 0.5 m from one end, so \(d = 1.5 - 0.5 = 1.0\) m from the centroid. Parallel-axis theorem: \(I = ML^2/12 + Md^2 = 15(3.0)^2/12 + 15(1.0)^2 = 11.25 + 15.0 = 26.25\) kg·m².

Numerical entry: accepted range 26.0–26.5 kg·m². Common wrong entries are 15.0 (using \(d = 0.5\) m, the distance from the end rather than from the centroid) and 45.0 (\(ML^2/3\), the end-axis value).

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Parallel-Axis Theorem; table of mass moments of inertia (slender rod).

B – Mass moments of inertia · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 5-9

questions.question: Two blocks of mass 4 kg and 6 kg hang from a cord passing over a pulley with mass moment of inertia 0.05 kg·m² about its axle and radius 0.2 m, as shown in Figure 5.9. The cord does not slip on the pulley, and axle friction is negligible. When the system is released from rest, the acceleration of the 6-kg block is ______ m/s². [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Because the pulley has mass, the cord tensions on the two sides differ. Let \(T_1\) act on the 4-kg block (which rises) and \(T_2\) on the 6-kg block (which descends), with common acceleration \(a\) and pulley angular acceleration \(\alpha = a/r\).

4-kg block (up positive): \(T_1 - 4(9.81) = 4a\)

6-kg block (down positive): \(6(9.81) - T_2 = 6a\)

Pulley: \((T_2 - T_1)r = I\alpha = Ia/r\), so \(T_2 - T_1 = Ia/r^2 = 0.05a/0.04 = 1.25a\)

Adding the three: \((6 - 4)(9.81) = (4 + 6 + 1.25)a\), so \[a = \frac{2(9.81)}{11.25} = 1.744\ \text{m/s}^2\] (The quantity \(I/r^2 = 1.25\) kg is the pulley’s “equivalent mass” at the cord.) Tensions, for reference: \(T_1 = 4(9.81 + 1.744) = 46.2\) N and \(T_2 = 6(9.81 - 1.744) = 48.4\) N.

Numerical entry: accepted range 1.72–1.76 m/s². The common wrong entry is 1.96 m/s², which ignores the pulley inertia (\(2g/10\)).

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Plane Motion of a Rigid Body (Equations of Motion); Particle Kinetics; Plane Circular Motion (\(a_t = r\alpha\)).

C – Force acceleration · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 5-13

questions.question: A construction hoist raises a 2000-lb load at a constant speed of 3 ft/s. The hoist mechanism is 80% efficient. The power that must be supplied to the hoist is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
At constant speed the cable force equals the load, so the output power is \(P_{out} = Fv = (2000\ \text{lb})(3\ \text{ft/s}) = 6000\) ft·lb/s. Converting with 550 ft·lb/s per hp, \(P_{out} = 10.91\) hp. Input power: \(P_{in} = P_{out}/\varepsilon = 10.91/0.80 = 13.6\) hp.

FE Reference Handbook: Dynamics — Power and Efficiency; separately, Units and Conversion Factors (hp = 550 ft-lbf/sec).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 8.7 hp multiplies by the efficiency instead of dividing—an input can never be less than the output.
  • (B) 10.9 hp is the output power, ignoring efficiency.
  • (D) 18.2 hp divides by 0.6 instead of 0.8, i.e., treats the 20% loss as if it were 40%.

D – Work, energy, and power · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 5-17

questions.question: For the beam in Figure 6.15 (pin at A, roller at B 8 m from A, overhang to C at 10 m; 6 kN/m on AB only; 20 kN at C), the maximum magnitude of bending moment in the beam is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Moments about A: \(R_B(8) = 6(8)(4) + 20(10) = 192 + 200 = 392\), so \(R_B = 49\) kN and \(R_A = 48 + 20 - 49 = 19\) kN. In span AB, \(V = 19 - 6x = 0\) at \(x = 3.167\) m, where \(M = 19(3.167) - 6(3.167)^2/2 = 60.17 - 30.08 = 30.1\) kN·m (positive). At B (from the right), \(M_B = -20(2) = -40\) kN·m. The maximum magnitude is 40 kN·m at B.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Beams — Shearing Force and Bending Moment Sign Conventions.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 30.1 kN·m is the maximum positive moment, smaller in magnitude than the support moment.
  • (C) 49 is the reaction \(R_B\) in kN, not a moment.
  • (D) 60.2 is \(R_Ax\) alone at the zero-shear point, omitting the distributed-load term.

A – Shear and moment diagrams · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 6-3

questions.question: A 25-mm-diameter steel rod carries an axial tensile force of 60 kN. The normal stress in the rod is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A = \pi(25)^2/4 = 490.9\) mm2. \(\sigma = 60{,}000/490.9 = 122.2\) MPa.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Uniaxial Loading and Deformation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 30.6 MPa uses \(A = \pi d^2\) (four times too large).
  • (B) 61.1 MPa uses \(A = \pi d^2/2\) (a factor-of-2 slip in the area formula).
  • (C) 96.0 MPa uses \(A = d^2\) (a square).

B – Stresses and strains · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 6-7
