questions.question: A steel wide-flange beam has an elastic section modulus of 54.6 in3 about its strong axis. Under a bending moment of 120 kip·ft, the maximum bending stress is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(M = 120\) kip·ft \(= 1440\) kip·in. \(\sigma = M/S = 1440/54.6 = 26.4\) ksi.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Stresses in Beams (\(\sigma_x = M/s\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 2.2 ksi forgets to convert kip·ft to kip·in.
  • (B) 13.2 ksi is half the correct value, from a section modulus twice too large (e.g., using \(2S\), or taking \(c\) as the quarter-depth, \(d/4\)).
  • (D) 52.7 ksi doubles it.

B – Stresses and strains · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-11

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each mechanical property (1–4) with the feature of the engineering stress–strain curve from which it is obtained (a–d).

  • (a) The intersection of the curve with a line parallel to the elastic portion offset by 0.002 strain
  • (b) The maximum engineering stress on the curve
  • (c) The permanent engineering strain after fracture, expressed as percent elongation
  • (d) The slope of the initial linear portion
pairs: Yield strength (for a material without a distinct yield point)
questions.explanation:
The modulus of elasticity is the slope of the linear elastic portion (d). The 0.2% offset method defines yield strength for materials without a sharp yield point (a). Ultimate tensile strength is the peak engineering stress (b). Ductility is the permanent strain at fracture, reported as percent elongation (c).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Uniaxial Stress-Strain; Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Properties of Materials — Mechanical.

E – Elastic and plastic deformations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 6-15

questions.question: A 20-ft simply supported steel beam (\(E = 29{,}000\) ksi, \(I = 500\) in4) carries a 20-kip concentrated load at midspan. The midspan deflection is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(L = 240\) in. \(\delta = PL^3/48EI = 20(240)^3/[48(29{,}000)(500)] = 2.765\times10^8/6.96\times10^8 = 0.397\) in.

FE Reference Handbook: Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections (midspan concentrated load).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.050 in uses \(PL^3/384EI\).
  • (B) 0.199 in is half (uses \(96EI\)).
  • (C) 0.248 in applies the uniform-load coefficient to the point load, \(5PL^3/384EI\).

C – Deformations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 6-19

questions.question: [Select all that apply] A simply supported beam of rectangular cross-section carries a uniformly distributed load. Which of the following changes, made one at a time, would produce the stated effect on the midspan deflection?
choices: Doubling the span increases the deflection by a factor of 16.
Doubling the width of the section reduces the deflection by a factor of 4.
Replacing the steel beam by an aluminum beam of the same dimensions increases the deflection by a factor of about 2.9.
Doubling the load intensity doubles the deflection.
Doubling the depth of the section halves the deflection.
questions.explanation:
\(\delta = 5wL^4/384EI\) with \(I = bh^3/12\).

FE Reference Handbook: Simply Supported Beam Slopes and Deflections; Material Properties Table 1; Statics — Moment of Inertia.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(L^4 \rightarrow 16L^4\).
  • (B) False — doubling \(b\) doubles \(I\) and halves the deflection (factor 2, not 4).
  • (C) True — \(E_{steel}/E_{al} = 200/69 = 2.9\) (Handbook Table 1).
  • (D) True — deflection is linear in \(w\).
  • (E) False — doubling \(h\) multiplies \(I\) by 8, so the deflection falls by a factor of 8.

C – Deformations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 6-23

questions.question: A plane-stress element has \(\sigma_x = 60\) MPa, \(\sigma_y = 0\), and \(\tau_{xy} = 40\) MPa. The angle from the \(x\) axis to the nearest principal plane normal is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\tan 2\theta_p = 2\tau_{xy}/(\sigma_x - \sigma_y) = 80/60 = 1.333\), so \(2\theta_p = 53.1^\circ\) and \(\theta_p = 26.6^\circ\). On Mohr’s circle (\(C = 30\), \(R = 50\)), the \(x\)-point (60, 40) lies \(53.1^\circ\) from the \(\sigma_a = 80\) MPa point, confirming the doubled angle.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Mohr’s Circle—Stress, 2D.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 33.7° is \(\arctan(2/3)\), omitting the factor 2 in the numerator.
  • (C) 53.1° is \(2\theta_p\), the angle on the circle, not on the element.
  • (D) 63.4° is \(90^\circ - \theta_p\), the angle measured from the \(y\) axis instead of the \(x\) axis.

D – Combined stresses, principal stresses, Mohr's circle · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 6-27

questions.question: A steel has a yield strength of 50 ksi and \(E = 29{,}000\) ksi. Its modulus of resilience is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(u_r = \sigma_y^2/2E = (50)^2/[2(29{,}000)] = 0.0431\) ksi \(= 43.1\) psi \(= 43.1\) in·lb/in3.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Elastic Strain Energy (\(u = \sigma^2/2E\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.72 is \(1000\sigma_y/E\), the yield strain expressed in thousandths — a strain, not an energy density.
  • (B) 21.6 in·lb/in3 is \(\sigma_y^2/4E\).
  • (D) 86.2 in·lb/in3 is \(\sigma_y^2/E\), omitting the one-half.

E – Elastic and plastic deformations · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 6-31

questions.question: For a metal whose stress-strain curve shows no distinct yield point, the property defined by drawing a line parallel to the initial elastic slope from a strain of 0.002 is the:
questions.explanation:
The Handbook defines yield strength as the engineering stress at which permanent deformation is first observed, calculated by the 0.2% offset method: a line parallel to the elastic portion, offset by 0.002 strain, intersects the curve at \(\sigma_y\).

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Properties of Materials — Mechanical.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) The proportional limit is where the curve first departs from linearity—no offset is involved.
  • (B) UTS is the maximum stress.
  • (C) Resilience is an area, not a stress read from an offset line.

C – Physical and mechanical properties · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 7-2

questions.question: A steel component in fully reversed loading has Basquin constants \(A=900\) MPa and \(B=-0.10\). At a stress amplitude of 250 MPa the predicted fatigue life is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[N=\left(\frac{\sigma_r}{A}\right)^{1/B}=\left(\frac{250}{900}\right)^{1/(-0.10)}=(0.2778)^{-10}=(3.60)^{10}=3.66\times10^{5}\ \text{cycles}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Properties of Materials — Mechanical (Fatigue, Basquin equation).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is \(3.6^{10}/10\), a decimal slip.
  • (B) is \(3.6^{9}\), one power short (miscounting the exponent).
  • (D) is \(3.6^{12}\), using \(1/B=-12\).

B – Test methods · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 7-6

questions.question: A 15.0-m concrete pavement slab (\(\alpha=10\times10^{-6}\)/°C) is free to expand. When its temperature rises 30°C, the change in length is ______ mm. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(\delta=\alpha\,\Delta T\,L=(10\times10^{-6})(30)(15{,}000\,\text{mm})=4.5\,\text{mm}\).

Accepted: 4.5 (4.4–4.6). An answer of 0.0045 indicates the length was left in meters.

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Thermal Properties; Mechanics of Materials — Thermal Deformations.

C – Physical and mechanical properties · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 7-10

questions.question: A sieve analysis of a concrete sand gives the following cumulative percent retained: 3/8 in, 0; No. 4, 2; No. 8, 12; No. 16, 30; No. 30, 52; No. 50, 74; No. 100, 90; pan, 100. The fineness modulus is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
FM = (0 + 2 + 12 + 30 + 52 + 74 + 90)/100 = 260/100 = 2.60.

FE Reference Handbook: not given—procedure must be known.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.70 omits the No. 100 sieve (260 − 90 = 170).
  • (C) 3.60 includes the pan (260 + 100 = 360).
  • (D) 4.40 sums the percent passing (100 + 98 + 88 + 70 + 48 + 26 + 10 = 440) instead of the cumulative percent retained.

B – Test methods · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 7-14

questions.question: A standard 6-in-diameter concrete cylinder fails at a load of 113,000 lb. The compressive strength of the concrete is ______ psi (nearest 10 psi). [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(A=\pi(6)^2/4=28.27\,\text{in}^2\). \(f'_c=113{,}000/28.27=3{,}997\approx4{,}000\) psi.

Accepted: 3,990–4,000. Using \(\pi d^2\) (113 in²) gives 1,000 psi; using \(\pi r^2\) with \(r=6\) gives 999 psi.

FE Reference Handbook: Materials Science/Structure of Matter — Properties of Materials — Mechanical (stress = force/area).

B – Test methods · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 7-18

questions.question: A compacted asphalt specimen has a bulk specific gravity \(G_{mb}=2.350\) and the loose mix has a theoretical maximum specific gravity \(G_{mm}=2.455\). The air-void content is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(V_a=100(1-G_{mb}/G_{mm})=100(1-2.350/2.455)=100(1-0.9572)=4.28\%\approx4.3\%\).

FE Reference Handbook: not given—definition supplied in the chapter.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 4.5% is \(100(2.455-2.350)/2.350\), the wrong denominator.
  • (C) 11.3% is \(100(1-G_{mb}/G_{sb})\), using the aggregate specific gravity of Question 7-23 in place of \(G_{mm}\).
  • (D) 95.7% is \(100\,G_{mb}/G_{mm}\), the percent solids rather than the percent voids.

A – Mix design · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 7-22

questions.question: A flat plate of area 0.40 m² moves at 3.0 m/s parallel to a fixed wall, separated from it by a 2.0-mm layer of oil with dynamic viscosity 0.10 Pa·s. Assuming a linear velocity profile, the force required to move the plate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Linear profile: \(\tau=\mu v/\delta=0.10(3.0)/0.0020=150\) Pa. \(F=\tau A=150(0.40)=60\) N.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Definitions — Stress, Pressure, and Viscosity.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) leaves the gap in millimeters.
  • (B) is a decimal slip.
  • (D) is the shear stress in Pa, not the force.

B – Fluid properties · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-2

questions.question: An open tank contains a 2.0-m layer of oil (SG = 0.80) floating on 3.0 m of water. The gauge pressure at the bottom of the tank is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(P=\gamma_w(SG_{oil}h_{oil}+h_w)=9{,}810\left[0.80(2.0)+3.0\right]=9{,}810(4.6)=45{,}126\ \text{Pa}\approx45.1\ \text{kPa}\).

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Characteristics of a Static Liquid — The Pressure Field in a Static Liquid.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) treats the oil as water.
  • (C) uses SG = 1.2 for the oil.
  • (D) is the absolute pressure (\(45.1+101.3\)); the question asks for gauge pressure.

C – Fluid statics · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 8-6

questions.question: A circular hatch 1.2 m in diameter lies in a vertical wall with its center 4.0 m below the water surface. The distance from the centroid of the hatch to the center of pressure is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
For a circle, \(I_{xC}=\pi r^4/4\) and \(A=\pi r^2\), so \(y_{CP}-y_C=I_{xC}/(y_CA)=r^2/(4y_C)=(0.6)^2/[4(4.0)]=0.0225\ \text{m}=22.5\) mm.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Forces on Submerged Surfaces and the Center of Pressure; Statics — Moment of Inertia (Area) (circle).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) treats the hatch as a 1.2-m square, \(I_{xC}/(y_CA)=d^2/(12y_C)=1.2^2/[12(4.0)]=0.030\) m.
  • (C) uses \(r^2/(2y_C)\) (wrong inertia).
  • (D) uses the diameter in place of the radius.

C – Fluid statics · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-10

questions.question: Water (\(\gamma=9.81\) kN/m³) flows without loss from point 1, where the pressure is 250 kPa, the velocity 3.0 m/s, and the elevation 0, to point 2, where the velocity is 6.0 m/s and the elevation 5.0 m. The pressure at point 2 is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Bernoulli in pressure form: \[\begin{aligned} P_2&=P_1+\frac{\rho}{2}\left(v_1^2-v_2^2\right)-\gamma(z_2-z_1)=250{,}000+500(9-36)-9{,}810(5)\\ &=250{,}000-13{,}500-49{,}050=187{,}450\ \text{Pa}\approx187\ \text{kPa} \end{aligned}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Principles of One-Dimensional Fluid Flow — Bernoulli Equation.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) omits the velocity-head change (\(250{,}000-49{,}050=200{,}950\) Pa).
  • (C) omits the elevation-head change (\(250{,}000-13{,}500=236{,}500\) Pa).
  • (D) adds the elevation term instead of subtracting it (\(250{,}000-13{,}500+49{,}050=285{,}550\) Pa), a sign error on \(z_2-z_1\).

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-14

questions.question: A 6-in-diameter cast-iron pipe with Hazen–Williams \(C=100\) carries 500 gpm. The pressure loss over 1,000 ft of pipe is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Pressure-loss form (USCS, \(Q\) in gpm, \(D\) in inches): \[P=\frac{4.52\,Q^{1.85}}{C^{1.85}D^{4.87}}=\frac{4.52(500)^{1.85}}{(100)^{1.85}(6)^{4.87}}=0.0144\ \text{psi/ft}\] Over 1,000 ft: 14.4 psi.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Hazen-Williams Equation — Circular Pipe Head Loss Equation (Head Loss Expressed as Pressure), U.S. Customary Units.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) reports the loss per 100 ft.
  • (B) uses \(C=145\) instead of the given \(C=100\): \(14.4(100/145)^{1.85}=7.2\) psi.
  • (D) uses the Handbook head-loss form \(h_f=4.73\,LQ^{1.852}/(C^{1.852}D^{4.87})\) (\(Q=1.114\) cfs, \(D=0.5\) ft), which gives 33.4 ft of water, and reports the feet as psi. Converting head to pressure (\(h_f/2.31\)) returns about 14.4 psi.

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 8-18

questions.question: A sphere 1.0 ft in diameter moves through air (\(\rho=0.00238\) slug/ft³) at 100 ft/s. The drag coefficient is 0.50. The drag force is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A=\pi(1.0)^2/4=0.7854\) ft². \(F_D=C_D\rho v^2A/2=0.50(0.00238)(100)^2(0.7854)/2=4.67\) lb.

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Consequences of Fluid Flow — Drag Force.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) omits the 1/2.
  • (C) uses the sphere’s surface area or quadruples through a radius/diameter error.
  • (D) uses the density in lbm/ft³ (\(0.00238\times32.2=0.0766\)) in place of slug/ft³, overstating the force by 32.2.

D – Energy, impulse, and momentum · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-22

questions.question: A sharp-edged orifice 2.0 in in diameter (\(C=0.61\)) is located in the side of a large tank, 9.0 ft below the water surface. The discharge is ______ ft³/s. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(A_0=\pi(2/12)^2/4=0.02182\) ft². \[Q=CA_0\sqrt{2gh}=0.61(0.02182)\sqrt{2(32.2)(9.0)}=0.01331(24.07)=0.320\ \text{ft}^3\text{/s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Fluid Flow Measurement — Orifice Discharging Freely into Atmosphere; Orifices and Their Nominal Coefficients.

A – Flow measurement · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 8-26

questions.question: The bearing of a property line is S 37°20′ W. Its azimuth from north is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
SW quadrant: \(Az=180°+\beta=180°+37°20'=217°20'\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Latitudes and Departures (quadrant figure).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the bearing angle itself (NE quadrant).
  • (B) is \(180°-\beta\), the SE quadrant.
  • (D) is \(360°-\beta\), the NW quadrant.

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 9-1

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A closed traverse has a perimeter of 2,450 ft. The sums of the latitudes and departures are +0.18 ft and −0.24 ft. Express the relative precision as 1:X and enter X to the nearest 10.
questions.explanation:
\(E_c=\sqrt{0.18^2+0.24^2}=\sqrt{0.0324+0.0576}=\sqrt{0.0900}=0.300\) ft. Precision \(=0.300/2450=1/8{,}167\), so \(X=8{,}170\).

Rounding: 8,167 to the nearest 10 is 8,170; entries in the 8,150–8,200 range reflect acceptable rounding of the closure.

FE Reference Handbook: none needed.

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 9-5

questions.question: A traverse line has azimuth 75°30′ and the next line has azimuth 48°10′. The deflection angle at the common station is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Deflection \(=Az_{\text{next}}-Az_{\text{prev}}=48°10'-75°30'=-27°20'\); negative means the line turns to the left: 27°20′ L.

FE Reference Handbook: none needed.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) has the correct magnitude but the wrong sense — a decrease in azimuth is a left turn.
  • (B) adds the two azimuths (75°30′ + 48°10′), a sum with no geometric meaning.
  • (C) is \(180°-27°20'\), the interior angle between the lines, not the deflection.

A – Angles, distances, and trigonometry · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 9-9

questions.question: [Numerical entry] The balanced latitudes and departures of a four-course traverse, in feet, are: course 1: Lat +280.00, Dep +150.00; course 2: Lat −120.00, Dep +260.00; course 3: Lat −310.00, Dep −90.00; course 4: Lat +150.00, Dep −320.00. Using the DMD method, enter the enclosed area in acres to two decimal places.
questions.explanation:
DMDs: course 1 = +150.00; course 2 = 150.00 + 150.00 + 260.00 = 560.00; course 3 = 560.00 + 260.00 − 90.00 = 730.00; course 4 = 730.00 − 90.00 − 320.00 = 320.00 (equals \(-\text{Dep}_4=+320.00\) ✓).

Double areas: 150(280) = 42,000; 560(−120) = −67,200; 730(−310) = −226,300; 320(150) = 48,000. Sum = −203,500.

Area \(=203{,}500/2=101{,}750\) ft² \(=101{,}750/43{,}560=2.336\) acres.

Rounded to two decimals: 2.34 acres. An entry of 2.33 reflects truncation and is accepted.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Area formulas; Units and Conversion Factors (acre).

B – Area computations · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 9-13

questions.question: Two cross-sections 25 m apart have areas of 64.0 m² and 98.0 m²; the section midway between them has an area of 80.5 m². The volume by the prismoidal formula is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(V=L(A_1+4A_m+A_2)/6=25(64.0+4\times80.5+98.0)/6=25(484.0)/6=2{,}017\) m³.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Earthwork formulas — Prismoidal Formula.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) drops the factor 4 on the mid-section area: \(25(64.0+80.5+98.0)/6=1{,}010\) m³.
  • (C) is the average end area result 25(64 + 98)/2 = 2,025 m³.
  • (D) omits the division by 2 in the average end area formula.

C – Earthwork and volume computations · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 9-17

questions.question: [Select all that apply] On a mass haul diagram, which statements are correct?
choices: A rising curve indicates that the roadway is in cut.
A maximum on the curve occurs where the profile changes from fill to cut.
A horizontal line intersecting the curve at two points defines a reach in which cut equals adjusted fill.
A negative ordinate at the end of the project indicates waste.
Fill quantities are increased by the shrinkage factor before the ordinates are accumulated.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (C), and (E) are correct. A maximum marks a change from cut to fill, and a negative final ordinate means borrow, not waste.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Earthwork formulas — Mass Haul Diagram.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the ordinate accumulates cut as positive, so it rises in cut.
  • (B) False — a maximum occurs where cut changes to fill (the curve stops rising and starts falling).
  • (C) True — this is the definition of a balance line.
  • (D) False — a negative final ordinate means adjusted fill exceeds cut, which is borrow; a positive ordinate is waste.
  • (E) True — the Handbook states that fill is increased by the shrinkage factor.

C – Earthwork and volume computations · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 9-21

questions.question: Point M has coordinates N 5,010.20 m, E 5,650.75 m; point N has N 4,321.55 m, E 6,874.30 m. The distance and azimuth from M to N are most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(\Delta N=4{,}321.55-5{,}010.20=-688.65\) m; \(\Delta E=6{,}874.30-5{,}650.75=+1{,}223.55\) m. Distance \(=\sqrt{688.65^2+1223.55^2}=1{,}404.0\) m. Direction: south and east → SE quadrant; \(\arctan(1223.55/688.65)=60°38'\) from south, so azimuth \(=180°-60°38'=119°22'\).

FE Reference Handbook: Mathematics — Trigonometry; Civil Engineering — Transportation — Latitudes and Departures.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) gives the bearing angle from south as if it were an azimuth.
  • (C) is the back azimuth from N to M.
  • (D) uses \(|\Delta N|+|\Delta E|\) instead of the root-sum-square.

D – Coordinate systems · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 9-25

questions.question: A 12-acre asphalt parking lot has a runoff coefficient \(C = 0.90\) and a time of concentration of 10 min. The site IDF curve gives a 10-year intensity of 5.5 in./hr at a 10-min duration and 3.1 in./hr at a 30-min duration. The 10-year peak discharge at the outlet is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Enter the IDF curve at the duration equal to \(t_c = 10\) min, giving \(I = 5.5\) in./hr. \[Q = CIA = 0.90(5.5)(12) = 59.4\ \text{cfs}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Rational Formula.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 5.9 cfs divides by 10, as if the acre·in./hr-to-cfs constant were 0.1 rather than ≈1.0.
  • (B) 33 cfs uses the 30-min intensity, 3.1 in./hr, instead of the intensity at \(t_c\).
  • (C) 46 cfs averages the two tabulated intensities, \((5.5 + 3.1)/2 = 4.3\) in./hr, instead of reading the curve at \(t_c\).

A – Basic hydrology · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-1

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about rainfall-runoff methods are correct?
choices: The rational formula yields a peak discharge, not a runoff volume.
The rainfall intensity used in the rational formula should be taken at a duration equal to the watershed time of concentration.
In the NRCS method the initial abstraction is taken as \(0.2S\), where \(S = 1000/CN - 10\) with \(S\) in inches.
Converting pasture to rooftops and pavement lowers the watershed curve number.
For a watershed with several land uses, the runoff coefficients should be averaged arithmetically.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B) and (C) are correct; (D) and (E) are not (see the rationale for each statement below).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Rational Formula; NRCS/SCS Rainfall-Runoff.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(Q = CIA\) returns a single peak flow; volume requires NRCS or a hydrograph.
  • (B) True — \(t_c\) is the shortest duration for which the whole watershed contributes, which maximizes the peak for a given return period.
  • (C) True — this is the Handbook form, valid with \(S\) in inches only.
  • (D) False — impervious cover raises CN (pavement approaches 98), which raises both runoff depth and peak.
  • (E) False — coefficients must be area-weighted, \(C_w = \sum C_jA_j/\sum A_j\).

A – Basic hydrology · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-5

questions.question: A 90° V-notch weir is used to gauge a small stream. The head on the notch is 0.35 m and the SI weir coefficient is 1.40. The discharge is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[Q = CH^{5/2} = 1.40(0.35)^{2.5} = 1.40(0.07247) = 0.1015\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Weir Formulas.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 0.172 m3/s squares the head instead of raising it to the 5/2 power.
  • (C) 0.184 m3/s applies the USCS V-notch coefficient 2.54 to SI data.
  • (D) 0.290 m3/s uses the rectangular-weir exponent 3/2 with the V-notch coefficient.

B – Basic hydraulics · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-9

questions.question: A centrifugal pump delivers 900 gpm of water against a total dynamic head of 120 ft. The pump efficiency at this point is 70%. The brake power required is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[Q = \frac{900\ \text{gpm}}{448.8} = 2.005\ \text{cfs}, \qquad \dot W_{fluid} = \gamma QH = 62.4(2.005)(120) = 15{,}020\ \text{ft·lb/s} = 27.3\ \text{hp}\] \[\dot W_{brake} = \frac{27.31}{0.70} = 39.0\ \text{hp}\] (Equivalently, hp \(= QH/(3960\eta) = 900(120)/(3960 \times 0.70) = 39.0\) hp.)

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Pump Power Equation (fluid, brake and purchased power are defined immediately above it, after the NPSHA equation).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 27.3 hp is the fluid (water) power, with efficiency ignored.
  • (C) 43.3 hp divides by an additional, unstated 90% motor efficiency — that would be purchased power, not brake power.
  • (D) 55.7 hp divides by the efficiency twice.

C – Pumps · Easy · target ~3 min · Book question 10-13

questions.question: A 5,000-ft length of 8-in.-diameter water main with a Hazen–Williams coefficient \(C = 100\) carries 1.2 cfs. The friction head loss is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Use the Handbook’s circular-pipe form with \(L\) and \(D\) in feet and \(Q\) in cfs: \(D\) = 8 in. = 0.667 ft. \[h_f = \frac{4.73\,L\,Q^{1.852}}{C^{1.852}D^{4.87}} = \frac{4.73(5000)(1.2)^{1.852}}{(100)^{1.852}(0.6667)^{4.87}} = \frac{23{,}650(1.4017)}{5058(0.13882)} = \frac{33{,}150}{702.1} = 47.2\ \text{ft}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Circular Pipe Head Loss Equation (Head Loss Expressed in Feet).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 2.6 × 10−4 ft enters \(D\) in inches in a formula that requires feet — the 4.87 exponent makes the error enormous.
  • (B) 20.5 ft is the correct head loss converted to psi (47.2 × 62.4/144), a units mismatch, not a head.
  • (C) 25.3 ft assumes \(C = 140\) instead of the given 100.

D – Water distribution systems · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-17

questions.question: An uncontrolled ogee spillway is 25 m long with a discharge coefficient of 2.1 in SI units. When the pool stands 1.2 m above the crest, the spillway discharge is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
An uncontrolled overflow spillway is a weir: \[Q = CLH^{3/2} = 2.1(25)(1.2)^{1.5} = 52.5(1.3145) = 69.0\ \text{m}^3/\text{s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Weir Formulas.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 76 m3/s squares the head (\(H^2\)) instead of raising it to the 3/2 power.
  • (C) 83 m3/s uses the V-notch exponent 5/2.
  • (D) 118 m3/s applies the USCS coefficient 3.6 to SI data.

E – Flood control · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-21

questions.question: A detention basin discharges through a 6-in.-diameter circular orifice (\(C_d = 0.61\)) whose center is 3.5 ft below the design water surface. The release rate at the design water surface is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[A_0 = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi(0.5)^2}{4} = 0.1963\ \text{ft}^2\] \[Q = C_dA_0\sqrt{2gh} = 0.61(0.1963)\sqrt{2(32.2)(3.5)} = 0.1198(15.01) = 1.80\ \text{cfs}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Fluid Mechanics — Orifice Discharging Freely into Atmosphere.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 1.27 cfs uses \(\sqrt{gh}\) instead of \(\sqrt{2gh}\).
  • (C) 2.95 cfs omits the discharge coefficient.
  • (D) 7.19 cfs computes the orifice area as \(\pi D^2\) instead of \(\pi D^2/4\).

F – Stormwater · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 10-25

questions.question: A storm sewer must carry 0.65 m3/s flowing just full. The concrete pipe has \(n = 0.013\) and will be laid at a slope of 0.006. Determine the required (unrounded) pipe diameter, in millimeters. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
For a just-full circular pipe, Manning’s equation with \(A = \pi D^2/4\) and \(R_H = D/4\) reduces (SI) to \(Q_f = 0.312\,D^{8/3}S^{1/2}/n\), so \[D = \left(\frac{Qn}{0.312\,S^{1/2}}\right)^{3/8} = \left(\frac{0.65(0.013)}{0.312(0.006)^{1/2}}\right)^{3/8} = \left(\frac{0.008450}{0.02417}\right)^{0.375} = (0.3497)^{0.375} = 0.674\ \text{m}\] The next commercial size, 750 mm, would be specified.

Accepted range: 665–685 mm. Using the USCS constant 0.463 in place of 0.312 gives 582 mm and a badly undersized pipe.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Manning’s Equation (the solved-out \(D^{8/3}\) form is a rearrangement, not printed).

G – Collection systems · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-29

questions.question: A well of 0.30-m radius fully penetrates an unconfined aquifer whose original saturated thickness is 30 m and whose hydraulic conductivity is 12 m/d. At steady state the drawdown in the well is 8.0 m and the drawdown at an observation well 200 m away is 1.0 m. The pumping rate is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Saturated thicknesses, measured from the impermeable base: \[h_1 = 30 - 8.0 = 22.0\ \text{m at } r_1 = 0.30\ \text{m}, \qquad h_2 = 30 - 1.0 = 29.0\ \text{m at } r_2 = 200\ \text{m}\] \[Q = \frac{\pi K\left(h_2^2 - h_1^2\right)}{\ln(r_2/r_1)} = \frac{\pi(12)\left(29^2 - 22^2\right)}{\ln(200/0.30)} = \frac{37.70(357)}{6.502} = 2{,}070\ \text{m}^3/\text{d}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Well Drawdown — Dupuit’s Formula.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 41 m3/d uses \((h_2 - h_1)\) rather than \((h_2^2 - h_1^2)\), i.e., the confined form without the aquifer thickness.
  • (B) 365 m3/d substitutes the drawdowns for the saturated thicknesses, computing \(s_1^2 - s_2^2\).
  • (D) 4,770 m3/d uses \(\log_{10}\) in place of ln.

H – Groundwater · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 10-33

questions.question: A stream flowing at 0.85 m3/s carries an ultimate BOD of 2.0 mg/L and 9.2 mg/L of dissolved oxygen. It receives 0.15 m3/s of treated effluent with an ultimate BOD of 120 mg/L and 2.0 mg/L of DO. The saturation DO after mixing is 9.8 mg/L. The ultimate BOD and the initial DO deficit immediately after mixing are most nearly:
choices: \(L_a\) = 19.7 mg/L, \(D_a\) = 0.60 mg/L
\(L_a\) = 19.7 mg/L, \(D_a\) = 1.68 mg/L
\(L_a\) = 61.0 mg/L, \(D_a\) = 1.68 mg/L
\(L_a\) = 120 mg/L, \(D_a\) = 7.80 mg/L
questions.explanation:
Both BOD and DO mix on a flow-weighted basis at the outfall: \[L_a = \frac{Q_sL_s + Q_wL_w}{Q_s + Q_w} = \frac{0.85(2.0) + 0.15(120)}{1.00} = \frac{1.70 + 18.0}{1.00} = 19.7\ \text{mg/L}\] \[DO_{mix} = \frac{0.85(9.2) + 0.15(2.0)}{1.00} = \frac{7.82 + 0.30}{1.00} = 8.12\ \text{mg/L}\] \[D_a = DO_{sat} - DO_{mix} = 9.8 - 8.12 = 1.68\ \text{mg/L}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Stream Modeling — Streeter Phelps.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) computes the deficit from the stream DO alone (9.8 − 9.2).
  • (C) averages the two BOD values arithmetically instead of weighting by flow.
  • (D) uses the effluent values undiluted, ignoring the 5.7:1 dilution the stream provides.

I – Water quality · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 10-37

questions.question: A circular primary clarifier 25 m in diameter treats 8,000 m3/d. The overflow rate (surface loading rate) is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[A_{surface} = \frac{\pi D^2}{4} = \frac{\pi(25)^2}{4} = 490.9\ \text{m}^2, \qquad v_o = \frac{Q}{A} = \frac{8000}{490.9} = 16.3\ \text{m/d}\] This is 400 gpd/ft2, well below the Handbook’s typical primary-clarifier range of 800–1,200 gpd/ft2 (32–49 m/d); the basin is conservatively sized.

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Clarifier; Design Criteria for Sedimentation Basins.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 4.07 m/d uses \(A = \pi D^2\) (four times too large).
  • (B) 12.8 m/d uses \(A = D^2\) (a square of side 25 m), omitting the factor \(\pi/4\).
  • (D) 65.2 m/d uses the 12.5-m radius in place of the diameter in \(A = \pi D^2/4\).

K – Water and wastewater treatment · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 10-41

questions.question: [Select all that apply] Which of the following statements about water and wastewater treatment are correct?
choices: In an ideal horizontal-flow sedimentation basin, every particle whose settling velocity exceeds the overflow rate \(Q/A_{surface}\) is removed, regardless of the basin depth.
Soda ash is required only for the portion of the hardness that exceeds the alkalinity, i.e., the non-carbonate hardness.
Removing magnesium carbonate hardness requires two equivalents of lime per equivalent of hardness removed.
Improving the baffling of a chlorine contact chamber lowers \(CT_{calc}\) at a given nominal detention time and chlorine residual.
Raising the applied pressure in a reverse-osmosis unit increases the water flux but not the salt flux, so the product water becomes less saline.
questions.explanation:
Statements (A), (B), (C) and (E) are correct; (D) is not (see the rationale for each statement below).

FE Reference Handbook: Environmental Engineering — Clarifier; Lime-Soda Softening Equations; Disinfection (baffling factors, \(CT_{calc}\)); Reverse Osmosis.

Option by option:

  • (A) True — the ideal-basin derivation gives the critical settling velocity as \(Q/A_{surface}\), independent of depth; depth governs detention time and scour resistance, not the cut-off velocity.
  • (B) True — carbonate hardness already carries its own carbonate ion, supplied by the bicarbonate alkalinity, so only non-carbonate hardness needs soda ash.
  • (C) True — one equivalent of lime converts the bicarbonate to carbonate and a second raises the pH enough to precipitate Mg(OH)2; calcium carbonate hardness needs only one.
  • (D) False — a higher baffling factor raises \(t_{10} = \theta\times BF\), which raises \(CT_{calc}\) at the same residual. That is why contact chambers are built long and narrow.
  • (E) True — water flux is \(J_w = W_p(\Delta P - \Delta\pi)\) and depends on pressure, while salt flux \(J_s = K_p(C_{in} - C_{out})\) is driven by concentration difference alone, so the permeate is diluted.

K – Water and wastewater treatment · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 10-45

questions.question: For the overhanging beam in Figure 11.15, the maximum positive (sagging) bending moment in span AB is ______ kN·m. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
From 11-2, \(R_A = 40.5\) kN. Within span AB the shear is \(V(x) = 40.5 - 12x\), which vanishes at \[x = \frac{40.5}{12} = 3.375\,\text{m}\] \[M^+_{max} = 40.5(3.375) - \frac{12(3.375)^2}{2} = 136.69 - 68.34 = 68.34\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}\] (For contrast, the moment at B is \(-30(2) = -60\) kN·m, a hogging moment caused by the overhang.)

Numerical entry: accepted answer 68.3 kN·m (range 67.5–69.0). A common wrong entry is 60 kN·m, the negative moment at B, and another is 96 kN·m, obtained by ignoring the overhang entirely (\(wL^2/8\) for the 8-m span).

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Shearing Force and Bending Moment Sign Conventions (\(dM/dx = V\)).

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-3

questions.question: The rigid frame in Figure 11.18 is fixed at A. A vertical load of 15 kN acts downward at the free end C, and a horizontal load of 10 kN acts to the right at joint B. The bending moment at the fixed base A is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Take moments of both applied loads about A. The 15-kN vertical load at C has a horizontal lever arm of 3 m; the 10-kN horizontal load at B acts 4 m above A. Both moments turn the frame the same way, so they add: \[M_A = 15(3) + 10(4) = 45 + 40 = 85\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}\] The base also carries an axial compression of 15 kN and a shear of 10 kN.

FE Reference Handbook: Statics — Equilibrium Requirements; Mechanics of Materials — Shearing Force and Bending Moment Sign Conventions.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 40 kN·m counts only the horizontal load.
  • (B) 45 kN·m counts only the vertical load.
  • (D) 100 kN·m uses a 4-m lever arm for the vertical load as well; the moment arm of a vertical force is a horizontal distance.

A – Analysis of determinate structures · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-7

questions.question:
The vertical deflection of joint G of a steel truss is to be found by the unit-load method. Only three members carry force under the unit load; their data are:

Member \(F\) (real load) \(f\) (unit load) \(L\) (m) \(AE\) (kN)
1 +50 kN +0.80 4.0 60,000
2 −60 kN −0.60 5.0 60,000
3 +30 kN +0.50 3.0 40,000

All other members have \(f = 0\). The vertical deflection of G is ______ mm. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
The unit-load method gives \(\Delta = \sum f(\Delta L) = \sum fFL/(AE)\). Note that member 2 has \(f\) and \(F\) both negative, so its product is positive. \[\begin{aligned} \Delta_G &= \frac{(0.80)(50)(4.0)}{60{,}000} + \frac{(-0.60)(-60)(5.0)}{60{,}000} + \frac{(0.50)(30)(3.0)}{40{,}000} \\ &= \frac{160}{60{,}000} + \frac{180}{60{,}000} + \frac{45}{40{,}000} = 0.002667 + 0.003000 + 0.001125 = 0.006792\,\text{m} \end{aligned}\] \(\Delta_G = 6.79\) mm downward (in the direction of the unit load).

Numerical entry: accepted answer 6.79 mm (range 6.6–7.0). A common wrong entry is 0.79 mm, obtained by subtracting member 2’s contribution because both of its forces are compressive; a compression member shortens under a compressive virtual force and therefore still moves the joint in the direction of the unit load.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Truss Deflection by Unit Load Method.

B – Deflection of determinate structures · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-11

questions.question: A solid circular steel rod 50 mm in diameter and 2.5 m long is fixed at its base and completely free at its top (\(E = 200\) GPa, \(F_y = 250\) MPa). Using the theoretical effective-length factor, the critical buckling load is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Section properties of a 50-mm solid round bar: \[I = \frac{\pi d^4}{64} = \frac{\pi(50)^4}{64} = 3.068 \times 10^5\,\text{mm}^4 \qquad A = \frac{\pi(50)^2}{4} = 1963.5\,\text{mm}^2\] Fixed at the base and entirely free at the top is the fixed-free case, \(K = 2.0\), so \(K\ell = 5000\) mm: \[P_{cr} = \frac{\pi^2(200{,}000)(3.068 \times 10^5)}{(5000)^2} = \frac{6.056 \times 10^{11}}{2.5 \times 10^7} = 24{,}220\,\text{N} = 24.2\,\text{kN}\] Validity check: \(\sigma_{cr} = 24{,}220/1963.5 = 12.3\) MPa, far below \(F_y = 250\) MPa, so the column is very slender (\(K\ell/r = 5000/12.5 = 400\)) and Euler’s formula applies.

FE Reference Handbook: Mechanics of Materials — Columns.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 48.4 kN uses \(K = \sqrt{2}\).
  • (C) 96.9 kN uses \(K = 1.0\), treating the free top as if it were pinned; a free end cannot supply the lateral restraint a pin does.
  • (D) 198 kN uses \(K = 0.7\), the fixed-pinned value; a free top provides neither the lateral restraint nor the rotational restraint that case assumes.

C – Column analysis · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-15

questions.question: A plane frame has \(m = 6\) members, \(j = 6\) joints, \(r = 9\) reaction components, and \(c = 2\) condition equations from internal hinges. The degree of static indeterminacy is:
questions.explanation:
For a plane frame the degree of indeterminacy is \[3m + r - 3j - c = 3(6) + 9 - 3(6) - 2 = 18 + 9 - 18 - 2 = 7\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Stability, Determinacy, and Classification of Structures.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 3 applies the truss criterion \(m + r - 2j = 6 + 9 - 12\); frame members carry moment and shear as well as axial force, so each has three unknowns.
  • (B) 5 counts each internal hinge as releasing two equations.
  • (D) 9 omits the condition equations entirely; each hinge that connects two members releases one moment and therefore supplies one extra equation.

D – Determinacy and stability · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-19

questions.question: A beam fixed at both ends spans 6 m and carries a uniformly distributed load of 30 kN/m. The magnitude of the fixed-end moment at each support is:
questions.explanation:
\[FEM = \frac{wL^2}{12} = \frac{30(6)^2}{12} = \frac{1080}{12} = 90\,\text{kN}\cdot\text{m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Member Fixed-End Moments.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) 135 kN·m is \(wL^2/8\), the simply supported maximum moment.
  • (C) 180 kN·m is \(wL^2/6\), twice the correct value.
  • (D) 540 kN·m is \(wL^2/2\), the support moment of a cantilever carrying the same load; the second fixed end shares the load and reduces the end moment sixfold.

E – Elementary indeterminate structures · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 11-23

questions.question: A floor system carries nominal loads \(D = 20\) psf, \(L = 50\) psf, and \(L_r = 20\) psf. Using the LRFD (strength design) load combinations, the governing factored load is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Evaluate the LRFD combinations, remembering that \(L_r\), \(S\), and \(R\) are alternatives:

  • \(1.4D = 1.4(20) = 28\) psf
  • \(1.2D + 1.6L + 0.5L_r = 24 + 80 + 10 = 114\) psf ← governs
  • \(1.2D + 1.6L_r + L = 24 + 32 + 50 = 106\) psf

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Load Combinations using Strength Design (LRFD).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 90 psf is the unfactored service load \(D + L + L_r = 20 + 50 + 20\), with no load factors applied; LRFD strength design requires the factored combinations.
  • (B) 106 psf is the third combination, which does not govern here because \(L\) is much larger than \(L_r\).
  • (D) 136 psf applies the 1.6 factor to \(L\) and \(L_r\) simultaneously; only one of them can carry the leading factor.

F – Loads and load combinations · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 11-27

questions.question: Figure 11.19 shows an overhanging beam (8-m span AB plus a 2-m overhang BC) together with the influence line for the reaction at B, whose ordinates are 0 at A, 1.00 at B, and 1.25 at C. A uniformly distributed live load of 12 kN/m may be placed over any portion of the beam. The maximum reaction at B is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Every ordinate of the influence line for \(R_B\) is positive (0 at A rising to 1.00 at B and continuing to 1.25 at C), so the uniform load is placed over the whole beam and the response is \(w\) times the total area: \[A = \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}(8)(1.00)}_{\text{span}} + \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}(2)(1.00 + 1.25)}_{\text{overhang (trapezoid)}} = 4.00 + 2.25 = 6.25\,\text{m}\] \[R_{B,max} = wA = 12(6.25) = 75\,\text{kN}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Influence Lines for Beams and Trusses.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 48 kN uses only the 8-m span area (4.00 m).
  • (B) 63 kN treats the overhang portion as a triangle of area \(\tfrac{1}{2}(2)(1.25) = 1.25\) m rather than a trapezoid.
  • (C) 72 kN treats the overhang ordinates as a constant 1.00 (a rectangle of area 2.00 m), missing the rise to 1.25 at C.

F – Loads and load combinations · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-31

questions.question: A bolted connection uses six 7/8-in-diameter bolts in double shear. The nominal shear stress is \(F_{nv} = 68\) ksi and \(\phi = 0.75\). The LRFD design shear strength of the bolt group is ______ kips. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Bolt area: \(A_b = \pi d_b^2/4 = \pi(0.875)^2/4 = 0.6013\,\text{in}^2\).

Per bolt per shear plane: \(\phi R_n = 0.75(68)(0.6013) = 30.67\) kips.

Double shear means two shear planes per bolt, and there are six bolts: \[\phi R_n = 30.67(2)(6) = 368\,\text{kips}\]

Numerical entry: accepted answer 368 kips (range 360–375). A common wrong entry is 184 kips, which counts one shear plane per bolt; the other is 491 kips, obtained by omitting \(\phi\).

FE Reference Handbook: Not in the Handbook; \(F_{nv}\) and \(\phi\) are given in the stem (AISC 360-16 J3.6).

G – Design of steel components · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 11-35

questions.question: The gusset plate in Figure 11.20 is 1/2 in thick with \(F_y = 36\) ksi and \(F_u = 58\) ksi, and is connected by a single line of three 7/8-in-diameter bolts at 3-in pitch with a 1.5-in end distance and a 2-in edge distance. Take \(U_{bs} = 1.0\) and use a hole allowance of \(d_b + 1/8\) in. The LRFD design block-shear strength is ______ kips. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
Hole allowance: \(d_b + 1/8 = 7/8 + 1/8 = 1.0\) in.

Shear plane (one plane, running from the end of the plate through all three bolts): length \(1.5 + 3 + 3 = 7.5\) in, crossed by \(3 - 0.5 = 2.5\) holes. \[A_{gv} = 7.5(0.5) = 3.75\,\text{in}^2 \qquad A_{nv} = [7.5 - 2.5(1.0)](0.5) = 2.50\,\text{in}^2\] Tension plane (from the last bolt to the free edge): length 2.0 in, crossed by half a hole. \[A_{nt} = [2.0 - 0.5(1.0)](0.5) = 0.75\,\text{in}^2\] Now take the smaller of the two nominal expressions: \[F_u[0.6A_{nv} + U_{bs}A_{nt}] = 58[0.6(2.50) + 0.75] = 58(2.25) = 130.5\,\text{kips}\] \[0.6F_yA_{gv} + U_{bs}F_uA_{nt} = 0.6(36)(3.75) + 58(0.75) = 81.0 + 43.5 = 124.5\,\text{kips} \leftarrow \text{governs}\] \[\phi R_n = 0.75(124.5) = 93.4\,\text{kips}\]

Numerical entry: accepted answer 93.4 kips (range 91–96). A frequent wrong entry is 124.5 kips, the nominal strength with \(\phi = 0.75\) omitted; another is 82.5 kips, from deducting a full hole on the tension plane instead of half.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Steel Components — Tension Members (block shear).

G – Design of steel components · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 11-39

questions.question: A reinforced concrete beam has \(b_w = 14\) in, \(d = 24\) in, \(f'_c = 4000\) psi, and #4 vertical U-stirrups (\(A_v = 0.40\,\text{in}^2\), \(f_y = 60{,}000\) psi). The factored shear at the critical section is \(V_u = 70\) kips. The required stirrup spacing, rounded down to the nearest inch and satisfying the maximum-spacing limits, is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Concrete contribution: \[V_c = 2\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_wd = 2\sqrt{4000}(14)(24) = 2(63.25)(336) = 42{,}500\,\text{lb} = 42.5\,\text{kips}\] \(\phi V_c = 0.75(42.5) = 31.9\) kips \(< V_u = 70\) kips, so stirrups must carry \[V_s = \frac{V_u}{\phi} - V_c = \frac{70}{0.75} - 42.5 = 93.3 - 42.5 = 50.8\,\text{kips}\] \[s = \frac{A_vf_yd}{V_s} = \frac{0.40(60)(24)}{50.8} = \frac{576}{50.8} = 11.3\,\text{in}\] Maximum spacing: \(4\sqrt{f'_c}\,b_wd = 85.0\) kips \(> V_s\), so \(s_{max} = \min(d/2, 24\,\text{in}) = 12\) in. Use 11 in.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components — Beams—Shear (required and maximum-permitted stirrup spacing).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 6 in omits \(V_c\) altogether, requiring the stirrups to carry \(V_u/\phi = 93.3\) kips: \(s = 576/93.3 = 6.2\) in.
  • (C) 12 in is the maximum-spacing limit \(d/2\), not the required spacing.
  • (D) 15 in comes from \(V_s = V_u - \phi V_c = 70 - 31.9 = 38.1\) kips (mixing factored and nominal quantities), giving \(s = 576/38.1 = 15.1\) in, which also violates \(s_{max}\).

H – Design of reinforced concrete components · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 11-43

questions.question: A clay has a liquid limit of 58 and a plastic limit of 24. The plasticity index is:
questions.explanation:
\[PI = LL - PL = 58 - 24 = 34\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Plasticity Index.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the plastic limit itself.
  • (C) is the liquid limit itself.
  • (D) results from adding rather than subtracting the limits.

A – Index properties and soil classifications · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 12-1

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A subgrade soil has 62% passing the No. 200 sieve, a liquid limit of 52, and a plasticity index of 24. Compute the AASHTO group index, reported to the nearest whole number.
questions.explanation:
\[GI = (F-35)\left[0.2 + 0.005(LL-40)\right] + 0.01(F-15)(PI-10)\] \[GI = (62-35)\left[0.2 + 0.005(12)\right] + 0.01(62-15)(24-10)\] \[GI = 27(0.26) + 0.01(47)(14) = 7.02 + 6.58 = 13.60\] Rounded to the nearest whole number, GI = 14.

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — AASHTO Soil Classification (group index equation). Accepted range: 13.5 to 14.0 for the unrounded value, or 14 as the reported integer. A common error is using \((LL-30)\) or \((PI-15)\) in place of the Handbook’s constants.

A – Index properties and soil classifications · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 12-5

questions.question: A soil has a water content of 22%, a specific gravity of solids of 2.72, and a void ratio of 0.72. The degree of saturation is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[S = \frac{wG_s}{e}\times 100 = \frac{0.22(2.72)}{0.72}\times 100 = \frac{0.5984}{0.72}\times 100 = 83.1\%\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Phase Relationships (degree of saturation).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits \(G_s\).
  • (B) divides by \((1+e)\) instead of by \(e\): \(0.5984/1.72 = 34.8\%\).
  • (C) uses \((G_s - 1)\) in place of \(G_s\).

B – Phase relations · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 12-9

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A constant-head permeability test on a sand specimen 10.0 cm long with a cross-sectional area of 30.0 cm² collects 250 cm³ of water in 120 s under a head difference of 25.0 cm. Determine the coefficient of permeability in cm/s.
questions.answer: \(2.78\times 10^{-2}\) cm/s (accept \(2.7\times 10^{-2}\) to \(2.8\times 10^{-2}\) cm/s)
questions.explanation:
\[i = \frac{\Delta h}{L} = \frac{25.0}{10.0} = 2.50\] \[K = \frac{Q}{iAt_e} = \frac{250}{(2.50)(30.0)(120)} = \frac{250}{9{,}000} = 2.78\times 10^{-2}\,\text{cm/s}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources — Hydraulic Conductivity/Permeability (from constant head test). Accepted range: 0.027 to 0.028 cm/s, equivalently \(2.7\times 10^{-4}\) to \(2.8\times 10^{-4}\) m/s. Omitting the gradient (using \(Q/(At_e)\)) gives 0.069 cm/s and is not accepted.

C – Laboratory and field tests · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 12-13

questions.question: A saturated sand has \(\gamma_{sat} = 19.62\) kN/m³. The critical hydraulic gradient at which a quick condition develops is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[i_c = \frac{\gamma_{sat} - \gamma_w}{\gamma_w} = \frac{19.62 - 9.81}{9.81} = 1.00\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Factor of Safety Against Seepage Liquefaction.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) uses \(\gamma_{sat}/\gamma_w\) without subtracting.
  • (C) adds \(\gamma_w\) instead of subtracting it: \((19.62 + 9.81)/9.81 = 3.00\).
  • (D) is the saturated unit weight, which is not dimensionless and cannot be a gradient.

D – Effective stress · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 12-17

questions.question: A flow net beneath a dam has 5 flow channels and 14 equipotential drops across a total head loss of 4.5 m. The foundation soil has \(K = 2.5\times 10^{-5}\) m/s. Using \(Q = KHN_f/N_d\), the seepage per meter of dam is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[Q = KH\,\frac{N_f}{N_d} = (2.5\times 10^{-5})(4.5)\,\frac{5}{14} = (1.125\times 10^{-4})(0.357) = 4.02\times 10^{-5}\,\text{m}^3/\text{s per m}\]

FE Reference Handbook: the flow-net discharge relationship is not in Handbook 10.6 and was supplied in the problem statement; Darcy’s Law (Civil Engineering — Hydrology/Water Resources) provides the underlying principle.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) omits the \(N_f/N_d\) ratio entirely.
  • (C) inverts the ratio to \(N_d/N_f\), which would make more equipotential drops increase the flow — physically backwards.
  • (D) multiplies by \(N_f\) but omits the division by \(N_d\): \((2.5\times 10^{-5})(4.5)(5) = 5.63\times 10^{-4}\) m³/s.

D – Effective stress · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 12-21

questions.question: For a soil with \(\phi = 30°\), the ratio of the Rankine passive earth pressure coefficient to the Rankine active earth pressure coefficient is:
questions.explanation:
\[K_A = \tan^2 30° = \frac{1}{3} \qquad K_P = \tan^2 60° = 3 \qquad \frac{K_P}{K_A} = \frac{3}{1/3} = 9\] Since \(K_P = 1/K_A\) always, the ratio is \(1/K_A^2 = 9\).

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Horizontal Stress Profiles and Forces (active and passive coefficients).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) inverts the ratio to \(K_A/K_P = (1/3)/3 = 1/9 = 0.11\).
  • (B) would require \(\phi = 0\).
  • (C) is \(K_P\) itself, or equivalently \(1/K_A\) mistaken for the ratio.

E – Stability of retaining structures · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 12-25

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A soil has effective strength parameters \(c' = 10\) kPa and \(\phi' = 28°\). On a potential failure plane the total normal stress is 180 kPa and the pore water pressure is 60 kPa. Determine the shear strength available on that plane, in kPa.
questions.explanation:
\[\sigma'_N = \sigma_N - u = 180 - 60 = 120\,\text{kPa}\] \[\tau_F = c' + \sigma'_N\tan\phi' = 10 + 120\tan 28° = 10 + 120(0.5317) = 10 + 63.8 = 73.8\,\text{kPa}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Shear Stress at Failure; Effective Stress. Accepted range: 73 to 75 kPa. Using the total normal stress gives \(10 + 180(0.5317) = 105.7\) kPa and is not accepted — effective strength parameters must be paired with effective stresses.

F – Shear strength · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 12-29

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each situation (1–4) with the most appropriate foundation type (A–D). Each type is used once.

  • (A) Mat (raft) foundation
  • (B) Deep foundation (piles or drilled shafts)
  • (C) Spread (isolated) footing
  • (D) Wall (continuous strip) footing
pairs: A single interior column bearing on competent dense sand 2 m below grade
A continuous masonry bearing wall on firm clay near the surface
A heavy building on weak, erratic soil, where individual footings would cover more than 60% of the plan area
A bridge pier where competent rock lies 25 m below soft alluvium
questions.explanation:
1 → C. A single column on competent shallow soil is the textbook case for an isolated spread footing sized as \(A = Q/q_{all}\). 2 → D. A continuous line load calls for a continuous strip footing designed per unit length of wall. 3 → A. When the required footing area approaches or exceeds about half the plan area, a mat is both cheaper and stiffer, and its stiffness limits differential settlement across erratic ground. 4 → B. Twenty-five meters of soft alluvium over rock is the classic deep-foundation case: piles or drilled shafts carry the load past the compressible soil.

FE Reference Handbook: not tabulated in Handbook 10.6; conceptual foundation selection.

H – Foundation types · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 12-33

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A 6.0-m-thick clay layer drains to sand on both faces and has \(c_v = 0.0025\) cm²/s. Using \(T_v = 0.286\) at 60% consolidation, determine the time in days required to reach 60% of the ultimate primary settlement.
questions.explanation:
With sand on both faces the drainage is two-way: \[H_{dr} = \frac{6.0\,\text{m}}{2} = 3.0\,\text{m} = 300\,\text{cm}\] \[t = \frac{T_v H_{dr}^2}{c_v} = \frac{0.286(300)^2}{0.0025} = \frac{25{,}740}{0.0025} = 1.030\times 10^7\,\text{s}\] \[t = \frac{1.030\times 10^7}{86{,}400} = 119\,\text{days}\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Variation of Time Factor with Degree of Consolidation (\(T_v = c_v t/H_{dr}^2\)). Accepted range: 117 to 121 days. Using \(H_{dr} = 6.0\) m gives 477 days and is not accepted; the layer drains on both faces.

I – Consolidation and differential settlement · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-37

questions.question: For the slope of Figure 12.18(a), the assumed planar slip surface is 20 m long and inclined at 30° to the horizontal, the weight of the wedge above it is 1,200 kN per meter, and the soil has \(c = 15\) kPa and \(\phi = 20°\). The factor of safety against sliding is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\[T_{FF} = cL_S + W_M\cos\alpha_S\tan\phi = 15(20) + 1{,}200\cos 30°\tan 20°\] \[T_{FF} = 300 + 1{,}200(0.8660)(0.3640) = 300 + 378.2 = 678.2\,\text{kN/m}\] \[T_{MOB} = W_M\sin\alpha_S = 1{,}200\sin 30° = 600\,\text{kN/m}\] \[FS = \frac{T_{FF}}{T_{MOB}} = \frac{678.2}{600} = 1.13\]

FE Reference Handbook: Geotechnical — Slope Failure Along Planar Surface.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits the cohesion term.
  • (B) uses \(\sin\alpha_S\) in the resistance term where \(\cos\alpha_S\) belongs.
  • (D) omits \(\cos\alpha_S\) from the friction term, applying \(\tan\phi\) to the full weight.

J – Slope stability · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 12-41

questions.question:
[Drag-and-drop / matching] Match each ground improvement measure (1–5) with the mechanism that makes it work (A–E). Each mechanism is used once.

  • (A) Cation exchange plus a pozzolanic reaction that lowers plasticity and builds strength
  • (B) Temporary stress greater than the design load, so most settlement occurs before construction
  • (C) Shortening of the drainage path so primary consolidation finishes far sooner
  • (D) An essentially impermeable membrane
  • (E) Tensile stress carried by an inclusion that the soil itself cannot carry
pairs: Lime treatment of a plastic clay
Geogrid layers in a steep fill
questions.explanation:
1 → C. Wick drains give the pore water a short horizontal path to a vertical drain instead of a long vertical path to a drainage boundary. Since \(t \propto H_{dr}^2\), cutting the drainage path by a factor of ten cuts the time by a factor of a hundred. They do not change the magnitude of settlement. 2 → A. Lime supplies calcium for cation exchange (immediate reduction in PI and swell) followed by a pozzolanic reaction with clay minerals (long-term strength gain). 3 → E. A geogrid is a tensile inclusion; soil has essentially no tensile strength, so the grid carries the tension that allows a steeper face than the soil could stand alone. 4 → B. A preload surcharge exceeding the design load forces most of the primary consolidation to occur before the structure is built, after which the surcharge is removed. 5 → D. A geomembrane’s defining property is very low permeability, making it a barrier for landfill liners, pond linings, and canals.

FE Reference Handbook: not covered in Handbook 10.6; conceptual ground improvement. The \(t \propto H_{dr}^2\) dependence used in item 1 follows from Geotechnical — Variation of Time Factor with Degree of Consolidation.

K – Soil stabilization · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 12-45

questions.question: A horizontal curve with \(R=800\) ft and \(I=30^\circ\) has its PI at station 32+50.00. The station of the PT, expressed in feet from the origin (e.g., 2718.30 for Sta 27+18.30), is ______. [Numerical entry]
questions.explanation:
\(T=800\tan15^\circ=214.36\) ft. \(L=RI\pi/180=800(30)(\pi/180)=418.88\) ft.

Sta PC \(=3250.00-214.36=3035.64\). Sta PT \(=3035.64+418.88=3454.52\), i.e., Sta 34+54.52.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves. The common wrong answer 3464.36 (Sta 34+64.36) comes from adding \(T\) to the PI instead of adding \(L\) to the PC.

A – Geometric design · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 13-3

questions.question: For a design speed of 40 mph on a level road, with a perception-reaction time of 2.5 s and a deceleration rate of 11.2 ft/s², the stopping sight distance is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(SSD=1.47(40)(2.5)+40^2/[30(11.2/32.2)]=147.0+1600/10.435=147.0+153.3=300\) ft.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Stopping Sight Distance.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is the reaction distance alone.
  • (B) is the braking distance alone.
  • (C) is the SSD on a 6% upgrade.

A – Geometric design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-7

questions.question: A crest vertical curve joins a +2.0% grade to a −1.5% grade. The required stopping sight distance is 425 ft. Using standard AASHTO eye and object heights, the minimum curve length is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(A=|-1.5-2.0|=3.5\). Assume \(S\le L\): \(L=AS^2/2158=3.5(425)^2/2158=293\) ft. But \(293<425=S\), so the assumption fails. Use \(S>L\): \(L=2S-2158/A=850-616.6=233\) ft, and \(233<425\) is consistent.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Vertical Curves: Sight Distance Related to Curve Length (Crest Vertical Curve).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) is the \(S\le L\) result, which is inconsistent with its own assumption.
  • (C) is simply \(S\).
  • (D) is \(2158/A\), the term subtracted from \(2S\).

A – Geometric design · Hard · target ~2 min · Book question 13-11

questions.question:
Match each horizontal-curve element (1–4) with its formula (a–d). [Drag-and-drop / matching]

  • (a) \(R\left(1-\cos\dfrac{I}{2}\right)\)
  • (b) \(2R\sin\dfrac{I}{2}\)
  • (c) \(R\tan\dfrac{I}{2}\)
  • (d) \(R\left(\dfrac{1}{\cos(I/2)}-1\right)\)
questions.explanation:
\(T=R\tan(I/2)\); \(E=R[1/\cos(I/2)-1]\); \(M=R[1-\cos(I/2)]\); \(LC=2R\sin(I/2)\). A quick check: \(E>M\) always, and \(E\) contains the secant while \(M\) contains the cosine.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Horizontal Curves.

A – Geometric design · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-15

questions.question: A pavement requires \(SN=4.0\). The design uses 4.0 in of asphalt concrete (\(a_1=0.44\)) and 8.0 in of subbase (\(a_3=0.11\), \(m_3=1.0\)). If the crushed-stone base has \(a_2=0.14\) and \(m_2=0.90\), the minimum base thickness is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Surface: \(0.44(4.0)=1.76\). Subbase: \(0.11(8.0)(1.0)=0.88\). Required from base: \(4.0-1.76-0.88=1.36\).

\(D_2=1.36/(0.14\times0.90)=10.8\) in; use 11 in.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Highway Pavement Design.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) subtracts the subbase credit twice and ignores \(m_2\): \((4.0-1.76-0.88-0.88)/0.14=3.4\) in.
  • (B) multiplies by \(m_2\) instead of dividing: \(1.36(0.90)/0.14=8.7\) in. Note that a poorly drained base needs more thickness, not less.
  • (C) ignores \(m_2=0.90\): \(1.36/0.14=9.7\) in.

B – Pavement design · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 13-19

questions.question: Traffic on a lane follows the Greenshields model with a free-flow speed of 55 mph and a jam density of 130 veh/mi/ln. The capacity of the lane is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(V_m=D_jS_f/4=130\times55/4=1{,}787.5\approx1{,}790\) veh/h/ln.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Traffic Flow Relationships (Greenshields Model).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) divides by 8.
  • (C) divides by 2.
  • (D) is \(D_jS_f\) without the factor of 4.

C – Traffic flow · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-23

questions.question: One direction of a six-lane freeway on level terrain carries 4,400 veh/h with \(PHF=0.95\) and 5% trucks. The free-flow speed is 70 mph and base conditions otherwise apply. Using the Handbook’s basic freeway segment procedure, the level of service is:
questions.explanation:
\(f_{HV}=1/[1+0.05(1)]=0.952\). \(v_p=4400/(0.95\times3\times0.952)=1{,}621\) pc/h/ln.

\(c=2200+10(70-50)=2400\) pc/h/ln; \(BP=1000+40(75-70)=1200\); \(v_p>BP\).

\(S=70-(70-2400/45)(1621-1200)^2/(2400-1200)^2=70-16.67(0.1231)=67.9\) mph.

\(D=1621/67.9=23.9\) pc/mi/ln, in the range >18–26: LOS C.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Basic Freeway Segment Highway Capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) would require \(26<D\le35\) pc/mi/ln, i.e., \(v_p\gtrsim1{,}740\) pc/h/ln; the correct \(v_p=1{,}621\) gives \(D=23.9\). Single slips do not reach it: \(E_T=3.0\) gives \(D=25.3\), and applying the PHF twice gives \(D=25.5\), both still LOS C.
  • (C) would require \(D>35\); \(v_p\) is well below capacity.
  • (D) uses \(N=2\) lanes: \(v_p=4400/(0.95\times2\times0.952)=2432\) pc/h/ln, which exceeds \(c=2400\). The six-lane freeway has three lanes in each direction.

C – Traffic flow · Hard · target ~3 min · Book question 13-27

questions.question: For an approach speed of 35 mph on a level grade, a driver reaction time of 1.0 s, and a deceleration rate of 10 ft/s², the yellow change interval is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(v=35\times1.47=51.45\) ft/s. \(y=t+v/(2a\pm64.4G)=1.0+51.45/(2\times10+0)=1.0+2.57=3.57\approx3.6\) s.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Traffic Signal Timing.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) omits the reaction time (2.57 s).
  • (B) enters \(v\) in mph instead of ft/s (\(1.0+35/20=2.75\) s).
  • (D) uses the 2.5-s SSD perception–reaction time instead of the 1.0 s given (2.5 + 2.57 = 5.1 s).

D – Traffic control devices · Easy · target ~1 min · Book question 13-31

questions.question: Zone 1 produces 2,000 trips. Zone 2 has 300 attractions and friction factor 60, zone 3 has 900 attractions and friction factor 30, and zone 4 has 600 attractions and friction factor 25. With all socioeconomic factors equal to 1.0, the number of trips from zone 1 to zone 3 by the gravity model is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Weights \(A_jF_{1j}\): zone 2, \(300\times60=18{,}000\); zone 3, \(900\times30=27{,}000\); zone 4, \(600\times25=15{,}000\); sum 60,000.

\(T_{13}=2000\times27{,}000/60{,}000=900\) trips.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Gravity Model.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) is zone 4’s share.
  • (B) is zone 2’s share (2,000 × 18,000/60,000).
  • (D) is the share by attractions alone (900/1800 × 2000), ignoring friction factors.

E – Transportation planning · Medium · target ~2 min · Book question 13-35

questions.question: A 4.5-mi segment with an ADT of 15,000 veh/day recorded 27 crashes over 2 years. The crash rate per million vehicle-miles is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
\(VMT=15{,}000\times(2\times365)\times4.5=49.275\times10^6\) veh-mi. \(R_{MVM}=27\times10^6/49.275\times10^6=0.548\approx0.55\).

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Transportation — Traffic Safety Equations (Crash Rates for Roadway Segments).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) uses one year of exposure for two years of crashes.
  • (C) omits the segment length.
  • (D) is the rate per 100 million vehicle-miles.

E – Transportation planning · Medium · target ~1 min · Book question 13-39

questions.question: An owner wants one firm to be contractually responsible for both the design and the construction of a new pump station, and wants construction of the foundations to begin before the mechanical design is finished. Which project delivery method best meets both objectives?
choices: Construction manager as agent with multiple prime contracts
Design-bid-build with an early-release bid package
questions.explanation:
Design-build places design and construction under one contract with a single entity, giving the owner a single point of responsibility, and it permits fast-tracking because the design-builder can release foundation design and begin construction while later packages are still being designed.

FE Reference Handbook: none (delivery-method definitions are not in the Handbook).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) Design-bid-build requires a complete design before bidding and keeps design and construction under two separate owner contracts.
  • (B) A CM as agent holds no trade contracts and gives the owner more contracts, not one.
  • (C) Early-release packages under DBB can overlap phases somewhat, but the owner still holds separate design and construction contracts, so responsibility is split.

A – Project administration · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-1

questions.question: A drywall subcontractor on a public school project has not been paid by the general contractor. Because the property is public, a mechanic’s lien cannot be filed. Which instrument protects the subcontractor?
questions.explanation:
The payment bond (labor and material bond) guarantees payment to subcontractors, laborers, and suppliers. On public work — where liens cannot attach to public property — the payment bond is the subcontractor’s substitute remedy (the federal analogue is the Miller Act).

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (B) A bid bond protects the owner if a successful bidder refuses to sign.
  • (C) A performance bond protects the owner against nonperformance, not subcontractors against nonpayment.
  • (D) Builder’s risk is property insurance on the work itself.

A – Project administration · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-5

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A 30-m-long trench 3.0 m deep with a 1.0-m-wide bottom is sloped at 1:1 (H:V) on both sides in Type B soil. The soil swells 30%. Determine the loose volume, in cubic meters, that must be hauled away.
questions.explanation:
Top width \(=1.0+2(1.0)(3.0)=7.0\) m. End area (trapezoid): \[A=\frac{(1.0+7.0)}{2}(3.0)=12.0\ \text{m}^2\] Bank volume \(=12.0(30)=360\ \text{m}^3\) (BCM).

Loose volume \(=360(1+0.30)=468\ \text{m}^3\) (LCM).

Accepted range: 465–471 m³. Reporting 360 m³ (bank, not loose) or 252 m³ (multiplying by \(1-0.30\)) is wrong; loose volume is always larger than bank.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Earthwork Formulas (Average End Area Formula; the prism of constant section is the limiting case).

B – Construction operations and methods · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-9

questions.question: The loader of Question 14-12 fills each haul unit in 5 passes. Each truck spends 18.0 min on haul, dump, maneuver, and return. The number of trucks required to keep the loader working continuously is:
questions.explanation:
Loading time per truck \(t_{load}=n_{passes}\times C_{loader}=5(0.60)=3.0\) min.

Truck cycle \(C_{truck}=t_{load}+(\text{haul, dump, maneuver, return})=3.0+18.0=21.0\) min. \[N=\frac{C_{truck}}{t_{load}}=\frac{21.0}{3.0}=7.0\rightarrow 7\ \text{trucks}\]

FE Reference Handbook: none.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 4 divides the 21.0-min truck cycle by the 5 passes instead of by the 3.0-min loading time (\(21.0/5=4.2\rightarrow4\)).
  • (B) 6 omits the loading time from the truck cycle, \(18.0/3.0=6\) — a common slip; a truck’s cycle includes the time it spends under the loader.
  • (D) 8 applies the rule \(N=(\text{haul, dump, return time})/t_{load}+1\) to the full 21.0-min cycle, \(21.0/3.0+1=8\); the “+1” already stands for the truck under the loader, so adding it to a cycle that includes the loading time counts that truck twice.

B – Construction operations and methods · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-13

questions.question: Figure 14.12 shows a precedence network in which all relationships are finish-to-start with zero lag. The project duration and critical path are:
questions.explanation:
Forward pass (\(ES=\) latest \(EF\) of predecessors; \(EF=ES+D\)):

A: 0–2. B: 0–5. C: 2–6. D: max(2, 5) = 5–11. E: 6–9. F: 11–13. G: max(9, 13) = 13–17.

Project duration = largest EF = 17 days. Path lengths: A–C–E–G = 13; A–D–F–G = 14; B–D–F–G = 17. The longest path is B–D–F–G.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — Nomenclature (ES, EF, LS, LF, Float).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 13 days is the A–C–E–G path.
  • (B) 14 days is A–D–F–G.
  • (D) 19 days adds A’s 2 days to the B–D–F–G path; A and B are parallel start activities, not sequential.

C – Project controls · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-17

questions.question: A project’s critical path has three activities with (optimistic, most likely, pessimistic) durations in weeks of (4, 7, 10), (6, 9, 18), and (2, 5, 8). Using PERT, the probability that the project finishes within 25 weeks is most nearly:
questions.explanation:
Compute \(t_e=(a+4m+b)/6\) and \(\sigma^2=[(b-a)/6]^2\) for each activity:

\(a\) \(m\) \(b\) \(t_e\) \(\sigma^2\)
4 7 10 7 1.00
6 9 18 10 4.00
2 5 8 5 1.00
Sum 22 6.00

\(T_e=22\) weeks, \(\sigma_{path}=\sqrt{6.00}=2.449\) weeks. \[z=\frac{25-22}{2.449}=1.22\quad\Rightarrow\quad\Phi(1.22)\approx0.89\]

FE Reference Handbook: Industrial and Systems Engineering — PERT; Engineering Probability and Statistics — Unit Normal Distribution (read \(\Phi(z)\) at \(z=1.22\)).

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 0.50 is \(P\) at the expected duration, \(z=0\).
  • (B) 0.77 comes from adding standard deviations (\(1+2+1=4\), \(z=0.75\)) instead of variances.
  • (D) 0.93 uses only the largest activity’s standard deviation (\(\sigma=2\), \(z=1.5\)).

C – Project controls · Hard · target ~4 min · Book question 14-21

questions.question: [Select all that apply] At the end of month 8 a project reports PV = $600,000, EV = $660,000, and AC = $640,000. Which statements are correct?
choices: The schedule variance is +$60,000, so more work has been earned than was planned.
The cost variance is negative, so the project is over budget.
The cost performance index is about 1.03.
questions.explanation:
\(SV=EV-PV=660{,}000-600{,}000=+\$60{,}000\): more budgeted work has been earned than was scheduled, so (A) is correct.

\(CV=EV-AC=660{,}000-640{,}000=+\$20{,}000\): the cost variance is positive, so (B) is false and (E) is false (\(AC=640{,}000<EV=660{,}000\)).

\(CPI=660{,}000/640{,}000=1.031\), so (C) is correct. \(SPI=660{,}000/600{,}000=1.10\), so (D) is correct.

Note that a favorable SV is measured in dollars, not days; the work earned early could be off the critical path, so always confirm schedule status against the CPM network.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — Earned-Value Analysis (Variances, Indices).

Option by option:

  • (A) True — \(SV=EV-PV=+\$60{,}000\).
  • (B) False — \(CV=EV-AC=+\$20{,}000\), so the project is under budget.
  • (C) True — \(CPI=660{,}000/640{,}000=1.031\).
  • (D) True — \(SPI=660{,}000/600{,}000=1.10\).
  • (E) False — \(AC=640{,}000\) is less than \(EV=660{,}000\).

C – Project controls · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-25

questions.question: [Numerical entry] A separate slab on grade, 12 m by 9 m in plan, is reinforced with a single mat of 12-mm bars at 200 mm on center each way, running the full plan dimensions. Bar mass is 0.888 kg/m. Using the convention that the number of bars along a length \(L\) at spacing \(s\) is \(L/s+1\), and neglecting laps, hooks, and cover, determine the mass of reinforcing steel in kilograms.
questions.explanation:
Bars running the 12-m direction are spaced across the 9-m width: \[n=\frac{9.0}{0.20}+1=46\ \text{bars}\times12.0\ \text{m}=552\ \text{m}\] Bars running the 9-m direction are spaced across the 12-m length: \[n=\frac{12.0}{0.20}+1=61\ \text{bars}\times9.0\ \text{m}=549\ \text{m}\] Total length \(=552+549=1{,}101\) m. Mass \(=1{,}101(0.888)=977.7\) kg.

Accepted range: 965–990 kg (report about 978 kg). Dropping the “+1” gives 45 and 60 bars, 1,080 m, 959 kg — about 2% low; using \(L/s\) with no correction is a common takeoff error on a bar mat.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Design of Reinforced Concrete Components — ASTM Standard Reinforcement Bars gives bar mass per unit length for USCS bar sizes; the SI bar mass is supplied here.

D – Construction estimating · Medium · target ~3 min · Book question 14-29

questions.question: A storm inlet is shown on a plan drawn at 1:500. Measured along the centerline from the point marked Sta 2+340, the inlet scales 84 mm up-station. The distance and the inlet’s station are:
questions.explanation:
At 1:500, one millimeter on paper is 500 mm on the ground: \[84\ \text{mm}\times500=42{,}000\ \text{mm}=42.0\ \text{m}\] Stations in SI are 1,000 m apart, so Sta 2+340 is 2,340 m from the origin. Adding 42 m up-station gives 2,382 m, or Sta 2+382.

Where a dimension is written on the drawing, use it; scale only when no dimension is given.

FE Reference Handbook: none — scales and stationing are drawing conventions.

Why the other options are wrong:

  • (A) 16.8 m applies 1:200.
  • (C) 84 m reads the paper measurement as meters.
  • (D) 420 m applies a 1:5,000 scale.

E – Interpretation of engineering drawings · Easy · target ~2 min · Book question 14-33

questions.question: [Point-and-click] Figure 14.15 is an activity-on-node network in which every relationship is finish-to-start with zero lag. Each node carries a circled label (A) through (E). Exactly one activity in this network has total float greater than zero. Name the labeled activity.
questions.explanation:
Forward pass (\(ES=\) latest \(EF\) of the predecessors, \(EF=ES+D\)):

Activity D ES EF
A 6 0 6
B 9 6 15
C 7 6 13
D 5 15 20
E 4 20 24

Activity D waits for the later of B (\(EF=15\)) and C (\(EF=13\)), so \(ES_D=15\) and the project duration is 24 working days.

Backward pass (\(LF=\) earliest \(LS\) of the successors, \(LS=LF-D\)): \(LF_E=24\), \(LS_E=20\); \(LF_D=20\), \(LS_D=15\); both B and C feed D, so \(LF_B=LF_C=15\), giving \(LS_B=6\) and \(LS_C=8\); \(LF_A=\min(6,8)=6\), \(LS_A=0\).

Total float is \(LS-ES\): \[TF_A=0,\quad TF_B=0,\quad TF_C=8-6=2\ \text{days},\quad TF_D=0,\quad TF_E=0\] Only activity C has float, so the answer is region (C). The critical path is A–B–D–E, 24 days.

(A), (D), and (E) each lie on the single chain that every path must use, so their float is necessarily zero. (B) is the longer of the two parallel branches (9 days against C’s 7), so it sets \(ES_D\) and is critical; the 2 days of float belong entirely to the shorter branch, C.

FE Reference Handbook: Civil Engineering — Construction — CPM Precedence Relationships; Nomenclature (ES, EF, LS, LF, Float).

C – Project controls · Easy · target ~3 min · Book question 14-37
